en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
The Illustrious Lamp of the Gems of Law (*Śrīmadanaratnapradīpa*: *Vyavahāroddyota*).
Having bowed to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati, the destroyer of the multitude of obstacles,
I shall now analyze right conduct and subsequently analyze legal procedure.
In order to facilitate easy understanding of those matters which have indeed been set forth in the *Vyavahāraviveka*, their sequential order is now demonstrated.
The nature of legal procedure and of the titles of legal procedure has been shown previously; now, however, [the nature] of the titles of legal procedure [is to be explained].
Immediately after that, the various divisions beginning with the non-payment of debts were shown,
followed by specific descriptions of the nature and characteristics of the judge (*prāḍvivāka*).
Furthermore, the description of the court has been properly provided here; thereafter, the procedure for the administration of justice is elaborated upon.
Thereafter, the enumeration of the limbs of legal procedure was set forth, together with considerations of time, place, local custom, caste-dharma, prohibition, and so forth.
The two sections known as Bhāṣā and Uttara have been explained in detail;
following that, in the Kriyāpāda, the Pratyākalita has been described.
Following the discussion on legal procedures and gifts, the classification of legal actions (*kṛtya*) and so forth was likewise explained;
thereafter, the witness was defined, and following that, the examination of written documents (*lekhya*).
Then follows the definition of inference in the form of enjoyment and so forth;
thereafter is the section on ordeals, wherein the manual of ordeals (*divyamātṛkā*) is set forth.
Then follows the procedure for the water-pot, the procedure for fire, and the procedure for water;
thereafter the procedure for poison is taught, and after that, the procedure for the divine ordeal is taught.
[2] Next, the rule for rice grains and the procedure for the heated gold coin (taptamāṣa) were declared;
then the rule for the ploughshare and the rule for the son of Dharma (Yama).
These matters have been explained in detail in the section on Action (Kriyāpāda);
therefore, no further exposition is made here for the section on Determination (Nirṇayapāda).
Thus has the matrix of correct legal procedure been explained;
following that, the specific points of legal procedure shall now be explained here.
First, the section on the non-payment of debts was fully explained therein;
thereafter follows the section on deposits, along with sealed deposits and so forth.
The joint undertaking has been correctly defined here;
thereafter, the breach of agreement, as well as repentance regarding what was purchased, have been defined. Then, the failure to deliver after having sold has been explained in detail.
Then, the dispute between owner and herdsman, as well as the dispute concerning boundaries, have been explained in detail.
Verbal abuse and physical assault have thus been defined;
now follows the definition of theft and violence in their proper order.
The examination of disputes concerning the seduction of women has been completed;
thereafter, the dispute regarding sexual union between men and women is examined here.
In this work, the exposition of the partition of inheritance has been set forth in detail, preceded by explanations of numerous topics such as the time of partition, the agent, and so forth.
Then follows the determination of the legal title known as "Gambling and Betting," and thereafter the determination of the dispute known as "Miscellaneous Matters."

In this regard, Kātyāyana demonstrates the essential nature of judicial procedure (*vyavahāra*): "When the extensive expansion of legal principles (*dharma*), which is accomplished through effort and has been interrupted, is the subject of dispute, that litigation rooted in the matter to be proven is called *vyavahāra*. Thus it is said.

It has the *sādhya* (the matter to be proven) as its root, meaning it is rooted in the purpose (*prayojana*). Here, by the word *vāda* (legal dispute), the fourfold set of categories consisting of the plaint (*pratijñā*), the subsequent procedure (*uttarakriyā*), and the final decision (*nirṇaya*) is understood; for in the statements of Yājñavalkya, Bṛhaspati, and others, these four are designated as the "feet" (*pāda*) of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*). Those texts will be shown later. In this verse, the portion ending with the words "in that which is called *dharma*" states the cause of legal procedure, which is the interruption of *dharma*. By the remaining portion, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of legal procedure is stated. And the explanation of these two sentences is as follows: in the "expansion of *nyāya*"—that is, in a subject matter where there is an expansion or operation of *nyāya*, i.e., the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—that *vāda* which is rooted in the *sādhya* is *vyavahāra*. And that occurs when *dharma*—the entity named *dharma*—which is to be accomplished through effort and produced by the performance of prescribed duties, has been "interrupted," meaning destroyed. Nārada also, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), states that the cessation of *dharma* is the cause of legal procedure.
In that time when Manu Prajāpati ruled the kingdom,
men were devoted solely to dharma and were speakers of truth.
"At that time, there was no legal procedure, nor hatred, nor even envy.
When dharma had perished among men, legal procedure came into being. [NSm Mā 1–2]

Alternatively, the verse beginning with "prayatnasādhya" (to be accomplished through effort) may be explained as follows, without resorting to two separate sentences: when a matter such as a house or a field—which is to be accomplished through effort, meaning difficult to accomplish—is interrupted and can no longer be enjoyed at one's will, then in the *nyāyavistara*—that is, in that place characterized as a court (*sabhā*) known as the *dharmādhikaraṇa* (the seat of justice), where *nyāya* (reasoning/evidence) is expanded, elaborated, and determined—the dispute concerning houses and other matters rooted in what is to be accomplished is called *vyavahāra* (legal procedure). Kātyāyana states that the site of investigation is the *dharmādhikaraṇa*.

"That place where the discernment of the essential and the non-essential is carried out through an investigation of the *dharmaśāstra* is indeed the *dharmādhikaraṇa* (the court of justice). Although this [definition] pertains to the general nature of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), it does not apply to a lawsuit concluded by mutual consent (*saṃpratipatti*), because Bṛhaspati describes it as "two-footed" in the statement, "In cases of mutual consent, there are two feet. Nevertheless, one should understand that the term "legal procedure" (*vyavahāra*) is applied there by way of a metaphorical designation of the whole upon its part.
This legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is of two kinds: with a superior (*sottara*) and without a superior (*anuttara*). And so says Nārada:
"It should be known as having two characteristics: with a superior and without a superior. He himself states the definition of these two: (Mā. 1.4).

*Sottara* (with a stake) is that case where the wager (*paṇa*) is preceded by a written record (*vilekhā*) and is greater than the fine (*daṇḍa*) resulting from defeat. Where the wager is greater than the substance of the fine caused by loss and is preceded by a written record, that is *sottara*. By implication, the meaning is that where a greater wager is not recorded in writing, that is *anuttara* (without a stake).
This concludes the definition of the nature of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*).
Now follows the determination of the titles of legal procedure.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya (2.5) states:
"One who has been oppressed by others through a course of action deviating from the traditional law and established custom..."

"For that which one reports to the king is indeed a subject of legal dispute (*vyavahārapada*). "Assaulted" (*ādharṣita*) means insulted. Regarding the eighteen-fold nature of these subjects of legal dispute, Uśanas says:
"Whoever should report a matter or a grievance to the king..."
That locus is proclaimed to be of eighteen kinds of disputes.

And Manu shows those eighteen divisions [of legal disputes] (8.4–7): "Of these, the first is the non-payment of debts; then deposits, sale without ownership, joint undertakings, and the non-delivery of what has been given."
Non-payment of wages, breach of contract,
rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between owners and herdsmen.
The law concerning boundary disputes, verbal and physical assault,
theft, violence, and the abduction of women.
"The duties of women and men, partition [of inheritance], gambling, and betting—
these eighteen are the topics in the administration of legal procedure here."

*Anapākarma* means non-payment [of a debt]. *Krayavikrayānuśaya* is the inclusion, as a single item, of both the rescission of a purchase (*krītānuśaya*) and the failure to deliver after sale (*vikrīyāsaṃpradāna*). By the term *strīpuṃdharma*, there is the inclusion of that title of dispute called *strīpuṃyoga*, wherein an investigation into the duties of husband and wife is conducted. *Vibhāga* is the partition of inheritance (*dāyabhāga*). *Dyūta* is gambling with inanimate objects; *āhvaya* is gambling with living creatures. Both of these constitute a single title under the category of gambling, though they are mentioned separately with the intention of indicating their internal subdivisions. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the statement that there are eighteen titles. In the compound *daṇḍavācike*, the word *daṇḍa* is placed first because it has fewer syllables. Thus, the order in which they appear in the recitation is not intended to be significant. For this very reason, by him (Manu, MDh 8.278):
This rule for punishment regarding verbal abuse has been declared according to the truth;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of punishment for physical assault.
Thus, following the determination of verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*), it was promised that the determination of physical assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*) must now be undertaken.
Now, one might object: theft, sexual intercourse with another's wife, verbal abuse, and physical assault—[as defined by Manu:
"Theft is the killing of a human being, the stealing of property, and the violation of another's wife."
Harshness and both [of these] constitute the fourfold *sāhasa* (outrageous act).

Thus, Bṛhaspati has stated that [theft and so forth] constitute acts of violence (*sāhasa*); how then is there a separate mention of these here? It is said in reply: those acts such as theft which are committed by force (*sahasā*), that is, by means of physical compulsion, are *sāhasas*; those which are not of such a nature are designated separately as heads of legal procedure (*vyavahārapada*). For this very reason, Manu himself has stated (8.332): "The forcible seizure of another's property in the presence of guards is *sāhasa*; the seizure of another's property not of such a kind is theft (*steya*)."

An act committed by force, provided it is accompanied by a claim of ownership, constitutes *sāhasa* (violence); however, if it is done without such a claim, or if one takes property and denies having taken it, it constitutes *steya* (theft).

Medhātithi has explained that "with its followers" means accompanied by guards, while "without its followers" means devoid of guards, using force. Nārada, however, having set aside three titles of law—dispute between owner and herdsman, theft, and adultery—and having accepted the fifteen remaining titles previously mentioned, further adopting two other titles called "non-service" and "miscellaneous," and specifying "selling what has not been delivered" as a distinct title, asserts that there are eighteen titles of law (NSm, Mā. 1.16–19).
Recovery of debts, deposits, partnerships,
resumption of what has been given, and the failure to perform agreed-upon service;
[6] Non-payment of wages, likewise sale without ownership, non-delivery after selling,
and rescission after buying;
Non-performance of agreements, disputes, and matters concerning sons born of the field; the legal relationship between men and women, the division of inheritance, and then violence.
"Harshness of speech, likewise harshness of physical punishment,
gambling, and miscellaneous matters— thus the Smṛti declares eighteen titles of law.
The specific nature of these titles of legal procedure and their particular details will be shown further on.

Thus ends the first section, "The Definition of the Nature and Varieties of Legal Procedure," in the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, a commentary on the *Vyavahāraviveka*, composed by Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva, the son of Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles such as "the Illustrious Kodaṇḍa-Paraśurāma."
Now, the *Vyavahāramātṛkā*, which is useful for all legal proceedings, is being described. At the beginning of the treatise is the description of the court (*sabhā*). Bṛhaspati says:
"One should construct a separate house in the middle of the fortress, situated near water and trees;
in the eastern direction of that [fortress], one should fashion a court facing east, endowed with auspicious characteristics."
It should be provided with garlands, incense, and seats, endowed with seed-syllables and jewels,
joined with deities in the form of images and paintings, and likewise with fire and water.

The house of the king; of that royal palace. A *lakṣaṇyā*—one endowed with the characteristics described in the treatises on architecture (*vāstuśāstra*). An assembly hall (*sabhā*) serving as the court of justice. Regarding the specific procedure for the king’s entry and seating in this assembly hall, Manu says (8.1–2):
"But a king desiring to see legal cases (*vyavahāra*), being modestly dressed, should enter the assembly hall together with Brāhmaṇas and ministers who are experts in counsel."
Seated there or even standing, having raised his right hand and wearing modest dress and ornaments, he should examine the legal cases of the litigants.
The examination of legal cases must be conducted by one free from anger and greed. And so says Yājñavalkya (2.1):
"The king shall examine legal cases together with learned Brāhmaṇas, in accordance with the Dharmaśāstras, and devoid of anger and greed."

Here, the mention of the "king" (*nṛpa*) is for the purpose of making it known that the administration of justice must be carried out even by one other than a Kṣatriya who is authorized to protect the subjects. And this administration of justice should be performed by one desiring righteousness (*dharmakāma*), assisted by the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*), the assessors (*sabhyas*), and others. Accordingly, Kātyāyana says:

"Accompanied by the presiding judge, the ministers, the Brāhmaṇas, and the family priest, and together with the assessors, the king remains in heaven as an observer [of justice] in accordance with Dharma."

In this context, there is no tautology regarding the word *brāhmaṇa*, for by the word *brāhmaṇa* those who are not appointed are included, whereas by the word *sabhyas* those who are appointed are included. Vyāsa has shown the true nature of a minister:

"One should appoint as a minister a twice-born man who knows the meaning of all the scriptures, is free from greed, speaks with justice, is wise, and has attained his position through a succession of learned men."

Furthermore, the mention of the "twice-born" (*dvija*) here is intended to include both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas in the absence of Brāhmaṇas. The nature of the *prāḍvivāka* (judge) has been stated by Bṛhaspati: "He who asks a question in a dispute, as well as a counter-question, and speaks first with kindness, is therefore remembered as a *prāḍvivāka*."
Vyāsa has also said:
"Because he carefully examines a matter under dispute after having questioned it before the members of the court,
he is therefore known as the *prāḍvivāka* (the presiding judge)."

Gautama, however, states that the king, together with the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*), questions both the plaintiff and the defendant; he is called *prāṭ* because he asks them, and *vivāka* because he speaks after having deliberated with the members of the court (*sabhyas*) upon what has been said by those two. Furthermore, the members of the court must indeed be endowed with qualities such as learning and so forth. Accordingly, Yājñavalkya (2.2) says:

"Those who are perfected in sacred learning and study, who know the Dharma, who speak the truth, and who are impartial toward both enemy and friend—such persons should be appointed as members of the court by the king."
*Śruta* is the hearing of treatises such as Mīmāṃsā and Vyākaraṇa; *adhyayana* is the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*). Kātyāyana (66, 67, 71):
"The king should appoint as members of the court those who are free from greed, wealthy, knowers of the Dharma, speakers of truth, and proficient in all branches of learning."
One who studies only a single treatise cannot know how to determine the outcome of a legal matter;
therefore, kings should ensure that those most proficient in many scriptures are employed in judicial disputes.
Where there is no learned Brahmin, one should appoint a Kṣatriya;
or a Vaiśya who knows the treatises on Dharma; but one should avoid a Śūdra with every effort.
One who has studied much and knows many branches [of the law]. Nārada (NSm Mā. 3.4–5):
But the king shall appoint righteous assessors who have been well-tested, who are capable of bearing the burden of legal proceedings like excellent oxen.

"Those who are skilled in the treatises on Dharma, of noble birth, speakers of truth, and impartial toward both enemy and friend should be the members of the king's assembly. Thus [it is said]. "Excellent oxen" refers to superior bulls. Bṛhaspati [says]:
The king should appoint as members of the assembly those who are engaged in performing virtuous deeds, devoted to truth and righteousness, free from anger and pride, and learned in the scriptures.

Those engaged in the performance of virtuous deeds—meaning those devoted to the practice of noble rites such as sacrifices—and these three types of members should constitute the assembly. Thus says Manu (8.11): "In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together, along with a learned official of the king, they know that to be a *sabhā* (an assembly)."
The *adhikṛta* is one appointed as a presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*). Bṛhaspati, however, speaks of an odd number of members of the court (*sabhya*), even more than three:
"That assembly in which Brahmins who know the worlds, the Vedas, the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), and the Dharma sit—whether they be seven, five, or even three—is equal to a sacrifice."
Bṛhaspati has stated those who should not be made members of the assembly:
those ignorant of local customs, atheists, those devoid of scriptural knowledge,
the insane, the angry, the greedy, and the afflicted— these should not be questioned in reaching a verdict.
Vyāsa:
[9] He who, setting aside the twice-born, should look after affairs together with Śūdras—
his kingdom becomes agitated, and his army and treasury perish.

The king should also appoint an accountant and a scribe. Thus said Bṛhaspati: "The king should appoint an accountant and a scribe who know the true nature of words and terminology, who are skilled in calculation, pure, and proficient in various scripts."

*Śabda* refers to grammar (*śabdaśāstra*). *Abhidhāna* refers to the lexicon (*kośa*). A king should also seat a few merchants in the assembly hall. Thus says Kātyāyana (58): "It should be presided over by a few merchants who possess noble lineage, good character, youth, proper conduct, and wealth, and who are free from envy, acting as if they were members of the royal family."

"By those belonging to the family" means by those gathered together in one place. Regarding the phrase "presided over," since that is indeed the court of justice (*dharmādhikaraṇa*), the term *dharmādhikaraṇa* is supplied here [from the previous context]. Their duty has also been stated by this very same [author]:
"The merchants there should be made the hearers, as they perceive what is just.
For the purpose of summoning witnesses and so forth, the king should also appoint some of his own officials. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
In matters of non-injury and protection, as well as regarding the testimony of plaintiffs and defendants,
one who speaks the truth and is dependent upon the members of the court should be appointed as a personal representative.

This royal officer named *sādhyapāla* must indeed be a *śūdra*. Thus says Vyāsa: "The king should appoint as *sādhyapāla* one who accomplishes the legal case; he should be hereditary, firm, a *śūdra*, and remain steadfast in the opinion of the court members (*sabhyas*)."

When the king is unable to act himself or is preoccupied with other duties, he should appoint a learned judge (*prāḍvivāka*) together with court members (*sabhyas*) and others to his own seat. Thus says Manu (8.97, 141; 8.10): "But when the king does not personally conduct the investigation of cases, then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to investigate the cases."
When weary from overseeing the affairs of men, he should appoint to that seat a chief minister who knows the Dharma, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth.
Surrounded by three members of the court, he should examine his legal cases,
having entered the foremost assembly hall, either seated or standing.

[10] "Wearied" means exhausted; and this is an epithet of the king. By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "only by the members of the court," the king is excluded. The meaning is that, unlike in other circumstances, the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*) need not wait for the presence of the king in this case. By the restrictive particle *eva* in "only to the court," other locations are excluded. Yājñavalkya (2.3): "But when the king, due to the pressure of business, does not personally oversee legal cases, he should appoint a Brāhmaṇa who knows all the laws, together with the members of the court."
Bṛhaspati says: The king, or else a judge, or a twice-born man, should oversee the legal matters,
having placed the constituent elements of justice at the forefront and remaining steadfast in the opinion of the learned members of the court.

In the absence of a Brāhmaṇa, one should appoint a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya as the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*), but never a Śūdra. Thus says Manu (8.20–21): "One who merely lives by his caste, or even one who calls himself a Brāhmaṇa, may at will be the expounder of dharma for the king, but a Śūdra should never be so under any circumstances."
The kingdom of that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma perishes, like a cow sinking in the mud while onlookers look on.

Demonstrating the status of these individuals— the king and the others— as members of the court, Bṛhaspati states their respective functions: "The king, the appointed official, the court members, the legal code, the astrologer, the scribe,
gold, fire, water, and one's own men— these are indeed the ten constituent elements of the means of proof."
Among these members of the body [of the court], the king is remembered as the head; the presiding judge is the mouth;
the members of the assembly are the arms; the legal code is the hands; and the astrologer and the scribe are the two shanks.
Gold, silver, water, the eyes, the heart, and likewise the feet and one's own person—
for these ten as well, the specific functions have been declared individually.
The king is the presiding speaker and the ruler; the members of the court are the examiners of the case.
Smṛti (the sacred law) declares the final decision, as well as the awarding of victory and the imposition of punishment.
Gold and fire are for the purpose of an oath; water is for those who are thirsty or agitated.
The accountant shall calculate the matter, and the scribe shall record the legal decision.
The king’s own officers shall summon the defendant, the court members, and the witnesses;
they shall always keep the plaintiff and the defendant under guard, ensuring they have no opportunity to escape.
That assembly hall, presided over by a king of resolute mind who, seated therein, examines legal cases according to this tenfold procedure, is equal to a sacrificial rite.

Here, by the two words *adhikṛta* (appointed official) and *adhyakṣa* (supervisor), the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) is understood. *Dama* means punishment (*daṇḍa*). This tenfold instrument (*karaṇa*)—meaning this body characterized as an assembly (*sabhā*) consisting of ten parts—is the "ten-limbed instrument. Within this body characterized as an assembly, Bṛhaspati describes the manner in which the king and others are to sit in this court:
"The king should sit facing the east, while the members of the assembly face north.
The calculator (*gaṇaka*) faces west, and the scribe (*lekhaka*) faces south."

The mention of the "court" (sabhā) is also indicative of the judge (prāḍvivāka). Bṛhaspati indicates that there are also certain other, non-principal venues for the adjudication of legal disputes besides the royal court.
Those families, guilds, assemblies, and so forth, who are well-known to the king, shall carry out the legal affairs of men, excluding cases involving violence or injustice.
The heads of families, guilds, and assemblies are declared to be the final arbiters;
the testimony of each subsequent group carries greater weight than that of the preceding one.

What has been done by guilds after deliberation but not decided upon by the families, what is unknown to the guilds though done by the corporations, and what is unknown to the corporations though done by the appointed officials; [these are matters for the king to decide].
The members of the assembly are superior to the family and other such groups; the presiding officer is declared superior to them;
and the king is superior to all of them, for he must diligently ascertain the law.
By investigating disputes among the superior, inferior, and middling,
those of lesser intelligence move about while the higher intellects remain above them.

A *kula* is a collection of kinsmen, relatives, and blood relations. A *śreṇi* is a collection of persons of different castes who subsist by the same occupation. A *gaṇa* is a collection of persons of various castes who subsist by various occupations and reside in the same village or similar locality. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), members of an assembly (*sabhyas*) and others are included. "Excluding cases of force" means excluding those legal matters known as *sāhasa*. "Appointed" refers to the members of the assembly. Yājñavalkya (2.30):
"Groups, guilds, and families appointed by the king—each preceding one is to be understood as more authoritative than each succeeding one in the judicial procedure for men."

Those appointed by the king, such as judges and others; the word *pūga* has the same meaning as the word *gaṇa*. Bṛhaspati states that for forest-dwellers and others, there shall be an assembly (*sabhā*) in the forests and similar places:
"For those who roam the wilderness, their court shall be in the forest;
likewise, for soldiers it shall be in the army, and for merchants in caravans."
The assembly hall is the instrument.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Description of the Assembly Hall, in the illustrious *Kodaṇḍa*, [in the commentary] called *Uddyota*.

**A possible reading of the defective text:** Thus ends the second chapter, "The Description of the Court," in the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, an exposition on the discernment of legal procedure (*vyavahāraviveka*), composed by Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "the Illustrious Kodaṇḍa-Paraśurāma."
Now follows the method for the administration of justice.
Regarding that, Kātyāyana states (verses 60–61) the time for the administration of justice:
"In the courtrooms, during the forenoon, the king shall decide the cases."
The subduer of enemies should act according to the path prescribed by the scriptures.
Excluding one-eighth part of the day, the remaining three parts constitute the time for legal proceedings as seen in the scriptures and traditionally remembered.

The eighth part consists of the first watch; the first half of that is three parts, and the subsequent portion prior to the sun's turning point (āvartana) is also three parts. Regarding this, Saṃvarta indicates the lunar days (*tithi*) to be avoided:
"On these lunar days—the fourteenth, the new moon, the full moon, and likewise the eighth—a wise man should not engage in legal transactions."
On a lunar day that is not prohibited, one should examine the scriptures in the forenoon for the purpose of reaching a definitive decision. And so Bṛhaspati also says:
"Having occupied that [throne] in the forenoon with his aged ministers and dependents, he should look upon and likewise listen to the ancient treatises on Dharma and Artha."
The phrase "for the sake of a definitive decision" is to be understood as the ellipsis. The treatises on Dharma have been indicated by Pitāmaha [Yājñavalkya]:
"The four Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, as well as Mīmāṃsā and the Smṛtis—these are the treatises on Dharma, along with the Purāṇa and the Nyāya philosophy. Thus it is said.

[13] The *arthaśāstra* is the science of polity (*nītiśāstra*). Regarding the resolution of contradictions between the *dharmaśāstra* and the *nītiśāstra*, Nārada says (NSm Nā. 1.39): "Where there may be a conflict between the *dharmaśāstra* and the *arthaśāstra*, one should set aside what is stated in the *arthaśāstra* and practice what is stated in the *dharmaśāstra*."
Yājñavalkya (2.21) states that when there is a conflict between two *dharmaśāstras*, logic (*nyāya*) is the deciding factor:
"In a conflict between two *smṛtis*, however, logic is stronger than [mere] legal practice (*vyavahāra*).

Logic consists of the nature of general rules (*utsarga*) and exceptions (*apavāda*), and so forth. "From legal practice" means from the traditional practice of the elders. Nārada also says: (NSm Mā 1.40)
But when there is a conflict with the Dharmaśāstras, a rule supported by reasoning is remembered as authoritative.
Bṛhaspati states that a fault arises in the absence of an investigation into logic:
"A legal decision must certainly not be made by relying solely on the scriptures."
But when an investigation is devoid of reason, the loss of Dharma arises.
A thief or a non-thief, a virtuous or a wicked person, is established by means of worldly convention;
without reasoning and investigation, Māṇḍavya was treated as a thief.
Unreal things appear like real ones, and real things appear like unreal ones;
they are seen as producers of delusion, therefore one should investigate with reason.

What is good may appear bad, and what is bad may appear good; such is the usage of the Vedic texts (*chāndasa*), where the elision of the case-ending *su* occurs. This is due to worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) and the lack of logical inquiry. Manu (8.3) states that one must also take into account local customs:
"Every day, by means of reasons observed in the country and those observed in the scriptures, [cases] are settled separately according to the eighteen titles of law."

The phrase "he shall examine the cases" is to be supplied [to each clause]. Regarding the paths, that is, the titles of legal procedure (*vyavahārapada*), Kātyāyana states the definition of what is observed in a particular region (*deśadṛṣṭa*):

"That custom which has been established in a particular region and has persisted at all times, provided it is not in conflict with the *Śruti* and the *Smṛti*, is called 'observed in the region' (*deśadṛṣṭa*). (46)
[14] But in the absence of a treatise, a decision must be made solely in accordance with local custom; thus he himself says (Kāt 45):
"Therefore, the king should settle legal cases in accordance with the treatises;
but in the absence of any scriptural statement, he should adopt the opinion observed in the land by all."
He (Kātyāyana, verse 47) also states that in disputes between people of different regions, the decision must be made solely according to the view of the *śāstra*:

"In districts, towns, cattle-pens, cities, or villages, the law for litigants shall be according to their own local customs; in other cases, [the law] shall be according to the *śāstra* in conjunction with them."

The word "must be determined" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. By "one's own conventions," he means the customs established in one's own country. Manu also states that the laws of caste and family must likewise be followed:
(8.41) "One who knows the law, having carefully examined the laws of castes and regions, the laws of guilds, and the laws of families, should uphold his own duty."

"Local laws" (*jātidharmān*) are those laws connected to specific birthplaces or regions. "Guilds" (*śreṇyaḥ*) are those who subsist by a single occupation, such as merchants, farmers, and so forth. "One's own law" (*svadharma*) refers to the form of punishment for the wicked. The definition of family law (*kuladharma*) has been stated by Kātyāyana (85):
"That which is the established status of a lineage, which comes down to them through tradition according to dharma—they call that 'family law,' and one should protect it in that very same way."
Bṛhaspati also says:
"The customs of regions, castes, and families that have been established from of old must be preserved exactly as they are; otherwise, the subjects become agitated."
The people become disaffected, and both the army and the treasury perish;
furthermore, the daughters of maternal uncles are married by twice-born men from the South.
In the Middle Country, laborers and artisans eat beef;
all its men are fish-eaters, and its women are devoted to adultery.
"Women who drink liquor in the north, as well as those who are menstruating, are untouchable by men;
because of this conduct, they are not eligible for the administration of penance. Thus [it is said].

"All" refers to the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes. The reading "pūrve" (in the east) is found in the *Kṛtyakalpataru*. "Pūrve" means in the eastern region. [15] "Dama" means punishment. As for the mention of penance and punishment for performing such acts in other Smṛtis, that refers to regions not included in this specific statement. In a dispute between merchants and others, the king, having considered their specific customs, must reach a decision through those who are experts in those very customs. Thus Vyāsa says: "In the case of merchants, artisans, and so forth, as well as those who live by agriculture or crafts..."
For it is impossible for others to determine; one should have it performed by those alone who possess knowledge of that subject.
Bṛhaspati also says:
Laborers, artisans, craftsmen, usurers, guilds, dancers, those wearing sectarian marks,
and thieves shall carry out a decision according to their own specific laws.

*Kīnāśas* are farmers; *kārukas* are artisans such as carpenters and the like; *śilpins* are craftsmen such as painters and the like; *kusīdinas* are usurers; and *liṅginas* are members of ascetic orders such as the Pāśupatas. When Brāhmaṇas are disputing among themselves regarding a matter pertaining to their own caste (*varṇa*) or stage of life (*āśrama*), the king himself shall not issue a decision. Rather, having informed them, he should cause that determination of the law to be made by the Brāhmaṇas alone. Thus says Manu (8.390–91): "When twice-born men are disputing among themselves regarding matters concerning their stages of life, a king who desires his own welfare and seeks to act according to dharma must not pronounce the law [himself]."
Having honored these men as was fitting along with the Brahmins,
and having first pacified them with gentle words, the king should establish them in their own duty.

Regarding duties in hermitages— that is, matters pertaining to the hermitages— he should not speak out or speak with partiality. Having pacified them by means of gentleness and conciliation, and having removed their anger— even Bṛhaspati himself should have the affairs of ascetics conducted only by those learned in the three Vedas,
and never by those skilled in the art of illusion, for fear of provoking his wrath.
Kātyāyana also says:
One who is endowed with perfect knowledge should provide instruction for those of superior birth and character, as well as for gurus, teachers, and ascetics.

The word ending in the third case is *samyagvijñānasampannena*. When there is a dispute between a teacher and pupil or others, the king should settle the dispute by considering the matter as requested in some manner; he should not conduct an investigation preceded by the formal writing of a plaint and a reply. Intending this very point, Bṛhaspati says:
"A teacher and a pupil, father and son, husband and wife, master and servant—among these who are assembled together, a legal proceeding is not established."
Regarding those who are assembled and disputing over a single matter, Nārada states that a dispute between husband and wife arising from jealousy and the like need not even be reported to the king:
"When a conflict arises from jealousy or malice, caused by passion, the husband and wife may dispute among their own kinsmen, but not before the king. (NSm 1.32)
In this context, the word *jñāti* indicates friends. Kātyāyana describes the manner of questioning one who has come to present the subject of a dispute (86–87):
"At the proper time, he should question the petitioner for justice as he stands before him, bowing down:
'What is your business? What is your grievance? Do not fear; speak, O man!'"
One who has entered the assembly should ask: "By whom, where, when, and for what reason?
At the time of the plaintiff's deposition, Uśanas prohibited [the following]:
being armed, being without an upper garment, having one's lower garment untucked, or sitting together [on the same seat].
Or, wearing a garland, if he speaks with his left hand, he shall receive the punishment for a staff-offense.

"Seated with his seat" means being established upon a seat; "raising his left hand with his left hand" means speaking while making his case known—this is the meaning. Kātyāyana states what must be done after the questioning (verses 87–88):

"When he has been questioned in this manner, whatever he may say, the judge, together with the members of the court and the Brāhmaṇas, shall deliberate upon the matter. If it is found to be just, then [the defendant] is to be summoned for further proceedings."
He should deposit a token there, or he should appoint a person [to do so];
that which is just and fit for investigation. Bṛhaspati also says: "Against whomsoever one brings a charge, whether on the basis of truth or even out of suspicion..."
The king should have that very person summoned by means of a seal or by a messenger.

If, after the plaint has been lodged, the defendant is not summoned by the king due to the king’s preoccupation with other affairs, then, by the king’s command, the plaintiff himself may have the defendant detained by some person until that [summons] is granted. And so says Kātyāyana (28.104): “He who inflicts injury or does not pay what is owed when asked for, because of his wicked conduct, shall be dragged forth by the king’s command.”
But once the matter has been reported to the king and he has given an unambiguous promise [to investigate],
the judge shall then issue an injunction of restraint until the defendant's appearance for trial.

Regarding that which is beyond doubt, that which has been promised, that which is determined to be subject to investigation, and that which has been declared to be subject to investigation—Nārada also [states] (Mā.
1.47): "The plaintiff shall restrain one who does not abide by the matter to be stated and who departs from his word, until the appearance of the summons for the trial."

Regarding what is to be said and what is to be decided: "not remaining" means not being occupied with the purpose of reaching a decision; "departing" means going beyond [the limits]. He himself states that there are four kinds of restraint (*āsedha*) regarding the speech of the litigant (NSm 1.48): "Restraint may be of four kinds: restraint of place, that determined by time, from travel, and likewise from activity. One who is restrained must not transgress that restraint."

The prohibition (*āsedha*) consisting in the form, "Without resolving this dispute, you must not set foot elsewhere than from this place," is the prohibition of location (*sthānāsedha*). The prohibition of time (*kālāsedha*) consists in the form, "Without having reached a decision on this matter, you must not take food on this day," and so forth. The prohibition of travel (*pravāsāsedha*) consists in the form, "Without reaching a decision, you must not go to another village. The prohibition of action (*karmāsedha*), which is devoid of specific restrictions of place or time, consists in the form, "Without making a formal determination, you must not perform [rituals] such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*). If one violates a restriction imposed by a person authorized by oneself, and possesses the capacity to prove one's own case, one may personally carry out the prohibition.
And likewise Kātyāyana says:
[18] "If one who has been restrained by a party seeking a legal remedy should violate that restraint,
he may be restrained even with his own hand, provided he admits that act."
That plaintiff should demonstrate that action; he must be capable of proving it. Regarding the punishment for one who obstructs what has not yet been proven, Kātyāyana says (105):

"One who is fit for obstruction, having failed to prove his case, deserves punishment if he transgresses. 'Fit for obstruction' refers to an action that is subject to restraint. There is no punishment for the transgressor in cases of restraining what is unfit for restraint, such as the voiding of feces or urine; on the contrary, the punishment falls upon the one who obstructed. Thus it was stated by him (Kāt. 106).

But he who, by restraining the senses through such means as silence or holding his breath, should obstruct those who ought not to be obstructed, shall be punished— not for the transgression itself, but for the obstruction.

"By those who are not subject to restraint" means by those who are unfit for restraint. Regarding the absence of punishment in certain cases of violating a restraint, Nārada states (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.49):
"In the case of crossing rivers, traversing wildernesses, difficult terrains, or during calamities and the like, one who violates a restraint while already constrained shall not be held at fault."

In the *Mādhavīya*, however, the reading is *durdaśā*; *durdaśā* means a miserable condition. Kātyāyana states (110) that one who seizes those who should not be seized shall be punished: "But he who seizes one who should not be seized is to be punished by the king; such is the settled rule. He himself (107–108) specifies those who should not be seized:
Those who have climbed trees or mountains, those stationed on elephants, horses, chariots, or boats,
and all those situated in difficult terrain— none of these should be obstructed by those seeking to accomplish their purpose.
Those afflicted by disease, those in distress, and likewise the sacrificer;
the sacrificer is one performing Vedic rites such as sacrifices. Vyāsa says:
"The seeker of yoga, the one desiring to sacrifice, the insane, the seeker of dharma, the one in distress, and the observer of vows."
One who is intent on giving should not be pressured, nor should he be obstructed, nor should he be summoned.
The yogi is one who is devoted to internal yoga. Nārada (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.52–54):
"One who desires to renounce, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to sacrifice, one situated in calamity, one assailed by another, and likewise one engaged in royal service."
[19] Cowherds [should go] where cattle graze; farmers when it is time to sow the grain;
artisans at their respective times; and those who bear arms during a conflict.
A messenger who has not yet attained legal majority, one intent on giving a gift, one observing a vow,
and those in a precarious situation must not be obstructed; nor should the king summon them, says Bṛhaspati.

One who has raised a weapon, one intent on battle, a sick person, those afflicted by grief, the insane, children, the intoxicated, the elderly, one engaged in royal business, and one observing a vow— [these are exempt from being summoned].
A soldier in the midst of battle, a farmer during the harvest, those in a precarious situation, and likewise women accompanied by their protectors, should not be obstructed.

Regarding the summary of the [rules for] sowing seeds and the collection [of debts]: "Women with a protector" refers to women of good family who have a protector, being dependent on others and subject to their father or other guardians. According to the Easterners, "women with a protector" means those who stay in secret with a woman. Kātyāyana (96–97): [One should avoid summoning] those who are incompetent, children, the elderly, those in distress, those occupied with religious rites, those preoccupied with business, those addicted to vices, and those overwhelmed by royal business or festivals.
A king should not summon those who are intoxicated, insane, negligent, or afflicted,
nor a young woman of noble birth who lacks protection, nor one who has recently given birth.
"A maiden of the highest among all castes is declared to be under the authority of her kinsmen.

Regarding one whose case is ruined when a restraint is imposed, he is called a "defaulter of duty" (*kāryātipātī*). He says the same regarding those who must be summoned: "Women who are dependent on others for their livelihood, unchaste women, and courtesans [must be summoned by their own kin]."

"And those who have been deprived of their families and those who are outcasts—their summoning is prescribed. Thus it is said. "Those dependent on a family" refers to women such as Ābhīras who support a household. "Svairiṇīs" are unchaste women. "Gaṇikā" means a courtesan. Regarding those who, being accused, take up renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and so forth out of fear of that accusation, he (the same author) states that they too may sometimes be summoned:
"Even those who, having learned of an accusation, have become forest-dwellers, renunciants, and so forth..."
The king should also summon them for important affairs, without provoking their anger.
The same author states that even those who are ill or otherwise incapacitated should be summoned without insistence:
"Having ascertained the time, the place, and the relative strength or weakness of the matters at hand,
the king should summon even those who are unfit [to appear in court] and so forth, but very gradually."

The reading in the *Mādhavīya* is: “He should cause him to be summoned by means of gentle vehicles. By “vehicles,” [Bṛhaspati] refers to swings and the like. Regarding the penalty for one summoned by the king who does not come, Bṛhaspati says:
“If one summoned does not come out of arrogance, even though supported by the strength of his kinsmen, the king shall determine his punishment in accordance with the nature of the legal claim.”
Kātyāyana states the differentiation of punishment according to the differentiation of the accusation (vv. 100–101):
"But if one who is summoned should disregard the king's command while being capable [of obeying], the king shall inflict upon him punishment according to the procedure prescribed by law."
For a minor offense, the fine shall be fifty; for a middling one, it shall be at least one hundred;
and for serious matters, the punishment shall always be at least five hundred.
Vyāsa states that there is no punishment for one who does not come when summoned in certain circumstances:
"In a region struck by an enemy army, or afflicted by famine and disease,
one should issue a summons again, but should not impose a penalty."
The Grandfather (Bṛhaspati) has stated what must be done when one who has been summoned fails to appear:
"The defendant must be placed before the assembly by the plaintiff, or in another designated location; otherwise, he is not considered authoritative."
Regarding the requirement as to who should speak when, and at what time, among the plaintiff and the others in the assembly, Kātyāyana says (121):
"In that case, the plaintiff should speak first, and the defendant immediately thereafter;
after those two, the members of the assembly [should speak], and after that, the presiding judge."

[21] Nārada also stated that the plaintiff is the one who possesses the right to the initial claim: "He who makes the first report to the king should be known as the plaintiff (*pūrvavādī*) by those who know the law. Thus it is said.

In certain cases, such as disputes over boundaries and the like, it is not necessarily the one who first brings the suit who is the plaintiff; rather, between the two parties, he who has the greater matter at stake or the greater suffering is the plaintiff. Thus, that same author says:
"To whichever party the greater suffering or the more significant matter belongs, to him the right of being heard (arthavāda) must be granted, not to the one who merely presented the case first."
Kātyāyana also says:
"He for whom there is greater suffering or whose case is more significant shall be the plaintiff;
it is not he who first makes a formal announcement."

In a case where these two are simultaneously acting as plaintiff and defendant due to a difference in their respective subjects, the claim of the higher caste or the one suffering greater hardship should first be scrutinized, and only thereafter should the position of the other party be adjudicated.
Thus says Bṛhaspati:

When the plaintiff and the defendant have both proceeded with a spirit of rivalry, the trial should be conducted according to their respective castes or by considering the degree of suffering involved. If either of these two—the plaintiff or the defendant—is unable to speak for himself, his representative may speak on his behalf. Thus says Bṛhaspati:

For those who are lacking in confidence, the dull-witted, the insane, the elderly, women, children, or the sick, a kinsman, an appointed official, or another person may state the preceding and following statements on their behalf.
The "prior and subsequent" refers to the plaintiff's plea and the defendant's reply. Kātyāyana (89–90) states:

"The right of representation belongs to the one who is formally accused, not to anyone else, as there would be no connection [otherwise]. However, even another person, if impelled by the accused, is considered authorized to act on his behalf."
Another person who is presented by the plaintiff before the judicial authority is to be known as the defendant (*prativādī*), as is one who has come forward of his own accord (*pratipanna*).

By the "accused," meaning the defendant (*pratyarthin*), or by the "plaintiff," meaning the proponent (*vādin*). Here, the term *prativādin* refers to a representative (*pratinidhi*) and not to the defendant. Furthermore, the "consenting one" (*pratipanna*) is one who has personally made an agreement, thinking, "I myself shall become his representative. In this context, the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and the consenting one" indicates that both being entrusted by the plaintiff and being a personal consent are jointly the grounds for representing another. Nārada states that victory and defeat in the case of a representative belong to the proponent and the defendant respectively (NSm Mā 2.22).
Whether commissioned by the plaintiff or even instigated by the defendant,
whoever litigates on behalf of another, victory and defeat belong to those two [parties].
Regarding those two, the plaintiff and the defendant:
"He who is neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor an appointed agent,
yet speaks on behalf of another, shall be punished if he speaks falsely in legal proceedings."
This statement of Kātyāyana refers to those who are not formally appointed [as witnesses], since it was stated by him alone (Kāt 92):
"Slaves, laborers, disciples, those who are appointed, and likewise kinsmen—these litigants shall not be punished; whoever is other than these is liable to punishment."
In certain disputes, the prohibition of a representative has been stated by that same [author] (Kāt 93–95):
"In cases of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife,
as well as in other disputes where it is impossible to argue, no opponent (prativādī) is permitted."
In the case of killing a human, theft, violating another's wife,
eating forbidden food, and the abduction or defilement of a maiden;
In cases of harsh speech, forgery, and likewise treason against the king, the defendant shall not be compelled to plead; rather, the perpetrator himself must dispute the matter.

The defendant (*prativādī*) is the representative. The repetition of the term "theft" (*steya*) is for the purpose of indicating that in such a case, a representative must not be appointed under any circumstances. After the legal proceeding has commenced, if either one or both of the plaintiff and defendant should die, their son shall carry out the determination of the lawsuit. Thus says Bṛhaspati: "When the plaint and the reply have been written down, if the plaintiff or the defendant dies, their son shall clear up the legal proceedings."

Having formulated a legal action whose outcome was previously undecided and having reflected upon it, one should establish—that is, prove—the proposition of the disputing plaintiff; this refers to the case of a "false" (mithyā) reply. The defendant should establish the "reason" (kāraṇa); this refers to the case of a "counter-attack" (pratyavaskandana). The "plaintiff regarding prior conduct" (prāgvṛttavādī), that is, the one who asserts a prior judgment (prāṅnyāyottaravādī), should prove his case by means of a certificate of victory; this is an elliptical expression for the judge and other officials. For this very reason, Vyāsa states:
"In a case of prior judgment, likewise by means of a certificate of victory from the judge and others. Nārada says:
In a case where the defendant admits the claim, the proof consists of a false plea;
however, when a matter is established by the procedure of a prior judgment, the proof shall be the written decree of victory.

"In the cases of *mithyā* and *mithyottara*, the burden of proof (*kriyā*) lies with the plaintiff (*pūrvavādī*). The meaning is that the document of victory (*jayapatra*) shall be the *kriyā*; it shall be the means of proof (*pramāṇa*). Vyāsa states: "But when the defendant asserts a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) or a valid defense (*kāraṇa*), he shall indicate the *kriyā*. In the case of a plea of denial (*mithyottara*), the burden falls on the plaintiff; in the case of a confession (*pratipatti*), it does not exist."

The *pratyarthī* is the defendant (*prativādī*). In the case of a "plea of admission" (*saṃpratipatti*), it is the answer of agreement. That is the legal action (*kriyā*). When two people, disputing over a single object—each saying "this is mine, this is mine"—arrive simultaneously in the court, the legal action belongs to the plaintiff (*pūrvavādī*) who says, "I obtained this first. And so Yājñavalkya (2.17) states: "When there are witnesses on both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff."

The word "become" (*bhavanti*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. The mention of "witnesses" (*sākṣin*) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other means of proof (*pramāṇa*). However, when one of those two says, "It is true that this was previously obtained by him, but it was obtained by another through a gift or similar means from him and given to me," then the burden of proof (*kriyā*) falls upon the defendant who claims it was obtained later. And so says that same author (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.17):
"When the plaintiff's case has been defeated, the means of proof belong to the defendant."

The word "witnesses" (*sākṣiṇaḥ*) is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. The *pūrvapakṣa* is the claim, "I previously obtained this"; its subordination occurs because, being admitted as true, it is no longer a matter to be proven. And this taking of proof (*kriyādāna*) must be performed by taking a surety (*lagnaka*) from both the plaintiff and the defendant. Thus says Yājñavalkya (2.10): "A surety capable of resolving the legal matter should be taken from both parties."

The function of the decision (*nirṇaya*) consists in the payment of the adjudicated wealth and the payment of the fine; this is *kāryanirṇaya*. Because the rule regarding the prior placement [of words] (*pūrvanipāta-śāstra*) is not absolute, in the sūtra *tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ savarṇam* (Pāṇini 1.1.9), the term *prayatna* is used where one might expect *yatnaprārambha* (the commencement of effort). Thus, it is *prayatna* as that which has arisen at the beginning (*prārambhautpanna*).

The author of the *Mahābhāṣya*, while speaking, has established that in certain instances within a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the word ending in the genitive case may be placed last; by virtue of this indication (*jñāpaka*), the word *nirṇaya* is placed at the end of the compound. Vijñāneśvara, however, states that because of its inclusion in the *āhitāgny-ādi* class of words, the word *kārya* should be placed first. Kātyāyana declares those who are not to be accepted as witnesses (114–116): Neither an owner nor an enemy, nor one appointed by the owner, nor one who is imprisoned, nor one who has been punished, nor anyone who is under suspicion.
Neither an heir nor one who is destitute, nor those residing elsewhere,
nor men appointed to royal service, nor those who have gone forth as renunciants [are entitled to inherit].
One who is incapable of paying the creditor and an equivalent amount as a fine to the king should not be accepted as a surety for the performance of the obligation,
nor should one who is unknown.

An heir (*rikthin*) is one who takes the inheritance, such as a brother or other relative; *rikta* means destitute. "Dwellers elsewhere" refers to those residing in another country. "Unknown" means not specifically familiarized with. Yājñavalkya (2.52): "Suretyship, debt, and witness testimony—these are indeed not recorded [as valid] among brothers, husband and wife, father and son, when they have not yet divided their property."
Nārada also says: "Being a witness, acting as a surety, giving, and receiving—
these brothers who are divided may perform among themselves, but not those who are undivided."

In the absence of a surety, the king’s officers shall be appointed for as long as it takes to reach a decision in order to protect him, and they shall receive their wages from those two parties. Thus says Kātyāyana (117): "If there is no surety suitable for the case of the litigant, he, having been protected, shall pay the wage to the servant at the end of the day."
"Fit for the task" means fit for the delivery of the adjudicated wealth and so forth. "Of the plaintiff" refers to the litigant;

here, the singular number is not intended to be restrictive. In the phrase "to the servant," the singular is likewise not intended to be restrictive. He (Yājñavalkya, verses 118–119) states the means of recovering the wealth and other assets in the event of defeat for one who lacks a surety:
"A twice-born man who lacks a surety should be guarded by external patrols."
But one should bind with fetters those such as Śūdras who are without sureties.
(25) "In cases of transgression or flight, one should fine him eight *paṇas*;
however, the obstruction of the daily duties (*nityakarman*) of any of the social classes (*varṇa*) must not be permitted.

This *kriyā* (proof), which is prescribed to be granted to either the plaintiff or the defendant as appropriate among the various types of false pleas (*mithyottara*), should be granted after imposing a fine upon that person who possesses the characteristics of a defeated litigant (*hīnavādī*), provided he is liable to punishment alone; but it should not be granted if he is liable to defeat. However, if he lacks the characteristics of a defeated litigant, it should be granted without delay. Regarding this, Kātyāyana identifies the defeated litigant (vv. 385–386):
One should discern his inner state through his facial expressions, gestures, and movements;
that the opponent has become defeated is indicated by inference.
Trembling, perspiration, discoloration, dryness of the lips,
scratching the ground, leaving one's place, looking sideways or upwards,
and hoarseness of voice— these the wise declare to be the signs of a corrupted [patient].

The mention of the "opponent" (*prativādin*) is illustrative [of other parties as well]. By "inference" (*anumāna*), one means through signs of corruption such as trembling and the like. "Touching" (*avamarśana*) means licking. Yājñavalkya also states other characteristics of a defeated litigant (2.13–15):
"He moves from place to place, and he licks the corners of his mouth;
his forehead perspires, and his face becomes discolored."
With speech parched and faltering, he speaks much that is contradictory;
he does not honor his words or his eyes, and he even distorts his lips.
He who undergoes a change from his natural disposition through actions of mind, speech,
or body during a legal proceeding or while giving testimony is proclaimed to be a wicked person.

"Sr̥kkiṇī" refers to the corners of the lips; the connection is "the mouth becoming parched. He does not honor speech or sight—that is, he does not honor the words spoken by another by giving a reply, nor does he honor the gaze with a look in return—except by his own nature, meaning without any agitation of the assembly or the like. As stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"One who is terrified does not speak; there is neither trembling nor perspiration, nor any transformation or pain in the limbs, nor would his gait be otherwise."
[26] He is victorious if he remains free from anger; otherwise, it is indeed the previous party who prevails. "The previous party" refers to the plaintiff. Nārada also says:
"He who, having abandoned the original plea, again resorts to another..."
Because he shifts the course of the debate, that man should indeed be known as a speaker of inferior discourse.
Kātyāyana (196):
One should not, having accused another of a matter, later speak against that very case;
one who speaks thus should likewise be declared defeated.
That same [person] (197):
But if a litigant, having caused a statement to be written, should then speak of it as deficient or excessive, he shall lose the case; he does not deserve to bring a formal accusation.
He who gives an instruction and then denies it after having pointed it out;
and he who does not comprehend matters that are contradictory, where the conclusion is contrary to the premise; [these are witnesses who should be excluded].
Furthermore, he who, having cited an authority, subsequently evades it;
or who, when questioned regarding a matter properly undertaken, does not acknowledge it.
He who converses secretly with witnesses in a place where conversation is forbidden,
he who does not wish to answer when questioned, or he who runs away;
If, when told "speak," he does not speak; or if, having spoken, he cannot substantiate what was said;
or if he cannot discern the consistency between what precedes and what follows—that person is defeated on account of that matter.
Having said, "There are witnesses," if one who is established in dharma does not point them out when told to do so, he too should be declared defeated for these reasons.
If the plaintiff does not speak, he shall be punished with death or a fine according to the law;
if he does not speak within three fortnights regarding the matter of justice, he is defeated.

*Ādeśyam abhiyogam*: *Ādeśa* refers to the place where the plaintiff and the defendant were present at the time of the loan or other transaction; thus it is defined in the *Kṛtyakalpataru*. In the *Smṛticandrikā*, however, reading it as *adeśa*, it is explained as "a witness who was not present at the time of the decision. *Adharottarān pūrvāparān*: Contrary, contradictory, and inconsistent. *Apadiśya uktvā*: Having stated, having made an excuse (*apadeśa*). *Apadhāvati apasarati*: He flees, he withdraws. *Samyak praṇihitam samyag abhihitam*: Properly set forth, properly stated. *Pṛṣṭaḥ san*: Being questioned—being asked, "What answer do you give here? By what evidence do you prove your own position? *Nābhinandati nottarayati*: He does not acknowledge it, he does not respond. *Asambhāṣye deśe sambhāṣaṇārhe pradeśe*: In a place where conversation is inappropriate, yet in a spot where conversation ought to take place. *Niṣpatet*: Without speaking, he goes away to another village. The repetition of the previously stated matter, such as "Speak! and so forth, is for the sake of emphasis. *Dharmastho dharmādhikaraṇasthaḥ*: A judge, one stationed in the court of justice. *Vadhyo vadhārhe viṣaye*: One deserving death, in a case where capital punishment is warranted. *Daṇḍyo daṇḍārhe viṣaye*: One deserving punishment, in a case where corporal or monetary penalty is warranted. Yājñavalkya (2.16).
He who proceeds independently regarding a doubtful matter,
he who absconds, or he who says nothing when summoned, is declared by the law to be defeated and liable to punishment.

"Independent" means not dependent on [other] means of proof (*sādhana*). "Should establish" means he should accept [the claim]. "Should flee" means he should run away. Since his inferiority is already established by the very mention of the "staff" (punishment), the repetition here is for the purpose of making known the loss of the subject matter at hand. For this very reason, Nārada says (Mā 1.46): "But he who proceeds with a doubtful matter without reporting it to the king shall be punished by force, and that matter shall not be established."
Kātyāyana (207): "But that plaintiff who, having pointed out witnesses, does not proceed to litigate by his own will—he is defeated after thirty nights have passed. Thus it is said.

Nārada (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 8.54): "One who speaks falsely, one who evades the legal procedure, one who does not appear, one who fails to provide an answer, and one who flees when summoned— these are declared to be the five kinds of defeated parties."
"One who hates the legal process" means one who hates the members of the court and so forth. And thus, that same [author] says:
"The wise should know that the members of the court and the witnesses constitute the legal process;
he who, out of delusion, hates that process is called 'one who hates the legal process.'"

One who is not present in court at the time appointed by the members of the assembly and others is considered non-appearing. Bṛhaspati states that there is no fault if one fails to appear due to divine or other such obstacles:
"When a decision has been made regarding the performance of customary rites or a divine ordeal, if someone does not appear, one should not employ a pretext in that case. (28)
If at that time a fault caused by fate or the king should occur,
he shall not be defeated merely by the abandonment of his life.

In a legal proceeding concerning conduct or a matter of dharma, one should not employ deception; the meaning is that one should not regard [the opponent] as guilty therein. In this statement of Nārada, the mention of "the defeated party is of five kinds" is not intended to be an exclusive limitation to only five types, since other defeated parties are also recorded in the tradition. What then? It is for the purpose of making known that among those, the defeat of each subsequent one is more serious than the preceding. And that is shown by the following: "One who changes his plea [is fined] five *paṇas*; one who shows hatred toward the judicial procedure, ten *paṇas*; one who does not appear, fifteen *paṇas* (ten plus two); and one who fails to provide an answer, sixteen *paṇas*."
And one who flees when summoned shall be made to pay a fine of twenty *paṇas*; this is stated by Kātyāyana to indicate the severity of the punishment. (202) Kātyāyana says:
One should not approach witnesses in secret as directed by another.
And one should cause it to be split by no other means; acting in this way, one will not come to ruin.
Nārada says: "When both parties have submitted their written statements and the decision on the matter has begun,
he who speaks there what was not previously stated shall be deprived of that object."
Bṛhaspati says: But he who, having designated witnesses, does not cause them to speak within thirty nights or three fortnights, his case suffers defeat.
One who flees when summoned, one who remains silent, a witness who is defeated,
and one who admits the claim by his own words— the defendant is of these four kinds.

One who flees loses his case after three fortnights; one who remains silent, after seven days; one whose testimony is contradicted by witnesses, at that very moment; and one who admits the claim, immediately.

One who has admitted his own statement and has himself accepted defeat—here, the specification of particular time limits, such as "within thirty nights," follows the relative lightness or gravity of the matter and is intended to indicate short or long durations respectively. Among these signs of a defeated litigant, some, such as being defeated by witnesses, serve to determine the non-existence of the claimant's intended object. Upon seeing such signs, two punishments are to be prescribed. And so Kātyāyana (206) states:
"Having seized him in accordance with the fault, a second trial is not permitted."

However, certain other matters, such as speaking of irrelevant subjects and so forth, serve as grounds for suspecting the absence of the intended meaning [of the claim]. Upon seeing these, punishment should be prescribed. For this very reason, Kātyāyana (202) states: "One who speaks inconsistently [is fined] five *paṇas*; one who hates the legal procedure, ten *paṇas*; one who does not appear, twelve *paṇas*; and one who fails to provide an answer, sixteen *paṇas*."
"And one who flees when summoned shall be made to pay a fine of twenty *paṇas*. Thus, the initiation of a legal proceeding occurs through fleeing,
through failing to provide a defense, and by resorting to the position of the opposing party.
The speech of an inferior person is refuted, but not that of one who has triumphed through his own words.

Where permission is granted by such statements of Bṛhaspati and others, there one should proceed; otherwise, a defeat must be declared. Furthermore, permission for a withdrawal from the lawsuit should be understood as applicable within a period of three fortnights or similar duration, but not beyond that; for "one who flees is defeated after three fortnights, and one who remains silent after seven days."

This is because of the previously cited statement. In legal proceedings concerning acts of violence (*sāhasa*) and the like committed out of anger, even if a party states otherwise due to negligence, there is both punishment and a reversal of the case. However, in proceedings concerning matters such as debts not committed out of anger, there is only punishment and no reversal. Thus says Nārada (Mā. 2.25):
"In all disputes concerning property, one does not fail on account of a verbal quibble;
however, in cases involving cattle, women, land, or the non-payment of debt, even if punished, one does not lose the matter at stake."

In all disputes concerning property (*arthavivāda*) that are not caused by malice, one does not fail, nor does one become defeated, even when employing verbal quibbles (*vākchala*) or speaking through negligence (*pramādābhidhāna*). Herein is an illustration: as in cases involving cattle, women, land, or the non-payment of debts, although one may be censured or even punished for speaking negligently, one does not lose the matter at issue according to one’s own intent. [30] By specifying "in disputes concerning property" (*arthavivādeṣu*), it is implied that in disputes caused by malice (*manyukṛta-vivāda*), there is a loss of the subject matter under consideration. Regarding the penalty for the plaintiff and defendant reaching a private settlement between themselves without informing the king after the written statements of the plaint and reply have been submitted, Kātyāyana says (206):
Those who, having presented their case and accepted its meaning, subsequently seek reconciliation with one another,
shall all be fined double, for they have deceived the king.
A matter that has been formally taken up and accepted by oneself; furthermore,
when a dispute has been set forth and the investigation between the plaintiff and defendant has commenced,
those who reach a settlement with one another shall be made to pay a fine double the amount [in dispute].

This statement of Bṛhaspati also refers to the context of deceiving a king; therefore, when two parties reach a mutual agreement by the king's command, there is no punishment, but rather merit itself. And so he says: "When the former and latter positions have been set down and the determination of the case has begun, a reconciliation between the two heated parties may occur like that of two iron balls."
But where there may be a choice between witnesses and assessors for both parties,
those two who, while wavering, bring about a settlement are to be considered wise.
Where there is equality of authority but a difference between the scriptures and the conduct, a reconciliation of both is recommended by royal decree.

The "deliberation of witnesses and assessors" (*sākṣisabhyavikalpa*) refers to the knowledge of the form: "What will these [witnesses] say? regarding both the plaintiff and the defendant. "Swinging" means being possessed by doubt as to how this legal matter will be resolved. "Equality of evidence" (*pramāṇasamatā*) refers to the assessors' perception of equality in the evidence on both sides. "Divergence" (*bheda*) refers to the conflict between the treatise (*śāstra*) and established practice (*caritra*); "practice" here means the treatise on legal procedure (*vyavahāraśāstra*), and the meaning is that there is a contradiction between that treatise and another treatise, or a contradiction between a legal proceeding and another legal proceeding. Thus concludes the determination of the *pratyākalita*.

Now, after the administration of ordeals, the various types of legal procedures (*kriyābheda*) and so forth that are to be performed have been indicated. Having thus described the administration of ordeals, Bṛhaspati says:

[31] "Having heard the plaintiff's and the defendant's statements as determined by the members of the court, he whose case is to be proven must substantiate his entire claim by means of written documents and other evidence."
"Bhāvanā" means the act of proving. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is an inclusion of those things that will be mentioned hereafter. Yājñavalkya also says (2.7):
"Then the plaintiff shall immediately have the proof of the matter asserted written down."

That which is sought or desired is called *artha* (the object); one who possesses such an object to be purified is an *arthin* (the plaintiff). Consequently, in the case of a false plea (*mithyottara*), the plaintiff is the *arthin* because he is the one who must prove his case; in the cases of a plea based on a cause (*kāraṇottara*) or a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāyottara*), the defendant is the *arthin*, as he is the one who must establish the cause or the prior judgment. This *arthin* should immediately, without delay, cause the proof—the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—for the matter asserted, the matter to be proven, to be written down. Vyāsa says:
"Whatever was stated in the initial pleading, that the *arthin* should present in its entirety through evidence in the third stage."

The mention of the plaintiff (*pūrvavādin*) is also an indication for the defendant (*uttara*). [He proves his case] by means of action (*kriyā*), that is, by means of evidence (*pramāṇa*). Bṛhaspati demonstrates the different types of action:
"Action is declared to be of two kinds: human (*mānuṣī*) and likewise divine (*daivikī*);
each of these has been divided into one kind by the sages who perceive the truth."
Human proof is threefold: written testimony, witnesses, and inference;
while divine proof is traditionally held to be ninefold, beginning with the water-pot ordeal and ending with that born of religious merit.

In this context, possession (*bhukti*) is not mentioned separately because it is included within inference (*anumāna*). The examination of the distinctions among witnesses and other means of proof will be treated in its own section. Kātyāyana (214) states:
"Witnesses, documentary evidence, and possession—they know these to be the three kinds of proof.
Yājñavalkya (2.22) declares the superiority of witnesses and the other means over divine ordeals (*divya*).
Written documents, possession, and witnesses are declared to be the means of proof.
In the absence of any one of these, one of the divine ordeals is prescribed.

The meaning is that scholars learned in the scriptures state that in the absence of even one of these, any one among the divine ordeals, such as the water-jar (*ghaṭa*) and others, should be accepted as the means of proof. Kātyāyana also, with this very intention, stated that when two people who are disputing over a single object—each saying "this is mine, this is mine"—arrive at court simultaneously, if one relies on evidence such as witnesses while the other relies on a divine ordeal, the witness-evidence alone must be accepted. Likewise, in a lawsuit where the defendant denies a claim that "on this day, a hundred gold coins were taken by you at such an interest rate, yet now you do not pay back the principal and the interest," if there are witnesses regarding the taking of the debt but none regarding the specific amount or the specific interest rate, and the plaintiff says, "In that case, I shall prove the amount and so forth by means of a divine ordeal," even then a divine ordeal should not be accepted there; for, according to the maxim of the grain in the cooking pot (*sthālīpulākanyāya*), certainty regarding the specific amount and interest is possible through other means. Thus he says.
If one person should state a human means of proof and another should state a divine one,
the king should accept the human means in that case, but not the divine procedure.

If even a human act of proof that has reached only one part of the case exists, it should be accepted by men who speak; however, even a divine act of proof, though complete, is not to be accepted. [Kāt 218–219]

Yājñavalkya also intends that where there is the possibility of witnesses and other means of proof regarding even a single part of the claim, an ordeal (*divya*) should not be accepted.
