Thus, in a lawsuit concerning multiple items such as gold or jewels, if the plaintiff proves a portion of the claim through witnesses and the like while the defendant denies all of it, but the plaintiff then seeks to prove the remainder by means of an ordeal, the king—without causing the plaintiff to undergo the ordeal—should cause the defendant to pay all of that gold, jewels, and so forth to the plaintiff. However, he states (YDh 2.20) that what was not recorded at the time of drafting the plaint (*bhāṣā*), but is subsequently asserted by the plaintiff, shall not be made the defendant pay.

"One who denies [a claim] is cleared by a written document; one who is proven on a single point must be made to pay the entire amount by the king, but he should not be made to pay what was not declared.
This does not mean that if the witnesses state an amount less than or greater than that indicated by the document, there is no proof of the entire matter to be established.
In disputes concerning debts and the like, when the matter is largely established and decided,
if the stated amount is either less or more than the truth, the claim to be proved shall not succeed.

It should not be said that this contradicts the statement of Kātyāyana (396), because that refers to a case where, after the plaintiff has asserted the entire matter, the witnesses produced as evidence establish only a portion of it. The statement of Yājñavalkya, however, concerns cases other than this. Furthermore, regarding crimes of violence (*sāhasa*) and the like, by this very same author it has been stated that even when witnesses produced to prove the entire matter testify to only a portion, the whole matter is established:
"Even if only a portion of the matter to be proved is spoken by the witnesses, the whole shall be [established]. [33]
"In matters involving association with women, acts of violence, and theft, that which is established [by witnesses] is declared to be valid.

By the term "acts of violence" (*sāhasa*), verbal abuse and the like are included. Furthermore, this indicates that success is achieved only for that portion which has been stated by the witness; even when multiple matters are being litigated, "the creditor shall prove only as much as he can establish."

"By means of witnesses alone, he shall obtain the debt as proven," says Kātyāyana (473). This statement refers to cases where a son or other heir must pay a debt incurred by his father or others, even though he was unaware of it; for in such instances, since the son and others cannot deny the debt, they are not at fault. He (Kātyāyana) also states (223) that between witnesses and documentary evidence, the document is more authoritative:
"When witnesses are available, no divine means of proof (*daivikī kriyā*) is prescribed."
And when a written document exists for the disputes, there shall be neither ordeal nor witnesses.
Likewise:

"The legal standing that has been proclaimed for guilds, trade associations, corporations, and the like, is established by documentary evidence; neither divine ordeals nor witnesses apply to it. (225)

In some cases, that same author states the superiority of witnesses (227–228): "When a dispute arises regarding ownership— such as when one takes back what was given, or when one has not received what was given—
or concerning the sale and delivery of goods, or when one has purchased wealth but does not wish to pay for it..."
In cases of gambling, challenges to combat, and when a dispute has arisen, witnesses are declared the sole means of proof; neither divine ordeal nor documentary evidence is required.

"Having given, he takes back"—that is, having said "this has been given to you," he takes it back before it has been formally delivered. He takes it back after having given; therefore, it is taken by force (*ācchidya*). The absence of the substitution of *t* for the root *dā* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). When there is a determination regarding owners—that is, when there is a legal decision concerning the owner—the meaning is: in a dispute regarding that [ownership]. "Having bought [something] and not wishing to give the wealth"—the word "wealth" refers to the form of the price; this is the ellipsis. In some cases, the same author (verse 226) states the superiority of possession (*bhukti*): "Likewise in the case of doors, paths, works, enjoyment, water-conduits, and so forth."
"Indeed, possession alone is weighty; neither a document nor witnesses [are sufficient].

[34] "Door-activity" refers to the act of exiting or entering; "path-activity" refers to a path for the exit of cattle and the like; "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) refers to that which is enjoyed, such as houses, fields, and so forth; "water-conduit" refers to a channel for the exit of water. In some instances, Bṛhaspati states the superiority of divine ordeals:
"One who forges gems, pearls, or coins, or one who misappropriates a deposit..."
One who is violent and one who consorts with another's wife must always be examined by means of oaths.
In cases of accusations of great crimes, as well as in the misappropriation of deposits,
the king should examine the matter by means of ordeals, even when witnesses are available.
Kātyāyana also states:
"Where there is equality among witnesses, one should verify even that by means of ordeals,
provided that witnesses are available in disputes involving the loss of life."
When a litigant invokes a divine ordeal, he need not question witnesses therein;
however, in all cases involving the highest degrees of violence (sāhasa), he should conduct an investigation.
"Bhṛgu indeed [declared] that the existence [of a fact] among the virtuous is [to be established] by divine means when witnesses are present.
Equality consists in similarity in terms of qualities and number. Bṛhaspati has also mentioned other matters pertaining to divine means:
"In cases of long-standing secret acts or where witnesses have long since perished..."
When the [witnesses] are equally corrupted, one should purify the matter by means of divine ordeals.
Regarding a document made long ago in secret, or one made long ago in private, Vyāsa states:
"This document was not written by me; it has been forged by this person.
Having set aside that document, a decision on the matter shall be reached through an ordeal.
Setting aside— that is, disregarding— that matter or subject, Nārada says: "In a forest,
in a secluded place, at night, inside a house,
in cases of violence, and likewise in the denial of a deposit, divine means of proof are applicable."
When no witness is found for men disputing in a legal case,
then one should examine them by means of ordeals and various kinds of oaths.
[35] This same rule is seen to apply in cases of women's violation of their character, as well as in theft and acts of violence, and in all instances of denial of facts.
Bṛhaspati says: Where doubt arises regarding a written document or the testimony of witnesses,
and where inference is confused, there divine proof (divya) is the means of purification.
In cases of injury to a man and in acts of violence, one should employ divine means of proof (*daivikī kriyā*).
In certain instances, he states the option between witnesses and divine proof (Kāt 229, 233):
"When a lawsuit concerning violence, verbal abuse, or physical assault has already been commenced..."
In matters arising from force, witnesses and even divine proof [are admissible].
A written document, witnesses, or even subtle arguments and the like,
as well as divine means of proof, have been declared for the benefit of the subjects.

“*Yuktileśaḥ*” means a portion of reasoning (*yukti*). By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*), the refutation of scriptural injunctions (*codanā-pratikalpa*) is included; its nature will be shown in the section defining inference (*anumāna-nirūpaṇa-prakaraṇa*). The plural number is used with the intention of referring to a plurality of instances. Here, by the inclusion of “verbal abuse” (*vācika-pāruṣya*), there is the inclusion of harsh speech in the form of insults such as “you are a drinker of *surā*,” and so forth. However, in the case of minor verbal abuse, or in cases of [other] verbal abuse and [disputes over] land, one should not employ an ordeal (*divya*).

Thus, because Kātyāyana has prohibited [the use of] ordeal (*divya*) in this manner (239), the mention of "land" (*bhūmi*) in this statement of Kātyāyana is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all immovable property (*sthāvara*). And so Pitāmaha says:
"In disputes concerning immovable property, one should avoid ordeals.
Furthermore, this prohibition of ordeal refers to cases where witnesses and other means of proof are available, since it has been stated by that same author:
"One should establish these [claims] by means of witnesses, a written document, or possession" (Kāt 240).

But when there is no existence of witnesses and the like, then an ordeal (*divya*) must certainly be accepted; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that such a dispute could never reach a decision. Nor should one suspect that this statement is redundant because there is no distinction between the case of immovable property and other disputes such as the non-payment of debts—wherein an ordeal is not taken when witnesses exist, but is taken when they are absent—since, in comparison to those cases, there is no difference here. Just as in disputes over debts and the like, even though witnesses exist, if the defendant accepts a specific penalty for defeat and declares, "I shall undergo an ordeal," then an ordeal is to be accepted. This is because human defects such as anger or greed are possible in witnesses, whereas an ordeal, being free from defects, is capable of making known the matter exactly as it is. Thus, regarding this very subject where the matter is to be proven by divine means, Kātyāyana has stated that one should not employ human evidence such as written documents; since he declares that witnesses and the like are inadmissible in such a case, an ordeal becomes acceptable. Similarly, in disputes concerning immovable property, even if witnesses exist and the defendant accepts a penalty and declares that he will undergo an ordeal, an ordeal is not to be accepted. This statement is intended to make known this specific distinction. However, Pitāmaha states that where, due to the insignificance of the matter, neither an ordeal nor witnesses and the like exist, the king’s own will alone is the authority.
Where neither a written document exists, nor possession, nor witnesses,
and where there is no application of divine ordeals, the king himself is the authority in that case.
"Those disputes which are of a doubtful nature and cannot be determined [by other means],
for those the king shall be the authority, since he is the lord of all.
Thus ends the third section, "The Determination of What Must Be Done Immediately After the Award of the Verdict," in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* by Śrī Kodaṇḍaparaśu.

**Proposed reading of the defective text:** Thus ends the third chapter, "The Determination of Duties to be Performed Immediately Following the Execution of Legal Proceedings," in the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "the Illustrious Kodaṇḍa-Paraśurāma."
Now follows the definition of witnesses. In this regard, Manu (8.74) sets forth the nature of a witness:
"Testimony is established through having seen something with one's own eyes and through having heard it."

The meaning is that he by whom the subject of dispute was previously cognized through the eye or the ear is a witness therein. Viṣṇu (8.13) states: "Testimony arises from seeing or hearing in person. Bṛhaspati shows the different types of witnesses:
The written, the copied, the secret, the reminded, that which is delivered by a kinsman or a messenger,
the incidental, the reply, and another which occurs in the midst of business.
"The king, the presiding officer (*adhyakṣa*), as well as the village, and the witness—thus it is remembered as twelvefold.

Here, "presiding officer" refers to the judge (*prāḍvivāka*). The mention of the "presiding officer" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the members of the court (*sabhyas*), the scribe (*lekhaka*), and others. For Kātyāyana says:
(355) [37] "The scribe, the judge, and the members of the court, in their proper order..."
"When the king examines that matter, the witnesses are formally cited.

From this, and from the forthcoming statement of Bṛhaspati—"the accountant, the messenger, and the chalk-bearer [are witnesses]"—it should be understood that the accountant possesses the status of a witness. The mention of the "village" is illustrative; by this, it is established that whoever has measured the subject of dispute becomes a witness therein, even if not formally appointed as such. Otherwise, in disputes such as the non-payment of wages, there would result an absence of witnesses due to the impossibility of written documents and the like. Having this very point in mind, Manu stated (8.76):
"Where one may see or even hear something unrecorded, there too, when questioned, one should speak of it exactly as seen and exactly as heard.

Here, "unrecorded" (*anibaddha*) means not committed to writing. The nature of the nine types of evidence, such as written documents and so forth, as well as the circumstances under which the three classes of persons, beginning with the king, serve as witnesses, have been shown by that very same author.
He by whom one's own [name], that of one's father,
and the place of residence are recorded— that person should be known as a witness designated as "written."
Having effected a transaction involving wealth through various acts such as lending money and the like,
that which is recorded in writing before one's eyes is declared to be "written" (lekhita).
He who is made to hear the debtor's statement while separated by a wall,
and who denies it as it truly was, is declared to be a hidden witness.
He who is summoned and made a witness in matters such as debts, deposits, and transactions,
and who is repeatedly reminded, is called a "reminded witness" (smārita).
In matters of partition, giving, or establishing a mortgage, where a kinsman is prescribed—
one who is common to both parties and knows the law— he is proclaimed a *kulya*.
He who, being sent by both parties, listens to the statements of the plaintiff and the defendant—
one who is virtuous and approved by both— is declared to be a *dūtaka* (messenger/witness).
But when a legal matter is being transacted, whoever happens to arrive of his own accord and says,
"I am your witness here," is considered an incidental witness.
[38] Where a witness, while departing for another direction or being on the verge of death,
causes another person to hear what he has heard, one should know that person to be a subsequent witness (uttara-sākṣin).

He whose confidence is placed by both [parties] and to whom their business is disclosed should be known as a secret agent (*gūḍhacārī*), as well as one who is situated in the midst of the undertaking.
The statement of both the plaintiff and the defendant which has been heard directly by the king himself.
He alone shall be the witness in a dispute between either of the two.
But when a legal case has been decided and a new trial is required, the presiding judge, together with the members of the court, shall act as witnesses therein; it cannot be otherwise.
Whatever has been stolen or destroyed on all sides within the boundary,
the village shall undoubtedly be the witness there, even if it was not formally appointed as such.

*Jāti* refers to [caste] such as Brāhmaṇa-hood and so forth. *Nāma* is [the personal name] such as Devadatta and so forth. *Sva* means one's own property. *Pitrya* means related to the father. *Nivāsa* is the place of residence, such as Vārāṇasī and so forth. Regarding the phrase "having performed the purposeful action" (*arthikriyām*), this is its meaning: having performed the purposeful action through various types of actions, specific means of knowledge, authoritative statements, and so forth; and having established the certainty of the matter connected to the claimant; whoever is recorded in writing regarding that claimant’s connection to debts and the like—that person is called "one who has been written down" (*lekhita*). "Denies" (*vinihnute*) means he does not disclose. "The matter as it is" (*yathābhūtam*) means the matter exactly as it was heard. "The act of deposit" (*nyāsakriyā*) refers to the legal proceeding characterized by a deposit. "In a pledge" (*ādhāne*) means in a mortgage or a security bond. "Sent" (*preṣitaḥ*) means sent by the claimant to the presence of the defendant, and by the defendant to the presence of the claimant—this is the remainder [of the sense]. "In what must be done" (*kartavye*) refers to a task consisting of the repayment of debt and so forth. "To another region" (*diśam*) means to another country. Regarding the phrase "he on whom [trust is placed] by both," this is its meaning: he upon whom trust has been placed by both the claimant and the defendant—namely, a trust of the form "this matter of his must be disclosed"—or to whom the matter has been entrusted; he who remains in that manner, i.e., in a state of non-disclosure, is to be understood as a "secret agent" (*gūḍhacārī*) situated in the midst of the case. The mention of the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) and the assessors (*sabhyas*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the accountant and the scribe. The inclusion of the term "together with the assessors" (*sabhya-sahita*) is intended to state that the assessors and others also serve as witnesses in the trial again, but it is not intended to indicate that the witnesshood belongs only to a judge specifically distinguished by the presence of the assessors and others.

[39] This is because it would result in a contradiction with the previously cited statement of Kātyāyana: "The scribe, the judge, and the members of the court, in their respective order. Furthermore, in response to the inquiry as to how many such witnesses should be accepted, Bṛhaspati says:
"There should be nine, seven, five, or even four or three."
Or both may be learned in the Vedas and renowned; one should never consult with only one.

In this context, a *śrotriya* is one who, while being a student of the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-veda*), performs the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti. He [Yājñavalkya] himself states that even a single person among those such as the *likhita* may be accepted as a witness:
"The *likhita*, the two kinds of *gūḍha*, three, four, or five *lekhitā*s, the *yādr̥cchaka*, the *smārita*, the *kulya*, and likewise the *uttara-sākṣin*."
The messenger, the scribe, and likewise one who is involved in the matter—
these alone shall be authoritative, as shall the king and the presiding official.

The accountant is one who holds a chalk-pen. The word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "one only" is intended to mean that one should not look for two or more witnesses. As for the restrictive rule—"Witnesses should be known as at least three" (YDh 2.69)—that refers to cases other than those involving written documents, such as the case of accidental witnesses (*yādr̥cchika*) and so forth. When accidental witnesses and others are learned Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), even two may be accepted, according to the cited statement: "Or both may be accepted if they are both learned Vedic scholars and renowned. Regarding written witnesses and the like, Yājñavalkya (2.72) states that even a single person may be accepted if there is mutual consent.
Even a single person who knows the law may be a witness if he is approved by both parties;
as Nārada also says (Ṛṇādāna 192):
"He who is approved by both of two litigants..."
Even if he is alone, he should be questioned as a witness in the assembly.

Vyāsa states that even a single witness may be accepted as valid if he has been determined by kings and others to be trustworthy: "One who is pure in conduct, knows the dharma, and whose speech is based on personal experience— even a single such person may be authoritative, especially in cases of violence."
Kātyāyana states that even a single witness who was previously unknown as being untrustworthy may be admitted in cases such as deposits (353):
"In the case of a deposit kept within [the house], even a single person may be declared a witness;
even a single person sent by the plaintiff may be a witness in the case of a requested loan."

That which is requested for the purpose of marriage and the like, or received through solicitation, such as ornaments and so forth—regarding a dispute over merchandise such as earrings and the like, that very author [of the work] is a witness; thus he himself says (Kāt 354):
"Whatever merchandise has been refined by whomsoever, that should be proven by him alone;
in a dispute concerning that, he alone is declared to be the authority."
The merchandise consists of earrings and the like. Vyāsa states who the witnesses should be:
"Those who know the Dharma, who have sons, who are hereditary residents, of noble birth, speakers of truth, engaged in the performance of Vedic and Smārta rites, and free from hatred and envy."
Those learned in the Vedas who are not dependent on others, wise men who do not travel abroad, and young men should be appointed as witnesses in matters such as debts by one who knows the law.
The *mūla* is the ancient account; those who know that are called *maula*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.59 (*tad adhīte tad veda*). Kātyāyana [states]:
"Those of renowned lineage and character, and free from greed and delusion..."
The word of those who are authoritative, refined, and awakened is undoubtedly [true].
The disputant must establish his case through witnesses who are exactly like himself;
he should never attempt to prove his case with witnesses who are either superior or inferior.

The *āptas* are those who speak of objects as they have been correctly cognized; the *śiṣṭas* are those who are devoid of the performance of prohibited actions; the *vibuddhas* are those possessing knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures. The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), with the intention of expressing the initial action [of becoming so] (Pāṇini 3.4.71).

71) Regarding the phrase *vibhāvya* ("having caused to be perceived"): the kind of person (*yādṛk*)—that is, the type (*yajjātīya*)—of opponent who must be made to perceive or accept by the proponent, that very same kind of person, belonging to the same class as the opponent, the members of the court (*sabhyāḥ*) should cause to be perceived or accepted; this is the ellipsis. The mention of "proponent" (*vādī*) is an illustration, and the mention of "opponent" (*prativādī*) is likewise an illustration; for the opponent, too, must be made to accept by those belonging to the same class as the proponent. Nārada (*Ṛṇādāna*, 155): "In guilds, the guildsmen [should decide]; in their own groups, the group members."
"Among outsiders, outsiders shall be witnesses; and among women, women. [This refers to] those who are "inferior," meaning those of lower castes. Manu (8.68):
"Women shall give testimony for women, and for the twice-born, similar twice-born men."
And those who are Śūdras among Śūdras are of the lowest birth among the lowest castes.

Although the members of a guild (*śreṇi*) are included within the category of "groups" (*varga*), they are mentioned separately according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*). Kātyāyana has shown who these group members are (349–350):

"Bhr̥gu declared those to be groups (*varga*) who wear sectarian marks (*liṅgin*), guilds (*śreṇi*), associations (*pūga*), merchant corporations (*vaṇigvrāta*), and others who stand in collective bodies."
The leaders of the various groups of slaves, wandering performers, wrestlers, and those who live by elephants, horses, and weapons are known as the *vargiṇas*.

"Their testimony is among their own groups, and those group members are the witnesses. This statement regarding the eligibility of witnesses only for those who are similar in caste and other attributes should be understood to apply when both similar and dissimilar persons are available. However, in the absence of similar persons, even dissimilar ones may be accepted as witnesses. With this very intention, Yājñavalkya (2.68–69) says:
"Ascetics, those of a charitable disposition, those of noble birth, and speakers of truth..."

"Those who are devoted to dharma, upright, having sons, endowed with wealth, at least three in number, and dedicated to the performance of Vedic and Smṛti rites—these are to be known as witnesses. They are prescribed according to their respective birth and caste, or all may serve for all [castes]. Thus it is said.

"Without overstepping their birth" means according to their respective castes (*jāti*). "Castes" refers to those born in the direct order (*anuloma*), such as the *Mūrdhāvasikta* and others, and those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), such as the *Sūta* and others. "According to class" (*yathā-varṇam*) means without overstepping their social class (*varṇa*). "Classes" refers to the Brāhmaṇas and so forth. All these include those of the same caste and different castes, those of the same class and different classes. Regarding those who must be excluded from serving as witnesses, Yājñavalkya says (2.70–71):
Women, children, the elderly, gamblers, the intoxicated, the insane, the accused; performers, heretics, forgers, and those with impaired senses.
[42] Those who have fallen from their caste, kinsmen, those with a personal interest in the matter, associates, enemies, thieves, violent persons,
and those whose guilt has been proven— these, beginning with the outcastes, are not to be admitted as witnesses.

A child (*bāla*) is one devoid of the discernment necessary for worldly affairs. An old man (*vr̥ddha*) is one devoid of the physical dexterity required for worldly affairs. A gambler (*kitava*) is a professional dice-player. One who is intoxicated (*matta*) is one whose mind is impaired by drinking and the like. One who is insane (*unmatta*) is one possessed by spirits or the like. One who is accused (*abhiśasta*) is one under charge of such crimes as the killing of a Brahmin. A stage-player (*raṅgāvatārī*) is a dancer. Heretics (*pāṣaṇḍinaḥ*) are those who follow paths contrary to the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. A forger (*kūṭakr̥t*) is one who produces fraudulent documents and the like. A friend of the plaintiff (*āpta*) is the plaintiff’s ally. A relative to the subject matter (*arthasambandhī*) is one connected to the object that has become the subject of dispute. An associate (*sahāya*) is one constantly intent on performing that person’s business. An enemy (*ripu*) is the adversary or foe of the defendant. A violent person (*sāhasī*) is one who commits acts such as the killing of living beings. One whose fault has been observed (*dṛṣṭadoṣa*) is one seen to have spoken falsehoods. One who is cast out (*nirdhūta*) is one abandoned by his own kin. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), slaves and others are included. Manu (8.65–66): [text follows]
A king shall not be made a witness, nor shall artisans or bards;
nor a learned Vedic scholar, nor one in a religious order, nor one who has renounced all worldly attachments.
"One who is not dependent on another, nor one who is censurable, nor a thief, nor one who performs forbidden acts. Thus it is said.

A *kāru* is an artisan; a *kuśīlava* is an actor; one who "dwells in signs" (*liṅgastha*) refers to an ascetic and the like; one who has "gone forth from attachments" (*vinirgata*) is one who has abandoned contact with elders such as his father; one who is "under another's control" (*adhyadhīna*) is one who has been made a debtor (*bandhakīkṛta*); and one who is "despicable" (*vaktavya*) is one who is blameworthy. This prohibition against a king acting as a witness applies to the time of lending money and the like, when he is being made a witness; it does not apply to his being a witness during a legal dispute regarding the actual facts, for that would result in a contradiction with the previously cited statement of Bṛhaspati. The prohibition against a *śrotriya* acting as a witness concerns a single *śrotriya* alone, in accordance with the forthcoming statement of Nārada; for if it applied to all *śrotriyas* in general, it would entail a contradiction with the previously cited statement of Bṛhaspati. Nārada (Ṛṇādāna, 178–): [text follows]
187, 156) | A slave, a deceitful person, one lacking faith, an elder, a woman, a child, a wheelman (chariot driver),
a hired laborer, one who is intoxicated, insane, or addicted to drink, one who is afflicted by disease, a gambler, and a village priest.
[43] Long-distance travelers, sea-merchants, renunciants, and the sick;
those with missing limbs, Vedic scholars (śrotriya), those lacking proper conduct, eunuchs, and actors.

Atheists, those who have abandoned their vows, those who have deserted their wives or the sacred fires, those who officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, those who eat from a single vessel, companions, enemies, those who live by wandering, kinsmen, and blood relations.
Actors whose faults have been previously observed, poison-sellers, snake-charmers,
those who administer poison, arsonists, usurers, the offspring of Śūdra women, and those guilty of minor offenses (upapātaka).
Those exhausted by rashness, those weary, those driven out, and those at the very end;
those who have broken their conduct, those who have not returned to it, the dull-witted, oil-pressers, and root-diggers.
Those possessed by spirits, those hostile to men, those who predict rain or the positions of the stars,
those who utter curses, those who sell themselves, those with deficient limbs, and those who live on the fortunes of others;

One with deformed nails, one with a dark-complexioned face, one afflicted with vitiligo, a betrayer of friends, a rogue, a vintner, a magician, a hunter, a fierce person, and those who oppose guilds or assemblies; [these are excluded].
A murderer, a painter, a conch-blower, one who has fallen from his caste, a forger, a cheat, a debtor, a thief, and a royal officer;
A Brahmin who sells human beings, cattle, meat, bones, honey, milk, water, or clarified butter, as well as a twice-born man who is a usurer;
One who has fallen from his own duty, a member of a guild, a slanderer, a servant of the low, one disputing with his father, and a creator of dissension— these are non-witnesses.
But if someone among groups such as guilds should become an object of hatred, he shall not be a witness for them; they are all witnesses to him.

A *naikṛtika* is one who is habitually seeking out the faults of others. An *aśraddha* is one devoid of faith. A *cātrika* is a bard or panegyrist. A *pramatta* is one whose mind is always inattentive. An *ārta* is one who is suffering. A *mahāpathika* is a traveler on a great road. A *sāmudravaṇik* is a sea-faring merchant. An *ātura* is one afflicted by disease. A *vyaṅga* is one with missing limbs. One *ācārahīna* is one lacking proper conduct. Regarding *ekasthālī*: here, by the word *sthālī*, the cooking of rice for the purpose of a meal in a pot is understood. He who has one pot is an *ekasthālī*; because the rule for the suffix *kap* in compounds is not universal, there is no *kap* here. There is no shortening of the vowel, as in the case of *ardhapippalī*. An *aricara* was formerly an enemy; the suffix *caraṭ* is used in the sense of "having been previously" (Pāṇini 5.3.53). However, in the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, it is read as *aridhara*, and explained as "one who bears weapons. *Jñātayaḥ* are those of the same lineage (*sagotra*) and blood relations (*sanābhi*), such as maternal uncles, their sons, and maternal cousins. A *śailūṣa* is a director of female dancers. A *viṣajīvī* is one who lives by selling poison. An *āhituṇḍika* is a snake-catcher. A *garada* is a poisoner. An *agnida* is one who sets fire to houses and so forth. A *kīnāśa* is a miser. An *upapātaka* is one joined with a minor sin; the analysis of the compound is "one for whom a sin is near. A *klānta* is one who is utterly exhausted. An *aśrānta* is one who performs work without ceasing. A *nirdhūta* is one cast out by kinsmen. According to the Easterners, a *lokabhayaśūnya* is one who is fearless of public opinion. An *antāvasāyī* is a barber. A *bhinnavṛtta* is one of reprehensible conduct. An *asamāvr̥tta* is one who has not performed the ritual of returning home from study (*samāvartana*). A *jaḍa* is a fool. A *tailika* is one who lives by selling sesame seeds. A *mūlika* is one who deceives with root-mantras; it is stated in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* that he is one who practices such things. A *varṣasūcaka* is a rain-predictor. A *nakṣatrasūcaka* is an astrologer. An *aghaśaṁsī* is one who proclaims the sins of others. A *hīnāṅga* is one with deficient limbs. A *bhagavr̥tti* is one who lives on the wages of sexual intercourse with his wife, slave-girls, and so forth. Here, a *śaṭha* is a rogue. A *śauṇḍika* is a seller of liquor. A *śaṅkha* is one who lives by dancing with bulls. A *kuhaka* is a hypocrite. A *pratyavasita* is one who has fallen away from the life of a renunciant. A *kulika* is one appointed to a corporation (*kula*), meaning one who holds office over a group of Brahmins and so forth. A *sūcaka* is one appointed by the king to report the faults of others. A *bhedakr̥t* is one who causes the breaking of friendships and the like. Regarding the phrase "in guilds and so forth" (*śreṇyādiṣu*): the meaning is this—that when a person has an enemy among members of a guild or similar body, even other members established in those guilds do not become witnesses in that dispute. Kātyāyana (361–364) says:
Those who live by that occupation, those who perform services for him,
his kinsmen, friends, servants, and trusted associates— these, however, are not witnesses.
Mothers' sisters' sons, uterine brothers' sons, and maternal uncles—these are declared to be sapindas; one should not employ them as witnesses.
Kinsmen, relatives by marriage, the husband of one's sister,
the father, a paternal relative, a paternal uncle, a father-in-law, and likewise teachers;
Those royal officers who have been appointed to positions in cities, villages,
and districts must not fail to question the favorites [of the king] when they are commanded.
Bṛhaspati says: The mother’s father, the paternal uncle, the wife’s brother and maternal uncle,
the brother, the friend, and the son-in-law are all non-witnesses in any legal dispute.
Those addicted to other men's wives or to drinking, gamblers, those who corrupt everyone,
the insane, the afflicted, the rash, and atheists are not to be witnesses.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The officers in charge of customs and military outposts, a messenger, those with their heads wrapped [in cloth], all women, students living in the house of a teacher, wandering mendicants, forest-dwellers, the Nirgranthas, and conch-blowers or snake-catchers"—the phrase "are not witnesses" is to be supplied here. The officer in charge of customs (*śulkādhikṛta*) is one authorized at a place for collecting tolls. The officer in charge of a military outpost (*gulmādhikṛta*) is one authorized over a *gulma*, which is a troop of infantry. A messenger (*dūta*) is a servant. Students living in the house of a teacher (*gurukulavāsinaḥ*) are celibate students (*brahmacāriṇaḥ*). A *nirgrantha* is a Jain ascetic (*kṣapaṇaka*). Nārada (on the non-payment of debts, verse 157): [text follows]
For even one who is not a witness is seen in the treatises to be of five kinds by the wise:
[the witness] through speech, through fault, through division, through self-accusation, and the one deceased in the interval.
And he himself explains these [categories] by distinguishing them (*R̥ṇādāna*, 158–162):

"In a dispute where there is a disagreement among witnesses due to differences— such as those who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and so forth on account of their verbal testimony, or thieves and so forth on account of the perception of their faults [as being biased]— " [so it is said].
A "self-accuser" is one who, not being previously identified, comes forward and speaks of himself;
he is considered as if dead while the claimant is still alive, except in the case of one who has been heard from while on the verge of death.
Vedic scholars, ascetics, the elderly, and those who have renounced the world and so forth are not witnesses; this is because of their own declarations, and no further reason need be cited here.
Thieves, violent men, the fierce, gamblers, and likewise executioners—these are not witnesses because of their wickedness; truth is not found in them.
When witnesses have been accepted by the king for the determination of a single matter,
if their statements should diverge, they shall be considered non-witnesses due to that discrepancy.
[46] But where, in a legal dispute, an equality of memory is observed among the witnesses,
the testimony is set aside from that case because of the subtle nature of the requirements for witness-status.
But he who, not having been designated as a witness, comes of his own accord and speaks—his statement is considered "self-accusation" in the treatises; he does not deserve the status of a witness.
If there should be a matter that ought to be heard, yet no witness exists for it, where could one exercise witnesshood? Thus, one who dies before the trial is not a witness.

The connection is that those beginning with the *śrotriya* are non-witnesses by virtue of their [specific] statements. Where there is a disagreement—meaning a contradictory statement—among those who have been cited as witnesses in a legal dispute, they become non-witnesses due to that division; this is the meaning of the phrase "disagreement due to division. "Unspecified" means not mentioned as a witness. "Having approached" means having arrived. One who possesses the knowledge, "This person here is a witness," is an "internal" (*āntara*) witness. "One whose internal witness has died" (*mr̥tāntara*) refers to one for whom the internal witness is dead. When the plaintiff (*arthin*) in whose favor a witness was known dies, that witness becomes a "one whose internal witness has died" and thus ceases to be a witness. Regarding the term "one about to die" (*mumūrṣu*), since it is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), even if informed by a healthy father or other relative that "this person is a witness in this matter," he remains a witness despite being a "one whose internal witness has died"; such is the meaning of the phrase "one whose internal witness has died in the plaintiff. Intending that the mention of "one about to die" is illustrative, it was stated by that same author:

Even if not made to hear by the dying man himself, that matter connected with dharma for which he was informed [by another] shall constitute evidence even after death; this applies in cases such as deposits (*nikṣepa*) and bailments for delivery (*anvāhita*).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), items such as borrowed goods are included. In the expression *mumūrṣuśrāvita* ("informed by one about to die"), the suffix *-kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) as that which is pervaded by the operation of the agent.

When [an action] has been stated or expressed, there is no further injunction; however, when a subordinate action (*guṇakarman*) is involved, the rule for *l*-suffixes and so forth applies. This is the teaching of the one of no small intelligence regarding those cases where there is a connection with constant or volitional activity, even in the absence of a subordinate quality (*aguṇa*). Remember this!

Thus, since it is stated in the *Vārttika* appended to the *Mahābhāṣya*—regarding roots derived from verbal bases other than those meaning "motion" (*gaty-artha*) or "intransitive" (*akarmaka*)—that when the primary object (*pradhāna-karman*) is expressed, the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) and so forth may optionally apply to both the secondary object (*guṇa-karman*) and the non-primary object, the series of sentences beginning with "learned Vedic scholars" (*śrotriya*) and "ascetics" (*tāpasa*) is intended to clarify the aforementioned grounds for disqualification as witnesses. In this context, those intended are the learned Vedic scholars and ascetics whose minds are solely absorbed in the Supreme Brahman and whose hearts are unattached to external objects. This is because it is impossible for them to remember matters regarding which there is disagreement, and because, if all such Vedic scholars and ascetics were included, it would contradict the previously cited statements of Bṛhaspati and Yājñavalkya. [The reason for their exclusion is] due to their statement, not due to any fault; the meaning is that the cause here is not of the nature of a defect. "Violent" (*caṇḍāḥ*) means extremely prone to anger. "Killers" (*vadhakāḥ*) means those who commit violence against living beings. The phrase "when a determination of a single fact must be made" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Witnesshood is not lost merely by a difference in testimony; rather, since it is difficult to ascertain witnesshood when there is a discrepancy in statements—due to the impossibility of discerning who is truthful and who is lying based on qualities such as the ability to remember long-observed facts and their number—the sentence "But the equality of a witness possessing memory... (*smṛtimatsākṣisāmyaṃ tu*) is intended to convey the meaning that they are disqualified as witnesses. Therefore, this does not constitute a redundancy in relation to the preceding statement. However, that which conveys the meaning that when one among many gives a different account, all of them are disqualified as witnesses— [End of provided text]
Among witnesses— whether they have been recorded in writing or specifically designated by the plaintiff—
if even one of them speaks otherwise than the rest, all are disqualified as witnesses due to that discrepancy.

This statement by Kātyāyana (359) refers to the case where, among five witnesses, one who possesses superior qualities speaks falsely; because the many witnesses of inferior quality state a matter contrary to the testimony of the one of superior quality, they all become non-witnesses, and because that single witness of superior quality states a matter contrary to the testimony of the many, he too becomes a non-witness. Otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with the statement of Yājñavalkya (2.78), which will be cited later: "In a conflict between two sides, [the testimony of] the many... and so forth. By the phrase "having come of his own accord," the absence of formal summons is indicated. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says (404):
"He who is neither designated as a witness, nor summoned, nor exhorted, yet speaks—whether falsely or truthfully—is also to be punished, for he is the lowest of men. Thus it is said.

The meaning of the phrase "the matter which is to be made known" is as follows: when a plaintiff must make a witness hear the nature of the matter—such as a claim for testimony—that he must state here, if that person has died, then because the one to whom it was to be heard is absent, and since no specific matter has been designated, one might ask, "In what [matter], being unindicated, should he speak as a witness? For this reason, one who is deceased is not a witness. Regarding those previously declared non-witnesses, such as slaves, the dishonest, and others, Nārada states that they may in certain cases serve as witnesses (*Ṛṇādāna*, 188):
[48] Those who have been designated as non-witnesses, such as slaves, the dishonest, and so forth...
Having encountered the gravity of the matter, even they may become witnesses.
In the absence of a woman, the task may be performed by a child, an elderly person,
a pupil, a relative, a slave, or even a hired servant.
Among them, neither a child, nor one who is alone, nor a woman, nor a forger,
nor a kinsman, nor an enemy shall give false testimony.
A fool may give false testimony through ignorance; a woman, through lack of truthfulness; one who has practiced evil, through habitual wickedness;
a kinsman, out of affection; and an enemy, for the sake of revenge.
But when [the judge] is unavailable, the task may be performed by a woman, or by a child, an elderly person,
a pupil, a relative, a slave, or even a hired servant.

Thus, the permission for women and others to serve as witnesses granted by Manu (8.70) is to be understood as applicable when there is no certainty regarding the absence of grounds for disqualification from witnesshood—such as those mentioned by Nārada concerning the tendency to speak untruth—and when other witnesses are unavailable. Yājñavalkya (2.72) also states that in cases such as adultery, everyone may serve as a witness:
"Everyone is a witness in cases of adultery, theft, verbal assault, and violence.
In this regard:
Killing a human being, theft, violating another's wife,
and both forms of harshness— these constitute the fourfold category of *sāhasa* (heinous crimes).

Because of this statement, although acts such as *strī-saṃgraha* (sexual intercourse with women) are indeed *sāhasa* (violent crimes), they are mentioned again for the purpose of including those instances where *strī-saṃgraha* and so forth are committed in secret, which otherwise would not be considered *sāhasa*. Uśanas says:
"A slave, a blind man, a deaf man, a leper, women, children, the elderly, and others like them—even if they are not [otherwise] related, these are held to be witnesses in cases of *sāhasa*."
"Unconnected" means devoid of a relationship with the matter at hand; that is to say, impartial. [As stated by] Manu and Nārada (*Manu* 8.72; *Nārada*, *Ṛṇādāna*, 189):
"In all cases of violence, as well as in theft and adultery..."
And in cases of verbal or physical assault, one should not examine witnesses.

[49] However, one should examine witnesses in cases such as debts and in matters of stable nature; it is recorded in the Smṛti that examination is prescribed only in some instances of violent acts and urgent matters. (Kāt 365)
Thus, the mention of "examination" refers to cases where there is the possibility of the fault of untruthfulness; for the absence of examination has been stated by that same author (Kāt.
366): "In cases of contradiction, in royal commands, in matters of seizure, in violent crimes, and in cases of theft or assault, one should not examine witnesses."

When witnesses have arrived in court, if the defendant knows them to be at fault, he should then expose their faults. However, if he imputes faults that do not exist, then the defendant should be punished by the king. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"One may expose the faults of witnesses designated by the plaintiff when such faults actually exist;
but a litigant who exposes those who are faultless deserves a punishment equal to the value of the claim."
The defendant (*pratyarthī*) is the one here. "Equal to that" (*tatsamaṃ*) means equal to the object of dispute, i.e., equal to the property in question. Vyāsa states:
"The defendant must set forth all the defects of the witnesses in the assembly; they should be stated in writing, and then the reply [to those charges] must be given."

The meaning is that the witnesses, having identified all the defects written in the document, should be made to state their answer—that is, their rebuttal—regarding those points by the members of the court (*sabhyas*). If the witnesses provide an admission as their answer, they do not function as witnesses; if they provide a denial (*mithyottara*), the defendant must prove the defects he has alleged by means of evidence. If he does not prove them, then he is to be punished; but if he does prove them, the witnesses are to be discarded because of their corruption. Furthermore, if the plaintiff fails to present other evidence, he suffers defeat; thus says the same author: "Having scrutinized all the defects written in the document, the witnesses should be made to state their answer regarding those points by the members of the court. In the case of an admission by the witnesses, they lose their status as witnesses; in the case of a denial, the defendant must establish the faults he has asserted through proof. If he fails to establish them, he is liable to punishment; however, if he establishes them, the witnesses are to be rejected due to their wickedness. And for the plaintiff, if he does not produce further evidence, there is defeat. Thus he [the author] states.
They are not entitled to act as witnesses in any way regarding the performance [of the rite];
otherwise, they must be made to perform the ritual action by the defendant.
If he fails to prove his case, the defendant shall be compelled to pay a fine;
witnesses who have been clearly proven [to be false] must be excluded, as they have been disqualified by the rules governing witnesses.
"If the plaintiff remains satisfied and relies solely upon the witnesses, then the defeated party shall be made to pay with due humility by means of the procedure prescribed in the scriptures. [50]

In the case of correct practice and proper adherence; otherwise, in the case of non-adherence. They are to be cultivated—that is, they are to be made to accept—by means of action, namely by the presentation of evidence. The syntactical connection is: "making the witnesses clearly perceive [the truth] as it is. The reading in the *Mitākṣarā* is "of the witnesses" (*sākṣiṇām*), where the genitive case is used in the sense of the object. "With humility"—humility (*vinaya*) means instruction; accompanied by that, he should be made to pay the wealth in dispute; this is the ellipsis. "Free from further expectation" means devoid of the desire to present other means of proof. As for the fact that Vyāsa’s own statement regarding the disqualification of witnesses—that [the matter] is not to be established by witnesses or other such means of proof—is intended to convey this very meaning.
Whether it be well-known among the members of the assembly or even established in common worldly usage,
the disqualification of witnesses should be accepted, since it cannot be remedied by the absence of fault.
But if the refutation of the earlier witnesses were to be established by other witnesses,
there would be the fault of infinite regress, because others could likewise be required for them.

This statement is intended to mean that one cannot establish the refutation of those witnesses who have been determined by the world to be authoritative because they are not suspected of defects; for such a refutation is "unprovable" (*asādhyam*) due to its being already established (*prasiddhatvāt*), and it is "fit to be proven" (*sādhayitum arham*) precisely because of the absence of defects, namely the absence of the defect known as infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor should it be said that the raising of a refutation of witnesses by the defendant constitutes a change of legal issue (*vyavahārāntarāpatti*); for since that refutation is useful to the present legal proceeding, it does not constitute a different matter (*arthāntara*). And so says Kātyāyana (381): "When the defendant or the plaintiff establishes a refutation of the witnesses..."
Nor is there any other conventional usage, because it is useful for the subject matter at hand.

Regarding the opponent's failure to point out existing defects, there are two optional penalties for defeat (*hāni*). He himself also states that if the opponent is unaware of the defects in the witnesses, those must be exposed by the members of the court (380, 275):
"One should not invalidate a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with a false defect;
rather, one who brings a false accusation shall be punished or shall lose the matter to be proven."
Indeed, those faults of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which are to be stated must be pointed out by the disputant;
however, those that are obscure should be made manifest by the members of the assembly at the proper time through the citation of authoritative treatises (śāstra).

[51] The meaning is that those points which are concealed by the presentation of the legal document (*śāstra*) must be clarified by the members of the court at the proper time through the testimony of witnesses; they should be stated prior to the witness-debate. Bṛhaspati states that one should not raise defects after the witness-debate has concluded: "Whatever defects of the document or of the witnesses are recorded, they must be stated at the time of the debate; once stated later, one may not invalidate them."

"Before the time of the witnesses' testimony," that is, prior to the time of the witnesses' testimony during the course of the trial. "Of one who has begun to speak what was said": the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) according to Pāṇini 3.4.71, *ādikarmaṇi ktaḥ kartari ca*, since it refers to the commencement of an action. Kātyāyana states the punishment for raising an objection regarding defects after the witnesses' testimony has been given (verse 379): "But he who, when the matter has been stated, seeks to impeach witnesses who were previously unimpeached, and does not state the grounds for doing so, shall incur the first amercement."

The first degree of fine is the highest fine. When witnesses are unable to defend themselves against self-incrimination due to the disturbance of the assembly or other such causes, the plaintiff shall provide that defense. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"In a legal dispute, if either the written document or the witnesses are found to be tainted, the case of that party shall not succeed until they have cleared them of suspicion."

Regarding that [document] and so forth: Kātyāyana states the punishment for a plaintiff who, having brought under his control—by means of gifts of wealth or other methods—those who are ignorant of the matter at dispute or those who have a perverted understanding of it, and then designates them as witnesses:
"Having seized all the property of one by whom false witnesses were designated out of greed for the case, he should thereafter banish him from the realm. (407)

"By greed for the matter," meaning by the desire for the accomplishment of one's own stated purpose; "false witnesses" refers to wicked witnesses. "Confiscation of all property" is an illustrative expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); therefore, the punishment should be determined after considering whether the dispute is serious or minor. "Deprived of his standing" means rendered destitute of the object that was the subject of the dispute. "Therefore," that is, for that reason consisting of the employment of false witnesses, even if no mental corruption is manifested in the witnesses who have come to the court, they must be examined by the King. And so says Kātyāyana (340):
"The king himself should examine the witnesses who have appeared," so says Bṛhaspati:
"Those who have appeared should be examined by their voice, complexion, gestures, and other such signs."
Nārada states the means for determining a corrupt witness (*Ṛṇādāna* 193–196):
"But he who, because of being corrupted by his own faults, appears as if unwell,
who moves from place to place, and who runs after each person individually..."
One coughs suddenly and excessively and frequently sighs;
one scratches the earth with the feet and shakes the arms or the garment.
The color of his face changes, and likewise his forehead perspires;
his lips become parched, and he looks upward and sideways.
One who speaks much without being questioned, as if in haste, even when not asked, should be known as a false witness; one should severely punish that sinner.
"Āviddham" means agitated. Śaṅkha and Likhita also [state this].

Ministers should discern signs of wickedness through the application of the treatises: he glances askance, looks about in all directions, voids urine or excrement unexpectedly, moves from place to place, squeezes one hand with the other, bites his nails, his face becomes discolored, and his forehead perspires; he does not acknowledge or respond to the sight or speech [of others], yet suddenly gives gifts or offers praise; he repeatedly dismisses another, gazes outside, touches weapons, scratches the ground, shakes his head, distorts his lips, licks the corners of his mouth, and appears excessively startled even at insignificant tasks; he knits his brows, laughs, remains silent and lost in thought, speaks with internal contradictions, and so forth—these are the signs of wickedness. Furthermore, when the master is angry, [the minister’s behavior] deviates from his natural character. Thus it is said.

"And such [signs] as these are the characteristics of a wicked master when he is angry"—this is the connection [of the previous statement]. "Except for one who is naturally well-disposed" (*prakṛtiśīla*): one whose disposition (*śīla*)—that is, whose nature (*svabhāva*)—consists of the previously mentioned qualities such as looking straight ahead and so forth, is "naturally well-disposed. Other than that, these characteristics of a wicked or angry master apply. The meaning is that one who possesses natural qualities such as looking askance and so forth is not wicked, nor is such a master angry.

When the witnesses have been thus examined and their corruption is not perceived, they should be questioned regarding the disputed matter. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the procedure (Manu 8.87, 79–80):
[53] In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, the judge, being pure, should question the pure twice-born men concerning the testimony at midday or in the forenoon, while they face north or east.
In the midst of the assembly, the judge, consoling them, shall examine all the witnesses in the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant according to this rule.
Whatever you know of the mutual conduct of these two regarding this matter, tell it all in truth; for you are the witnesses here.

He (Kātyāyana) also states that in disputes concerning cattle, horses, and the like, the presence of the parties involved in the contested matter is required at the time of questioning the witnesses (Kāt 388–390): "In the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, and in the presence of the matter to be proven, one should cause the witness to testify directly; never indirectly."
In some cases, this duty may be performed even without those two [parents] for the sake of the purpose;
this law applies to quadrupeds as well as to bipeds and immovable beings.
For one may indeed act as a witness in all formal agreements (kriyākāra), even in the absence of balances, weights, or measures; but not otherwise than this.

"Even in the absence of those two"—that is, even without the presence of both disputants (*vādinau*). The word "even" (*api*) indicates the maxim of *kaimutika-nyāya* (how much more so), thereby making known the necessity of the presence of the subject matter to be proven (*sādhyārtha*). Therefore, the intent is not that testimony must be given even when neither is present; rather, the absence of both should be understood as the absence of the presence of one of the two—the defendant (*pratyarthin*)—and not merely the absence of each individual disputant or respondent. Thus, even if the defendant is absent due to flight or other reasons, testimony may still be given. In some cases, the meaning of the words has been shown by the phrase "in matters involving four parts" (*catuṣpādeṣu*). "Weighable" (*taulya*) refers to gold and the like, which are fit for weighing. "Countable" (*gaṇima*) refers to coins and the like, which are to be counted. "Measurable" (*meya*) refers to rice, wheat, and the like, which are fit for measurement. "Even in its absence"—that is, even in the absence of the presence of the subject matter to be proven. "In transactions involving formal agreements" (*kriyākāreṣu vyavahāreṣu*). Regarding the legal point (*vivādapada*) concerning killing, he (Kātyāyana) himself states that the testimony of witnesses should be given in the presence of Śiva (Kāt 391).
If there is a killing of living beings, one should cause the testimony to be proclaimed in the presence of Śiva;
in the absence of that, however, it should be proclaimed by means of a mark, and not otherwise.

[54] That testimony of witnesses must be taken in the absence of a branding mark serving as a sign of capital punishment; this is the remainder of the sense. Otherwise, when such a branding mark exists, no delay should be made in questioning the witnesses, as stated by that same author (Kāt 339): "The king must not cause a delay in the examination of witnesses;
through delay, a great fault arises characterized by the subversion of dharma."

Nārada states (Ṛṇādāna 198) that witnesses should be questioned individually after restraining them from speaking untruth by means of oaths: "Having summoned the witnesses— who are known for their conduct and who understand the matter— one should question them all together, having bound them firmly with oaths, and then [question them] individually."
Vasiṣṭha states that in some cases testimony must be given by those assembled together, while in others it may be given individually:
"That which has been seen by those gathered together must be stated in exactly that manner;
but that which is to be done by each separately must be stated individually."
But when a matter is proven by witnesses at different times, one should have each individual party plead their case; this is the rule proclaimed for such a situation.

The phrase "whatever task has been observed" is to be supplied [to the verse]. Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 200) states that fear must be instilled in witnesses by means of their speech being augmented with dharma:
"One should greatly terrify these [witnesses] with ancient declarations of dharma, demonstrations of the majesty of truth, and censures against falsehood."
Manu has stated those words which should be made to be heard [by the litigant]: "The judge, soothing him, should interrogate him according to this rule. (8.79–86)
"Whatever you know of the mutual conduct of these two regarding this matter,
tell it all in truth, for you are witnesses here.
By speaking the truth in testimony, a witness attains abundant worlds."
And here, this speech, honored by Brahmā, brings about unsurpassed fame.
A witness who speaks falsehood while giving testimony shall be bound by the nooses of Varuṇa, rendered helpless for a hundred births; therefore, one should speak the truth in testimony.
A witness is purified by truth; dharma increases through truth.
Therefore, witnesses must indeed speak the truth among all social classes.
For the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self is likewise the refuge of the self. Do not despise your own self, the supreme witness of men.
Evildoers indeed think, "No one sees us";
yet the gods see them, as does the inner person within oneself.
The sky, the earth, the waters, the heart, the moon, the sun, fire, Yama, and the wind,
as well as night and the two twilights, and Dharma— these are the knowers of the conduct of all embodied beings.
Bṛhaspati says: He should be admonished by court members who are experts in the Dharmaśāstras, through words that praise truth and reject falsehood, [and] regarding his births and lives.
Whatever merit has been acquired from birth until death,
all of that goes to ruin through the accusation of falsehood.
Vasiṣṭha said: Now, if one should speak untruth, which is characterized by falsehood in every respect,
he goes to hell after death and immediately thereafter enters the state of an animal.
For ten years he is a pig, for ten years a donkey;
for ten years he is a dog, and for twenty years a vulture.
Likewise, for forty years among worms, insects, and moths;
then he is born as a wild animal for ten years, and after that, as a human being.
Even if he attains human birth, he may become mute or blind;
subsequently, he is born as a low-born person, utterly abandoned by his kinsmen.
Lame, blind, deaf, mute, afflicted with leprosy, naked, thirsty,
and hungry, he begs for alms together with his wife in the house of an enemy.
Having understood the faults of falsehood and having understood the excellent qualities of truth,
one should therefore speak the truth in testimony, for it is conducive to welfare both in this world and the next.
Baudhāyana:
A witness who speaks falsely destroys three generations of ancestors and three generations of descendants— seven in total, both those already born and those yet unborn.
Manu and Nārada (Manu 8.97–101; Nārada, Ṛṇādāna 207–209):
Listen, O gentle one, to the sequence of the number of kinsmen whom a person slays by speaking falsely in testimony, starting from the first.
He kills five cattle by lying; he kills ten by lying regarding a cow;
he kills a hundred horses by lying; he kills a thousand men by lying.
One who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both those already born and those yet unborn;
one destroys everything by lying regarding land. Therefore, do not utter a falsehood concerning land.
Regarding food, women, sexual enjoyment, and all gems— whether born of water or made of stone— they say that these are like the earth.

One should behave toward honey and ghee as toward cattle; likewise toward vehicles as toward horses; toward silver and clothing as toward cows; and toward grain and Brahmins indeed as toward Brahmins.
"Consider all these faults in speaking untruth;

speak only the truth exactly as it was heard and exactly as it was seen. Thus [it is said]. Regarding water-born gems such as pearls and the like, and regarding the Brahman, that is, the Veda—Yājñavalkya (2.75).
"Whatever merit has been performed by you through hundreds of previous births,
know that all of it belongs to him whom you defeat falsely.
Thus, Nārada stated (Ṛṇādāna 198) that witnesses should be questioned after being bound by oaths.
"Having summoned the witnesses, he should question them after binding them firmly with oaths.
Regarding this, a distinction based on the difference of castes has been stated by that Manu and by Nārada (Manu 8.113; Nārada, *Ṛṇādāna* 199).
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by [the truth of] the Vedas, a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons,
a Vaiśya by his cattle, grain, and gold, and a Śūdra by all [the aforementioned] sins.

The meaning of this is as follows: one should administer an oath to a Brāhmaṇa by saying, "If you speak otherwise, your truthfulness shall perish"; to a Kṣatriya, "Your vehicles and weapons shall become useless"; to a Vaiśya, "Your cattle, seeds, and gold shall become useless"; and to a Śūdra who speaks otherwise, one should administer an oath by saying, "All manner of sins shall fall upon you. As for the statement by Gautama (13.12–13)—"Some say that the act of proving truth through an oath should take place in the presence of the King of the Gods and Brāhmaṇas, but not for those who are not Brāhmaṇas"—which declares the absence of oaths for a Brāhmaṇa, that refers specifically to a Brāhmaṇa who is recognized by all as being trustworthy. "Proving truth" (*satyakarma*) means the establishment of the facts exactly as they occurred. However, Manu states that even Brāhmaṇas who are degraded by such occupations as cattle-tending and the like should be made to undergo an oath just like Śūdras.
Those who have fallen away from their own duties, who subsist on the food of others,
and yet desire the status of the twice-born— one should treat them like Śūdras.
The mention of "Brahmins" is an elliptical expression intended to include Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well. Bṛhaspati states the manner in which questioned witnesses should speak:
having removed their shoes and turbans, they should raise their right hands;
taking gold, cow-dung, and *darbha* grass, they should speak the truth.

Bṛhaspati states the method for examining the testimony provided by a witness: "If what has been declared is not deficient in terms of place, time, age, substance, name, caste, and quantity, one should determine that the matter to be proven is established."
If a witness, when questioned regarding the matters specified,
does not state the testimony in accordance with the facts, that testimony shall not be considered properly delivered.
In cases where there is disagreement regarding place, time, age, substance, quantity, appearance, or caste,
even that testimony is contemptible.
"Whatever the witnesses may state, whether less than or more than [the truth], that too is to be understood as unspoken; this is the rule for witnesses as recorded in the Smṛti.
Regarding the question of how a decision is reached when there is a conflict among witnesses, Yājñavalkya says (2.78):

[58] In a dispute between two parties, the testimony of the majority should be accepted; if the numbers are equal, that of those possessing superior qualities; and if there is a conflict even among those of superior qualities, the testimony of those who are most virtuous should be adopted.
The phrase "of those who possess the highest qualities" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 229) states:
"In the case of a conflict among witnesses, many are considered authoritative;
when they are equal in number, those who are pure should be accepted; when they too are equal, those with superior memory."

Yājñavalkya (2.76) states the punishment for one who accepts to testify but then fails to do so: "For a man who does not give testimony, the king shall cause him to pay the entire debt along with ten percent interest on the forty-sixth day."

"Everything is accompanied by interest (*vṛddhi*). Together with the *daśabandha* [penalty], it is free from the tenth part (*daśamāṃśa*). The tenth part is to be taken by the king; the debt along with its interest is to be taken by the creditor (*uttamarṇa*)—so say the teachers beginning with Vijñāneśvara. The mention of 'debt' (*ṛṇa*) is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for legal disputes (*vivāda*) in general. For this very reason, Manu (8.108) states: 'A man who, being healthy, does not state his testimony regarding debts and other matters within three fortnights, shall be liable for that entire debt and the *daśabandha* penalty in every respect.'"

The mention of "disease" (*gada*) is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for any unavoidable obstacle. Regarding one who, though knowing the facts, refuses to accept the role of a witness out of malice, Yājñavalkya (2.82) states the punishment:

"He who, having been summoned to give testimony, denies it to others while being shrouded in darkness [of ignorance], shall be made to pay a fine eightfold; but in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, he shall be banished."

One who, having accepted the role of a witness and being made to hear the testimony by reliable witnesses, at the time of formal recitation—being shrouded in darkness and possessed of passion, hatred, and other such defects—denies that testimony before other witnesses, saying, "I am not a witness in this matter," shall be compelled to pay eight times the fine that is imposed upon defeat in the lawsuit. As for a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is capable of paying the fine, he should be banished rather than fined. Banishment (*vivāsana*) consists of being made naked, the destruction of his house, or exile from the country; the determination among these depends on the specific circumstances of the case. Regarding Kṣatriyas and others, however, if they are incapable of paying the fine, the teacher Vijñāneśvara states that they should be made to perform the duties appropriate to their respective castes, or be subjected to fetters, imprisonment, and so forth. Nārada says:

He who, having caused others to hear [the testimony], then denies his status as a witness, should be punished most severely; for he is one intent on perjury. [59] Having caused others to hear the testimony—having made others know, "I am a witness here"—if, when the witness has delivered his deposition, he should fabricate a pretext such as greed for the defendant's side, and if within seven days the witness suffers from a disease or other affliction resulting from that [falsehood], then he is to be punished for being a false witness. Otherwise, however, the defendant alone is at fault; thus says Manu (8.108).
If, within seven days of the witness having given his testimony,
disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman should befall him, he shall be compelled to pay the debt and a fine.

The mention of "taking a loan" (*rṇagrahaṇa*) is merely an illustration for the entire scope of legal disputes. Kātyāyana states (406): "Those who, having stated the matter as it truly is before witnesses, later state it otherwise out of greed or other motives, shall be punished.
This means that those who speak falsely after having spoken are to be punished for engaging in verbal deception.

Kātyāyana further states (408) regarding the falsity of the former witnesses when the testimony has been given by witnesses and the opposing party establishes the contrary fact through witnesses of superior quality or double the number: "In such a case, the former witnesses are considered false witnesses (*kūṭasākṣin*)."
When the matter to be proven has indeed been established by witnesses for the plaintiff,
if the defendant then proves the matter otherwise;

The syntactical connection is: "There may be many witnesses from that same family for that legal matter. The term "from that family" (*kulīnaiḥ*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other qualities as well. Yājñavalkya (2.80) states:
"Even when the testimony has been given by the witnesses, if there are others who possess superior qualities..."
Or if they should state it otherwise as double, the former witnesses would be considered fraudulent.
And this presentation of perverted testimony is to be understood as occurring prior to the conclusion of the legal proceeding;
for once the case has been decided, even documentary evidence or witnesses would be fruitless if they were not previously presented.

As it has been stated by Nārada (Vyavahāramātṛkā, 1.62–63): "Just as the qualities of the rainy season are fruitless for crops that have already ripened, so too is evidence useless for those whose legal proceedings have already been settled. Regarding the specific punishments for false witnesses when their particular motives, such as greed, are known, Manu says (8.119–124):
[60] Testimony is declared to be false through greed, delusion, fear, friendship, desire, anger, as well as through ignorance and childishness.
I shall now declare, in due order, the specific punishments for anyone who gives false testimony in place of any one of these.
For taking [something] out of greed, one should be fined a thousand; for out of delusion, the first *sāhasa* fine;
for out of fear, two middle *sāhasa* fines; and for out of friendship, four times the first *sāhasa*.
From desire it is said to be tenfold; from anger, three times more than that;
from ignorance, two full hundredfold; and from childishness, indeed a hundredfold.
The wise have declared these punishments for those who give false testimony,
in order to ensure that dharma does not deviate and to restrain unrighteousness.
A righteous king, having punished them with a fine, shall banish members of the three [lower] castes who give false testimony, but he shall only exile a Brāhmaṇa.

The teacher Vijñāneśvara explains that *lobha* is the desire for wealth, *moha* is false knowledge, *maitrī* is an excess of affection, and *kāma* is the longing for sexual union with women. In the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, *ajñāna* is defined as indistinct knowledge; it is the temporary delusion of the moment. Southern scholars such as Vijñāneśvara and others maintain that *bālabhāva* is the absence of the arising of specialized knowledge. As for the statement found in Eastern treatises such as the *Ratnākara*—that *bālabhāva* is intoxication resulting from the onset of youth—that is incorrect, because it would render the prescription of a lesser fine in comparison to other causes logically untenable, as it would imply a mere hundred-fold [reduction] due to childishness alone. In this context, copper *paṇas* are to be understood as the objects of the numbers "thousand" and so forth. The first *sāhasa* (fine) is two hundred and fifty *paṇas*; the middle *sāhasa* is five hundred *paṇas*.
"Two hundred and fifty *paṇas* are declared to be the first *sāhasa*;

five [hundred] are to be known as the middle; and a thousand shall be the highest," according to the statement of Manu (8.139). By changing the word "five" (*pañca*) to "five hundred" (*pañca śatāni*), the word "hundred" (*śata*) is to be supplied. However, Yājñavalkya (1.366) has stated that their measure is slightly more than this.
"A fine of eighty-five thousand is the highest amercement;
half of that is declared the middle, and half of that is remembered as the lowest. Thus it is said.

The settlement of these two cases is according to the degree of their respective offenses. "Two middle [fines] for fear" means that for false testimony caused by fear, the fine is double the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*). "The first fourfold" refers to the first amercement (*prathama-sāhasa*) mentioned by Manu, meaning four times one thousand *paṇas*. "The highest threefold" means the highest [fine], which is the middle amercement, tripled—that is, fifteen hundred. The meaning of the word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "one should banish the Brāhmaṇa, but not punish him" is as follows: as for the one who...
The forger and the false witness are each to be punished separately;
the fine shall be double the amount in dispute, and a Brāhmaṇa is ordained to be banished.

Thus, the double fine mentioned by Yājñavalkya (2.81) is to be understood as applicable when the specific motive, such as greed, is not known. One who makes witnesses false through the giving of wealth and other means is a "false-maker" (*kūṭakṛt*). A man who speaks thus regarding matters of dharma, even if he knows otherwise, does not fall from the heavenly world; they call that the speech of the gods.

Regarding the statement of truth (*ṛtoktau*) or the speaking of truth (*satyoktau*): the meaning is that where there would be the killing of a *śūdra* or others due to the deposition of truth in cases such as a charge of suspicion, one should speak untruth. However, Gautama states that where the killing of a thief or another highly censurable person would occur through the speaking of truth, untruth should not be spoken: "There is no fault in speaking untruth if one's livelihood depends upon it, but not if it is for the livelihood of a more wicked person" (GDh 13.24–25). But where the death of either the plaintiff or the defendant would result from the speaking of truth, even then nothing should be said. If he does not relinquish his position without the king’s command, then the witnesses must be declared non-witnesses because of their mutually contradictory statements; and if even that is impossible, then truth alone must be spoken.
