Regarding the fault of death incurred by speaking the truth, the preceptor Vijñāneśvara has stated that the prescribed expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed. Yājñavalkya (2.83) declares this expiation for the speaking of untruth specifically for the twice-born (*dvijāti*).

"The members of the court, vehicles, weapons, cows, seeds, and gold;
the feet of deities and ancestors, and [images of] meritorious deeds."

In cases where it is possible to bring charges against them, he may touch the heads of his sons, his wives, and likewise his friends; or else, he may undergo the ordeal of drinking from the royal vessel.
Thus these oaths have been proclaimed by Manu for minor matters. Thus [it is said].

It is true that those oaths, such as touching the assembly members and so forth, serve as causes for a determination occurring at a later time; however, since it is here intended to speak of *divyas* (ordeals) as causes for an immediate determination, and since that quality belongs only to the *ghaṭa* (water ordeal) and others, the statement that there are nine *divyas* is not inconsistent. Although the *kośa* (sacramental oath) is also a type of oath, its inclusion among the *ghaṭa* and others is due to the similarity of being subject to "great charges" (*mahābhiyoga*) and the similarity of being subject to "charges made with firm resolve" (*sāvaṣṭambhābhiyoga*). Yājñavalkya states (2.95–96) for the purpose of establishing the rule that the *ghaṭa* and other ordeals are to be employed in cases of great charges and charges made with firm resolve, but not in cases of charges based on mere suspicion (*śaṅkābhiyoga*).
The balance, fire, water, poison, and the sacred ordeal (kośa) are the divine ordeals used here for the sake of purification;
these are employed in cases of serious accusation when the accuser has placed his head upon the stake.
Or, by mutual consent, one party may pay [the fine] and the other may accept the "head" (*śiras*).

The term *śīrṣakastha* means that the penalty, which is the cause of defeat, resides there; the meaning is that he becomes the bearer of the aforementioned penalty. By "consent" (*rucyā*), meaning by desire, either one of the two—the plaintiff or the defendant—may act. The other shall "accept the head," meaning he shall take upon himself the penalty. In this statement, the mention of the *kośa* (oath or ordeal) is for the purpose of establishing its applicability to a case involving a defiant accusation, and not for the purpose of excluding its applicability to a case involving a mere suspicion.
One should point out jars and the like for those intent on defiance;
and in cases of suspicion, one should employ rice and a treasury.

Thus, because the Grandfather (Bṛhaspati) has prescribed the application [of ordeals] as being subject to charges based on suspicion (*śaṅkābhiyoga*), "avaṣṭambha" refers to one who is under oath (*śīrṣastha*). He (the same author) also states that in some cases, the balance and other ordeals may be used even for charges based on suspicion (YDh 2.96): "One may administer them even without an oath (*śīrṣaka*) in cases of treason against the king or in mortal sins (*pātaka*). This means even without an oath, and even in the absence of a plaintiff who would otherwise be liable for the punishment resulting from defeat, in cases such as the murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and so forth. Kātyāyana also says: (412)
For those suspected by kings, for those pointed out by bandits,
and for those intent on proving their own purity, the divine ordeal should be administered, provided it does not involve the head.

In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "O King, in cases of false accusation regarding another's wife, in theft, in approaching women who should not be approached, in those condemned for mortal sins (mahāpātaka), and in acts of violence, the ordeal shall be administered."
When a dispute has arisen and an accusation of infamy has been established,
the lord of the earth shall first administer the ordeal upon that very person who initiated it.
In cases of violating another's wife where there are many disputants,
the ordeal of the headless man (śirohīna) shall be employed for the sake of one's own purification.

In cases of misconduct, such as the accusation of adultery with another's wife; in disputes concerning the payment of debts and the like; and in cases of defamation—where "defamation" refers to slander, and the phrase "in the case of violating another’s wife" is an elliptical expression that includes [offenses against] honor and so forth—Viṣṇu (9.22) states: "In treason against the king and in acts of violence, [the ordeal may be performed] even without the application of the *śīrṣa* [or *śiras*].
Pitāmaha, however, specifies the scope for the *taṇḍula* (rice-grain) ordeal.

In cases of theft, however, rice is to be administered as the ordeal, and not otherwise; this is the settled rule. "Otherwise" refers to cases such as adultery with women, but not to the denial of a gift (*dattāpahnavah*). For in that latter case, the administration of the rice ordeal is prescribed by the forthcoming statement of Kātyāyana (verse 420): "In that case, rice is used for half of that [the former] half. This, moreover, should be understood to apply when there is suspicion of a minor theft. But when there is suspicion of a major theft, it is stated:
"For those accused on suspicion of theft, the ordeal of the heated metal ball (*taptamāṣa*) is ordained."

This is because the procedure for the heated gold coin (*taptamāṣa*) is prescribed by that very same authority. Kātyāyana states the scope of the ordeal by sacred libation (*kośa*): "In cases of suspicion, the establishment of trust, partition among heirs, and when one is the performer of a series of transactions, one should always cause the ordeal by sacred libation to be administered."
Regarding the agency in a collection of actions— that is, performing a single action collectively— the Grandfather (Brahmā) has said:
"In matters of trust, in all types of suspicion, and likewise in the business of making peace,
the ordeal by sacred libation (*kośa*) must always be administered for the sake of purity of mind."
Having carefully considered the relative value of the property and other factors, a divine ordeal should be administered accordingly; thus says Bṛhaspati:
"In matters such as debts where there is mutual disagreement, the ordeal should be assigned according to the quantity of the property and likewise in consideration of the person involved."

The phrase "divine procedure" (*daivikī kriyā*) is to be supplied [to the verse]. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), disputes concerning immovable property (*sthāvara*) are also included here. As for the statement: "In disputes concerning immovable property, one should avoid divine ordeals" (Kāt. 240), its purpose is simply to indicate that an ordeal should not be employed when documentary evidence (*likhita*) and other such means exist.

If it is argued: "But even in disputes over debts and the like, an ordeal is certainly not resorted to when human means of proof (*mānuṣapramāṇa*) exist; therefore, this specific rule would be redundant," [the response is as follows:]...

It is said: In disputes concerning debts and the like, when the plaintiff has presented witnesses and the defendant, accepting the penalty for defeat, says, "I shall undergo an ordeal," then—even though witnesses exist—the possibility of suspicion regarding their defects arises; whereas in the case of an ordeal, there is no suspicion of defect. Thus it is said: "In that case, *dharma* (truth/righteousness) resides in truth, but judicial procedure (*vyavahāra*) resides in witnesses. When a matter is to be settled by divine means, one should not employ human evidence, nor should one employ written documents. [82]

The divine ordeal (*divya*) is to be accepted based on the words of Nārada. Similarly, in a dispute concerning immovable property (*sthāvara*), even if the defendant, in the presence of human means of proof (*mānuṣapramāṇa*), resorts to a divine ordeal after first accepting the penalty, this statement is intended to mean that the divine ordeal should not be accepted in such a case; it does not mean that a divine ordeal is never to be accepted in a dispute over immovable property, for if there were no written documents, neighbors, or other evidence, it would follow that the dispute could never be decided. Although we have already stated this previously, it is mentioned again here to reinforce the point established by the teacher Vijñāneśvara and others. Viṣṇu also states (9.1–3) that when administering a divine ordeal, one must take into account the relative value of the property involved and other such factors.
Now, regarding the performance of oaths (*samayakriyā*): in cases of treason or violent crimes, it may be administered at will; in cases of deposits or theft, it depends on the value of the object.

Thus, in disputes concerning cloth and similar items, the measure of the raw material from which they were made should be taken. Bṛhaspati states the specific ordeals according to the scale of the value of the property: poison [is used] when a thousand [paṇas] have been stolen, and fire when three-quarters of a thousand have been stolen.
Water should always be provided at one-third [of the distance], and a water-jar should be placed at the halfway point.
In a lawsuit involving four hundred [paṇas], the ordeal of the heated metal ball (taptamāṣaka) must be administered;
for three hundred, rice grains (taṇḍula) are to be given; and for half of that [two hundred], the ordeal of the sacred water (kośa) is prescribed.
When a hundred [panas] have been taken and denied, the means of purification according to dharma must be administered;
for a cow-thief, the immediate licking of a plowshare [red-hot with fire] must be imposed.
This number is prescribed for those of inferior quality; it is remembered as double for those of middling quality, and fourfold for those of superior quality—thus should it be calculated by experts.

The purification of the *dharma* is the purification by means of the divine ordeal born of *dharma*. For those of low status, it is determined by their birth, qualities, and conduct; for those of middling and superior status, it is likewise by those same criteria.

As for the statement of Yājñavalkya (YDh 2.99), "One should not administer the plowshare, nor the balance, nor the poison for less than a thousand," that refers to persons of middling status. The teacher Vijñāneśvara explains that "a thousand" means a thousand *paṇas*. As for [the verse]:
[83] One should administer a water-pot for a thousand [palas], likewise iron for half a thousand;
for half of that, water is prescribed, and for half of that, poison is traditionally taught.

Thus, regarding even a small charge, the preceptor Vijñāneśvara maintains that Pitāmaha’s statement prescribing the ordeal by poison or divine test applies specifically to cases where the theft of a particular object results in loss of caste (*pātitya*). Regarding the denial of what was given, Kātyāyana states (vv. 416–420): "Where there is a denial of what was given, one should determine the means of proof.
In cases of theft or violence, one should cause a divine test to be administered even when the matter is of small value."
Having ascertained the measure of all the substances, one should fashion the gold;
then, endowed with the proper measure of gold, one should employ that divine [mantra].
Having ascertained the number of gold pieces, it is traditionally taught that one should administer poison in the event of a loss of one hundred;
however, in the event of a loss of eighty, one should certainly not administer fire.
In the case of a loss of sixty [paṇas], water is to be known as the ordeal; for a loss of forty, indeed, the balance;
but for a loss of twenty or ten, the drinking of holy water (kośapāna) is prescribed.
Or, upon the destruction of more than five [vārāha measures], rice is prescribed for half of that half;
furthermore, when half of that half is destroyed, worldly rites are ordained.

And here, the word *suvarṇa* refers to a specific measure stated as sixteen *māṣas*. Regarding "the loss of twenty or ten": the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* states that this means the loss of thirty. "Worldly transactions" refers to such things as [threats] during a denial: "There shall be an eightfold loss of goods for you. As for the legal injunction: "When a hundred has been taken and denied, it must be paid."

Thus, regarding the denial of a hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*, this procedure for divine ordeal (*divya*) prescribed by Manu pertains to the case of an inferior person; or rather, it should be understood as pertaining to cases where the denial of a particular object involves great sin. Therefore, there is no contradiction [with other texts]. Bṛhaspati states that the measurements mentioned by Manu regarding both the divine ordeal and the fine are to be adopted:
"The enumeration [of fines] was set forth by Manu as being based on the *raśmi* and the *rajas*;
that enumeration, ending with the *kārṣāpaṇa*, is to be applied in the divine ordeal as well as in judicial punishment."
[84] Number, measure, and the sequence beginning with the *raśmi* and *rajas*, starting from the *trasareṇu*, are established in the Vinaya and the legal codes (*daṇḍa*).
Manu demonstrates that sequence of measures, beginning with the *trasareṇu*, by means of formal propositions (8.131–137):
"Those designations which are well-known on earth for the sake of worldly transaction..."
I shall explain those [measures] for copper, silver, and gold in their entirety.
The minute particle of dust that is seen when the sun shines through a lattice opening— that first measure is called a *trasareṇu*.
Eight *trasareṇus* should be known as one *likṣā* in measurement;
three of those [likṣās] are a *rājasarṣapa*, and three of those [rājasarṣapas] are a *gaurasarṣapa*.
Six mustard seeds make one medium-sized barleycorn; three barleycorns make one *kṛṣṇala*;
five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*; and sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*.
Four suvarṇas make one pala; ten palas make one dharaṇa.
Two kṛṣṇalas weighed together are to be known as one silver māṣaka.
Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* shall be one *purāṇa*;
ten *dharaṇas* of silver should be known as one *śatamāna*.
"A *niṣka* made of four *suvarṇas* should be known by its measure;
a *kārṣāpaṇa*, however, is to be known as a copper coin weighing one *kārṣika*. Thus it is said.

In this context, regarding the phrase "of copper, silver, and gold," the words *tāmra* and *rūpya* are placed first because they have fewer syllables (*alpāctvāt*), and not for the purpose of indicating their sequence. The section ending with "ten *dharaṇas* are a *pala*" defines the measurement of gold; the section ending with "four *suvarṇas* are a *niṣka*" defines the measurement of silver; and by the remainder, the measurement of copper is defined. That minute particle of dust which is seen when a sunbeam enters through a lattice window is known as a *trasareṇu*. Eight *trasareṇus* make one *likṣā*; three *likṣās* make one *rājasarṣapa*; three *rājasarṣapas* make one *gaurasarṣapa*; six *gaurasarṣapas* make a middle-sized barley grain (*madhyamo yavaḥ*)—neither too large nor too small. Thus, the measurement of the middle-sized barley grain has been stated by the teacher Vijñāneśvara. However, in the *Manusmṛti-bhāṣya*, it is said that the word "middle" (*madhya*) is merely for the purpose of completing the verse. Three barley grains make one *kṛṣṇala*; eight *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*; sixteen *māṣas* make one *suvarṇa*; four *suvarṇas* make one *pala*; ten *palas* make one *dharaṇa*. Two *kṛṣṇalas* constitute the weight of a *rūpya*.

Sixteen silver *māṣas* constitute a *dharaṇa* of silver; its other name is *purāṇa*. Ten silver *dharaṇas* constitute a silver *śatamāna*; it also has the designation of a silver *pala*, for ten *dharaṇas* indeed make one *pala* and one *śatamāna*.

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Yājñavalkya (1.365): one *rājaniṣka* is equal to the four *suvarṇas* mentioned previously. A *kārṣika*—meaning measured by a *karṣa*—is to be understood as a copper coin (*tāmrika*) made of copper, and it is also to be understood as a *kārṣāpaṇa*; the word "and" (*ca*) is to be supplied [to connect these meanings]. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya has shown another designation for it, namely *paṇa*. Bṛhaspati also states: "A *niṣka* consists of four *suvarṇas*; a *kārṣika* is a copper *paṇa*.
A *kārṣika paṇa* is to be known as a stamped coin (*mudrā*) made from a *karṣa* of copper."

A *karṣa* is a fourth part of a *pala*; for Amarasimha states: "Sixteen of those [māṣas] are a *karṣa*, which is not feminine; four *karṣas* are a *pala*. The meaning is that sixteen of those *māṣas* are called a *karṣa*. By this, it is understood that the words *akṣa* and *karṣa* denote a measure of gold (*suvarṇa*). Alternatively, a *pala* is measured as five *suvarṇas*, for it is proclaimed: "A *pala* is said to be four or even five *suvarṇas*."
Thus, according to the statement of Yājñavalkya (YDh 1.364), a quarter of that [kārṣāpaṇa] consists of twenty māṣas; a kārṣāpaṇa is measured by that amount. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states:
"A twentieth part of a kārṣāpaṇa should be known as a māṣa;
a fourth part of both a māṣaka and a paṇa is a kākiṇī."
Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 334) states the divine ordeals according to the established distinction of eligibility beginning with the Brāhmaṇas:
"The *dhaṭa* ordeal is to be given to a Brāhmaṇa; the fire ordeal to a Kṣatriya;
water is to be given to a Vaiśya; and poison alone to a Śūdra."
[86] The treasury of all [the castes] has been declared by the wise to be common;
however, for a Brāhmaṇa, ordeal by poison is excluded, while for all others, the balance is prescribed.
Yājñavalkya (2.98):
"The balance [is prescribed] for women, children, the elderly, the blind, the lame, Brāhmaṇas, and the sick.
As for that which...
If dharma is indeed taken into account, the divine ordeal shall not be administered to those who observe vows, those who are severely afflicted, the diseased, ascetics, or women.
Thus, regarding the statement of Nārada (*Ṛṇādāna* 256), the venerable Vidyāraṇya in his *Mādhavīya* has stated that it pertains to the cases of fire and water. Pitāmaha says:
"The purification by ordeal (*kośa*) is prescribed for all castes;
all these [ordeals] apply to everyone, except for the Brāhmaṇa, in the case of poison."
Kātyāyana (423): One should cause those twice-born men who are cattle-herders, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, or usurers to be treated like Śūdras.
In the *Kālikāpurāṇa*:
"A *māṣaka* of refined gold (*taptahema*) should always be given for each unit of the lowest *varṇa*.
The author of the *Kṛtyakalpataru* explains that "the end of the *varṇas*" refers to the lowest *varṇa*. Nārada (*Ṛṇādāna* 255, 313–315): [text follows]
One should always examine eunuchs, men devoid of strength, those afflicted on all sides, children, the elderly, the sick, and women by means of the water-pot.
For women, however, poison is not prescribed, nor is water;
one should examine their inner nature through the use of a jar, a chest, and other such means.

For those who are afflicted, purification by water is not prescribed; for those suffering from bile disorders, poison is not used; and for those with vitiligo, blindness, deformed nails, and the like, cauterization by fire is not ordained.
Women, children, those who are ill, the elderly, and men who are weak should not be made to bathe by those who are experts in the Dharmaśāstras.
One should not submerge those who are lacking in vitality, afflicted by disease, or distressed in water;
for they are known to possess very little life-force and would die instantly while drowning.
Even when these have arrived for an ordeal of daring, one must not submerge them in water,
nor cause them to carry fire, nor purify them by means of poison.
Hārīta states: One should avoid fire for those suffering from leprosy, water for those with asthma and coughing,
and one should always strictly avoid poison for those with an excess of pitta and kapha.

Water [should not be drunk] by those afflicted with phlegm, those who are ill, the timid, those suffering from asthma or cough, those who subsist on water, and during the seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira. Kātyāyana (424): [Water should not be drunk] by those afflicted with phlegm, the ill, the timid, those suffering from asthma or cough, those who subsist on water, and during the seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira.
One should never give fire to metalworkers, water to those who subsist on water,
nor poison to those who know the application of mantras.
One should always avoid divine [substances] that cause an increase in the bodily constituents;
one should not prescribe rice for a patient observing a vow who suffers from diseases of the mouth.
[Regarding one] observing a vow, such as being established in the discipline of the milk-vow and so forth— Pitāmaha says:
"The wise should not administer an ordeal to those addicted to liquor or women, nor to gamblers, nor likewise to those who follow the conduct of atheists."
Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 332):

One should avoid administering an ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) in cases involving a grave offense, one devoid of dharma, an ungrateful person, a eunuch, a contemptible person, an atheist, or one whose guilt has already been proven.
Kātyāyana (427–430):
[The property] of those who have killed their mother, father, a twice-born, a guru, an elder, a woman, or a child;
of those guilty of the great sins (mahāpātaka); and especially of atheists—[is forfeit].
Of those wearing sectarian marks, of women, of those skilled in the practice of mantras and yoga,
and of those born of mixed castes who are intent on the habitual practice of evil.
In these very cases of accusation, which are indeed blameworthy, a king devoted to righteousness should never, even with effort, administer an ordeal.
[88] Those virtuous persons appointed by these very [officials] deserve divine ordeals. Where there are no virtuous persons, one should be cleared by means of one's own men.

The meaning is that the king ought to provide a divine ordeal for the virtuous; this is the remainder [of the sense]. To further strengthen the point that the ordeal should be administered through these proxies, the same author (Kātyāyana, 431–32) says again:
"Bhṛgu states that a divine ordeal must not be given to those guilty of mortal sins, especially to atheists, nor to one who is devoted to the habitual practice of sin."
In those cases where divine ordeals are strictly prohibited for sinful acts, a man should have them performed by virtuous persons; he must not abandon one who has been falsely accused.

"Should deliver" means he should purify. The meaning is that one should not abandon an accused person without having them undergo purification through a representative. He states another method in the same work (Kāt 433): "For those who are untouchable, for low-caste slaves, for Mlecchas, for evildoers, and for those born of inverse unions, there is no judicial determination by the king."
One should point to those well-known divine [omens] when there is doubt regarding them.

It is stated in the *Smṛticandrikā* that this is to be understood as applying when virtuous persons (*sādhu*) appointed for the task are unavailable. He (the same author) also permits a substitute (*pratinidhi*) in the event that even virtuous persons lack the capacity:
"But in case of conflict with time or place, one should determine what is appropriate."
One should cause another to perform the divine ordeal; such is the rule in the case of the opposite situation.

One should cause [the ordeal] to be performed or cause it to be removed. In the opposite case, there is an absence of efficacy. Regarding specific times, Pitāmaha states the distinction for divine ordeals:
"Caitra, Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise Vaiśākha—these are the common months, not incompatible with divine ordeals."
The Dhaṭa ordeal is declared suitable for all seasons, but one should avoid it when the wind blows;
the Agni ordeal is proclaimed for the cold, winter, and rainy seasons.
In autumn and summer, however, water [is the means of proof]; in early winter and late winter, poison [is used]. Nārada says:
"The ordeal by oath (kośa) may be administered at all times, while the balance (tulā) may be used throughout the year."

[89] Viṣṇu (9.25–30): Fire must not be administered to those suffering from leprosy, the infirm, or blacksmiths during the autumn and summer. Poison must not be administered to those suffering from leprosy or bilious disorders, nor to Brāhmaṇas, during the rainy season. Water must not be administered to those of phlegmatic constitution, those afflicted by disease, the timid, those suffering from dyspnea or cough, those who live by water, or during the winter and early spring. Thus it is said.

The prohibition regarding the winter season here refers exclusively to the month of Pauṣa, and not to Mārgaśīrṣa as well; for in the previously cited statement of Pitāmaha, "Caitra and Mārgaśīrṣa," it is declared that Mārgaśīrṣa is common to all divine ordeals. Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 259):
"There should be no purification by water during the cold season, nor purification by fire during the heat;
one should not administer poison during the rainy season, nor likewise a balance scale in a strong wind."

Neither in the afternoon, nor at twilight, nor ever at midday [should one perform the ordeal]. The prohibition regarding midday applies specifically to divine ordeals other than those involving water. For this very reason, Pitāmaha states:
"The fire-ordeal should take place in the forenoon, and the balance-ordeal should likewise be held in the forenoon."
At midday, however, water should be given by one who desires to understand the true nature of dharma.
"The purification by the [divine] vessel (kośa) is prescribed for the forenoon of the day;
however, at night, during the last watch, poison that has been well-cooled should be administered.

Although no specific rule regarding the days of the week for divine ordeals (*divya*) is heard in the texts, nevertheless, Master Vijñāneśvara stated that based on the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), the divine ordeals should be administered on Sundays. Pitāmaha describes the specific locations for the divine ordeals:
The balance-beam (dhaṭa) should always be placed facing east, kept steady, in a clean location—
either in the place of Indra, in an assembly hall, at the king’s gate, or at a crossroads.

The mention of the *dhaṭa* ordeal is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of other divine ordeals as well; likewise, the mention of the "place of Indra" (*indrasthāna*) is an elliptical indication of other shrines of well-known deities. For this very reason, after introducing the category of divine ordeals in general, Nārada says (Ṛṇādāna 265):
"In the assembly hall, at the gate of the royal palace, in a temple, or in a public square.
Kātyāyana states the specific application of the place of Indra and other such locations according to particular circumstances:

[90] One should employ this at the royal gate for men who have been accused in the abode of Indra, those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin), and those who have engaged in treason against the king.
"For those born of inverse unions (prātilomya), the ordeal should be administered at a crossroads;
for other matters, however, the wise know it should be conducted in the midst of the court.

Regarding the administration of an ordeal by disregarding the prescribed place, time, and so forth, Nārada states that such an act results in the failure of the legal purpose: * *vihitadeśakālādyanādareṇa divyadāne tathā kṛtasyārthavyabhicāritām āha nāradaḥ* ||* [The wise] declare that when an ordeal is administered by disregarding the prescribed place, time, and other requirements, it thus results in the failure of the legal purpose.
Gifts given at an improper place or time, and those bestowed while residing abroad,
undoubtedly cause deviation from the true purpose of wealth in this world.

"Vāsaḥ" means a dwelling place; "outside of that" (vāsād bahiḥkṛtāni) means performed in uninhabited regions—this is the meaning. By this, it is stated that the ordeal must be administered only in the presence of people. This point has also been shown by Pitāmaha: "The king, or his appointed official, shall cause the ordeal to be administered in person before learned Brāhmaṇas and likewise before the subjects."
The Grandfather (Brahmā) has declared the procedure common to all divine [ordeals]:
"Then the judge, who knows the Dharma, facing east and with palms joined in reverence, shall invoke the gods according to this rite. Thus should he speak.
Come, come, O Blessed One, O Dharma; enter into this divine [image], together with the world-protectors and the hosts of Vasus, Ādityas, and Maruts.

Having invoked Dharma into the balance, one should subsequently assign the limbs [of the deity]. This refers to the procurement of all materials necessary for the ordeal; here, the mention of "taking hold of the balance" (*dhaṭagrahaṇa*) is an elliptical expression for all ordeals. Since these rites—beginning with the invocation of the deity—are common to all ordeals, one should apply this entire procedure of mantras to every type of ordeal.
And in the same manner, one should likewise perform the invocation of the deities.

Because it has been stated by that very [author]: "The mantra, however, begins with 'the sun and the moon' and so forth," as will be shown later. He himself describes the method for the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the deities of the limbs:
"Having established Indra in the east, likewise Yama (the Lord of the Dead) in the south, Varuṇa in the western quarter, and Kubera in the north."
And one should place the world-protectors, beginning with Agni, in the corner regions:
Indra is yellow, Yama is dark, Varuṇa has the luster of crystal,
Kubera is gold-colored, and Agni is also gold-colored.
In the same way, Nirṛti is dark, and Vāyu is praised as smoky;
Īśāna, however, should be red—one should meditate upon these in this sequence.
On the right side of Indra, the wise one should invoke the Vasus:
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, and Anala.
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
Between Deveśa and Īśāna is the course of the Ādityas:
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga.
Indra, Vivasvat, and Pūṣan; Parjanya is remembered as the tenth;
then Tvaṣṭṛ, and then Viṣṇu, who is not the youngest, though born last.
Thus these twelve Ādityas have been proclaimed by their names;
one should know that the abode of the Rudras is in the western part of Agni.
Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, and the highly illustrious Giriśa; Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and Aparājita.
Bhuvanādhīśvara, Kapālī, Viśāmpati,
Sthāṇu, and the lord Bhava— these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
One should designate the station of the Mothers (Mātṛsthāna) between the Lord of the Dead (Preteśa) and the Rākṣasa;
[namely] Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā, accompanied by her hosts, are situated in the northern part of Nairṛti; they know that to be the abode of Gaṇeśa.
In the northern region of Varuṇa, the abode of the Maruts is said to be located;
[the names of the Maruts are] Gaganas, Sparśanas, Vāyu, Anila, and likewise Māruta.
[92] Prāṇa, Prāṇeśa, Jīva, and the eight Maruts are proclaimed;
the wise man should invoke Durgā on the northern side of the balance.

The wise know that the worship of these deities is performed by their own names, ending with ornaments and garments; then, having offered [the gifts] for Dharma, one should present the *arghya* and other offerings in due order.
Thereafter, one should prepare the offerings for the limbs (aṅgas), beginning with the arghya and ending with ornaments;
then one should perform the service consisting of scents and so forth, ending with the food offering (naivedya).
Likewise, the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed in the four directions by those who have mastered the Vedas,
using clarified butter, sacrificial offerings, and fuel-sticks as the means for the oblation.
One should perform the oblation with the Sāvitrī mantra and the Praṇava, ending with *svāhā*.

The meaning is that one should recite the Gāyatrī preceded by the Praṇava, and then again recite the Praṇava ending with the utterance of *svāhā* and offer it. Fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked rice (*caru*) should each be offered one hundred and eight times;
for where no specific number is mentioned, one hundred and eight is traditionally prescribed.

Thus it is from the Smṛti. He (the same author) states what must be done immediately after the oblation: "Whatever matter the accused may have been charged with, having written that upon a leaf together with this mantra, that document should be placed upon his head."
And the mantra:
"The sun and the moon, wind and fire, heaven, earth, water, the heart, and Yama."
"Day and night, and both twilights, as well as Dharma, know the conduct of a man. (Mahābhārata, Ādiparvan 74.30)
All of this must be performed by the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*) preceded by observances such as fasting. And so says Nārada:
"Then the presiding judge shall be a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, endowed with learning and good conduct, tranquil in mind, and free from envy."
Truthful to his word, pure, skillful, and devoted to the welfare of all living beings,
he has fasted, wears wet clothes, and has cleansed his teeth.
"Having performed the worship of all the deities according to the prescribed rule," thus [it is said].
Yājñavalkya (2.97) states the fasting and other requirements for the performer of the divine rite:
"Having summoned one who has fasted and bathed with his clothes on at sunrise..."
One should cause all the divine ordeals to be performed in the presence of the king and the Brahmins.
The Grandfather [Brahmā] also said:
"To one who has fasted for one night or three nights,
who is pure and wears wet clothes, divine [offerings] should always be given."

These two options—the three-night and the one-night periods—should be understood as being established according to the capacity or incapacity [of the accused]. After the performance of the ordeal, Pitāmaha describes the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the reward for the king who causes the ordeal to be performed according to the prescribed rule:
"The king, surrounded by virtuous men, should honor this purification;
he should satisfy the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the family priest (*purohita*), and the teachers (*ācārya*) with sacrificial fees."
Having caused this to be done, the king, after enjoying delightful pleasures,
attains great fame and is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
Thus ends the determination of the divine ordeal (*divya-mātṛkā*) in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* [composed by] the illustrious Kodaṇḍa-Paraśurāma. Section 7.

**Possible reading of the defective text:** Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Exposition of Ordeals (*divyamātṛkānirūpaṇam*), in the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*, composed by Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva, son of Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "The Illustrious Kodaṇḍa-Paraśurāma."
Now, the procedure for the ordeal by balance (*dhaṭavidhi*). Regarding this, Pitāmaha states:
"One should have a large, elevated, and bright hall for the balance constructed."
Wherever he stays, he shall not be harmed by dogs, outcasts, or crows.
The king should ensure that it is provided with door-bolts, guarded by attendants, supplied with water and other necessities, and never left empty.
The five seeds are rice and so forth. Regarding the wood for the balance, Nārada says (Ṛṇādāna 264–265):
"One should have it made of khadira wood there, free from wounds and devoid of white [sap];
or, in its absence, of śiṃśapā or śāla wood, provided they are without hollows."
Añjana, the heartwood of *tindukī*, *tiniśa*, red sandalwood (*raktacandana*),
*arjuna*, *tilaka*, *uśoka*, and *tiniśa*— red sandalwood being the reading in the *Mādhavīya*—
one should prepare such types of wood for the balance-beam (*dhaṭa*).

[94] *Śāṃśapa* means pertaining to the *śiṃśapā* tree; the substitution of the vowel *i* with *a* occurs according to the rule of Pāṇini (7.3.1), *devikā-śiṃśapā*. By the phrase "of such a kind," there is the inclusion of other sacrificial woods as well, such as *audumbara*, which possess sap. For this very reason, the Grandfather [Brahmā] said: "Having cut a sacrificial tree, like a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), preceded by the recitation of mantras..."
Having prostrated before the guardians of the world, the wise should prepare the scales.
When cutting down a tree, one should mutter the gentle mantra dedicated to the Vanaspati.

By the phrase "as with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), preceded by mantras," the application of the cutting mantras beginning with "O herb, protect him" (*oṣadhe trāyasvainam*, Vājasaṃhitā 4.1) and so forth is indicated. Regarding the *vānaspatya* [oblation], there is the mantra "O Lord of the Forest (*vanaspate*), grow with a hundred shoots" (*RV* 3.8.11). Some maintain that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the *saumya* and the *vānaspatya* offerings, based on the principle: "Mantras with identical purposes may be treated as optional alternatives" (*Jaimini Sūtra* 12.3.10). Others hold that there is a combination (*samuccaya*), because the word *ca* ("and"), which indicates conjunction, connects even separately with the term *vānaspatya*. The ellipsis "when the cutting has been performed" is to be supplied. Although the procedure for the *vānaspatya* is already established by the extension (*atideśa*) from the sacrificial post immediately following its cutting, this rule is stated again so that there may be no suspicion of the archetypal (*aupadeśika*) offering dedicated to Soma subverting the extended (*ātideśika*) one. Pitāmaha describes the method of constructing the balance-beam (*dhaṭa*) and its dimensions.
The balance-beam should be made four cubits long, and its two supports should be made likewise;
the distance between them should be two cubits, or indeed one and a half.

The two pillars named *tulādhāra* and *akṣa* are for the purpose of supporting the beam (*kāṣṭha*). They are likewise four cubits (*hasta*) in length. The interval—the middle space—is two cubits, or one and a half [cubits], which is two and a half cubits. The measurement of the beam (*akṣakāṣṭha*) has been indicated precisely by the description of the dimensions of the middle of the foot-pillars; therefore, it is not mentioned separately. Consequently, by considering the measurement of the intervening space, the beam should be made slightly longer than that. The author of the *Smṛticandrikā* states that the beam should be fashioned such that it does not protrude outward from the top region of the two foot-pillars. In this context, the statement that the foot-pillars are four cubits long should be understood as excluding the portion buried in the ground. For this very reason, Vyāsa stated:
"Two cubits are prescribed for the depth of the two *muṇḍakas*;
however, their measurement in terms of size is said to be six cubits. Thus [it is stated]. The *muṇḍakas* are the pillar-bases. This has also been stated by Pitāmaha:
"Two cubits [of earth] should be dug out for both feet as well. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the measure of a cubit is shown in another Smṛti:
"Eight horizontal barley-grains [in breadth], or three vertical rice-grains [in depth]."
The measure of a finger has been stated; a span (vittasti) consists of twelve fingers.
"Two *vitastis* make a *hasta*; four *hastas* make a *daṇḍa*;
two thousand of those [daṇḍas] make a *krośa*; and four of those [krośas] make a *yojana*. Thus it is said.
A *hasta* is two *vitastis*, meaning that a *hasta* consists of twenty-four *aṅgulas*. Regarding the balance scale (*tulā*), Pitāmaha states another specific distinction:
The balance-beam should be made square, firm, and straight;
likewise, rings should be carefully attached at the three locations.

The rings are made of iron. They are placed in three locations: at the two ends and in the middle. The mention of "rings" (kaṭaka) is intended as an illustration for other useful iron items such as pins and the like. Therefore, an iron loop should be provided in the middle of the axle-wood for the purpose of attaching the balance-beam. In this manner, other necessary iron parts should also be affixed in their respective places. Regarding the thickness of the supporting pillars and so forth, since no specific rule is recorded, it should be made to whatever extent ensures stability; or rather, the specific details should be understood from established custom. Having positioned the two supporting pillars facing east and west, the balance-beam should be made with its length oriented toward the north.

"One should place a man on the northern side and a stone on the southern"—according to this statement by Nārada which will be cited later (*R̥ṇādāna* 272). Having constructed two pillars for the feet situated in the north and south, the balance should be made with its beam pointing eastward; one should weigh the litigants on the western side and auspicious earth on the other.
This is because of the following statement by Pitāmaha: "Pitāmaha prescribes the arches and other features as integral parts of the balance: 'The two arches should likewise be made on both sides;
they should always be ten finger-breadths higher than the balance.'"
"Two supports should be made from the two arches, facing downwards;
they should be made of clay, connected by a cord, and touching the top of the balance-beam.
Thus Pitāmaha first describes the mounting of the balance-beam, which is necessary for the determination [of guilt].
Having suspended two loops on both sides,
one should arrange darbha grass with tips pointing eastward upon both loops.
In the western [scale] one should weigh the makers, and in the other, auspicious earth that is free from bricks,
ashes, stones, potsherds, and bones.

The mention here of the prohibition against using bricks and stones is for the purpose of ensuring they are not used in conjunction with clay; it is not intended to exclude them as optional alternatives, since Nārada has prescribed their use as well. Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 271–72): "Having firmly attached two sets of scales to the hooks of the balance-beam, one should place a man on one scale and a stone on the other."
One should place a man on the northern side and a stone on the southern side;
one should fill that pit with bricks, sand, and clods of earth.

Vijñāneśvara and others maintain that there is an option regarding the materials, such as clay, stone, or brick. Pitāmaha states that for the purpose of ensuring impartiality, the king should appoint examiners therein:
"Examiners skilled in weights and measures should be appointed—merchants, goldsmiths, and likewise bell-metal workers."
He himself states the method of examination:
"The balance-beam must always be made equal to its support by the examiners;
and water must be poured upon the beam by the learned."
That balance on which water does not drip is to be known as even.
It is "equal to the suspension" when it is level with two earthen suspensions hanging from the two arches. Nārada also says (Ṛṇādāna 273):
"At the first weighing, the measurement should be recorded by experts together."
It should be equal in measure to the two heads of the balance-beam, with the auspicious marks placed upon the archway.
[97] Pitāmaha states what must be done immediately after the weighing:
"Having first weighed the man and then having lowered him,
one should always cause the balance (dhaṭa) to be decorated with banners and flags."
Then, the knower of mantras should invoke the deities according to this rite,
accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments and drums, and with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.

The entire series of ritual acts common to all ordeals, beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the binding of the document upon the head of the litigant, has already been explained in detail. Regarding the specific offerings for the worship of the balance (*dhaṭapūjā*), Nārada says:
"One should first worship the balance with red perfumes, garlands, curds, cakes, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and so forth; thereafter, one should worship the remaining [deities]."
The remaining ones are Indra and the others. Pitāmaha states that immediately after the binding of the leaves, the judge shall address the balance:
"The knower of the scriptures, the judge, shall address the balance according to this rite;
'according to the rite' means with the mantra. And the knower of the scriptures refers to the judge. Furthermore, the mantra has been shown by him [Pitāmaha] himself:"
You, O Dhaṭa, were created by Brahmā for the purpose of testing the wicked-minded;
you are the embodiment of Dharma because of the letter *dha*, and you are the crookedness of men because of the letter *ṭa*.
Because you sustain that which is held [in being], you are therefore called Dharma;
you know the sins and the good deeds of all living beings.
O God, you alone know those things which human beings do not understand; this man, accused in a legal proceeding, desires purification.
Yājñavalkya also states the invocation of the balance for the person to be tested and the mantra to be recited therein (2.100–102):
"The accused, having mounted the balance, shall be attended by experts in weighing;
once he has been balanced with the counterweight, a mark shall be made, and he shall be lowered."
O Tula, you are the abode of truth, fashioned of old by the gods;
therefore, speak the truth, O auspicious one, and release me from my doubt.
"If I am a doer of evil, O Mother, then lead me downward;
if I am pure, lead me upward"—with these words, one should consecrate the balance.

"Resting on the balance" means having mounted the scale; "made level with the counterweight" means made even by means of a counterweight such as clay or other materials. Here, the verb *bhavati* refers to the activity of the agent who causes the action. Having drawn a line—that is, having made a mark for the sign of equality on the arch—the subject is understood from the appearance of the *kta* suffix in the word *avatāritaḥ* ("having been lowered") to be the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) immediately after the lowering. Then, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) should cause the accused, whose document is placed upon his head, to mount the balance again. And so says Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 276): "Then, having secured him with the oaths (*samaya*), he should cause him to mount the balance again."
Having placed the leaf upon his head in a windless place free from rain.

Having secured the weigher with oaths and bound him by solemn pledges, for Viṣṇu has shown these pledges: "Those worlds that are ordained for the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, and those worlds for the false witness—those same worlds shall belong to the weigher who holds the scale falsely. (10.9)
Furthermore, regarding the consecration at the time of mounting [the scales], Nārada says (Ṛṇādāna 278–279):
"You know the sins and the good deeds of all living beings;
you alone, O God, perceive those things which human beings do not know."
This man, accused in a legal dispute, is being weighed by you;
therefore, you ought to protect him, who has fallen into doubt, according to dharma.
Among gods, asuras, and humans, you excel through your truths;
O Blessed One, you are true to your word in discerning the auspicious and the inauspicious.
The sun and the moon, wind and fire, heaven, earth, water, and the heart; Yama,
day and night, and both twilights.
"And Dharma knows the conduct of a man.
Thus [it is said]. Pitāmaha states what must be done immediately after the re-installation:
"An eminent Brāhmaṇa who is an astrologer should perform the examination of the time."
These five should be understood as deficient by those skilled in the examination of time.
The king should appoint as witnesses the best of Brahmins, who speak of matters exactly as they have seen them, who are wise, pure, and free from greed.
At that time, all the witnesses declare the purity or impurity before the king.
A *prāṇa* is a period of time measured by the utterance of ten long syllables (*gurvakṣara*). Six *prāṇas* constitute a *vināḍikā*. Likewise, another *Smṛti* states:
"A *prāṇa* consists of ten long syllables; six *prāṇas* shall be one *vināḍikā*."
In the Viṣṇudharmottara as well: "A measure equal to a short syllable is proclaimed to be a nimeṣa;
a time more subtle than this cannot be perceived, O best of the Bhrigus."
Two *nimeṣas* should be known as one *truṭi*; ten *truṭis* are remembered as one *prāṇa*.
"Six breaths constitute one *vināḍikā*, and sixty of those are known as a *nāḍikā*;
sixty of those are always proclaimed to be a day and night (*ahorātra*).
Thus [it is said]. Nārada states the means for determining purity and impurity (*Ṛṇādāna* 283):
If, when weighed, it increases, that man will be purified, without a doubt;
but if it remains equal or decreases, he would not be purified.
It would increase if it went upward; if diminishing, it would go downward. Vyāsa says:
One who goes downward is not purified, whereas one who goes upward is purified. For there can be no purity through mere association; this is declared to be true purification.
Bṛhaspati says: If one accused in a case is weighed in a jar and found to be lighter, he shall suffer loss;
if he is equal, he should be weighed again; if he is heavier, he shall be victorious.

The meaning is that he should be weighed again, after performing all the ritual acts together with the preliminary rites such as the invocation of the deity (*devatāvāhana*). As for the claim made by certain Easterners (*paurastya*) regarding a second weighing within that very same procedure, that is incorrect; for the deficiency in the ritual (*karmavaiguṇya*), which is the cause of equality [of the scales], remains in the same state. Furthermore, even if equality occurs in two or three procedures, the possibility of ritual deficiency is refuted by the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthāpatti*); thus, even in the case of equality, there is defeat. However, Pitāmaha stated that the punishment and penance (*daṇḍaprāyaścitta*) are smaller in comparison to those of the one who loses, having in mind their relative insignificance.
If, when weighed, it increases, it is pure according to the nature of things;
if it decreases, it is not pure; but for some, that which remains equal is pure.
"One who has committed a small offense should be known as equal [to the accused], but one who has committed a great offense is inferior.

Regarding the mention of "some" (*ekeṣām*), the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* states that this is for the sake of honoring their view, and not to indicate that, in his own opinion, one who is equal is pure; for even one who has committed a small offense is impure. As for the statement in the *Ratnākara-nibandha* that the phrase "for some, one who is equal is pure" means that when there is equality, it refers only to a state of doubt—this is incorrect, as it results in a lack of straightforwardness in the interpretation of the sentence. Furthermore, Kātyāyana says that if the scale-pan or other components are broken, they should be repaired and weighed again. (440)
In the event of the breaking of the sling, the fracture of the balance-beam, or likewise the snapping of the cord,
or when there is doubt regarding purity, one should examine the man again.
The causes for doubt regarding purity have been explained by Nārada:
when the two ends of the scale are agitated, wavering, or marked by instability,
or when it is shaken by the wind, then one should not declare either side as the winner.

The meaning of this is as follows: when the two ends of the scale move sideways, when the mark placed for the purpose of determining balance disappears, and when the scale, impelled by the wind, oscillates upward and downward—at those times, one should not declare victory or defeat. Vyāsa says:

"In the case of a fracture of the arms, a breakage of the scale, or likewise of the two *karkaṭa*-hooks, or upon the snapping of the cord or the breaking of the pivot, the king shall cause the ordeal to be performed again."

The *kakṣya* is the bottom of the sling. The two *karkaṭas* are iron pins located at the ends of the balance-beam, serving as supports for the sling; they are slightly curved and resemble the horns of a crab. The *akṣa* is the crossbar fixed above the two leg-pillars, serving as a support for the balance-beam. Furthermore, one should declare the scale impure if there is a break in the *kakṣya*, a fracture of the balance-beam, likewise in the case of the *dhaṭa* or the *karkaṭas*, or if there is a severing of the cord or a breaking of the *akṣa*.

[101] Thus, the statement from another *Smṛti* refers to cases such as the sudden breaking of a garment, whereas the statement of Kātyāyana refers to cases such as the breaking of a sling where a visible cause is observed; so say the venerable teachers beginning with Vijñāneśvara.
Thus ends the eighth section, the Procedure for the Balance (*dhaṭavidhi*), in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* by the illustrious Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma.

**Possible reading of the defective text:** Thus ends the eighth chapter, "The Procedure for the Balance," in the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*, composed by the Great King Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of the Great King Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "the Illustrious Kodaṇḍa-Paraśurāma."
Now follows the procedure for the fire. Regarding this, Pitāmaha says:
"I shall proclaim the procedure for the fire exactly as it is enjoined in the scriptures."
One should cause eight mandalas to be made, and likewise a ninth one in front.
The first mandala belongs to Agni, the second likewise to Varuṇa;
the third has Vāyu as its deity, and the fourth has Yama as its deity.
The fifth, however, has Indra as its deity; the sixth is said to belong to Kubera;
the seventh has Soma as its deity; and the eighth belongs to all the deities.
That which is the ninth [altar] in front, they know to be the great earthly one;
it should be made with cow dung and sprinkled with water.

“Those who know the divine [ordeals] understand that the eighth is dedicated to Sāvitrī, and likewise the ninth belongs to all the deities (*sarvadaivatyam*); thus it was read by the teacher Vijñāneśvara. Having performed the purification of the ground in the previously mentioned location for the ordeal, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), endowed with the aforementioned observances, should draw nine circles there. And since it is stated that the ninth is "in front" (*purastāt*)—meaning it is to be made in the eastern part of the eight circles—and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the forthcoming statement, "standing in the western circle," they should be drawn facing east. These eight are, in order, dedicated to the deities beginning with Agni; the ninth is the "great" one, which, in comparison to the other circles, is of greater dimension, consisting of an indefinite number of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and is *pārthiva*, meaning its deity is the Earth (*pṛthivī*). Although these circles do not possess the status of being dedicated to Agni and others in the same way that sacrificial oblations (*havis*) do—either by being offered with reference to them or by having mantras that reveal them—nevertheless, their status as being dedicated to Agni and others should be understood on the strength of the designation (*samākhyā*) characterized by the use of words ending in patronymic suffixes (*taddhita*) such as *āgneya* (dedicated to Agni). This is just as in the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā, where it was established as a settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the Hotṛ, the Brahman, and others consume from their respective cups (*camasa*) on the strength of the designations found in the injunction-mantras (*praiṣamantra*), such as "the cup of the Hotṛ" and "the cup of the Brahman. Therefore, the worship of the deities beginning with Agni must be performed within those circles. He [Vijñāneśvara] himself states the dimensions of the circles:
[102] They say that the distance from one mandala to the next is thirty-two finger-breadths;
thus, with eight mandalas, there are two hundred finger-breadths.
The conceptualization of the earth, however, consists of fifty-six [units].

One *maṇḍala* is another *maṇḍala*; each individual *maṇḍala*, together with its intervening space (*antarāla*), measures thirty-two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Thus, with eight *maṇḍalas* accompanied by eight intervening spaces, there are two hundred and fifty-six finger-breadths. However, the ninth *maṇḍala* is of unlimited finger-breadths, and therefore it is not included in this calculation. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says (2.106): "A *maṇḍala* together with its intervening space measures thirty-two finger-breadths; therein, the *maṇḍala* is sixteen finger-breadths and its intervening space is sixteen finger-breadths."

The maṇḍala should be known as sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in size, and the space between them should likewise be sixteen finger-breadths. "Space" (*antara*) means the middle. If the footprint of the one performing the divine ordeal exceeds sixteen finger-breadths, then the maṇḍala should be measured according to that footprint, and the remaining finger-breadths shall constitute the intervening space; thus, the maṇḍala together with its intervening space must be completed at thirty-two finger-breadths. For this very reason, Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 299) states:
"One should make the measurement of the maṇḍala equal to the size of that [person's] footprint."
The Grandfather [Brahmā] also said:
"They say the distance from one mandala to the next is thirty-two finger-breadths;
however, the mandala should be made according to its proper measure, equal to the step of the performer."
As for the statement of Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 285–286): "They say that the distance from one circle to the next is thirty-two finger-breadths;
thus, with eight circles, there are two hundred finger-breadths."
It is forty finger-breadths more than the measurement of the ground. Thus.

In this regard, there is no contradiction in counting the finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) by excluding the sixteen-finger space that lies between the ninth and eighth mandalas, because that space is to be traversed and thus not included [in the count of the ground]. As for the fact that this same passage is read in the *Kalpataru* as "the calculation of the ground is declared to be twenty-four," there too there is no contradiction; for the first sixteen-finger mandala is the place where one stands, and since it is to be approached, it is excluded from the calculation of the finger-breadths of the ground to be traversed. The measurement of a finger-breadth has been shown in the section on the procedure for the balance ordeal (*dhaṭavidhi*). As for the statement of Viṣṇu (11.2), "one should make seven mandalas with an interval of sixteen fingers each," that refers specifically to the mandalas to be traversed.

"Taking that [the heated iron], he should walk slowly for exactly seven circles"—this statement by Yājñavalkya (YDh 2.106) should be understood as having the same meaning. In the *Ratnākara*, however, it is stated that these seven circles are [prescribed] in the event of an inability to leap over the eight auspicious objects (*maṅgalāṣṭaka*). Upon these [circles] being sprinkled with water, *kuśa* grass blades with their tips pointing eastward should be spread out;
*kuśa* grass, as enjoined by the scriptures, is to be placed in each circle.
And then the performer should place [the offerings] upon them; this is the established rule for the daily rite.

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Pitāmaha. Thereafter, the judge (prāḍvivāka), having established the common fire (laukikāgni) to the south of the first circle, shall offer clarified butter (ājya) one hundred and eight times for the sake of pacification, because of the scriptural injunction: "For the sake of pacification, he should offer clarified butter into the fire one hundred and eight times. And regarding this oblation, it has been stated by the teacher Vijñāneśvara that it should be performed with the mantra: *agnaye pāvakāya svāhā*. Immediately after the oblation, the heating of the iron ball (ayaḥpiṇḍa) must be carried out by the smith in that very same fire. Likewise, Nārada states (Ṛṇādāna 288–289):
One who is a blacksmith by birth, skilled in the work of fire, and experienced in other practical applications— by him one should heat iron in the fire.
A ball of iron, glowing with the color of fire and emitting sparks, must be well-guarded;
it must be protected in such a way that contact with outcasts (*cāṇḍāla*) and others does not occur. Regarding the dimensions and other characteristics of the iron ball, Pitāmaha says:
"Having made it smooth and free of edges, [one should prepare] a ball of iron eight fingers in length."
One should heat a uniform ball weighing fifty palas in the fire.

"Even" means not deficient, devoid of protuberances on all sides, and perfectly round—that is to say, symmetrical. "Eight fingers" means eight finger-breadths in length. "Fifty palas" means measuring fifty palas in weight. The repetition of the word "even" is for the purpose of indicating that one should heat it thoroughly on all sides. However, in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*, the length of the iron ball is stated to be twelve fingers:
"A ball of iron, weighing fifty palas, circular, twelve fingers long, forged from fire-refined metal, should be given by the king to the accuser."
There is an option between these two alternatives. Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated that the iron ball shall weigh sixteen palas;

or else, having taken with both hands a red-hot iron ball weighing sixteen palas enclosed within seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, one should walk until the seventh step is reached as the limit. Thus it is said.

The seventh circle extends up to the limit of the seventh step; here, the word "limit" (*maryādā*) is intended in the sense of inclusive extension (*abhividhi*). Here too, there is an option. However, in the *Paurastya-nibandha*, it is stated: "This count of sixteen *palas* applies in cases of incapacity. Furthermore, this heating of the iron ball must be performed three times, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the forthcoming statement of Nārada: "being heated during the third heating. The threefold heating is for the purpose of purifying the iron. Having cast the well-heated iron ball into water, one heats it again and casts it back into water; this is the third heating. At the time of the third heating, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) shall perform the entire set of common preliminary rites for all ordeals, beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the binding of the document to the head of the accused, as previously described. Regarding the specific flowers and other items for the worship of Fire (*vahnipūjā*), Pitāmaha says:
There, the lord of men should perform worship of the Fire-god with red sandalwood and incense, and likewise with red flowers.

In that context, regarding the iron ball (*ayaḥpiṇḍa*) which is the fire of the invoked Fire-god in his form as Dharma— immediately following this, Hārīta states what must be performed by the accused:
"Then, wearing wet clothes and being pure, he should stand facing east with his fingers and limbs extended, having placed the leaf [of evidence] upon his head."
And one must take one’s position within the first maṇḍala; for thus says Pitāmaha:

"In the first maṇḍala, one should stand facing east, pure and with palms joined. He [Pitāmaha] further states that while the person to be examined stands there, the purification of his hands must be performed.
They should observe the wounds and other marks on the hands of that perpetrator—those "perpetrators" being the persons appointed for the purpose of the task. Nārada also says:
"One should observe the signs on both his hands."
And those that are natural, hidden, with wounds, and without wounds.
Viṣṇu (11.10) states the method of purification:
"At the very beginning, one should examine his two hands while they are rubbing rice grains.

Those [hands] by which the rice grains are rubbed are so described. Rubbing them with rice grains is for the purpose of ascertaining their true condition. Thus, when those two are being purified and signs such as scars are present, they should be marked with the juice of lac and other substances before the application of fire, in order to know that 'these were already there. And so says Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 301):"
Upon all wounds caused by hands, one should apply *dhaṃsapada* ointments;
having applied them, one should observe that the two hands are indeed variegated with drops.

These are the previously established marks. Again, after the fire has been maintained, Yājñavalkya states what must be done by the judge immediately following this (YDh 2.103): "Having observed the hands of one who has rubbed grains of rice, he should then place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree upon them and wrap them with a thread for that same duration."

"‘Tāvat tāvatkr̥tvaḥ saptakr̥tvaḥ’ (so many times, up to seven times). Master Vijñāneśvara explained the meaning by taking *tāvat* as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) of the action [of wrapping]. However, for us, the meaning appears to be supported by other scriptural statements: *tāvat-sūtram* is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvigu*) of those threads; thus, "one should wrap with *tāvat-sūtreṇa*" means one should wrap with seven threads. Since the word *tāvat* is a numeral, it forms a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collection, and because it lacks the feminine gender, the suffix *ṅīp* is not applied, just as in the case of *tribhuvanam*. Furthermore, although there is no explicit statement regarding the sevenfold wrapping, it should be adopted based on the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). One should wrap both hands together with the seven white threads along with leaves of the *aśvattha* tree and so forth.

"One should wrap the hands with seven white threads of silk," as stated by Nārada. Furthermore, the seven *aśvattha* leaves must also be equal to one another; having filled the hollowed palms (*añjali*) with seven equal *aśvattha* leaves.

Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. One should place seven *śamī* leaves, seven unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and seven *dūrvā* leaves, along with unbroken grains mixed with curd, upon the *aśvattha* leaves: "Seven *pippala* leaves, then *śamī* leaves and unbroken grains, seven *dūrvā* leaves, and unbroken grains mixed with curd—one should set these down."

Because of this statement, Pitāmaha says that flowers should also be placed there: "One should place seven pippala leaves, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), flowers, and curd into the two hands, and likewise wrap them with a thread."

*Sumanas* refers to flowers. In the phrase "with a thread" (*sūtreṇa*), the singular is used to denote the class. As for the following: "But if one carries [something] heated with iron, covered by seven lotus leaves held in both hands, he is pure if he is not burned by the time he reaches the seventh step."

Thus is the rule regarding *arka* leaves; it should be understood that this applies when *aśvattha* leaves are unavailable. For this very reason, the Grandfather (Brahmā) praises them in order to demonstrate the preeminence of *aśvattha* leaves:
"Fire is born from the *pippala* tree; the *pippala* is remembered as the king of trees.
Therefore, a wise person should place its leaves upon his two hands. Thus [it is said].

Then, once the iron ball has been thoroughly heated, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) shall consecrate the fire situated therein with the mantra beginning "O Agni, you are the Vedas... This mantra was shown by Pitāmaha (Bṛhaspati):
"O Agni, you are the four Vedas; you are that which is offered in sacrifices.
You are the mouth of all the gods; you are the mouth of those who discourse on Brahman."
For, residing within the bellies of all beings, you therefore know their good and evil;
since you indeed purify sin, you are called Pāvaka.
Reveal yourself among the wicked, O Purifier; become radiant, O Fire! Or else, toward those of pure disposition, become cool, O Consumer of Oblations!
O Agni, you move within all beings like a witness;
O God, you alone know those things which human beings do not know.
This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification;
therefore, you ought to rescue him from this uncertainty in accordance with dharma.

Immediately after this, the person to be tested should also consecrate the fire with a mantra. Once it has been consecrated, one should place a ball of iron into his hands. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says (2.104–105):
“O Agni, Purifier, you move within all living beings.
Like a witness, O Sage, declare the truth to me concerning my merits and sins.”
When he has spoken thus, one should place a lump of iron weighing fifty palas and heated to the color of fire equally upon both hands.

The ablative case in *puṇyapāpebhyaḥ* is used with the elision of a gerund (*lyablope*), meaning "having reflected upon merits and demerits. *Brūhi* means "speak" or "reveal. *Hastayoḥ* means "in the hands," specifically those hands which hold an *aśvattha* leaf and so forth, and are bound with threads. The placing of the iron ball must be performed by the king, the presiding judge, or another official, holding it with tongs. And so Pitāmaha says: "Then, having taken that [ball], the king devoted to dharma..."
Or, being appointed with a pair of tongs, one should place it upon his two hands.
The syntactical connection is: "having taken it with a pair of tongs. Viṣṇu states what must be done for the accused who has grasped the iron ball (Viṣṇu 11.5–7):

"Then one should place there an iron ball, red-hot like fire, weighing fifty *pala*s and perfectly symmetrical. Having taken hold of it, he should walk, placing his steps upon the circles neither too quickly nor too slowly. Then, having passed the seventh circle, he should drop the iron ball onto the ground. Thus it is said.

"In the circles" means in the second and subsequent circles. "Having passed the seventh circle" means having traversed the seventh circle and gone to the eighth; this is the meaning, in accordance with the statement to be cited later. "On the ground" means on ground provided with a heap of fresh, dry grass, which constitutes the ninth circle; this is the meaning, following the words that will be spoken. Nārada also says (2.296–299):
"Taking hold of him with both hands, impelled by the presiding judge, he should then stand still and walk seven steps in a straight line toward the others."
Unperturbed and free from anger toward the fire, he should proceed slowly;
he must not let go of that [fuel] before reaching the ground that was intended.
One should not step beyond the mandala, nor should one place a foot before it;
having reached the eighth mandala, the person should then extinguish the fire.
One should release the fire in the first maṇḍala; the remainder [of the distance] is in the ninth maṇḍala. For this very reason, Pitāmaha says:
"One should not walk in haste, but one who is healthy should walk very slowly.
One should not skip over a maṇḍala, nor should one place a foot down between [the lines]."
Having gone to the eighth mandala, the wise one should deposit [the fire] in the ninth.
In the ninth mandala, which is provided with fresh grass, the relinquishing of the fire (agnivisarga) should be performed.
Likewise, seven mandalas should be made, measuring sixteen finger-breadths each.

"One should go inside for that duration, and having gone, one should cast it onto fresh grass"—so says a passage from the *Kālikāpurāṇa*. Nārada states what must be done by the examiners immediately after the casting of the iron ball:
"Once the ball has been released in this manner, one should perform an examination of the hands."
One should then observe it in the previously seen signs, and also elsewhere.
A mandala that appears red, or one where fire is produced,
should be known as impure, even if it is established according to the true Dharma.
But when the two hands cannot be distinguished as being burnt,
then one should rub grains of rice with great effort for seven times.
If he is not burnt when subjected to the ordeal, it is thus determined by the members of the court:
he is to be cleared; having been cleared, he is to be purified; if he is burnt, he is to be punished according to the sequence of the rules.
Therefore, even in another place devoid of such marks, they are not perceived—that is, they are not ascertained. Regarding Viṣṇu (11.8):
"The wise know that man to be impure whose hands are burnt in some place;
but he whose [hands] are not burnt at all shall be a pure man."
The Grandfather (Pitāmaha) has declared that one should perform the crushing of barley;
then, one should place either rice grains or barley into his two hands,
once they have performed the crushing with their hands without hesitation.
One should declare its purification at the end of the day when it is free from alteration.

[109] *Prāsyet* means one should throw. In some places, the reading is *nirvikāro yadā hastaḥ*. In that reading, since there is no indication of the time characterized as the end of the day, the determination of purification occurs at that very moment. And it is not the case that, according to the reading *dinānta*, one who has husked the rice and [is] unburnt (*adagdhaḥ*) would obtain purification today.
(One would attain purity?)

Thus, there is a contradiction with the statement of Yājñavalkya (YDh 2.107). Regarding this, one might argue that by the use of the suffix *ktvā* in the word *muktvā*, which signifies immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), and because no transformation of the hands is observed after the threshing of the rice, it must be understood that purification occurs immediately after releasing the heated iron ball. However, this must be refuted. For the meaning of the suffix *ktvā* is "prior time" (*pūrvakālatva*) and not "immediate sequence," according to Pāṇini’s rule: *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle* (Pā. 3.4.21). This is evident from the Vedic usage: although the sacrifice of the *dhāriyojana* is separated from the release of the *saṃsrāva* and *sruc* by the throwing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the suffix *ktvā* is seen used as *prahr̥tya paridhīñ juhoti*; likewise, in common usage, even when eating is separated from going by other actions such as sitting down, the expression *bhuktvā gacchati* ("having eaten, he goes") is observed even in the absence of immediate sequence. Furthermore, if the suffix *ktvā* signified immediate sequence, it would contradict a point in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā*. There, regarding the sentence *vājapeyeneṣṭvā bṛhaspatisavena yajeta* ("Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava"), a doubt arises: should the Bṛhaspatisava, enjoined by this sentence, be performed in the autumn—the time of the principal rite as heard in *śaradi vājapeyena*—and thus be included in the same performance (*ekaprayoga*) as the principal rite; or should it be performed in its own time, spring, because it is an archetypal (*prakṛta*) rite obtained through extension (*atideśa*)? Having raised this doubt, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established as follows: By the phrase *śaradi vājapeyena*, it is not the Vājapeya as an instrument (*karaṇa*) that is enjoined as something to be performed in autumn. Rather, the time is enjoined for that human activity—which is characterized by the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) having the Vājapeya as its instrument, designated by terms such as "productive operation" (*bhāvanā*) directed toward the fruit, and intended for the sake of the result. Since this activity, as a whole including its constituent parts, is indicated by the instrumental case-ending in *vājapeyena*, and since it is desired for the sake of the fruit and requires that specific time, the time of the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) is the same as the principal rite (*pradhāna*) because they are all involved in that activity. Therefore, the time of the Bṛhaspatisava, being directly taught (*aupadeśika*), sets aside the time obtained through extension (*ātideśika*). It cannot be argued that this directly taught time does not prevail over the extended time for the Bṛhaspatisava because it finds scope in the auxiliary rites other than the Bṛhaspatisava itself. For it is easy to say that since the extension also finds scope in the auxiliaries other than time, it has the power to restrict the injunction of time—even in the case of the Bṛhaspatisava—just as it does for the other auxiliaries. Therefore, since the lack of scope (*sāvakāśatva*) is not a determining factor, the extended time is set aside by the directly taught time, and the Bṛhaspatisava must be performed in autumn along with the principal rite. However, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is established as follows: It is true that the directly taught sets aside the extended, but in this case, the directly taught time is not possible. To explain: the human activity consisting of the productive operation (*phalabhāvanā*) having the Vājapeya as its instrument and the procedure as its adjunct, which is enjoined as to be performed in autumn by the injunction of time *śaradi vājapeyena*, is referred to by the suffix *ktvā*. The Bṛhaspatisava, being enjoined subsequently by *vājapeyeneṣṭvā bṛhaspatisavena*, falls outside the performance of the Vājapeya and therefore does not share its time. Thus, the Bṛhaspatisava must be performed in the spring following the Vājapeya, because the cause for the lapse of the immediate sequence—the inclusion of the auxiliary time of spring provided by the extension—is present. Furthermore, the suffix *ktvā* is traditionally remembered to signify "prior time" (*pūrvakālatā*) and not "immediate sequence. Even though the *apūrva* (transcendental merit) of the Vājapeya is produced first, it is strengthened by the Bṛhaspatisava performed in the subsequent spring. In certain circumstances, however, the maintenance of the sacred fires (*agnidhāraṇa*) must be performed again. Thus says Kātyāyana (441): [text omitted].
If one who is prosecuted falters, he is burned in a place other than his own;
the gods do not consider him truly burned, for they may cause him to be burned yet again.
Yājñavalkya (2.107):
"If the funeral cake falls in between, or if there is doubt, one should take it up again.

If the funeral cake falls in between and is taken up again, it should be understood that there is no impurity provided the hands are not burned; however, if they are burned, there is indeed impurity. For this very reason, Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 298) says:
But if one causes it to fall in between and it is not perceived as burnt, one should cause that fire to be carried again; this rule has been firmly established.
