Thus ends the ninth chapter, the ritual for fire, in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*, known as the *Śrīkodaṇḍaparaśurāma*.

**Proposed reading of the defective text:** Thus ends the ninth chapter, "The Procedure for Fire," in the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*, composed by Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva, son of Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "The Illustrious Kodaṇḍa-Paraśurāma."
Now follows the procedure for the water offering (*jalavidhi*). Regarding this, Pitāmaha says:
"Therefore, I shall proclaim the righteous and eternal procedure for the water offering."
The wise one should cause the mandala to be prepared with incense and lamps.
One should worship the arrows and the bamboo bow with devotion, using auspicious flowers and incense; thereafter, one should perform the ritual act.

[111] The grammatical connection is that one should worship the arrows with incense and lamps. The meaning is that, having prepared a consecrated ground near water and drawn a mandala, one should worship the arrows and other implements before commencing the ritual application (*prayoga*). The dimensions of the bow and the location of the target have been shown by Nārada (in *R̥ṇādāna* 307): "A fierce bow is known to be seven hundred [units], a middling one six hundred, and a mild one five hundred; this is to be understood as the rule for bows."
But with a medium bow, the discerning practitioner should discharge three arrows, having set the target at a distance of one hundred and fifty cubits.
However, there would be a fault if one throws the arrows either too short or too long;
[the distance] is seven hundred and seven fingers. Likewise, it may be six hundred or five hundred. The arrows should indeed be made of bamboo with tips not of iron. And so Kātyāyana says:
"For the sake of purification, one should prepare arrows with tips not of iron."
And he who throws [the targets] made of bamboo shafts should throw them very firmly.
Near the mandala, a gateway (toraṇa) should be erected, rising to the height of an ear-measure (karṇa). Thus says Nārada:
"Having gone to that body of water, one should erect a gateway on the bank, measuring only an ear's length, upon a clean and level portion of ground."
The Grandfather (Brahmā) shows the specific requirements regarding water:
"One should immerse oneself in still water that is neither turbid nor too shallow."
In a place free from grass and moss, and devoid of leeches and fish.
One should perform purification using water from natural pools;
one should always avoid water that has been drawn up, as well as that from rivers with swift currents.

In a place possessed of aquatic creatures known as "graspers" (*grāha*), [the ordeal] is to be prepared by bringing [water] from a river or similar source and placing it in a large vessel or the like. Nārada (*Ṛṇādāna* 305):
"One should cause men to immerse themselves in rivers that are not too swift, and in tanks, lakes, and ponds containing still water."
[112] In waters that are not too swift and which are free from the force that causes instability, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) should worship Varuṇa. Regarding this, Nārada says:
"With fragrant perfumes and garlands, and with honey, milk, clarified butter, and so forth, one should, being composed, first perform the worship of Varuṇa."
Then, a person of sturdy physique should be placed in water reaching up to the navel. And so says Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 308):
"A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, free from passion and hatred—a strong man—should be placed in water reaching the navel like a pillar."
"By this man, having supported the pillar of Dharma made from a sacrificial tree, he must stand facing the east;

and standing in water facing the east, he should hold onto the pillar of Dharma"—so says the scriptural injunction. Thereupon, the judge (prāḍvivāka), having performed the rites beginning with the invocation and worship of Dharma up to the end of the oblation (homa) according to the previously stated sequence, and having placed the written confession upon the head of the person to be purified, shall perform the consecration of the water. And so says Pitāmaha:
The king should first cause the man to stand in water like a pillar,
having made him who has arrived face the east while standing in the midst of the water.

Then he should invoke the deities and consecrate the water with mantras. The mention of the "stump" refers to the person together with the stump; the invocation of the deities is an illustration of the entire set of rites previously described, which are common to all divine ordeals and conclude with the binding of the written pledge (*pratijñāpatra*). The mention of "water" is also an illustration of Varuṇa, who is the deity of the water. And the mantra for consecrating the water has been shown by Pitāmaha (Bṛhaspati):
"O Water, you are the life-breath of living beings, created as the very first of all things."
You are declared to be the cause of purification for both material substances and embodied beings.
Therefore, reveal yourself for the examination of the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Also by Viṣṇu (12.7–8):
"O Water, you move within all beings like a witness."
You alone know the waters, those which human beings do not know.
This man, accused in a legal dispute, is sinking into you;
therefore, you ought to rescue him from this peril according to the Dharma.
Because these two mantras have the same meaning, there is an option between them. And the mantra for the consecration of the water by Varuṇa has been shown by Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 316–317):
"Water and fire are the most effective means of distinguishing truth from falsehood;
since fire arose from the waters, it is especially so in the case of water."
The purification of those who have been defiled is performed by those who know the true nature of reality;
therefore, O Blessed One, Lord of Waters, you ought to save us through the truth.

Also from Śaṅkha and Likhita: "O Varuṇa, you alone are both the existent and the non-existent; you are established in both. Truth is yours, O divine Varuṇa; you alone know that, O most excellent one; therefore, ordain it.
There is an option between these two [mantras]. Then, the judge shall cause the person to be purified to enter the water consecrated with the mantra. And so it is stated in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*:
"O Varuṇa, protect him from this curse;
if he is pure, then out of great compassion, consecrate him with mantras and cast him into the water."

The meaning is that, having consecrated [the water] with the mantra beginning with "Protect him" (*pāhy enam*) and ending with "out of great compassion" (*atikāruṇyāt*), one should cause the person to enter the water. Furthermore, this mantra is optional; Yājñavalkya states (2.108):
"Having sworn an oath over the water, saying 'O Varuṇa, protect me by truth,' the one to be purified, standing in water reaching the navel, should enter the water after grasping his thighs."

Having consecrated the water by reciting the mantra beginning with "By truth... (*satyena...*) and so forth, one should immediately thereafter discharge three arrows at the previously mentioned target location. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"Having caused the man to enter the water, one should cause him to discharge three arrows.
Pitāmaha states the specific requirements for the one who discharges the arrows:
The one who casts [the lot] should be a Kṣatriya, or else a Brāhmaṇa of that same conduct;
he must be of gentle heart, tranquil, fasting, and likewise pure.
The same author prohibits the discharge of an arrow at specific times and in specific places:
"A wise man should not discharge an arrow when the wind blows violently, nor on uneven ground, nor where it is crowded with trees and stumps. Thus it is said.

When all three arrows have been discharged, one of the two running men shall go to the spot where the middle arrow fell, retrieve that arrow, and stand there; while the other running man stands near the archway, the judge shall clap his hands to signal the timing. At the third clap of hands, the person undergoing the ordeal shall submerge himself by grasping the thighs of a man standing in water reaching up to his navel. At that very same moment, the running man standing near the archway shall run toward the spot where the middle arrow fell. Thus says Kātyāyana (443):
When the arrows have been shot, one should perform the immersion and the movement simultaneously.

When the arrows have been shot, as soon as the runner who was near the archway reaches the spot where the middle arrow fell, the other runner should take that middle arrow from that place and run back toward the archway. Upon his arrival, if he does not see the accused because the latter has completely submerged in the water, then he is acquitted. However, if any part of the accused's body, such as an ear, is visible after he has emerged, or if he moves to another location from where he submerged, then he is not acquitted. Thus say Nārada and Pitāmaha (Nārada, Ṛṇādāna 309–312).
From the point where the arrow was released, a youth endowed with speed should go with his utmost power to where that middle arrow has fallen.
Then another man of similar appearance, taking up a middle-sized arrow,
should return with speed from the direction where that first man had gone.
But when the arrow-catcher has entered and does not see [the arrow] clearly within the water,
then one should declare him pure.
[115] Otherwise, it would not be pure, because even a single factor might be seen—
either by remaining in its place or by moving elsewhere— from that in which it was previously established.

The phrase "of one limb" refers to the ears and so forth. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states: "If only the head is seen, but neither the ears nor the nose, one should declare that person pure even if he has entered the water."
The hitting of a medium-range arrow is determined from the point of its fall alone, not from the point where it glides. For this very reason, the Grandfather [Bhīṣma] said:
"One should take the falling of the arrow as the mark and avoid its gliding;
for as it glides and glides, the arrow goes further and further away."
Nārada states the characteristics of the two messengers appointed for the purpose of bringing back the arrow:
"Of the fifty messengers, those two who are superior in speed should be appointed there for the sake of retrieving the arrow."
Thus ends the section on the rules for water [offerings] in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* by the illustrious Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma. 10.

**A possible reading of the defective text:** Thus ends the tenth chapter, "The Rules for Water [Oaths]," in the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, an exposition on the discernment of legal procedure (*vyavahāra-viveka-uddyota*), composed by Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "the Illustrious Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma."
Now follows the procedure for poison.
Regarding this, Nārada says (Ṛṇādāna 318–320, 322, 324):
"Henceforth, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for poison."
At what time, in what manner, and of what kind that which is to be given has been proclaimed.
Whatever measure has been prescribed by those who understand the true nature of reality,
this should be given after stirring it at the desired time, during the arrival of winter.
One should avoid [gathering] in the afternoon, at midday, and during the twilight;
that which comes from the Himalayas, belonging to the Śārṅga species, and endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and taste is recommended.
That which is unadulterated, not confused,
and not impaired by mantras is prescribed as a dose of four barley grains during the rainy season and five barley grains in summer.

In the winter it is seven barley-grains; in the autumn it is even less than that. "At the onset of cold" refers to the winter and the cool season (*hemanta-śiśira*). "Śārṅga" means produced from horn. "Haimavata" means originating from the Himalayas. By saying "in the winter," both winter and the cool season are included. "In the autumn it is even less than that" means it is six barley-grains. Pitāmaha states that even the *vatsanābha* variety may be taken: "Without doubt, seven barley-grains should be given for the sake of purity."
Of the horned [poison], of vatsanābha, or of the poison born of snow.

"Seven barley-corns" refers to the dosage for the cold season, according to the previously cited statement. Kātyāyana describes the nature of *śārṅga* poison (446–447): "That which originates from a horn is dark like a goat's horn, or very yellow; when broken, it resembles ginger—that is known as *śārṅgiṇa* poison."
One should make the black [substance] reside in blood and harden it instantly;
by this method, poison is to be recognized by those expert in the divine [sciences].

*Abhaṅge* means "when broken. *Śr̥ṅgaverābham* means "resembling ginger (*ārdraka*). The grammatical connection is: "when broken, it resembles ginger and is very yellow. *Śārṅgiṇam* means "belonging to those with horns" (*śr̥ṅgin*). According to the rule *inaṇyanapatye* (Pāṇini 6.4.164), there is no elision of the suffix *ṭi* because the base form remains unchanged. The connection is that whatever is situated in the blood shall instantly make the blood black and thick. He [the author] also shows the nature of *vatsanābha* (Kāt 448–449): "It resembles *vatsanābha*, is yellow, and is determined by the knowledge of its color."
One should recognize that which is shaped like a pearl-oyster shell or a horn when broken as being *vatsanābha*.
Combined with honey and milk, it shall become clear in that very instant.
Thus has the external characteristic been described by those who accomplish the Dharma.
Nārada points out the poisons that must be avoided:
one should carefully avoid poison that has been fried, processed, fumigated, or mixed, as well as kālakūṭa and alābu poison.
The Grandfather also said:
One should avoid all poisons that have been administered, those that have become stale, those that are artificial, and likewise all those produced from the earth.
And this poison, having been properly ground and mixed with thirty times its weight of clarified butter, should be administered. Thus says Nārada:
"In the forenoon, in a cool place, poison should be given to living beings, finely ground and combined with thirty times its weight of clarified butter."

And this poison, in the previously mentioned divine place in the presence of deities and twice-born brahmins, shall be administered by the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*) after performing worship of Śiva and placing the poison before him; having performed the entire sequence of rites previously described, beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the binding of the document of the oath (*pratijñāpatra*), the poison—having been consecrated with mantras—should be given by one facing north or east to a person facing south. Thus says Nārada: "Fasting, he should give the poison in the presence of deities and brahmins, after worshipping Maheśvara with incense, offerings, and mantras."
In the very presence of the twice-born, while standing facing south,
the Brahmin, composed in mind, should give [the gift] while facing north or east.
And the mantra for consecrating the poison was spoken by Nārada (Yājñavalkya Smṛti, Ṛṇādāna 325):
"O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in truth and righteousness;
cleanse this man of sin, and through his truth become nectar."
And by Viṣṇu as well (13.6–7):
"O Poison, because of your poisonousness, your unevenness, and your cruelty toward all embodied beings,
you alone know those things which human beings do not know."
"This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification;
therefore, you ought to rescue him from this doubt in accordance with dharma."
The Grandfather (Brahmā) shows the mantra for consecrating the one to be tested:
"Having placed the poison in his hand as it is being given, he should cause him to swear:
'O Poison, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of testing the wicked-souled. [118]
Reveal yourself to the wicked; for those who are pure, become nectar.
Yājñavalkya also says (2.110):
"O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in truth and righteousness;
protect me from this curse; by truth, become nectar for me."
Having consecrated it thus, he himself said that it should be consumed (YDh 2.111):
"Having spoken thus, one should consume the Śārṅga poison, which is born from the snowy mountains.
If the consumed poison is digested, then one is pure; otherwise, one is impure. And so says Bṛhaspati.

He by whom poison administered according to the prescribed rite has been digested without mantras or medicines shall be considered pure; otherwise, however, he shall be punished and made to pay that wealth.
Yājñavalkya also (2.111):
"One should prescribe purification for him by whom [the food] is digested without [natural] urges.
'Urge' (vega) means the movement of one bodily humor (dhātu) into another."

"From one constituent element (*dhātu*) to the attainment of another constituent element is known as the 'force of poison' (*viṣavega*)," according to this statement. The constituent elements (*dhātavaḥ*), however, are seven, beginning with the skin:
skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the constituent elements.
Thus it is stated. There are seven stages of the poison's onset (*viṣavega*), and their characteristics are shown in the *Viṣatantra*:

"The first stage of the poison produced by the venom causes horripilation; the next two stages thereafter produce perspiration and dryness of the mouth, and subsequently cause discoloration of the body and trembling."

This fifth stage brings about the loss of control over the eyes and the breaking of the throat; the sixth bestows hiccups, labored breathing, and delusion; and the seventh brings death to the consumer.
Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 326) states that the purity of the person undergoing purification is established when there is an absence of the effects of the poison until the end of the day:
"He should be placed in the shade and guarded for the remainder of the day without food;
once he has passed beyond the stages of the poison's effect, Manu declared him to be pure."
Viṣṇu (13.5):
[119] If the poison, having passed its stage of violent onset, is digested easily,
one should recognize it as pure and discharge it at the end of the day.
The Grandfather said: If, after consuming it, he remains healthy, free from fainting and vomiting, and shows no abnormal symptoms by the end of the day, one should designate him as pure.

The person to be examined by the king should be protected from deceivers and the like for some time. And so says Pitāmaha: "For three nights or five nights, the king should keep the one undergoing the ordeal under the supervision of his own men, out of fear of deceivers and the like."
One should examine medicinal herbs, mantra-applications, and poison-removing gems that have been secretly produced and placed within the body of the perpetrator.
But according to Vijñāneśvarācārya:
"When one remains free from modification for a period of one hundred five-tālas, then one becomes completely purified; thereafter, one should undertake medical treatment."

Having recited these words of Nārada, [the author] stated: "If one remains free from any physical change for a period measured by five hundred hand-claps (*karatālikā*), then he is pure; otherwise, he must be treated. Furthermore, it was said that the statement which specifies the limit as the end of the day refers only to cases involving a small quantity [of poison].
Thus ends the section on the procedure regarding poison in the *Vyavahāraviveka* composed by the illustrious Kodaṇḍaparaśurāma. 11.

**A possible reading of the defective text:** The section on poisons (*viṣavidhi*) in the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*, composed by Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "Śrī Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma"— [Chapter] 11.
Now, the procedure for the ordeal by sacred libation.
On this matter, Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 327–328) states:
"Henceforth, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for the sacred libation."
Just as it has been declared by those learned in the scriptures, [this practice] is not in conflict with any time.
In the forenoon, for one who has fasted, bathed, and is wearing wet clothes— one who is conscientious and free from vices— the drinking of the ordeal-substance (kośapāna) is prescribed.

For one who desires [the ordeal], is faithful, is in the presence of gods and Brahmins, possesses a sense of shame, and—due to the possibility of untruth—is apprehensive of an undesirable outcome during a divine test (*divyakaraṇa*), there is the "drinking of the *kośa*," which is the drinking of water from the bathing-vessel of a fierce deity (*ugradevatā*). It should be understood that three handfuls (*prasr̥ti*) of the water used for the deity’s ablution are to be consumed.
Thus Viṣṇu (14.2–3):

Having worshipped the fierce deities (*ugrā devāḥ*), one should face the deity and drink three *prasṛti* measures of the water used for their ablution while declaring, "This was not performed by me. Thus [it is said]. The fierce deities are Durgā and others. Regarding the specific rule concerning the deities to be bathed, Pitāmaha says:
"Whichever deity a devotee is devoted to, one should have that person drink the water belonging to that deity."
But when there is equality among the gods, one should cause [the patient] to drink from the vessel of Āditya.
One should cause thieves and those who subsist by weapons to drink the water of Durgā;
however, one should not cause a Brāhmaṇa to drink that which belongs to the Sun.

When there is equality among all deities—that is, when devotion is equal—Kātyāyana states that if the offense is slight, one should bathe the weapons of the subordinate deities and have [the offender] drink that water: "In the case of a very slight offense against the gods, having bathed their weapons, the water [from them] should be made to be drunk; if there is a transformation [of the offense] and he remains impure, he must be restrained; otherwise, he is pure. (452)

*Pāyyaḥ* means one who is to be made to drink. *Niyamyaḥ* means one who is to be punished. The mention of "taking up weapons" (*āyudhagrahaṇam*) is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇam*) for the solar disc fashioned from copper and other metals. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati states: "The accused shall be made to drink that which he worships—the solar disc, the weapon of the gods—after having washed it; from that water, he shall drink three handfuls (*prasṛti*)."
Regarding this, the Grandfather (Brahmā) states the specific rule:
one should bathe the trident of Durgā and the mandala of Āditya;
for other deities as well, one should bathe their weapons.

This procedure for bathing and drinking the water is to be performed by the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) who has observed a fast: having prepared a mandala near a temple and placed the person to be purified (*śodhya*) therein, he should worship the deity with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, bathe the deity, and then bring that bathing water into the mandala. Having performed the rites beginning with the invocation of Dharma as previously described and ending with the binding of the written pledge (*pratijñāpatra*), he should address the person to be purified, declaring the undesirable consequences of falsehood in this divine ordeal. Then, after consecrating the water with the mantra prescribed for the water-ordeal, beginning with "O Water, you are the life-breath of living beings," the rite should be carried out. The person to be purified, having been consecrated with the mantra previously mentioned beginning with "Of truth and untruth, the division... and so forth, shall drink the water. On this point, Nārada says:
Having summoned that accused person and placed him within the circle,
one should have him face the sun and drink three handfuls of water.
The Grandfather [said]:
Having positioned the patient facing east, one should have him drink three handfuls [of the medicine],
provided he has been bathed according to the previously mentioned procedure, is wearing wet clothes, and is pure.
By what was previously stated, meaning by that which was mentioned before as being common to all divine [deities]. Yājñavalkya (2.112):
Having worshipped fierce deities, one should take their bathing water;
having made [the person] hear [the mantra], one should have them drink three *prasṛti* measures of that water.
Nārada said: Having worshipped that deity and washed him with water,
one should cause [the person] to hear of their transgression and then make them drink three handfuls of water.
Sin is the fruit of evil, manifesting in the form of leprosy and other such ailments, as has been shown by that very [author]:
"If a man who is defiled should drink from a vessel at any time,
and if that man, out of greed, does not speak [of it], that evil-minded person becomes afflicted with vitiligo."
"Knowing [the truth], if one drinks from the treasury [of the king] out of self-will and gives false testimony,
he is born poor, diseased, and foolish for seven births. Thus,
in a lawsuit concerning the head (a capital offense), that same text shows the undesirable consequence for the accuser.
If a twice-born man, having forcibly provided the treasury, should desire his own welfare,
he shall come to ruin and that business shall not succeed.
Viṣṇu (14.4–5) states the time limit for purification for one who has drunk the ordeal-substance and is to be cleared:
"If, within two weeks or even three weeks,
one should see illness, fire, the death of a kinsman, or even a royal calamity [befall the accuser], [then he is purified]."
One should know that to be impure, and likewise pure in the opposite case. Kātyāyana (456):
Now, if there is a discrepancy with fate, one should cause the payment to be made after three weeks.
One should diligently investigate that matter and the punishment as well.
There is a contradiction with fate and the emergence of divine diseases; and those divine diseases have been shown by that very same [author]:
fever, diarrhea, eruptions, pain in the vital organs and bones, eye disease, forehead ailments, and likewise insanity arise.
Headaches, paralysis of the arms, and other divine diseases afflict men. Pitāmaha said:
After three nights, seven nights, or even fourteen days, [the patient recovers].
That man in whom such a transformation is observed is indeed a doer of evil.
Bṛhaspati states that even for the son of the person to be cleared and others, there is defeat if excessive suffering occurs:
"If within seven days or fourteen days no affliction arises for him, nor for his sons, wife, or wealth, he shall be pure; of this there is no doubt."

The determination of these four periods, beginning with three nights, should be understood according to the smallness or greatness of the intensity of the attack. Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 331) states that there is no defeat if a disease or similar condition arises after the fixed period has elapsed: "If, after two weeks have passed, a very great abnormality should occur, he should not be accused by a wise man, because of the lapse of the agreed time."

In this context, the phrase "two weeks" (*dvisaptāha*) is merely an illustration of the maximum time limit, because the reason given is "due to the lapse of the fixed period at the end. Therefore, since twenty-one nights constitute the maximum time limit, it is established that if a deformity (*vaikṛta*) arises after fourteen nights, there is defeat; whereas in the cases of three or seven nights, there is no defeat even if a deformity arises before fourteen nights.
Thus ends the section on the procedure for the ordeal of the balance (*kośavidhi*) in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* by Śrī Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma. 12.

**A possible reading of the defective text:** In the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various birudas beginning with “Śrīkodaṇḍaparaśurāma”— this is the twelfth chapter, the *Kośavidhi* (The Procedure for the Treasury), within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*.
Now follows the procedure for rice grains. Regarding this, Pitāmaha says:
"I shall declare the procedure for rice grains as enjoined by their defining characteristics."
In cases of theft, however, rice grains must be given; it is certain that it is not otherwise.
One should have white śāli rice prepared by no one other than [the officiant];
having placed it in an earthen vessel, he, being pure, should stand before the sun.
Having mixed [the materials] with bathing water, one should let them remain in that very place during the night;
having first performed the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites according to the rules at night.

The judge, having fasted, shall perform at night in the temple of the Sun the procedure common to all ordeals previously described, beginning with the invocation of Dharma and ending with the oblation (*homa*). The meaning is that he should mix white, husked rice with the water used for the Sun’s ablution and keep it there until morning. He himself states what must be done by the judge in the morning:
"At dawn, [the rice] should be given to the litigant who is facing the Sun."

The phrase "rice should be given to the one performing the ordeal" is to be supplied [to the verse]. This must be done by fastening the document of the claim (*pratijñāpatra*) upon the head of the person undergoing the ordeal. And so says that same author:
"Having fasted and bathed while facing the east, with the document placed upon his head, he shall eat the rice and then spit it out onto the document."
"Only on birch bark, and not on any other; but in its absence, on *pippala* [leaves].

Regarding the phrase "having eaten" (*bhakṣayitvā*), this is the usage of the root *bhakṣ* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), meaning "having caused [the person] to eat. Bṛhaspati states the means for determining purity and impurity:
"Fasting and purified, one should eat rice grains in the presence of the sun."
One becomes pure by spitting out white phlegm, but if it is mixed with blood, one incurs the fault.
Kātyāyana also says:
"If one eats rice grains smeared with the water used for bathing or drinking a deity, or if one swallows pure saliva, one becomes pure; otherwise, one must be restrained as impure."
The Grandfather said: One in whom blood is seen, whose jaw and palate waste away,
and whose body trembles— him one should designate as impure.
[124] Thus ends the procedure for rice (*taṇḍulavidhi*) in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* by the illustrious Paraśurāma, the wielder of the bow. 13.

**A possible reading of the defective text:** The Procedure for Rice (*taṇḍulavidhi*), Chapter 11, from the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, specifically the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*, composed by Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "Śrī Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma."
Now follows the procedure for the heated gold-piece ordeal (*taptamāṣa*). Regarding this, Pitāmaha says:
"I shall describe the auspicious procedure for the extraction of the heated gold-piece."
One should have a vessel made of iron or copper, measuring sixteen finger-breadths.
One should fill a circular pit, either earthen or made of clay, four finger-breadths deep,
with twenty palas of clarified butter and oil.
Then, one should cast a gold māṣaka into that well-heated [liquid];
thereafter, one should extract the heated māṣaka using the thumb and finger.

The *maṇḍala* is circular in shape. A *suvarṇamāṣaka* is a measure equal to one-sixteenth of a *karṣa*. The mention of *suvarṇa* (gold) is for the purpose of excluding a silver *māṣa*. The meaning is that one should place therein, in a lumped form, gold or copper measured by a *suvarṇamāṣa*. "By the joining of the thumb and finger" means by the thumb, forefinger, and middle finger. And this extraction of the heated *māṣa* must be performed by the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) after having performed the common procedure for all ordeals—beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the binding of the document of the defendant's oath—and after consecrating it with the previously mentioned mantra beginning with "O Agni, you are the four Vedas. The person to be purified (*śodhya*), however, should extract the heated *māṣa* after consecrating it with the mantra spoken by Yājñavalkya beginning with "O Agni, you are [the witness] of all beings. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
One should extract a heated māṣaka-weight from well-heated oil or ghee.
This method for determining purity or impurity was stated by Bṛhaspati and Pitāmaha:
"He who does not shake his fingertips, on whom no eruption appears, [is pure]."
He becomes pure through the Dharma, according to the word of his grandfather.
Also in the *Kālikā-purāṇa*:
"He who does not shake off [the impurity] during the night, from whom blood does not arise,
and from whom it has been cast out along with defects such as eruptions— he is pure."

"Red" means red-colored. The grammatical connection is: "whose fingertips are free from eruptions and the like. Thus is one method of the heated-coin ordeal (*taptamāṣa*). Pitāmaha also states another method:
"Having taken cow's ghee in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay, the pure person should heat it over a fire."
One should cast into it a beautifully adorned ring made of gold, silver, copper, or iron, having washed it once with water.
In a place rich with swirling ripples and waves, beyond the reach of the touch of a fingernail,
one should examine [the water] with a moist leaf, listening for the distinct "curu" sound.
Then, one should consecrate that [ghee] once with this mantra:
"O ghee, you are the supreme purifier, the immortal, among the sacrificial rites."
O Purifier, may you become more purifying; may you be cool as snow in the heat.
Then, [he should approach] one who has fasted, bathed, and arrived wearing wet clothes.
One should cause that seal to be placed inside clarified butter;
then the examiners shall examine its index finger.
"He whose boils do not appear is pure; otherwise, he is impure.

In this case as well, the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and other rites are the same. For the person to be tested (*śodhya*), the mantra for consecrating the fire is the same [as before]; however, for the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), the mantra for consecration here is "the supreme purifier" (*paraṃ pavitram*). Here, the extraction of the ring must be done with the index finger alone, because of the statement that "they should examine the forefinger," which indicates that it is the one to be examined. Thus ends the procedure for the heated gold coin (*taptamāṣa*).
Now follows the procedure for the ploughshare. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"A ploughshare made of iron, weighing twelve palas, is so called."
It should be eight finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width.
The thief shall lick that [gold] once with his tongue when it is red-hot like fire;
if he is not burned, he attains purification, but otherwise he is defeated.

In this case as well, once the heating of the ploughshare has commenced, the judge (prāḍvivāka) shall perform the rites beginning with the invocation of Dharma (dharmāvāhana) and ending with the formal deposition of the defendant's plea (pratijñāpatrāropaṇa). The mantra for the consecration (abhimantraṇa) of the judge is the one previously mentioned, beginning with "O Agni, you are the Vedas... and so forth. The mantra for the consecration of the person to be purified (śodhya) is the one previously mentioned, beginning with "O Agni, you are among all beings... and so forth. Thus ends the procedure for the ploughshare ordeal (phālavidhi).
[126] Now follows the procedure for the ordeal by sacred libation (dharmaja).
Regarding this, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) says:
Now I shall fully explain the examination of dharma and adharma for men who have committed killings, those who are seeking refuge, and those desiring expiation.
One should have the Dharma fashioned from silver and Adharma from lead;
one should write Dharma and Adharma, white and black respectively, upon birch bark or cloth.
Having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship it with perfumes and garlands;
for Dharma is represented by white flowers, while Adharma is the bearer of black flowers.
Having prepared them in this manner and smeared them, one should place those two balls [of food] there;
the two balls should be made entirely of either cow dung or clay.
They should be placed in an undamaged earthen vessel, unobserved,
in a clean, plastered place in the presence of the gods and Brahmins.
Then one should invoke the gods and the world-protectors as before;
however, one should first perform the invocation of Dharma and then write the document of oath.
"If I am purified of evil, may the Dharma come into my hand;
then, being challenged, let one person seize it without delay."
When dharma is upheld, one becomes pure; but when there is adharma, one is diminished.
Thus has the examination of dharma and adharma been briefly explained.

By the mention of "of the slayers," it is indicated that this ordeal applies to those accused of a violent crime; by "of those who beg," it refers to those accused of a civil offense; and by "of those seeking expiation," it refers to those accused of a mortal sin (*pātaka*). The [balance] is made of lead and iron—that is, fashioned from lead and iron. Bṛhaspati also states:
"Justice (*dharma*) and injustice (*adharma*) should be inscribed upon two leaves, one white and the other black.
[The balance is consecrated] with mantras such as the 'Gift of Life' (*jīvadāna*), and with Sāman chants beginning with the *Gāyatrī*."
Having addressed [the deity], one should worship with perfumes and white and black flowers;
then, having sprinkled them with the five products of the cow, they should be enclosed within lumps of clay.
Having made two new jars equal and placed them out of sight,
one should then take a single ball from one of the jars without delay.
[127] When the *dharma* has been grasped, it becomes pure and worthy of worship by the investigators.

This refers to the meaning of performing the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) with mantras such as those beginning with "jīvadāna," or with the Ṛgvedic hymns recited in the *sūkta* starting with "mā pragāma" (RV 10.57), or with other *ṛc*-mantras.
Thus ends the procedure for the knower of *dharma*.

Thus ends the section on Ordeals (*divya*) in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* [of the *Madanaratnapradīpa*]. **Alternative reading:** Thus ends the procedure for the *taṇḍula* (rice) ordeal in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* of the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva—the son of Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "Śrī Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma. ||14||
And the exposition of the section on action (kriyāpāda) is completed. || 14 ||
Now follows the exposition of the determination of legal issues.
Regarding that, Bṛhaspati states the methods of determination:
"By means of dharma, by means of judicial procedure (vyavahāra), by means of custom (caritra), and by the king's command."
The determination of a doubtful matter has been declared to be of four kinds.
Each one is declared by the great seers to be of two kinds according to the distinction of action;
and one should determine the punishment in accordance with the offense.
That same author shows two types of legal determination (*dharmanirṇaya*):
"Having properly investigated the matter and having determined it through reasoning,
and then having examined it by means of oaths— that is to be known as legal determination."
Where the defendant admits the claim, that is a decision;
the second type, which is properly purified by ordeals, has been described.

The phrase "the defendant should accept" (*prativādī prapadyeta*) is connected to both parts [of the sentence], like the eye of a crow. Where the defendant, having investigated thoroughly through reasoning, accepts—that is, agrees to—a matter that has been fully considered and examined by means of oaths such as touching the head of one's son, that is the first kind of legal decision (*dharmanirṇaya*). Where the defendant, purified by ordeals such as the balance (*dhaṭa*) and so forth, should accept it, that is declared the second kind of decision called "dharma. Thus, two varieties of the decision known as *vyavahāra* (legal procedure) have been shown by that very same author.
That which is a determination by means of valid cognitions is called conventional practice (vyavahāra);
the second [type of nigrahasthāna] is proclaimed as such because it lacks a response to a quibble (vākchala).

In this context, the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) are the witnesses and the written document. The meaning is that the determination reached through verbal quibble (*vākchala*)—that is, by means of a verbal quibble and by not providing a proper reply—is the second type of legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*). Two varieties of determination based on conduct (*caritra*) have been shown by that same author:
[128] "Determination established by inference is called *caritra*; however, the second variety, established by local custom, has been illustrated by those learned in the scriptures."

A decision reached through inference in the form of a logical application of possession is *caritra*. A decision reached by virtue of local custom is the second type of *caritra*; such is the meaning. That same author shows two varieties of decision by royal decree (*rājājñā*):
"The first is declared to be a decision by royal decree accompanied by means of proof;
the other is proclaimed as such when there is no conflict with the scriptures or the members of the court."

A royal decree supported by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the first form of judicial decision. When there is a mutual conflict between the scriptures and the court members, that which is the royal decree is the second form of decision, namely a royal decree; this is the meaning. Nārada (Mā. 1.10) states that among the four types of decisions—dharma, legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), custom (*caritra*), and royal edict—the preceding one is weaker in relation to each subsequent one: "Dharma, legal procedure, custom, and royal edict: this legal process has four feet, each subsequent one setting aside the preceding."
Four-footed means of four kinds. Here, *vyavahāra* refers to the judicial decision. Bṛhaspati states that *vyavahāra* can override *dharma*:
"Where a decision is made by relying solely upon the technical treatises (*śāstra*), that is to be known as *vyavahāra*; by it, *dharma* is set aside."

*Śāstra* refers to the evidence such as witnesses and so forth as declared in the treatises on law (*smṛti*). By means of that *vyavahāra* (legal procedure), one is defeated or sublated. Kātyāyana also says: "But where a matter is joined with reason and divine proof is avoided, there *dharma* is sublated by *vyavahāra*, and not otherwise."
Bṛhaspati states that good conduct (caritra) can override judicial procedure (vyavahāra):
"When a decision is made based on local custom, inference,
or the consensus of merchants, the judicial procedure therein is set aside."

The *naigamas* are the merchants of the city. The terms *naigama-anumatena* and *anumānena* are in apposition. Kātyāyana also states (40–41): "In the case of those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*) and likewise those dwelling in forts, they invariably declare what is contrary [to the general rule]; one should not overturn that custom."
But when the king shall issue a final decision according to that dharma,
then the legal proceeding is superseded by that very conduct.

By that term, "customary practice" (*deśācāra*), Bṛhaspati states that royal edict supersedes established custom: "Where a king, setting aside established custom, issues a decision, that is a royal decree; by it, the custom is superseded."

[This refers to] local custom (*deśācāra*), which is practiced and handed down through tradition. Kātyāyana also says: "But when a practice that is contrary to justice is established by kings, such a practice should be set aside there by the king's command."
If it is thus determined that a practice contrary to justice (*nyāya*) should not be accepted by kings, then by the king's command that practice is set aside; the meaning is that it is annulled.
Vyāsa states what must be done after the decision:
"The king shall punish the defeated party and shall confer honor upon the victor."
The victor’s worship proceeds with perfumes, garlands, garments, and so forth.
Kātyāyana (262): Having joined the plaintiff with the proven matter, the king, preceded by marks of respect, should give him a written document bearing his own hand.

"By the proven matter" means by the wealth that has been established [as due]. "Document" refers to the *jayapatra* (document of victory); its specific nature has been shown in the section defining documents. "Established wealth" means it must be caused to be paid together with its interest. And so says Nārada:
"Whatever property was deposited in the interim, whether movable or immovable, that shall later be made to be paid with interest to the victor, along with the document of victory."
That which was deposited in the interim during the time of dispute is what was placed with the mediator. Kātyāyana states the method for the recovery of wealth:
[130] "The king, however, should cause the Brāhmaṇa to pay the debt to the owner by means of gentle persuasion alone;
but others who are wicked, he should cause to pay by means of coercion according to local custom."
One should cause even an heir or a friend to pay by means of stratagem.

Not only should one defeated by the king be made to pay the debt with interest to the creditor, but he should also be fined by the king himself. If the dispute involved a wager, then the staked amount must also be recovered from him. Thus says Yājñavalkya (2.18):
"If the dispute should involve a wager, the judge should cause the loser to pay it."
The staff, one's own wager, and the wealth itself must be returned to the creditor.
Nārada also says:
"In a dispute involving a counter-stake, whichever of the two parties loses,
he shall be made to pay the stake he himself undertook, as well as a fine for his defeat."

Regarding punishment (*daṇḍa*): when one who has been defeated fails to return the property or other items that were adjudicated [to him], the surety (*tallagnaka*) for that must be made to pay that wealth. If he is dead or absent, his son must be made to pay. And thus Vyāsa says:
"The sons of the two sureties—one for payment and one for dispute—likewise must be made to pay.

Here, "the two sons" refers to the sons of the surety for payment and the surety for dispute. The surety for payment will be shown later; the surety for dispute has already been shown. Nārada states the twofold nature of punishment in the *Parīṣiṣṭa* (53–54):
Punishment is traditionally held to be of two kinds: corporal and monetary.
Corporal punishment is proclaimed to range from flogging to the point of death.
The monetary fine begins at one kākiṇī and extends up to the loss of all property;
likewise, corporal punishment is said to be of ten kinds, while the monetary fine is of many varieties.

The phrase "tenfold" (*daśadhā*) is not an exhaustive enumeration, because other corporeal punishments (*śārīradaṇḍa*), such as branding with a mark (*bandhanāṅkakaraṇa*) and so forth, also exist. Manu indicates some of these corporeal punishments (8.124–125):
"Manu, the son of Svayambhū, has declared ten places for punishment:
the genitals, the stomach, the tongue, the two hands, and the feet as the fifth."
"The eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body;

the *upastha* (genital organ) is the mark of men and women. Regarding these punishments—such as the restraint of the *upastha* and so forth—which concern matters like approaching those who should not be approached (*agamyāgamanādi*), they apply to the Kṣatriyas and other castes, but not to Brāhmaṇas.
"Those [punishments] may apply to the three [lower] castes, but a Brāhmaṇa should depart unhurt. [131]
For this has been stated by that same author (Manu 8.124). Furthermore, regarding a Brāhmaṇa, the punishment is exile, as stated by that same author (Manu 8.380):
"One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is guilty of every possible crime;
one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him with all his wealth and his body unharmed."
Śaṅkha also says:
"For the three [lower] castes, there shall be the seizure of property, execution, imprisonment, banishment, and branding; but for a Brāhmaṇa, [only] these actions.
Here, the word *kriyā* is a separate term. Gautama also states (12.43): "There is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa. As for that which...
For members of all four castes who fail to perform penance,
the king shall prescribe lawful punishment consisting of both corporal and monetary fines.

This statement—that corporal punishment in the form of imprisonment should be inflicted upon one who is excessively arrogant, possesses great wealth, and fails to perform the prescribed expiation—refers specifically to this subject and not to the breaking of limbs and the like, because of the following statement by Hārīta: "The wise do not prescribe the breaking of limbs for a Brāhmaṇa. As for the previously cited statement of Śaṅkha which indicates that imprisonment applies to the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya, that refers to Brāhmaṇas other than those [of the aforementioned type]. Nārada describes the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa as consisting of shaving the head and so forth (Sāhasa 10).
The punishment for him shall be the shaving of the head, banishment from the city,
branding on the forehead with the mark of his crime, and travel upon a donkey.
Regarding that Brāhmaṇa: Manu states that shaving the head serves as a substitute for the execution of a Brāhmaṇa (8.379):
"Shaving the head is ordained as the capital punishment for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the other castes, the punishment may be one that ends in death."
Intending this very point, Bṛhaspati said:
"Even if he is guilty of a mortal sin (mahāpātaka), a Brahmin does not deserve the death penalty;
the king should instead impose banishment, branding, and shaving his head."
Regarding the specific marks for branding, Nārada says (Manu 9.237; Nārada, Pariśiṣṭa 44):
"For violating the Guru’s bed, the mark of a vulva should be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag;
for theft, the footprint of a dog should be made; and for killing a Brāhmaṇa, the figure of a headless man."
Yājñavalkya also mentions other types of punishment (1.367): "The punishment of speech, the punishment of reproach, the punishment of fines, and likewise corporal punishment—
these should be applied individually or collectively according to the nature of the offense."

The punishment of speech (*vāg-daṇḍa*) consists of harsh words; the punishment of reproach (*dhig-daṇḍa*) is the censure "fie! The specific scope of these punishments is to be observed in their respective contexts. The particular types of punishment regarding the titles of law (*vyavahāra-pada*), such as the non-payment of debts (*r̥ṇādāna*) and others, will be shown in the detailed exposition of each. Regarding the determination of victory or defeat through divine ordeals, a specific punishment has been shown by Kātyāyana (vv.
459–461): "He who is purified shall be made to pay half a hundred [paṇas]; he who is not purified shall be subject to the penalty.
This applies in the case of poison, water, fire, the balance, the sacred vessel (*kośa*), and rice."
In the ordeals of the heated ball and the ordeal by balance, one should prescribe punishment in sequence:
one thousand, six hundred, and likewise five hundred [paṇas].
In this manner, one should calculate four, three, two, or even one unit for those of lower status among the lowly.

For a pure person, the payment of fifty [paṇas] is intended as wages (*bhṛti*), and not as a fine (*daṇḍa*). This fine based on the divine ordeal is to be combined with the fine based on denial or a false accusation, because of the conjunction of the grounds for punishment.
In another place, however, Nārada states the application of legal reasoning:
"A legal transaction entered into with women, at night, outside the village, within the house, or with enemies— even if completed, it shall be subject to being done again."

Bṛhaspati says: The argument of one who is defeated is accepted [as lost] due to fleeing, failure to respond, or resorting to another side; however, this does not apply to one who has been defeated by his own statements.
[133] Nārada (Mā 2.40): In the case of witnesses, assessors, or those who have withdrawn, there is a retrial upon their disqualification;
however, for those defeated by their own statements, no rule for a second trial has been declared.

The meaning is that if one loses a case due to the testimony of witnesses or members of the court (*sabhyas*), and subsequently points out defects in them, there shall be a resumption of the legal proceeding; however, if one loses due to their own statement, there is no such resumption. Nārada (Mā 1.65) states that a matter already decided may be reopened by accepting a double fine:
"If anyone considers a decision or a judgment to have been rendered contrary to the law, he may have that matter reopened by imposing a double fine."

"Decided" means brought to a conclusion, determined—that is to say, finalized. "Instructed" means declared by the witnesses. Yājñavalkya (1.305): "But if lawsuits have been wrongly decided, and are reviewed again by the king, the judges, together with the winner, shall be fined double the amount of the dispute."
Those who have been defeated are joined with those who have won. Kātyāyana (496):

But the king should investigate the case of one who, even after being dismissed by his family and others, has not attained satisfaction; he should reconsider what was done and rectify any wrongful act.
"If ministers or the judge should decide a case otherwise than it ought to be,
the king himself shall decide that case and fine them one thousand [paṇas]."
In some instances, Nārada states the rescission of what has been done (*kṛta-nivṛtti*) (Ṛṇādāna 39–41,
29–30): "Whatever transaction a minor (*bāla*) performs, or likewise one who is not independent (*asvatantra*),
that also they declare to be 'not done' (*akṛta*) in the legal treatises, according to those people who are experts in the treatises."
For even that which is independent, if it performs an effect while having fallen into an unnatural state,
they say that too is unproduced, because of its lack of independence.
Those who are overcome by desire and anger, afflicted by distress, fear, and calamity,
and enveloped by passion and hatred, should be known as having fallen into an unnatural state.
[134] Likewise, a task performed by a slave is declared to be as if unperformed, except by the master’s command;
for a slave has no authority over himself.
If a task has been performed by a son that was not according to the father’s will, they say that it is as if it were unperformed; a slave and a son are equal in this regard.
Nārada states [in *Ṛṇādāna* 33–37] regarding those who are not independent:
"A pupil is declared to be dependent upon his teacher;
all women, sons, slaves, and dependents are dependent."
A child (śiśu) should be known as being similar to one in the womb until the eighth year;
a boy (bāla) is proclaimed to be so until the sixteenth year, and thereafter he is called a youth (pogaṇḍa).
One who is knowledgeable in legal affairs is independent after the death of the father;
while both parents are alive, he shall not be independent, even if he is advanced in age.
Of those two as well, the father is superior, because the importance of the seed is observed;
in the absence of the progenitor, the mother [is superior], and in her absence, the elder brother.

"Parigrahas" refers to the attendants. The singular form "of the father" (*pitur*) is Vedic; its meaning is "of the parents," as will be stated later. "Until death" means starting from the time of death. Kātyāyana (466):

"The father is not independent [in this regard], nor is one who has a father, nor a brother, nor even a nephew, nor a younger brother who has divided his property, nor a slave, nor likewise an attendant."

"Dependent on the father" (*pitṛsvatantra*) means that one who has a father is not independent while the father is alive, even if he has produced sons; "having undivided property" (*avibhaktasva*) means having undivided wealth. Regarding the fact that transactions made even by sons and others who are dependent are not nullified, the same author states (Kāṭ. 468–470): "All these [dependents] are authoritative in the buying and selling of commodities, provided they have previously engaged in such trade and their actions were approved."
In the same manner, the brother, the brother’s son, or the son may act as representatives for the field and other assets,
having been authorized by the elder who is departing on a journey to perform necessary duties.
But he to whom a matter has been entrusted and who is its master in that matter is its lord;
he ought not to undo the business performed by him.
[135] Bṛhaspati also says:
"He who is appointed by a master to the management of income and expenditure,
as well as to money-lending, agriculture, and trade, is known as one to whom the matter has been entrusted (nisr̥ṣṭārtha)."
"Whatever has been done by him [the judge] is authoritative regarding all gain, loss, expenditure, and income, whether in one's own country or abroad; the master shall not contradict that.
Thus, Bṛhaspati demonstrates the fruit for a king who renders a decision according to the manner described.
Thus, a king should carry out the preservation of judicial decisions as taught in the scriptures;
by spreading his fame throughout this world, he shall become a minister to Mahendra.
By settling legal cases through the testimony of witnesses, written documents, and inference,
a king spreads his fame in this world and attains the realm of the Sun.
Thus concludes the exposition on the determination of the legal issues.
Thus ends the exposition on the *Vyavahāramātṛkā* (the Matrix of Legal Proceedings) within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* [composed by] the illustrious Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma. 15.

**Possible reading of the defective text:** In the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "Śrīkodaṇḍa-Paraśurāma"— this is the fourteenth chapter, the Exposition of the Categories of Legal Procedure (*vyavahāramātṛkānirūpaṇam*), within the Illumination of the Analysis of Legal Procedure (*vyavahāravivekoddyota*).

Now, the titles of legal procedure (*vyavahārapada*), beginning with the non-payment of debt (*r̥ṇādāna*), are defined. Among these, first the primary title of legal procedure called "non-payment of debt" is defined. Nārada shows its essential nature (*svarūpa*) [in *R̥ṇādāna* 1]:
"The debt that is to be paid and that which is not to be paid, by whom, where, in what manner, and what [it is]..."
The rules concerning the giving and receiving of gifts, as well as the non-payment of debts, are recorded in the Smṛti.

The meaning is that this title of legal dispute called *ṛṇādāna* (non-payment of debt) refers to that subject matter of litigation which concerns all matters related to the repayment of a debt by the debtor—such as "this much debt is to be paid," "this much is not to be paid," "it is to be paid by this person," "it is to be paid at this time," or "it is to be paid in this manner"—as well as the rules regarding the giving and receiving of gifts related to the creditor. Since the acts of repayment and receipt are preceded by the act of giving, this sequence of recitation is not intended to be significant. Bṛhaspati describes the manner of giving a debt:
"Having received a pledge or a mortgage in its entirety, along with a virtuous guarantor..."
The creditor shall always pay back the debt, whether it be recorded in writing or witnessed by witnesses.

"Complete" means sufficient for the principal amount together with the interest. "Pledge" (*ādhi*) means a security. The specific distinction regarding that will be shown later. By the word "pledge" (*bandha*), what is intended here is the object deposited by the debtor in the hand of a third party chosen by him for the sake of the creditor's confidence. Regarding this meaning, the word *bandha* was employed by Nārada:
"A deposit placed in the hand of a friend is known as a pledge for the purpose of inspiring confidence."

The meaning is that a "deposit" (*nikṣepa*) is a pledge (*bandha*) held in the hand of a friend for the sake of creating trust; a "surety" (*lagnaka*) is a guarantor (*pratibhū*). The specific distinction between these will be shown later. The meaning is that the creditor (*uttamarṇa*), having received a full pledge, a superior pledge, or a surety, shall deliver the debt either as recorded in a document written by the debtor's own hand or accompanied by witnesses. While explaining the meaning of the word *kusīda*—which is a synonym for the word *ṛṇa* (debt)—Nārada demonstrates its purpose under that pretext in verse 98 of the *Ṛṇādāna*.
That which is intended as the acceptance of gifts for the sake of obtaining a position should be known as usury; by that, the livelihood of usurers is defined.

*Sthāna* is the preservation of the principal capital; *lābha* is the interest or profit. Bṛhaspati explains the etymological meaning of the word *kusīda*: "Because it is seized by those who are undaunted from that which is base (*kutsita*) and from that which decays (*sīdat*), therefore this debt is called *kusīda*, [yielding] fourfold or eightfold [interest]."

The words *kutsitāt* (from one who is contemptible) and *sīdataḥ* (from one who is in distress) are qualifiers of the debtor; he [Yājñavalkya] himself states the various modes of interest according to different opinions.
Growth is said to be fourfold by some, proclaimed as fivefold by others, and described by me as sixfold; therefore, learn it from me as such.
In my opinion, he himself demonstrates those three types:
bodily interest, periodic interest, and the wheel-interest which is different from these;
as well as stipulated interest, interest on the principal, and likewise interest on profits.
He himself shows the nature of these [types of interest]:
"Corporeal interest is connected with labor; monthly interest is to be taken month by month;
interest upon interest is 'wheel-interest' (cakravṛddhi); and that which is stipulated by the debtor is 'contracted interest' (kāritā)."
That which is received daily is known as the increase of the crest (śikhā-vr̥ddhi).
Satisfaction from the house is proclaimed as the fruit, and the acquisition of enjoyment from the field is likewise declared.

The meaning of *kāyikā* (bodily interest) is as follows: it is that interest which, together with the enjoyment consisting of acts such as milking or driving, belongs to one who has established [the loan] on the basis of the object being enjoyed. For this very reason, Vyāsa says:
"That which is joined with the act of milking or driving is declared to be *kāyikā*."

In the *Smṛticandrikā*, however, it is stated that where physical labor—such as milking cows, horses, and the like, which have been made into collateral—is calculated as interest, that interest is called "bodily" (*kāyikā*). As for "periodical" (*kālikā*), the meaning is that it is an interest to be taken month by month, calculated as being receivable every month. For this very reason, Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 103) says:
"That interest which flows month by month is considered periodical."
When interest itself accrues further interest month by month upon the principal, that is *cakravṛddhi* (compound interest). For this very reason, Nārada says:
"Interest upon interest is declared to be *cakravṛddhi*.
*Kāritā* means interest made by the debtor; the meaning is that it is interest established by the will of the debtor, the *adhamarṇa*.

"That interest which is called 'caused' (*kāritā*) is that which is personally agreed upon by the debtor," according to the statement of Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 103). Kātyāyana (498) states that only the interest caused by the debtor is to be paid, not that caused by the creditor:
"But whatever additional interest has been stipulated by the debtor..."
But that which is performed during a time of distress must always be given as a loan at the borrower's request.

Interest stipulated otherwise must never be paid. Interest known as *kāritā*—which, for the purpose of enticing the creditor during times of distress, is voluntarily agreed upon by the debtor even if it exceeds the rate prescribed by the scriptures—must be paid. "Otherwise" means that what was not voluntarily agreed upon—that is, what was stipulated at a higher rate by the creditor himself—need not be paid. The phrase "taken every day" is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the time for taking interest associated with the number of days promised by the debtor. For this very reason, Kātyāyana (499) has made a reference to time alone.
"He indeed gives [interest] at the proper time; that is known as *śikhā-vr̥ddhi*.
The similarity of this interest to a crest (*śikhā*) has been stated by Bṛhaspati himself:
"It increases constantly like a crest, but it ceases upon the cutting off of the head."
When the root is given in that same manner, this is traditionally known as the "increase of the crest" (śikhā-vṛddhi).

The satisfaction arising from residing in a house that has been taken as a pledge, or the fruit consisting of crops and the like from a field—that is the interest known as *bhogalābha* (gain through enjoyment). Thus, the meaning of the phrase "satisfaction from a house" is as follows. However, in the *Kalpataru*, having read: "Satisfaction (*stoma*) from a house, and *sada* from a field, is proclaimed as *bhogalābha*," it is explained that "*stoma*" means rent (*bhāṭaka*) and "*sada*" means the fruit of crops and the like. The mention of "house and field" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all immovable property (*sthāvara*) held as a pledge for enjoyment.
But that which is designated as interest is entirely usufructuary;
wherever such a thing occurs in a loan, it is called *ādhibhoga*.

Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Kātyāyana (501): "In whatever transaction for the recovery of a debt, where the enjoyment of the pledge alone is calculated as interest in relation to immovable property, there that interest is called 'pledge-enjoyment' (*ādhibhoga*). This is the meaning. Regarding the measure of interest, Yājñavalkya (2.37) says:
"The monthly interest shall be one-eightieth part [of the principal] when there is a pledge;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent per month."

In a loan secured by a pledge (*sabandhaka*), the interest (*vṛddhi*) is the eightieth part of the principal amount lent. This means that when one hundred *paṇas* are lent, one and a quarter *paṇas* increase per month. "Otherwise" refers to the case where there is no pledge. According to the order of the castes (*varṇakramāt*)—that is, according to the sequence of the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa—the amounts are two, three, four, and five [per cent]; that is, two, three, four, and five additional [paṇas] per hundred. The suffix *kan* is applied here according to Pāṇini 5.1.47: *tad asmin vṛddhyāya lābhaśulkopadā dīyate*. Thus, the meaning is that in a loan of one hundred *paṇas* without a pledge, two *paṇas* per month may be taken from a Brāhmaṇa, three from a Kṣatriya, four from a Vaiśya, and five from a Śūdra. Vyāsa states the limit of interest for a loan accompanied by a guarantor (*pratibhū*).
[139] When there is a pledge, the interest is one-eighth; when there is a mortgage, it is one-sixth.
In the case of an unsecured loan, a monthly profit of two percent is declared.

"In connection with a pledge" means secured by a pledge. "Aśītaḥ" means the eightieth; "ṣāṣṭaḥ" means the sixtieth. "Lagnakaḥ" means a guarantor (*pratibhū*). The mention of "pledge" (*ādhāna*) is also indicative of the guarantor. In the *Kalpataru*, however, reading "sāṣṭabhāgaḥ," it is stated that when there is a guarantor, the monthly interest is the eightieth part together with one's own eighth part. As for the verse: "A moneylender may take the eightieth part from a hundred per month, or he may take two percent, remembering the law of the virtuous."

In this statement by Manu (8.140–141), the alternative option of "two per cent" is permitted; however, based on the previously cited text, that should be established as referring to cases where no security has been provided. Regarding the amount of interest, Yājñavalkya (2.38) states another measure in certain cases:
"Those traveling through forests [should pay] ten percent, while those traveling by sea [should pay] twenty percent."

The verb "they shall give" (*dadyuḥ*) from the subsequent sentence is to be supplied here. The meaning is that those traveling on difficult roads after taking a loan shall pay ten *paṇas* per month as interest on a hundred *paṇas*, while those going by sea shall pay twenty *paṇas*. He (the author of the Yājñavalkya-smṛti) states another alternative view, characterized by the acceptance of stipulated interest, that all debtors—beginning with Brāhmaṇas—whether lending with or without collateral, shall pay the interest they themselves have agreed upon to creditors of any caste (YDh 2.38).
"Or they may pay the interest agreed upon by themselves, regardless of all types of debts or species [of the object]. Thus [it is said].

A specific rule regarding interest for cattle and other livestock, as well as female slaves, when given as a form of debt, has been stated by that same author (YDh 2.39): "But the offspring of livestock and women [is the interest]. And the giving of cattle and such as a debt is possible; one who is unable to maintain them might take them with the intent of obtaining their growth and progeny, while one who desires milk, transport, service, and so forth, would accept them. Regarding the fact that interest must sometimes be paid even when not explicitly stipulated, Viṣṇu says (6.40): [text omitted].
He who, having taken a loan with the agreement "I shall repay the whole amount tomorrow," does not pay it later out of greed, shall incur interest for that very day.

[140] "Tomorrow" (*śvaḥ*) is an indicative term for the time-limit set for the repayment of what has been promised. "Evenly" (*sāmakam*) means at the same time. The meaning is that if one, having taken a loan after promising, "I will give you your wealth back on such-and-such a day equally," should subsequently delay out of greed, he must pay interest starting from the date of that deadline. Kātyāyana states that if someone, having borrowed money by requesting it to perform his own business, should go to another country without returning it, then that wealth begins to accrue interest after one year has passed. (502)
If one who has taken a borrowed item should depart for another region without returning it,
that property shall accrue interest for him after the lapse of one year.

This rule, however, concerns property that has not been formally requested. If one who has been requested fails to return a borrowed item and departs for another country, then after three months that wealth begins to accrue interest; so it was stated by that same author (Kātyāyana, 503):
"If one who has been requested, having made an advance but failing to repay it, should depart for another region, after three months his debt shall begin to bear interest."

The syntactical connection is as follows: having made a deduction (*uddhāra*) and having taken what was borrowed, even when requested [to return it], he does not give it back. He himself (Kātyāyana, verse 504) states that if, having taken what was borrowed, he remains there and does not return it even when asked to do so, he shall pay interest on that wealth starting from the day of the request:
"But he who, though residing in his own country, does not give when requested at any time..."
One should compel him to pay that interest which was caused to accrue, even if he is unwilling.

Therefore, from that day forward, all of this should be understood to apply when a loan is obtained without having fixed any specific term. However, if a term is accepted and it is exceeded, interest on that capital must be known to begin from that very day; for the maxim "one shall obtain interest starting from that day" applies equally here. Regarding that which is given out of affection by friends and others at weddings and similar occasions for the sake of splendor and so forth, Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 108) states that even if it is taken without a fixed interest being stipulated, it begins to increase after six months.
Interest on gifts made out of affection shall never accrue if not requested;
however, even if unrequested, it increases after half a year has passed.
"Unsummoned" means not brought forward. Regarding the non-payment of what was given out of affection or requested, Kātyāyana states (505):
[141] "That which is given out of affection shall not increase until it has been requested;
if, when being requested, it is not returned, it increases by five percent per month."

"Five more than five" means that for every hundred *paṇas*, an additional five *paṇas* increase every month starting from the day the loan was requested. Regarding the interest on a purchased commodity when one departs for another country without paying its price, the same author (Kātyāyana, 507) says: "He who, having taken merchandise, should depart for another region without paying the price, shall pay interest on that debt after three seasons have passed."

And this [interest] is to be understood as applicable if the seller has not requested it; however, if he has requested it, then for that [loan], for the remainder of the interest, and for deposited goods, starting from the day of the request, five percent per month accrues—so says the same author (Kāt. 506): "A deposit, the remainder of interest, and likewise in the case of purchase and sale—if these are not returned when requested, they increase by five percent per hundred."

In this case, where interest has not been stipulated and no specific measure such as "one hundred and five" is taught, the measure stated by Yājñavalkya—that the interest shall be one-eighth part—should be adopted. For this very reason, Viṣṇu (6.3–4) states: "They shall pay interest even if it was not stipulated, upon the lapse of a year, as prescribed. The meaning of "as prescribed" is "as declared by the scriptures," that is, of that kind. Regarding certain exceptions to unstipulated interest, Nārada (Mā. 2.36) says:

The price of goods, wages, deposits, fines, and whatever has been specifically determined— as well as gifts made in vain, stakes at dice, and gambling bets— do not increase unless they are intended to do so.

The price of merchandise is the value of what has been purchased; wages are remuneration; a deposit is a pledge. A gift made in vain is that which is promised to actors and the like. The stake of a gambler is the gambling material. Those [items] not intended for mention are those where interest was not promised. Here, the statement regarding the absence of interest on the price of merchandise should be understood to apply when there is neither travel nor a formal request for repayment. Regarding a deposit, the absence of interest applies when there is no request for repayment, based on the previously cited statement of Kātyāyana: "A deposit and the remainder of interest on what was pledged."

[142] There is no interest on woman's property, nor on a profit, nor on what has been cast away and remains as it is, nor on a doubtful debt, nor on a suretyship, unless it be one contracted by the debtor herself.

This should be understood from the statement of Saṃvarta and from the absence of any change in the specific nature of the transaction. *Lābha* means interest. Regarding a doubtful suretyship—where there is doubt as to whether it is appropriate or inappropriate to provide the money for the payment of a debt or other obligations—Vyāsa states that in some other cases there is no interest: "Interest does not accrue on a suretyship for which the debt has been enjoyed, nor on one not yet received, nor on a fine or a promised fee when the debtor has surrendered himself."

The phrase "enjoyed pledge" (*bhuktabandha*) is intended to mean that no interest accrues on items such as clothing or ornaments when they have been used as a pledge by way of deposit. For this very reason, Gautama (12.29) stated: "A pledge that has been enjoyed, such as clothing or ornaments, does not increase. And the phrase "if he wishes to give it back without having taken [it]" is an exception to the rule regarding established interest. The meaning is that if the creditor, out of greed for interest or other motives, does not take back the item from the debtor even though the latter desires to return it, then the interest already stipulated shall not be paid. Thus says Yājñavalkya (2.44):
When one's own wealth that has been lent out is not accepted when being offered back, it shall remain deposited with a neutral third party; it does not increase beyond that point.

Because of the qualification "deposited by a neutral third party," if the debtor were to deposit it in his own hand, interest would indeed accrue. Regarding a debt that has been paid and remains outstanding for a long time without the taking of interest month by month or year by year, Bṛhaspati states the maximum interest according to the difference in the substance:
"Interest on gold is double; on clothes and base metals, triple;
on grain, fourfold; and likewise on beasts of burden and wool."
It is said that [the potency] in leafy vegetables (śāka) is fivefold; in seeds and sugarcane, it is traditionally held to be sixfold;
in salts, fats, and liquors, an eightfold increase is considered appropriate when used over a long period; and this is likewise stated for molasses and honey when administered over a long duration.
Base metals (*kupya*) refer to tin, lead, and so forth. *Sada* refers to the produce of the field, such as flowers, fruits, roots, and the like.

[143] Although grain is also the produce of the field, it is mentioned separately according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull. "External" (*bāhya*) refers to horses and the like.
