"Wool" (*lava*) refers to wool, yak-tail hair, and so forth. As for that which, whether grain, wool, or an external animal, does not exceed the number five—

This statement of Manu (8.151) is intended to prohibit [the application of] the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) and so forth. However, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* says that it refers to a case where the debtor has become wealthy at the very time the debt is to be returned. Here, by the word "long period" (*cirakāla*), a duration exceeding that time at which the promised interest—such as the one-eighth part (*aśītibhāga*) and so on—reaches the point of doubling the principal is understood. Vasiṣṭha also states that for diamonds (*vajra*), mother-of-pearl (*śukti*), corals (*pravāla*), gold, and silver, the interest is desired to be twofold, following the agreed-upon time limit: "For diamonds, mother-of-pearl, corals, gold, and silver, a twofold interest is prescribed, provided it conforms to the fixed time."

In this context, by the word *śukti* (oyster shell), the pearl is indicated due to its association with the diamond (*vajra*). For this very reason, Kātyāyana (510) states: "The interest on gems, pearls, corals, gold, silver, and also on silk, woven cloth, and wool is double."

*Kaiṭa* refers to that which originates from insects, such as silk thread and the like; *āvika* refers to woolen products, such as blankets and the like. Regarding copper and other metals, Vasiṣṭha states that the interest is threefold:
"For copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin, and lead, the interest remains at threefold after a long period of time has passed."
*Rīti* refers to brass. Vyāsa states that for cotton, the interest is sixfold:
"For vegetables, cotton-seeds, and sugarcane, a sixfold increase is proclaimed.
Kātyāyana states that for oil and similar items, the interest is eightfold. (511)
The increase for all types of oils, as well as for liquors, clarified butter,
jaggery, and salt, should be known to be eightfold.
Vyāsa also says: "They say that at the proper time, liquors made from grain, oil, meat, and molasses possess eight qualities."

* Sneha refers to oil and the like; *rasa* refers to liquids such as milk and the like. Viṣṇu (6.11–15) states: “The interest on gold is twofold, on cloth threefold, on grain fourfold, on liquids eightfold, and for women and cattle, it is offspring. As for the statement in the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti* (2.44–47)—“Grain is threefold by means of grain alone; liquids, flowers, roots, and fruits are explained in the same way; that which is weighed on a scale is eightfold”—the mention of a threefold rate for grain and so forth applies specifically to those regions where it is the established custom that only a threefold amount of grain and the like must be paid back. “That which is weighed on a scale” (*tulādhr̥tam*) refers to sugar and similar substances. In this manner, there are other [texts] as well which establish maximum rates of interest that are either lower or higher.

"The maximum [interest] on clothes, grain, and gold is four, three, and two times [the principal], respectively"—such statements by Yājñavalkya and others (YDh 2.39) are to be applied as referring to specific regions. Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 105–106) has stated that the distinction in the maximum interest arises from differences in local custom: "This rule for the accumulation of interest is recorded as being universally applicable to debts."
But the established custom of the region is another matter, wherein the debt remains.
"Twofold, threefold, and likewise fourfold in another;
likewise eightfold in yet another—thus the interest remains fixed according to the region.
Viṣṇu (6.17) states: "For those for whom a rate such as twofold is not prescribed, a twofold rate is to be understood," saying: "For those not mentioned, it is twofold."

It should be understood that this cessation of interest in the form of doubling and so forth occurs only if the interest has not been transferred to another person or converted into principal. Therefore, if the debtor causes another person to accept the interest by saying, "I shall pay it," or if he himself accepts it as principal, or if the creditor, having obtained the debtor's consent, takes his own wealth by making that interest a pledge with some other person, then from that day until its repayment, that debt continues to increase. For this very reason, Manu (8.151) states:
Interest on a loan, when lent at once, shall not exceed double the principal if the creditor remains idle.

*Kusīda* is debt; its *vṛddhi* (interest) is *kusīdavṛddhi*. The mention of "doubling" (*dvaiguṇya*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for tripling (*traiguṇya*) and so forth. "Laid out once" (*sakṛd āhitā*) means employed once, that is, without being subjected to another transaction such as transfer to another person. Some, however, read *sakṛd āhr̥tā*; in that case, the meaning is this: if it is not taken month by month or year by year, but rather is taken all at once, then it does not exceed the state of doubling. By this, it is indicated that in the absence of taking it all at once, it does exceed doubling. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says that in some cases there is no cessation of interest.
The growth of grass, wood, bricks, thread, yeast, leather, bone, armor, weapons, flowers, and fruits does not cease.

*Kiṇva* is a specific kind of fermenting agent that serves as the cause for producing *sura*. *Carman* is a shield used for warding off arrows and the like. *Varman* is armor. *Hetis* is a weapon. Vasiṣṭha says:
"The growth of ivory, leather, bone, horn, as well as earthenware, and likewise of flowers, roots, and fruits, is inexhaustible."

Viṣṇu (6.16) states: “There is no cessation [of interest] on fermenting agents, cotton, thread, leather, armor, weapons, bricks, and charcoal. In this regard, the statement that there is no cessation of the increase of flowers, fruits, and cotton refers either to the case of an extremely prosperous debtor or to a specific region; thus, it does not contradict the previously cited texts. Bṛhaspati declares the non-cessation of interest on the crest-lock (*śikhā-vṛddhi*) and so forth: “The creditor may continue to collect the crest-interest, bodily labor, and likewise the profit from enjoyment, as long as the principal has not been cleared.”
It has neither been cleared nor returned.
Bṛhaspati shows the nature of a pledge (ādhi) and its classifications:
"A pledge is declared to be a bond (bandha), and it is said to be of four kinds."
Both movable and immovable property, as well as that which is merely to be guarded and that which is to be enjoyed.
Whether spontaneous or with a fixed term, whether recorded in writing or witnessed by witnesses;

Although eight types of pledge (*ādhi*) have been shown, the *Smṛticandrikā* states that they are described as being of four kinds in order to emphasize their primary importance here for the sake of various practical applications, and not because the others do not exist. A pledge (*ādhi*) is so called because it is "placed" (*dhīyate*) or "deposited" (*sthāpyate*) with a creditor by a debtor for the sake of inspiring confidence regarding the money received. It is "to be guarded" (*gopya*), meaning it must be protected. It is "at will" (*yādr̥cchika*), meaning it is established without a fixed term. It is "with a term" (*sāvadhi*), meaning it is established having set a limit such as: "On such-and-such a day I shall repay the debt and release this pledge; otherwise, it shall belong to you alone. Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 124–25) demonstrates these four principal varieties.
That which is pledged is known as *ādhi*; it should be understood as having two characteristics:
that for which a time limit has been set, and that which remains until the debt is paid.

Furthermore, that [pledge] is said to be of two kinds: the secret (*gopya*) and likewise the one for use (*bhogya*). "Adhi" means it is placed above or established. "To be delivered at a fixed time" (*kr̥takālopaneya*) means it is to be brought near, or the debtor is to be released, once the appointed time limit has been reached. "As long as the debt remains to be paid" (*yāvaddeyodyata*) means it is established without a time limit as long as the debt persists. Regarding the pledge received, it must be maintained according to the agreement; otherwise, there is a loss of interest or a loss of the principal. Thus says Hārīta.
One should maintain a bond exactly as it has been established;
otherwise, by transgressing that, one's profit or even one's capital is lost.

"From its transgression" means from the transgression of the agreement (*samaya*). Here, the mention of "increase" (*vṛddhi*) and "decrease" (*hāni*) should be understood as referring to the enjoyment of a pledge (*ādhi*) that was established for the purpose of secrecy. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya (2.59) states: "There is no interest on the enjoyment of a pledge kept in custody; likewise, [no interest] when a pledge with benefit is lost. The meaning is: even upon the slightest enjoyment of a pledge kept in custody, no interest whatsoever should be paid; and in the case of a pledge with benefit—that is, a pledge to be used—when it is "lost," meaning rendered unfit for transaction, no interest should be paid, even if it was originally subject to interest. And this refers specifically to cases of forceful seizure. Thus says Manu (8.144):
A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.

The meaning is that for the debtor who, having transgressed the creditor’s command, uses the pledge despite the prohibition against its use, there is an extreme offense such that even a small amount of use results in the loss of all interest. However, in the absence of forceful compulsion, it has been stated by that same author (Manu 8.150):
"The foolish man who uses a pledge without the permission of the owner..."
Therefore, half an increase must be released as compensation for that enjoyment.

The mention of "half" (*ardha*) is an illustration for the portion of interest calculated in accordance with the unauthorized use of the pledge (*ādhi*). As for the statement of Bṛhaspati which speaks of the loss of the principal, that refers to a case of forced use or non-use, as stated in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Some hold it refers to the subject of the destruction of the pledge. Kātyāyana states a specific rule regarding the employment of a female slave or similar property deposited as a pledge for protection (*gopyādhi*): (525) He who, without desire and without permission, causes labor to be performed on a pledge, [is liable].
The enjoyer shall be made to pay the fruit of the action, or he shall not receive the interest.

"Unwillingly" means without desire. "Fruit of the work" refers to wages. "He shall be made to pay"—the remainder is that it is to the debtor. Thus, when a horse or similar object has been placed as a pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*), its rental fee must be made over, or interest (*vṛddhi*) must be relinquished. Regarding one who causes either kind of pledge to undergo alteration or the like, Yājñavalkya says (2.59):
"If [the pledge] is lost or destroyed, except by act of God or the king, it must be restored."

If [the pledge] is lost or has undergone transformation, it should be restored by making it as it was before. If it is destroyed—meaning it has reached total ruin—it must also be restored by means of its value or other such compensation. The meaning is that this does not apply in cases of destruction caused by divine forces, such as fire, water, or natural calamities, nor by the king. Regarding the loss of profit when the pledge itself is returned in a transformed state, Nārada says (Ṛṇādāna 125–126): "In the same way, there is a loss of profit for him [the creditor] in the opposite case; likewise, if the pledge undergoes transformation through the negligence of the debtor."

In the same manner, the treatment—that is, the legal procedure—regarding this pledge (*ādhi*) occurs precisely through the transgression of its conditions. In the opposite case, there is loss of interest. Likewise, the meaning is that when the pledge undergoes deterioration due to the negligence of the creditor (*dhanin*), there is a loss of profit. Bṛhaspati states that if [the pledge] has reached a state of deterioration through use and is returned in that very condition, there is a loss of the principal (*mūla*). Vyāsa says that upon the destruction of the pledge, its value must be paid.
If the pledge, such as gold or other valuables, has been destroyed due to the fault of the borrower,
the creditor, having recovered the debt along with its interest, shall cause the value of that pledge to be paid.

The meaning is that after clearing the debt along with the profit (*salābham*), and having properly investigated the matter, one should pay the value of the lost pledge; if there remains anything among the debts owed by the debtor, then that [remainder] should be taken. Regarding the loss of a pledge when its principal value, including interest, has been exhausted, Nārada says (Ṛṇādāna 126):
"If [the pledge] is destroyed, the principal shall be lost, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
Hārīta also says:

"When the pledge is lost, the wealth is lost, or the pledge itself belongs to the creditor. Regarding this, in the event of the loss of a pledge of high value relative to the principal and interest, one should pay the principal along with the interest and also pay the remainder of the value. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"In a case where a pledge of high value is lost, [the debtor] should satisfy the creditor there."
Manu also says (8.144):

"He should satisfy him with the value [of the pledge]; otherwise, he who steals the pledge becomes liable to punishment. Kātyāyana states that the creditor who, even upon the loss of the pledge, desires to seize wealth from the debtor by relying on the promissory note, is to be punished. (528)
When a creditor enjoys the use of a pledge by means of a fraudulent document from the debtor,
the king, having caused him to pay a fine, shall cause that pledge-document to be destroyed.

Damadaṇḍa (Punishment for Damage). When a pledge is destroyed due to acts of God or the king, the debtor shall give another pledge along with the interest to the creditor; or else, he shall pay the debt together with the interest. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"Where a pledge may meet its destruction through an act of God or the king, there the debtor shall cause another pledge to be given, or he shall pay the debt together with the interest."
"Royal calamity" refers to a disaster caused by a king who has become unrestrained, and not one resulting from the fault of the creditor. For this very reason, Vyāsa stated:
"In the event of calamity caused by fate or the king, there is never any fault on the part of the creditor.

Likewise, when a loss occurs due to causes such as thieves or one's own kinsmen, since there is no fault of the creditor, the debt or another pledge must be provided. For this very reason, Kātyāyana [says] (524):
If, however, [the debtor] should fall into misfortune or die due to a fault of the creditor,
the debtor shall be released from the debt, and the creditor shall be made to provide another pledge.

[Nipatet] means it would fall down; [naśyet] means it would perish; [mriyeta] means with the intention that it might die, referring to livestock and the like. Therefore, the meaning is that if the pledge is not returned, one shall not be released from that debt. Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 130) states that even if a pledge is being properly maintained, if it becomes worthless, the debtor must provide the value or another pledge: "If, despite being maintained, a pledge should become worthless over time, then another pledge must be provided, or the wealth of the creditor must be paid."
Regarding worthlessness—the state of the original property being insufficient to cover the interest along with the principal—Yājñavalkya (2.60) also states:

"The validity of a pledge arises from its acceptance; even while being guarded, if it reaches a state of worthlessness, another pledge must be provided, or the creditor shall become a sharer in the debtor's wealth."
The meaning is that the establishment [of ownership] over a pledge (*ādhi*) results from its acceptance or its enjoyment, not by the document alone.
And so says Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 139):
"A pledge is said to be of two kinds: movable as well as immovable."
The accomplishment of both of these occurs if there is enjoyment; it is not otherwise.

In the case of a pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*), "use" (*bhoga*) means physical possession; in the case of a pledge for enjoyment (*bhogyādhi*), it means the enjoyment of the fruit (*phalabhoga*). This demonstration of the validity [of ownership] through the use of the pledge is for the purpose of establishing the legal decision stated in such passages as: "In the case of a pledge, a gift, or a purchase, the prior [title] is indeed more powerful" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.23). For this very reason, Viṣṇu (5.184) states that when a debtor, being wicked, offers a pledge to two creditors, the decision is made on the basis of possession (*bhoga*).
When two men dispute over a pledge that has been deposited with them,
victory belongs to him whose possession has been established without force.
Regarding the method of decision when both parties possess equal rights to enjoyment, Bṛhaspati says:
"When a single field has been mortgaged to two parties at the same time, it shall belong to that one by whom it was first enjoyed; he shall obtain its established ownership."
The mention of "field" is illustrative [of other property]. Vasiṣṭha also says:
"When documents for the act of pledging are produced at the same time, that pledge which has been possessed first is the stronger."

The phrase "even though there exists" is to be understood as referring to documents that have been executed and delivered. Regarding the case where both parties, having made a single field a pledge, point it out, and it comes into the possession of both simultaneously for the purpose of enjoyment, Vasiṣṭha says:
"If the two should arrive on the same day desiring to enjoy it, the pledge must be enjoyed by them equally; this is the settled rule."
The word *tena* [is used] for those two; the substitution of *su* for *sa* is Vedic. Kātyāyana has stated the punishment for a debtor who makes a single pledge subject to both creditors (517):
"If one should make a single pledge subject to two [creditors], what should be the course of action?
Of those two, that which was made first is to be accepted; the maker thereof shall be liable to the punishment of a thief."
Viṣṇu states the specific punishment for a specific type of pledge (5.181–182):
"He who gives land pledged to one person to another when it exceeds the measure of a cow-hide is to be executed; if it is less than that, he shall be fined sixteen suvarṇas."

If a pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*) is not released until the principal debt has doubled, and if a pledge with a fixed term (*sāvadhi*)—whether for custody or for use (*bhogyādhi*)—is not released by the expiration of the stipulated time, then it is lost to the debtor and becomes the property of the creditor. However, a pledge for use without a fixed term (*niravadhika bhogyādhi*) never becomes the property of the creditor; as Yājñavalkya (2.58) states:
"A pledge for custody is lost when the debt has doubled, provided it is not released;
one made for a fixed period is lost at the end of that time, but a pledge for use is never lost."

The meaning is: "when the time limit has arrived. It is "time-determined" (kālakṛta), meaning one for which a limit has been set. According to the statement of the author of the *Vārttika*, "The word following [the compound] is placed last after words denoting genus, time, pleasure, and so forth," the past participle (*niṣṭhānta*) is placed at the end of the compound. Vyāsa and Bṛhaspati state that after the debt has doubled and after the time limit has passed, one must wait fourteen days before releasing the pledge:
"When the gold has doubled and the time limit set by the agreement has expired, the creditor becomes the owner of the pledge; however, he must wait for two weeks (fourteen days)."
Having paid that amount in the interim, the debtor shall obtain release from the pledge.

"The creditor" (dhanī) refers to the lender (uttamarṇaḥ). "For that reason" (tat) means for that cause. "In the interim" (antarā) means within the fourteen days; however, when the full term has expired and the profit has ceased, the owner of the pledge becomes the creditor.
But before ten days have passed, the debtor ought to be released.

Thus, the statement of Bṛhaspati prescribing a ten-day waiting period refers to items such as clothing, whereas the statement of Vyāsa and Bṛhaspati regarding gold refers specifically to gold, since it is stated therein: "when the gold has doubled [in value]."

When the profit has ceased due to the maximum increase of threefold interest and so forth, it is said "when the profit has ceased. And this payment of double the amount is to be understood as occurring after three fortnights have passed. Thus say Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana: "If one who has been pressed for payment gives a surety, he is entitled to receive double that amount after three fortnights have elapsed. (Kāt. 539)

*Prātibhāvya* refers to becoming a surety, and *prātibhāvyāgataṃ dhanam* is the wealth received on account of being a surety. One who has been made a surety (*pratibhū*) by virtue of his status as such must, after three fortnights have passed, pay double the amount; this rule regarding doubling applies specifically to gold. However, items such as clothing and the like must be returned together with the maximum interest previously specified for each. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya (2.57) demonstrates the maximum interest payable by a surety: "In the case of female slaves and cattle, offspring [is the interest]; grain is tripled; clothing is declared to be fourfold; and liquids are traditionally held to be eightfold."
Bṛhaspati states the method for recovering a debt that has been granted:
"A debtor who has acknowledged the debt should be made to pay through conciliatory means and other such approaches,
as well as by means of moral pressure, stratagems, force, and confinement in the house."

One who has entered upon the obligation and is currently fulfilling it; "should be made to pay" means he should be induced to give by means of "expedients," that is, by various methods. These methods have been shown in detail through the passage beginning with "the acquisition of dharma" (*dharmopadhi*) and so forth. By "imprisonment at home" [160], the method known as *ācarita* (customary practice) is indicated. He himself shows the nature of these four expedients, beginning with *dharma*:
"By means of messages sent through friends and relatives, and by following the path of conciliation (*sāma*), a debtor should generally be made to pay; this is declared to be the rule of *dharma*."
Where a creditor, having requested a debt under a pretext,
brings back the object from the debtor after first seizing collateral such as a pledge, that case is known as *sopadhi* (fraudulent).
Where a debtor is compelled to pay by being bound, brought to his own home, and subjected to measures such as flogging,
that is declared to be duress (*balātkāra*).
Having bound his wife, sons, and cattle, and having caused him to sit at the door, the creditor causes the debtor to pay the debt; this is called *ācarita* (customary practice).

The words of venerable persons sent by friends and relatives constitute conciliation (*sāma*). *Priyavākya* means pleasant speech. *Anugama* means following after. *Prāya* refers to an abundance of entreaties. *Chadma* is a pretext such as a festival or the like. *Anvāhita* is that which has been entrusted to another for the purpose of being given away. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), other similar modes are also included. The meaning is that *upadhi* is that [fraudulent device] by which, having brought the debtor's wealth under one's own control through any means whatsoever, the debtor is made to pay the debt. Regarding the rules for the application of *dharma* and the others, Kātyāyana says: (587–588).
One should cause a king, a master, or a Brahmin to pay by means of conciliation alone;
however, one may cause an heir or a friend to pay even by means of deception.
Bhṛgu said to merchants, farmers, and artisans:
"They should be made to pay according to local custom; having oppressed those who are wicked, one should cause them to pay."

The construction is as follows: by means of conciliation, gentleness, and the method known as *dharma*, a kinsman here is the heir; merchants and others should be made to pay according to local custom. The term "by oppression" includes both force and improper conduct. He (Kātyāyana) himself shows the local custom (Kāt. 580): "But the debtor should be kept confined publicly in an assembly of people until he pays that which is due, according to the established practice of the country."

By the word "yathā" (as), it is shown that he should be detained in the same manner as when he is detained by the creditor himself in a particular place; and in a place where he is detained by another cruel person seeking wages from the debtor, he should likewise be detained. He himself (Kātyāyana, 581) states that one must not obstruct the detainee’s urge for excrement or urine:
"Wherever there is a suspicion of excrement or urine for the person being detained, he should either follow behind him or release him even if he is bound."

"Bound" (*nibaddha*) means one who is indeed fettered by chains or other restraints; the meaning is that such a person should be sent out for the purpose of voiding urine and so forth. In this context, the second alternative refers to a low-status individual. Regarding the release of a prisoner (*avaruddha*) at the time of meals and the like, the same author (Kātyāyana, 582) states that he should be released after taking a guarantor (*pratibhū*): "He should be released day after day once a guarantor has been provided;
at the time of eating and at night, the guarantor remains in charge of his confinement."

Regarding "nibandhe," which means in the act of preventing escape; he (Kātyāyana, verse 583) states that there are two methods when a surety for appearance is absent, or when the debtor does not produce him:
"He who cannot find a surety for appearance, nor provide security, shall be confined in prison or kept under guard after being notified."

"In a *cāraka*," that is, in a prison; "guards" means protectors—having appointed men for the purpose of guarding him, he should be sent away; such is the meaning. Someone states an exception to this very rule (Kāt. 584): "A noble person who is trustworthy and pure should not be detained in a prison. "Trustworthy" (*prātyayika*) means reliable. To the inquiry, "How then should he be released? he says the same (Kāt. 584):
Therefore, that bond must be released, whether it was contracted by a formal agreement or by an oath.

"Unsecured" means devoid of a guarantor (*rakṣaka*). Here, regarding the nobleman’s confinement, although a restriction on the means such as religious duty (*dharma*) and so forth has been stated for Brahmins and others, it is nevertheless indicated that in certain specific regions, the employment of other means exists even for Brahmins and others. A debt with a fixed term becomes "without a fixed term" upon the expiration of that term; and when the maximum interest—such as doubling the principal—has been reached, if a particular business emergency arises, the debt may be collected with interest by these aforementioned means even if that [maximum limit] has not yet been reached. Alternatively, having made the total amount including the maximum interest the principal, another document (*lekhyāntara*) should be obtained. Or else, a pledge (*ādhi*) in the form of a field or similar property suitable for the enjoyment of the principal plus interest should be taken. And so says Bṛhaspati:
When the term has expired, the creditor may recover the debt with the interest ceased;
or the debtor may execute a new document according to the arrangement for compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*).
When interest at double the principal is stipulated,
as well as the profit from use, in that case the debt shall consist of the principal together with the interest.

The mention of "peaceful acquisition" (*śāntalābha*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes even non-peaceful acquisitions. The phrase "twofold" (*dviguṇa*) is an elliptical expression for any maximum increase, such as threefold and so forth. The meaning is that when interest is taken by the wheel-method (*cakravṛddhi*) or when a pledge to be used (*bhogyādhi*) is held, the debt shall consist of the principal plus interest. If the debtor is destitute, Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 131) states the method of collection:
"If, however, the debtor becomes devoid of capacity due to the lapse of time, he should be made to pay the debt according to his capacity, from time to time, in proportion to his income."
"According to income" means according to the production of wealth; and this refers to the case of one of superior caste. Thus Manu (8.177) says:
"A debtor of equal or inferior caste may discharge his debt to the creditor even by manual labor;
but one of superior caste should pay it gradually."
But one may compel a man of low birth who is impoverished to perform labor for the sake of a debt;
however, a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually, according to his means.

In this statement by Yājñavalkya (2.43), the mention of the *brāhmaṇa* refers to those of the highest caste. As for the statement of Kātyāyana (586), "One should cause farmers—whether they be *kṣatriyas*, *vaiśyas*, or *śūdras*—who are equal or inferior [in status], to pay," that should be understood to apply to them according to their means, provided they have the capacity to pay the fine. A person of the highest caste must not be made to perform labor even when he lacks the capacity to pay the fine gradually.
"Having ascertained that he is unable to pay the fine, one should compel him to perform labor under one's own supervision;
if he is incapable of that, he should be cast into prison, with the exception of Brāhmaṇas. Thus [it is said].

[163] Because this was stated by Kātyāyana himself (479). Regarding this, it is stated in the *Smṛticandrikā* that when the creditor is unable to perform the act of seizing [the debtor], the mention of entering the prison is intended for some means of recovering the debt once the capacity [to pay] has arisen. A creditor who recovers his own wealth through these means—such as [peaceful] methods beginning with *dharma*—should not be restrained by the king. And thus Viṣṇu (6.18) says: “A creditor recovering his lent property by any means whatsoever should not be censured by the king. “By any means whatsoever” means by a path not contrary to the *smṛtis*, local custom, or established practice. Manu also (8.50):
A creditor who recovers his own property from a debtor shall not be prosecuted by the king for recovering his own wealth.

A debtor who, when being requested for the admitted debt by means of lawful methods such as [moral] persuasion (*dharma*) and so forth, goes to the king and brings a suit against the creditor, shall be punished by the king. And thus says Yājñavalkya (2.40): "One who enforces a debt that has been admitted need not be censured by the king;
but one who goes to the king while the debt is being enforced shall be made to pay a fine and that [outstanding] wealth."

The measure of the fine for the substance [in dispute] has been stated by Viṣṇu (6.19): “If one being sued approaches the king, he should be fined an amount equal to that. “Equal to that” means equal to the debt or the substance. As for the verse: “He who, at his own will, informs the king against a creditor who is recovering his debt, shall be made to pay to the king a fourth part of the debt and that money to the creditor.”

The punishment mentioned by Manu (8.176) applies to the case of an indigent debtor. "At will" means according to his own desire. If the debtor should deny the debt, then he should recover his property by establishing his claim in court through the presentation of witnesses and other evidence. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"This is the rule for one who admits [the debt]; but one who denies it in court must be made to pay after proving it by means of a document or by witnesses."
And thus:
"One should accomplish one's purpose by means of legal procedure, by artifice, by conduct, and by force as the fifth."

It should be understood that the method characterized by legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), as stated by Manu (8.49), pertains to cases where there is disagreement. Legal procedure consists of the presentation of witnesses and other evidence. Bṛhaspati prohibits the use of methods such as confinement against one who lacks such disagreement:
"One who asserts his case in a doubtful matter must never be confined in any way.
But he who restrains one who should not be restrained becomes liable to punishment according to the law."

The term "obstruction" (*rodhana*) is an indication of any means other than legal procedure (*vyavahāra*). He himself explains the meaning of the two terms "one who insists on proof" (*kriyāvādī*) and "one with doubtful words": "Whatever is to be given according to justice, that I shall give"—where a debtor speaks thus, he is called one who insists on proof.

That matter is declared to be "doubtful" in which there may be a confusion between two parties regarding the acquisition of form, number, and so forth, or even concerning what is to be given and what is not to be taken.
Regarding the case of one who employs force when the matter is contested, Kātyāyana states (589):
"But where a creditor harasses a debtor who speaks justly,
he shall be deprived of that property and shall incur a fine equal to its value."
Bṛhaspati also says:
"But he who proceeds with regard to a doubtful matter without having informed the king should be forcibly punished, and that matter shall not be accomplished."

Regarding what must be done when a debtor fails to pay a debt that has been proven by the creditor even after it was reported to the king, Yama says: "But a debtor who possesses wealth yet does not pay out of wickedness should be compelled by the king to pay, having first seized [the property] from him, and then [the debt] shall be doubled."

The mention of "double" is an indication of the principal amount together with the interest. Viṣṇu states that for a king who causes a debtor to pay a debt proven by witnesses and other means through the creditor, there shall be a taking of a fine from the debtor and a taking of a fee from the creditor (Viṣṇu Smṛti 6.20–21): "If the creditor should approach the king, then, when the matter has been proven by him, the debtor shall pay to the king a fine equal to one-tenth of the sum; and the creditor, having recovered the sum, shall pay a twentieth part. The phrase "when proven by him" (*tadvibhāvite*) means when it has been established by the creditor. Yājñavalkya also says (2.42):
The king shall compel the debtor to pay ten percent on the amount recovered;
and the creditor, even upon having obtained his wealth, shall be made to pay five percent.

The meaning is that one should take as a fine the tenth part of the amount recovered from the debtor, and as wages the twentieth part of the amount recovered from the creditor. As for the verse: "Whatever amount one may deny, or whatever amount one may falsely claim, those two, being ignorant of dharma, shall be made by the king to pay double that amount as a fine."

This statement of Manu (8.59) refers to a case involving a debtor who possesses great wealth and is extremely wicked. "As much as he might deny" means as much as he might conceal; "as much as he might speak falsely" means he would speak untruthfully, saying, "I have given this much. The meaning is that both of them should be fined twice that amount of wealth. As for the verse: "If [the defendant] denies [the debt] and is proven [guilty], he shall pay the wealth to the king and an equal amount;
the one who makes a false accusation shall carry twice the wealth of the claim."

Thus, in the statement of Yājñavalkya (2.11), the prescription of an equal fine for one who denies [a debt] refers to the case of a debtor of wicked conduct who lacks sufficient wealth to pay a double fine; for otherwise, it would result in a contradiction with the previously cited texts. "From the accusation" means from the wealth [claimed] by the accuser. "The one who makes a false accusation shall pay double the wealth from the accusation. This rule applies to the one party who has been defeated when there is a valid ground [for the claim].
Likewise, in a plea of prior judgment, as well as in that which involves falsehood;

Furthermore, this would result in a contradiction with the statement of Vyāsa: "In the case of a plea of denial (*kāraṇa*), a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*), and a plea of falsehood (*mithyā*," among the plaintiff and defendant, "whichever one of the two suffers defeat, that person shall be fined double the amount of the property under dispute. As for what the teacher Vijñāneśvara stated—that in a plea of falsehood, the fine for the defendant who denies is equal [to the claim], while the fine for the plaintiff who makes a false accusation is double; and likewise, in the cases of a plea of prior judgment and a plea of denial, because the plaintiff is the one denying, if the defendant proves the grounds for the prior judgment, the fine is only equal to the principal amount; but if the defendant does not prove the grounds for the prior judgment, then he is indeed a false accuser, and his fine is double—this should not be respected, as it contradicts the statement of Vyāsa. Moreover, as for that which was stated by Manu (8.51):...
But if the debtor is found to have misappropriated the wealth and the matter has been proven by evidence,
the judge shall cause him to pay the creditor's debt and a small fine according to his capacity.

Thus, this refers to a debtor of good conduct who is unable to pay a tenth part [of the debt]. Regarding one who denies it—that is, one who conceals it: however, he who, out of arrogance due to power or other such reasons, does not acknowledge a claim when requested by the creditor, but upon being brought before the royal court, acknowledges it himself, shall be fined a twentieth part of the amount claimed. And so says Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 132): "But a debtor who possesses wealth yet does not pay due to wickedness, shall be compelled by the king to pay after taking a twentieth part [for the state]."
Manu also (8.139):
"When a debt is admitted as due, one deserves a fine of five percent;
in case of denial, that amount is doubled—such is the ordinance of Manu."

The meaning of this is as follows: A debtor who, having previously failed to acknowledge a debt, is brought before the royal court and admits that he owes it, saying, "Truly, I owe him," deserves to pay five percent (*pañcakaṃ śatam*)—this is the remainder of the sense. But he who denies it even in court, saying, "I do not owe him," and subsequently admits it, deserves a fine double that [five percent], namely ten percent (*daśakaṃ śatam*), which is double the previously admitted five percent. Regarding the order in which a debtor should be made to pay when several creditors arrive simultaneously, Yājñavalkya says (2.41):
A debtor shall be made to pay the creditors according to the order in which they presented their claims;
however, after paying the Brāhmaṇas, he shall pay the king immediately thereafter.

Regarding a Kṣatriya king: among creditors of the same caste, the repayment shall follow the very same order in which the money was received; among those of different castes, it shall follow the order of the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa—this is the meaning. Kātyāyana also says:
"But when there is a concurrence of multiple debts, whatever was contracted first must be paid first; and in the case of a king, as well as for a Śrotriya, the same rule applies."

"Immediately after the *śrotriya* Brahmins. When creditors to whom debts were given on a single day all present themselves simultaneously, they should be made to pay at once; however, if there is a disparity between the smallness or greatness of their respective sums, they should be made to pay after apportioning shares according to that disparity. And thus says the same author (Kāt. 513): "Where a debt is recorded for payment on a single day, one should make the repayment equal [for all]. Otherwise, the taking, the securing, and the profit shall be according to the order [of the dates]."

One should perform the taking [of the pledge], the giving of the pledge, its protection, the maintenance of the pledge, the profit, and the enjoyment of the pledge all equally and simultaneously. Otherwise, in the case of a difference in time, one should act according to the stated order; this is the meaning. Even when there is a convergence of multiple debts, the debtor shall give to that creditor whose wealth enabled him to acquire a particular object, and he should give the money obtained from the sale or other means of that object specifically for the discharge of that debt, rather than distributing it among all creditors. Thus it has been said by that same author (Kāt. 515):
If one should prove that a commodity was acquired by means of another's property, that property must be returned by the debtor alone; it cannot be otherwise.

The mention of "merchandise" (*paṇya*) is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*). The particle *eva* (only) is displaced [in the compound]. Bṛhaspati states what must necessarily be done by the debtor at the time of repayment:
"A debt contracted must be paid when requested, even if it is not the appointed time; once the deadline has expired, the profit ceases, and in the absence of the father, it must be paid by the sons."

"Untimely" means for a short time, that is to say, for an indefinite period. "Indefinite" means that once the request has been made and the interest has increased to its maximum, it becomes "definite"; upon the expiration of that limit, the debt must indeed be paid and not deferred. Even before the request or the like, repayment should be made if possible, because a debt must necessarily be discharged. Regarding the method of repaying a debt for one who is destitute, Manu (8.154) says:
"He who is unable to pay the debt but wishes to enter into a new transaction, shall, after paying the interest accrued, renew the bond."

The meaning is this: he who, due to a lack of wealth, is unable to pay the debt with interest and wishes to avoid the lapse of time by securing the creditor’s peace of mind through a formal act such as a written document, should—after paying the accrued interest—execute that act again, marked with the current date and so forth. But regarding one who is incapable of paying even the full interest, the same author says (8.155):
"Without producing the gold there itself, he may renew the transaction;
he ought to pay as much interest as has accumulated."

If, without having shown the gold, one fails to pay the accrued interest, then in that very same document previously executed, one should cancel that interest and record it as principal. The meaning is that only that portion of the interest which is impossible to pay should be recorded, and not an amount equal to the interest on the principal. As for one who is able to pay some portion of the interest, he should pay that much and record the remainder of the interest as principal, because the principle is the same. However, regarding one who is unable to pay the entire principal along with the interest at the time of repayment, Yājñavalkya says (2.93):
Having paid the debt, the debtor should write on the back of the document;
and the creditor, upon receiving the payment, should provide his own signature as a mark.

The debtor, having given small amounts as he is able, time and again, should write on the back of the original document: "I have paid this much, together with interest. Alternatively, the creditor should write on the original document, marked with his own hand-signature, "I have received this much"; the meaning is that he should give to the debtor the document known as an *upagata*—a receipt written in his own hand. And this granting of a receipt is to be understood as occurring when the original document is not present. Thus Viṣṇu (6.26) states: "In the case of non-payment, or when the document is not present, the creditor shall give a document written in his own hand. Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 114) speaks of the fault in not giving the receipt:
Having received the pledge, the creditor shall return it to the debtor at the time of repayment;
but if, when requested, he does not return it, he shall incur the loss of the interest.

"Interest" refers to the wealth given by the debtor. The phrase "having taken interest" implies this sequence. Furthermore, this designation of "loss" (or forfeiture) should be understood to apply when the remainder is very small; however, if it is substantial, the creditor must simply provide the interest on the portion received. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati states:

[169] "He who, having recovered a debt through righteous means and other such methods, does not record it in writing, nor delivers the acknowledged amount, shall incur interest on that [unrecorded balance]."
"Having extracted," that is, having taken back; the remainder is "the debt that is not yet fully paid. Regarding what must be done after the full repayment of the debt, Yājñavalkya (2.94) says:
"Having paid the debt, one should tear up the document; for the sake of purification, one should cause another [document] to be made.

The "document" (*lekhyam*) refers to the original bond (*mūlapatram*). "For the sake of purification" means for the purpose of making known the discharge of the debt; the meaning is that one should receive from the creditor (*uttamarṇāt*) another document, namely a certificate of clearance (*viśuddhipatram*). Regarding the alternative course when the original bond is situated in another country and even a certificate of clearance is somehow impossible to obtain, Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 116) says:
One should provide a written document for the sake of purification regarding the debt; in its absence, there should be a verbal acknowledgment.
In this way, there shall be mutual purification between the creditor and the debtor.

*Pratiśravaḥ* (a promise) is the declaration by witnesses to the effect that "the repayment has been made. However, the repayment of a debt (*karṇapratidāna*) accompanied by witnesses must be performed in the presence of the same witnesses who were present at the original transaction; if those are somehow unavailable, it may be performed in the presence of other witnesses. And so says Yājñavalkya (2.94): "Whatever [debt] there may be with witnesses, that should be repaid in the presence of witnesses. Regarding the undesirable consequences of failing to repay a debt, Kātyāyana (591) states:
He who takes a loan or other property and does not return it to the owner shall be born in that person's house as a slave, a servant, a woman, or an animal.

By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "recovery of deposits and so forth," items such as deposits (*nikṣepa*) are included. There is a distinction between these two: the *krīta* (bought) slave and the *vaitanika* (hired for wages) servant. Nārada also states (Ṛṇādāna 7–8): "If one does not pay a debt or a gift when it is demanded, that property shall increase until it reaches a hundred crores."
Then, when a full hundred million [lives] have passed, being bound by that karma,
he shall become a horse, a donkey, a bull, or a slave in birth after birth.

"Acceptance" refers to wealth promised. Vyāsa also says: "If an ascetic who maintains the sacred fires dies while still in debt, both his asceticism and his fire-sacrifice shall belong entirely to the creditor."

[170] In the absence of the debtor, the debt along with interest must be paid by his son. Thus says Bṛhaspati: "A debt incurred must be paid upon request even if it is not yet due; when the term has expired, it must be paid with the profits ceased, and in the absence of the father, it must be paid by the sons."
The meaning of this has been explained previously; it is as follows: A debt incurred by one's father, once established, must be paid by the sons as if it were their own.
A debt of a grandfather must be paid equally [by his grandsons], but the son of such a grandson need not pay it.
The meaning is that it is like one's own property, together with interest. Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 5) states the necessity of repaying a debt incurred by a father:
"For this reason, fathers desire sons for their own sake, thinking:
'He will liberate me from both the creditor and the debtor.'"
Therefore, once a son is born, he should diligently set aside his own interests and liberate his father from debt so that he does not go to hell.

"By whatever means possible" means by any means whatsoever. The *uttama-ṛṇa* (highest debt) is the debt to the ancestors, as stated in the Taittirīya Śruti: "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born burdened with three debts" (TS 6.3.10.5). The *adhama-ṛṇa* (lowest debt) is money borrowed at interest. "By one who has been born" means by one who has become proficient in worldly transactions. Kātyāyana also states (vv. 551–52):
"Since sons, once born, liberate their fathers from the lowest debt through the very act of giving [gifts], for that reason the ancestors desire sons."
But when the father has died, the inheritance should never be given at an improper time to those who have not attained the capacity for legal affairs;
rather, it should be given according to the rule at the proper time. Otherwise, they shall dwell in hell.

The meaning is: those who have attained legal capacity (*vyavahāra*), that is to say, those sixteen years of age who possess the specific knowledge of what is to be avoided and what is to be adopted. Nārada states [in *Ṛṇādāna* 35–36] regarding the legal competence of a sixteen-year-old:
"A child is to be known as equal to one still in the womb until the eighth year;
a minor (*bāla*) is so called until the sixteenth year, and thereafter he is termed a *pogaṇḍa*."
One who knows legal procedure is independent from others until the death of the father.

[171] Even though a son whose father has died may possess independence during childhood, he has no authority to discharge debt; rather, it has been stated by that same author that only one who has attained legal capacity [is so authorized]:
"For even if he is independent, a minor is liable for debt."
For sovereignty is traditionally held to belong to the eldest, and seniority is determined by both merit and age.
Regarding the repayment of a debt incurred by a father during his absence, or when he is overcome by an incurable disease or similar calamity, Yājñavalkya (2.50) states:
"When the father is abroad, deceased, or overwhelmed by misfortune, the debt must be paid by the sons or grandsons; however, if it is denied, it is established through witnesses."
The repayment that is due when [the father] has gone abroad should be understood as being after twenty years from the time of his departure. And so says Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 14):
"A son shall not pay the debt, nor a paternal uncle, nor even an elder brother, before twenty years have passed while the father has been away."
Kātyāyana also states:
"Even when [the father] is present, or is afflicted by disease, or likewise resides abroad from his own country,
a debt incurred by the father shall be paid after twenty years."
"Even though he is present," that is, even though he is alive; "after twenty years"—this is the ellipsis. For this very reason, Viṣṇu (6.27) states:

"When the one who took the property has died, or has renounced the world, or has been away for twenty years, the property must be returned by his sons or grandsons; beyond this time, it need not be given by those who are no longer living."

"Twelve years" means twenty years (*viṃśatiṃ varṣāṇi*) for one who has gone forth (*pravrajita*) or renounced the world (*saṃnyasta*). This is connected with the phrase "if he remains away" (*asya proṣite*). "Beyond this" means after twenty years. And the grammatical connection is that [the debt] should be paid by those who do not wish [to pay]. However, if a man has many sons, they should pay the debt according to their respective shares if they are divided (*vibhakta*). If they are undivided (*avibhakta*), then, since they exist in a state of equal primacy, the payment is made through collective effort (*sambhūyasamutthāna*). If they exist in a relationship where some are subordinate and others are primary, then the principal person among them shall pay. Thus says Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 2):
When the father has passed away, the sons shall pay the debt according to their respective shares,
whether they are divided or undivided, or whoever may have taken up that burden.

[172] In the absence of a son, the grandson who inherits the estate shall pay the debt without interest; however, upon inheriting the estate, he must pay it with interest. If a son inherits the estate, or in his absence, [the grandson], it must be paid with interest. But if the great-grandson inherits the estate, even the principal need not be paid, according to the previously cited statement of Bṛhaspati: "A debt to one's father is like one's own. Kātyāyana states that even in the absence of inheritance, the son must repay the debt: (559) [text follows].
While the debt to the ancestors remains unpaid, a son shall not take the wealth;
that property must be given to the creditor, but if [the father] has died, the son is made to pay it.

"Property" refers to paternal property. A son who has been separated [from his father] shall not take that property when he dies while remaining liable for a debt contracted by the father after the partition; rather, he must pay it to the creditor. If anything remains from that, then he may take it. The meaning is that even one who is not an heir (*rikthagrahaṇarahita*) should give from his own wealth in the absence of paternal property. Here, the mention of the "son" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the grandson as well, because Yājñavalkya, in the verse "The debt is to be paid by sons and grandsons" (YDh 2.50), mentions both with equal status. However, while the payment of the debt by the grandson without interest is based on a specific scriptural injunction (*vācanika*), the exclusion of the other [the son] from interest follows from this parallel reading. When there is a concurrence of the father’s own debt and the debt contracted by the father, the son must first pay the debt contracted by the father; but when there is a concurrence of the debt contracted by the grandfather, the debt contracted by the father, and the debt contracted by himself, the grandson must first pay the debt contracted by the grandfather. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
The debt due to the ancestors must first be paid, and then one's own personal debt;
between those two, the ancestral debt must always be paid first.

Yājñavalkya (2.47) shows that a debt incurred by a father should not be paid by sons or grandsons: "A son shall not pay for his father’s debts contracted through liquor, lust, gambling, fines, or remaining balances of taxes, nor for gifts made in vain."

That which is incurred through liquor, desire, gambling, drinking intoxicants, addiction to women, and defeat at dice; that which remains unpaid of fines and taxes; and "useless gifts"—that which is promised to rogues, bards, and the like—for it is said:
"What is given to a rogue, a bard, a wrestler, a quack physician, a gambler, a cheat, a flatterer, a wandering minstrel, or a thief, becomes fruitless."

Thus it is stated. Bṛhaspati also says: "One should not compel a son to pay a debt incurred through gambling, a gift made in jest, a promise made under the influence of passion or anger, a suretyship, or the remainder of a fine or a tax."

The *saura* [oath] is for the purpose of drinking liquor. Kātyāyana has shown the nature of promises made out of lust and anger (564–565): "Whether it be a written document or one delivered orally, that which is given to a woman who previously belonged to another, one should know that to be a promise made by men out of lust."

"For that which is spoken after having committed violence or destroyed property out of anger, even if it appears to bring satisfaction, one should know that it is produced by anger. Thus [it is said].
*Muktaka* means without a written document. *Prātibhāvya* refers to what arises from being a surety for appearance. Āhośana states that neither fine nor tax is to be paid in these cases.
Neither a fine nor the remainder of a fine, nor a toll nor its remainder, should be paid by a son; nor that which is not subject to legal proceedings.
The meaning is that it pertains to worldly transactions (*vyāvahārika*), such as those occasioned by the drinking of liquor and so forth.
Regarding the sequence [of liability] when there is a concurrence of many persons entitled to repay a debt, Yājñavalkya (2.51) states:
"The heir to the estate (*rikthagrāha*) shall be made to pay the debt, and likewise the one who takes the wife (*yoṣidgrāha*)."
A son whose property is not dependent on others is the heir to one who dies without a son.

Wealth obtained through the process of inheritance is *riktha*; he who takes that is the *rikthagrāha* (heir). He who, out of passion or other motives, accepts another’s wife as his own wife is the *yoṣidgrāha* (one who takes a woman). A son is one whose wealth is not dependent on another. "Dependent on another" (*anyāśrita*) means wealth belonging to another—namely, wealth related to the mother or father, since the word "another" (*anya*) here refers to the parents. The meaning is that a son such as a eunuch (*klība*), who lacks such parental wealth because he is unfit to receive an inheritance, is one whose wealth is not dependent on another. Regarding the heir of one who is sonless—that is, one who lacks a son eligible to inherit—the rule is: the *rikthagrāha* shall be made to pay the debt; in his absence, the *yoṣidgrāha*; and in his absence, the son who is otherwise ineligible for inheritance. This sequence follows the order of the text. The fact that a eunuch and others are ineligible to receive an inheritance has been stated by Manu (9.201).
Those who have no share [in inheritance] are the impotent, the outcaste, those born blind or deaf,
as well as the insane, the mentally dull, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of sense organs.

As for the statement of Viṣṇu (6.29), “Whether he has sons or is sonless, the heir to the estate shall pay the debt,” that is intended to mean simply that “the heir to the estate shall pay the debt,” regardless of whether there exists a son who is unworthy of inheritance or whether no such son exists at all. Regarding the point that in the absence of an heir to the estate, the one who takes the wife should be made to pay, Viṣṇu also states (6.30): “In the case of one without property, the one who takes the wife. This means “in the case of one who lacks an heir to the estate. Bṛhaspati also says:
“And the one who takes the wife shall likewise [pay] in the absence of the one who takes the wealth.”

Regarding the point that a son who is not entitled to a share of the inheritance must be made to pay [the debt] in the absence of a wife as a creditor, Nārada also states (Ṛṇādāna 23): "Among those who take the wealth, the wife, or the son, he who takes the wealth shall bear the burden of the debt; in the absence of both the wife and the one possessing wealth, the son bears it; and in the absence of both the wife and the son, the one possessing wealth bears it."

The term *strīdhaninau* means "the woman and the wealth," i.e., the woman and the property; *tadvatoḥ* means "of those two who possess them," that is, of the woman and the one who takes the wealth. Here, the statement that the woman (*yoṣidgrāha*) is liable for the debt in the absence of the son refers to the case where there is no son entitled to inherit (*dāyārha*). This is because Viṣṇu states (6.30): "In the case of one who has no wealth, the woman takes [the property]," while Kātyāyana (557, 576) says: "The son [takes] when the woman and the heir are absent"—which would contradict his own statement if the former applied even when an heir exists. Furthermore, even when a son is entitled to inherit, if he is incapable of paying the debt due to an affliction such as an incurable disease or due to childhood, then at that stage, a paternal uncle or other relative who keeps the father's wealth in his own custody shall pay the debt; and in the absence of such a person, the woman shall pay it. Thus says Kātyāyana.
One should compel the son to pay the debt if he is free from affliction, capable of wealth, and fit for the burden; otherwise, one should not compel the son to pay.

When a son is seen to be overwhelmed by calamity or is a minor, one who has taken property should be made to pay that; in his absence, one who has taken it from the household (purandhi) shall be made to pay.
[175] He (Kātyāyana, verse 577) states that even one who is unworthy of a share in the inheritance shall not give the wife [to the claimant] if he possesses abundant wealth:
"The claimant of the property shall give her first; after him, the son;
then the claimant of the wife, in the absence of a son or when the son is utterly destitute."

First, the heir to the estate (*rikthagrāha*) shall pay; in his absence, the son who is unworthy of inheritance but possesses greater wealth shall pay; in his absence, the one who takes the wife (*yoṣidgrāha*) shall pay—this is the meaning. In response to the inquiry as to what kind of *yoṣidgrāha* has the authority to discharge the debt, Nārada says (Ṛṇadāna 21):
"But if a woman who possesses property, or one who has offspring, should resort to another man, he [the new husband] shall pay her husband's debt, or she may abandon him in that same manner."

"Sapradhānā" means accompanied by excellent wealth; the syntactical connection is that she shall pay the debt of her husband. He himself [states] (NSm, Ṛṇadāna 22): "The last among the *svairiṇīs* and the first among the *punarbhūs*—he who enjoys these two shall pay the debt incurred by their husbands."
Even for one who dies without wealth or sons, he who approaches the wife inherits the debt; that alone is recorded as his wealth.

Of the four types of *svairiṇīs*, the last three are included; of the three types of *punarbhūs*, it is the first one [that is relevant]. The meaning is that he who "incurs the debt" (*ṛṇa*) created by the husband for those two—that is, he who enjoys [the woman] as a husband—must pay it. He "approaches" (*upaiti*) means he enjoys her as a husband. The *punarbhūs* and *svairiṇīs* have been demonstrated by that same author (Nārada, Strīpuṃsa 45–52): "Other women who have previously belonged to another are said to be sevenfold in order:
among them, the *punarbhū* is of three kinds, while the *svairiṇī* is of four kinds."
A maiden who, though her virginity remains intact, has been defiled by the taking of the hand in marriage,
is declared to be the first type of *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) by virtue of the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*).
When a woman is given by her elders after disregarding the laws of the country, having been impelled by reckless passion toward another man,
she is proclaimed the second [type].
When no suitable brothers-in-law are available, the woman who is given by her kinsmen to a sapinda of the same caste is proclaimed as the third [form of marriage].
[176] A woman, whether she has borne children or not,
who out of lust resorts to another man while her husband is still alive, is indeed a *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman) of the first degree.
She who, having abandoned her husband from childhood, resorts to another husband and then returns again to her husband's house, is proclaimed as the second [type].
But she who, upon the death of her husband, having rejected the brother-in-law and others,
approaches another out of desire, is proclaimed as the third [type].
"She who has come from another country, purchased with wealth, and afflicted by hunger and thirst, approaching you saying 'I am yours'—she is proclaimed as the fourth. Thus [it is said].

"Utpannasāhasā" means one who has lost her virginity, that is to say, one who is mature. "To another husband" refers to a brother-in-law (*devara*), because of the subsequent statement, "in the absence of brothers-in-law. Furthermore, this mention of the "seizer of a woman" (*yoṣidgrāha*) having the authority to pay the debt does not lack a subject; for while the seizure of another's wife is impossible for Brāhmaṇas and others who possess knowledge of what is prescribed and forbidden and do not transgress the path declared by the scriptures, it is certainly possible for commoners and those blinded by passion. For this very reason, in the context of stating the seizer of a woman’s authority to pay the debt, Kātyāyana includes the vintners and others [as examples]. (567)
Whatever debt has been contracted by those who are destitute, childless, or such as liquor-sellers and the like,
the one who enjoys the property of their wives must indeed pay that very debt.

A *śauṇḍika* is a liquor-distiller; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of leather-workers and others is intended. However, the teacher Vijñāneśvara, having provided an alternative explanation for the rule "the inheritor of the estate shall be made to pay the debt," established a different legal arrangement as follows:
"The inheritor of the estate shall be made to pay the debt, and likewise the one who takes the wife;
the son, provided his property has not been encumbered by others, [shall pay] for an estate-holder who is without a son."

"One whose property is not dependent on another" (*ananyāśritadravyaḥ*): "dependent on another" (*anyāśrita*) means that which is dependent upon another. Here, by the word "property" (*dravya*), the property related to the mother and father is intended. One whose property is dependent on another—that is, property related to the mother and father—is "one whose property is dependent on another," meaning he is unworthy of inheritance. Conversely, one whose property is not dependent on another is worthy of a share of the inheritance; this is the meaning. Regarding the heir (*rikthin*) of one who has no son: the taker of the inheritance (*rikthagrāha*) must be made to pay the debt; in his absence, the taker of the wife (*yoṣidgrāha*); in his absence, the son who is entitled to the inheritance. Now, if these [categories] were to coincide, this sequence would indeed apply. However, that very situation is not possible.

[177] "Neither brothers nor fathers, but sons are the heirs of the father" (MDh 9.185). Since it is impossible for anyone else to inherit when a son exists, even the taking of a wife is not appropriate; for a second husband is nowhere prescribed for virtuous women.

Thus it is from the Smṛti (MDh 5.162). Furthermore, the claim that "the son alone should be made to pay the debt" is also improper, because Yājñavalkya has already stated (2.50): "The debt must be paid by sons and grandsons. Moreover, the qualification "one whose property is not dependent on others" is redundant; for as long as there is a son, it is impossible for the property of the parents to go to another. Even if such a transfer were possible, since this is already established by the term "the heir" (*rikthagrāhī*), the phrase "the son whose property is not dependent on others" would be meaningless. As for the statement "of one who is without a son, the heir," this too is redundant; for even when a son exists, the authority to discharge the debt belongs solely to the heir, as established by the rule "the heir shall be made to pay the debt" (YDh 2.51), and by the logic of *kaimutika-nyāya* (a fortiori), this is proven all the more so when no son exists.

To this it is replied: Even when a son exists, another may become the heir (*rikthagrāhin*) because eunuchs and others are ineligible for inheritance. Furthermore, the taking of a wife is possible for one whose mind is defiled by passion and who has transgressed prohibitions. The restatement that "the debt shall be made payable by the son" is intended to establish the following principle: the son's authority to pay the debt exists only in the absence of a person who takes the wife, not when such a person exists. The phrase "one whose property is not dependent on others" is not redundant; its purpose is to demonstrate that even in the absence of paternal property, the authority to pay belongs only to that son among many who is fit to receive the inheritance, and not to one ineligible for inheritance, such as a eunuch. Nor is the statement "of one devoid of a son, the heirs" redundant. Here, the mention of the "son" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the grandson as well. For those who—namely the great-grandsons and others—who are designated in the treatises on inheritance as the immediate successors to take the estate after one who lacks both son and grandson, all of them must be made to pay the debt according to the order prescribed in the law of inheritance *if* they take the estate; if they do not take the estate, they are not liable. However, the son and grandson must be made to pay even in the absence of taking the estate. This is intended to show the distinction between the great-grandsons and others, on the one hand, and the son and grandson, on the other. This distinction between the great-grandsons and others compared to the son and grandson was also shown by Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 4).
"Successively, that debt which has been obtained without obstruction and discharged by sons should be paid by grandsons; it ceases with the fourth generation.

Alternatively, since it was stated that "in the absence of a woman-creditor (*yoṣidgrāha*), the son shall be made to pay," and "in the absence of a son, the woman-creditor shall be made to pay," the phrase "the heir of one who is sonless" is used for this purpose. On this view, the word "heir" (*rikthin*) refers to the woman, because of the traditional legal authority (*smṛti*) stating, "She alone is declared to be his wealth. Thus, the meaning is that in the case of one who is sonless but possesses a wife, the woman-creditor shall pay the debt.

[Objection: But surely, if there is no one who has taken the woman, the son should be made to pay; if there is no son, the one who took the woman should be made to pay. Thus, when both are present, no one at all would be liable to pay.

[Response: This is not a fault, because the legal settlement is as follows: the son is made to pay in the absence of the one who took the woman along with her property, the last of those who took a *svairiṇī* (a woman of loose character), and the first of those who took a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman); however, in the absence of a son, the one who took the woman who is destitute of wealth and offspring is made to pay. This very point was stated by Nārada (Ṛṇādāna 23): "Among the heirs of the property, the woman, and the son, the one who takes the property shall take the debt."
"The son of two who have no property takes the woman's wealth; the husband of two women who have no sons takes the wealth of both. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that when there is no one who abducted the woman, the son must be made to pay; or, if there is a son, someone else who abducted the woman must be made to pay. Alternatively, it should be explained differently as "of one who has no son, the heir. It was stated previously that the heirs and others are to be made to pay the debt in due order; in that context, when there is an absence of both the creditor and his son, the question arises as to whom they should be made to pay. This [verse] applies here: "of one who has no son, the heir. The meaning is that they are to be made to pay him who is the heir—that is, one entitled to inherit the estate—of the creditor who has no son. Thus, everything is consistent.
A debt contracted by paternal uncles and others for the sake of maintaining the family must be paid by the head of the household. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"A householder ought to pay a debt contracted for the sake of the family by paternal uncles, brothers, sons, wives, slaves, pupils, or dependents."
In this context, the "householder" (*kuṭumbī*) is the one referred to; for this very reason, Nārada (Ṛṇadāna 12) states:
"Whatever has been incurred by a pupil, a resident student, a slave, a wife, a servant, a messenger, or a laborer for the sake of the family, that must be paid by the householder."

In this context, a *śiṣya* is one seeking knowledge of the Vedas, while an *antevāsī* is one seeking knowledge of the arts (*śilpa*). "Utkṣiptam" means raised up or performed; that is to say, incurred. Kātyāyana states (545) that even in the absence of the head of the household (*kuṭumbin*), if his consent was not obtained, a debt contracted for the sake of the family must be paid by the head of the household: "A debt contracted for the sake of the family by a slave, a wife, a mother, a pupil, or a son—even without the consent of one who is away—must be paid," says Bhṛgu.
[179] Even one who is dependent may conduct legal business for the sake of his family, whether in his own country or abroad; a learned man shall not set such a person aside.

One who is under the authority of another is a slave and so forth. Kātyāyana also indicates that other debts incurred for the sake of the family must be paid by the head of the household (542–543): "However, one should know that what is borrowed for the sake of the family when [the head] is incapable, as well as when he is ill, or on account of a calamity, is a debt contracted in times of distress."
Whatever was performed for the marriage of a daughter or in funeral rites—
all this that was done by the family must be given to the master, O Lord.

"In the case of one who is incapable," meaning one unable to maintain the family—the word "wife" being understood as the subject—of the master of the household; Yājñavalkya (2.46) states that a debt incurred by anyone other than these, such as a son and so forth, need not be paid:

"A father shall not pay a debt incurred by his wife or son, nor a son for one incurred by his father, except for the sake of the family; likewise, a husband shall not pay what was incurred by his wife."
Kātyāyana states that even something done for the sake of a son may be required to be paid:
"That debt which is incurred by a son need not be paid according to the law;
however, that which was promised or which was subsequently approved must be paid."

That which is promised, that which is authorized, that which is consented to, and that which is accepted immediately after the contracting of the debt— Nārada states (Ṛṇadāna 11) that even what was contracted by a son for the purpose of rescuing himself from calamity must be paid.
Or, whatever debt was contracted at the father’s command or for the maintenance of the family,
the father shall pay that to the son in times of distress.
Bṛhaspati states that even for a debt contracted by a son, there is the obligation to pay out of affection:
"A debt incurred by a son must be cleared by the father if it was approved;
or he may pay it out of love for his son, but otherwise he is not required to pay."
The meaning is that it is not by affection, but by the nature of things (*dharmatā*). A debt contracted even by a wife for the sake of extricating herself from a calamity must be paid.
[180] "And a debt contracted by a wife shall never become the husband's obligation, except for what was done during a time of distress; for the expansion of the household depends upon men. (Kāt. 569)

"Ābhavet" means "it must be given. The prohibition against a husband paying a debt contracted by his wife applies to cases other than those involving Ābhīras and similar castes. Thus states Yājñavalkya (2.48): "The husband shall pay the debt of a cowherd, a vintner, an actor, a washerman, a hunter, or a woman, because their livelihood depends upon him."

An actor (*śailūṣa*) is a dancer. "Livelihood" (*vṛtti*) means the means of subsistence. The mention of cowherds and others is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for oil-pressers and others whose livelihood depends upon their wives. Kātyāyana states an exception to the rule that "a woman [is not liable] for debts incurred by her husband or son" (546):
"A debt contracted in this manner—whether jointly with the husband or the son, or solely by herself—must be paid by the woman; otherwise, she is not liable for what was contracted by them."

The meaning is this: a debt contracted by a husband together with his son must be paid in the absence of either of them; however, a debt contracted by himself must be paid even when they are present. Yājñavalkya also states (2.49): "A debt acknowledged by a woman, or one contracted jointly with her husband, or one contracted by herself, must be paid by her; she is not liable for any other."
"Accepted" means that which has been agreed upon with the words, "I shall give. Even that which is not accepted must be given by her upon the inheritance of the estate. And so says Kātyāyana (547):
"If a woman who wishes to die is told by her husband, 'You must pay this debt,' she must be made to pay it even if she did not accept it, provided that the wealth remains with the woman."

A debt incurred by a mother must be paid by her son. Likewise, Viṣṇu (6.35–36) states: “The sons of a father and those of a mother who have not been divided [from their mothers], as well as those who have been divided, shall pay a share corresponding to their inheritance. The word “shall pay” (*dadyuḥ*) is to be supplied from the context. Nārada (Ṛṇadāna 20) declares that even if a mother is wicked, her debt must still be paid by her son if she is destitute: “But if a woman who has a son abandons her son and resorts to another man, her son alone shall pay the entire debt of that woman if she is without means.”

[181] "Another husband"—this is the ellipsis. Regarding the specific case where that very woman possesses wealth, Kātyāyana says: "If a woman who has young children or excessive debts has resorted to another husband, the man she has resorted to shall pay her debt; this is the rule prescribed for women with young children."

A debt contracted for the maintenance of the family by those whose wealth has not been partitioned must be paid by all the heirs to that property once the head of the household—who is authorized to give—is absent. Thus says Yājñavalkya (2.45):
"If a debt should have been contracted for the sake of the family by those who are undivided, the heirs shall pay it when the head of the household has died or is away on a journey."
Nārada also [states] (Ṛṇadāna 3):
"A debt contracted by an undivided paternal uncle, or by a brother,
or by a mother for the sake of the family, all the heirs shall pay."
