In the absence of all those whose property has not been divided, he who remains shall alone pay the entire debt. Thus Viṣṇu (6.34) states: "He who remains among those undivided [heirs] shall pay the debt contracted for the sake of the family. And this repayment of the debt must be performed by the sons and others who are entitled to inherit the estate in the absence of the creditor; in their absence, it must be performed by his *sagotras*; and in their absence, it must be performed by his kinsmen (*bandhus*), such as maternal uncles and so forth. Thus says Nārada (Ṛṇadāna 112):
If there is no one belonging to the lineage of a Brāhmaṇa to whom a gift should be given, he should bestow it upon his kinsmen (sakulyas);
in their absence, upon his relatives (bandhus).

The mention of the *brāhmaṇa* is an illustration for the creditor (*uttamarṇa*). "Lineage" (*anvaya*) refers to the line of sons and the line of daughters. He states what must be done even in their absence (Yājñavalkya Smṛti, Ṛṇadāna 113):
"But when there are no *sakulyas*, nor kinsmen or relatives, then one should give [the debt] to twice-born men; if they too are absent, one should cast it into the water."
Prajāpati also says:
"In the absence of relatives, however, the wealth should be given to Brahmins or cast into the water;
for wealth cast into water or likewise into fire becomes beneficial for the next world."
[182] The remainder of the phrase is "offered into the fire" (*agnau hutaṃ*); there is no connection with the word "thrown" (*kṣiptaṃ*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Smṛtisaṃgraha*:

"If property belonging to a debtor should somehow come into the possession of a Brāhmaṇa, when there is an absence of heirs ranging from the son down to a Brāhmaṇa who would otherwise be entitled to inherit the estate..."
"One should offer an oblation with the middle leaf of the *palāśa* tree, saying:
'Whatever debt...'; then one should cast it [into the water], for that wealth is indeed water.

According to Gobhila, this mantra is connected specifically with the *homa* (fire-oblation), not with the casting into water, because Gobhila (Gobhilagṛhya 4.4.26) records it as being connected to the *homa*: "One should offer an oblation with the middle leaf, saying: 'Whatever debt... This rule is to be understood as applying even to property such as deposits when there is no owner, since the underlying principle is the same.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Legal Head of Non-payment of Debt," in the *Vyavahāravivekadīpikā* by the illustrious Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma.

**Possible reading of the defective text:** In the Madanaratnapradīpa composed by Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with “Śrīkodaṇḍa-Paraśurāma”— this concludes the sixteenth section, the exposition of the legal title known as Non-payment of Debt (*ṛṇādāna*), within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*.
Now follows the determination of the legal title known as "deposit" (*nikṣepa*).
Nārada shows its essential nature [in *Nikṣepa* 1]:
"When one deposits one's own property with another out of trust, free from apprehension..."
This is declared by the wise to be the legal head of dispute known as "deposits."

One's own property placed with another person out of trust is a *nikṣepa* (deposit). This very same thing, when placed as an uncounted amount of property, is called an *upanidhi* (sealed deposit). And so it has been stated by that same author:
"That which is deposited as an uncounted and undisclosed mass is to be known as an *upanidhi*; the wise know a *nikṣepa* to be that which is counted."
That which has its verbal meaning unexplained, though revealed by Bṛhaspati;
that which is unmentioned, remote, uncounted, or not shown;
and that which is given marked with a seal—this is known as *aupanidhika* (a sealed deposit).
"Separated" means situated in a casket or similar container; for this very reason, Yājñavalkya (2.65) states:

"When an object placed in a container and unobserved is handed over into the hand of another, that property is termed *aupanidhika* (a sealed deposit), and it must be returned in exactly that same manner."
[183] A *vāsana* is a container such as a basket that serves as a receptacle for goods. The mention of "taking by the hand" is illustrative. For this very reason, Nārada stated (*Nikṣepa* 5):
"That which is deposited in another's house is known as *aupanidhika*. This same thing, when delivered in the absence of the recipient, is called a *nyāsa*. For this reason, Bṛhaspati says:
When property is deposited in another's house due to fear of kings, thieves, or enemies, or for protection against the deception of heirs, that is proclaimed as a *nyāsa* (deposit).

Thus, a deposit (*nikṣepa*) is that which is placed before the recipient after being counted; an open deposit (*upanidhi*) is that which is placed before him without being counted but marked with a seal. A trust (*nyāsa*) is that which, whether counted or uncounted, is delivered into the hands of another—such as a son or relative—with the instruction, "This must be returned to the house-owner when he arrives. This is the distinction between them. Furthermore, Nārada states that there are two kinds of deposits and the like (*nikṣepādi*):
"That [deposit] is declared to be of two kinds: one with witnesses and likewise the other."
In the opposite case, a counter-offering would likewise serve as the condition for it.
In the case of the opposite, there is a failure of proof; [the word] *pratyaya* means divine [proof]. Manu (8.179) states the manner of depositing [property] and so forth:
"A wise man should make a deposit with one who is of noble birth, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in dharma, truthful, possessed of a large following, wealthy, and honorable."

"In one who has a great following and is joined with many kinsmen. The mention of "receiving a deposit" is illustrative. Bṛhaspati says: "Having examined the location, the house, the householder, his caste, various virtues, truthfulness, purity, and kinsmen, one should entrust a treasure."

A "deposit" (nidhi) and a "sealed deposit" (upanidhi)—this is also an illustration. Bṛhaspati states that a depositary must properly protect items such as deposits: "It is declared to be of two kinds: that given in the presence of witnesses and that given in secret;
it must be protected like a son, for it perishes through neglect."
The fruits and faults of protecting and failing to protect have been shown by that very same [author]:

"Whatever merit may arise from giving gold, base metals, garments, and so forth, that same merit would accrue to one who protects a deposit, just as it does for one who protects one who has come for refuge."

[184] Just as there would be guilt for a woman in betraying her husband, or for a man in killing his son or a friend, so too is there guilt for men in consuming or neglecting a deposit entrusted to them.
One should not take back a deposit; its loss brings dishonor.
Once accepted, one should protect it with care and return it when requested even once.
The mention of "deposit" (*nyāsa*) is illustrative. He himself states that whatever has been received by the recipient must be returned exactly as it was:
"By whatever procedure, by whom, what, and in whatever manner it was deposited, in that very same way it must be returned to him; it should not be given to his successor."

The immediate successor, other than the depositor, is the owner of the deposited property, such as his son or others. Manu (8.180) states that even the depositor must accept [the deposit] exactly as it was deposited: "In whatever manner a person places an object into the hand of another, in that very same manner it must be received; as the delivery was, so shall be the recovery."
*Ādāya* means giving, that is to say, depositing. Kātyāyana states (601) why [the deposit] must not be returned by the depositor during the period when it remains due to some fear:

"But a pledge (*upanidhi*) may be taken back at the [stipulated] time; however, one should avoid returning it before the time has elapsed. One who returns it prematurely shall be fined and made to pay double [its value]."

Even when there is danger, what has been requested must be given, because Bṛhaspati stated: "One should deliver what has been requested once. Regarding what must be done if that which was requested is not given, Nārada says: "But he who, being requested by the giver, does not return the deposit, shall be punished by the king and, if it is lost, shall be made to pay an equivalent amount."
The phrase "lost through fate or by the king" is the remainder [of the sentence]. Yājñavalkya also states (20.66):
"If there is loss when [the object] has been sought but not returned, the borrower must be made to pay [its value] and a fine equal to that.

The meaning is: if there is loss—meaning destruction caused by fate, the king, or other such factors—even though the object was sought and requested but not returned, nevertheless the borrower must be made to pay the owner the calculated value of that property, and a fine equal to that to the king. Manu also says (8.191):
"He who does not return a deposit, and he who demands it without having deposited anything—both of them should be punished like thieves, or made to pay a fine equal to the value of that [deposit].

Regarding the phrase "to be punished like thieves," this means they are to be penalized as thieves would be. Kātyāyana states what must be done when a deposit or similar item is lost through the fault of negligence: (594) [text follows].
If anything is lost or someone dies through the fault of another,
that person shall be made to pay the value of the property along with interest, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
He alone (Kāt. 596):
he by whom another's property, such as a deposit and so forth, has been consumed, neglected, or destroyed through ignorance, must be made to restore that very thing.
Bṛhaspati says: If a depositary, having neglected it through indifference or by means of separation, should destroy it,
or if he does not return it when requested, he shall be made to pay it back along with interest.

In this context, the mention of "neglect" (*upekṣayā*) as distinct [from consumption] is for the purpose of making it known that if a thing is destroyed along with one's own property through neglect, there shall be no repayment with interest. For this very reason, Vyāsa states:
"If [the object] is consumed, he should be made to pay with interest; if neglected, he should be made to pay the same amount;
if destroyed through ignorance, he should be made to pay a small portion less."
The teacher Vijñāneśvara states that "somewhat less" means less than one-fourth. Yājñavalkya (2.67) speaks regarding one who uses the deposited principal for enjoyment and so forth:
"If he lives at his own will [on it], he is to be punished and made to pay that [principal] along with interest.

"Living" means subsisting by means of lending money or other transactions for the sake of profit from enjoyment; "at his own will" means without the permission of the owner. Nārada also [says] (Nikṣepa 8):
If one should realize a profit there without the consent of the depositor,
he shall be punished for that as well and shall restore that profit along with interest.
The fine is in accordance with the value of the property recovered. And Kātyāyana has shown [the rule regarding] interest on a deposit:
"If one does not pay a deposit, the remainder of the interest, or [the proceeds from] a purchase or sale when asked for it, the debt increases by five percent per hundred. Thus [he says].

Regarding one who misappropriates a deposit, Viṣṇu (5.164) says: "The misappropriator of a deposit shall be made to pay the money to the creditor along with the interest. Manu (8.192) also prescribes a punishment for this:
"The king shall cause a fine equal to that [amount] to be paid by the misappropriator of a deposit, and likewise especially by the misappropriator of a sealed deposit (*upanidhi*)."
Vyāsa states what should be done in the case of denying a deposit:
"If a man, supported by the strength of his kinsmen, denies a deposit,
he should be made to restore it after being investigated through witnesses or by means of an ordeal."
Regarding the punishment for this, Bṛhaspati says: "Where one, having taken [a deposit], denies it— whether by means of witnesses or by oath—
one should cause that person to restore the deposit after it has been proven, and likewise impose a fine equal to its value."

Regarding deposits and the like made in the presence of witnesses, Manu (8.194) states that if the depositor is found to be wicked, the king, having ascertained the matter exactly as it was from the witnesses, should punish him: "Whatever deposit was made by someone, and of whatever amount, in the presence of witnesses—that same amount must be recognized; he who speaks falsely deserves punishment."

A family [of witnesses] is a group of witnesses. But regarding a case without witnesses, Bṛhaspati says: "When a dispute arises concerning a secret deposit, it is traditionally held that divine proof (divya) is the means of determination for both parties."

The meaning is "of one of the two. Bṛhaspati states that there is no fault for the borrower if there is destruction due to divine or royal calamity: "If it should meet its destruction through divine or royal calamity, along with the property of the borrower, no fault is found therein."

The phrase "accompanied by the appropriator and the object" is stated for the purpose of ascertaining the absence of negligence (*upekṣā*) and other such factors. Therefore, it should be understood that even if the deposit itself is somehow destroyed, if the absence of negligence is ascertained through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the appropriator is not at fault. Yājñavalkya (2.66) also states:
"But he shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by kings, by fate, or by thieves.
And Manu (8.189) has shown an example of what constitutes an act of fate (*daivika*).
If it has been stolen by thieves, carried away by water, or consumed by fire, he need not give it back; for he did not take anything from that person himself.

Therefore, the meaning is that if he does not recover or take back even a small amount of wealth from that deposit, then he need not pay it; that is, if someone deposits something knowing that its destruction is possible there due to the king, thieves, calamities, and so forth, then the receiver shall not be made to pay for the loss of what was deposited there, regardless of the cause—so says Kātyāyana (599):
"But where a depositor, having known the potential loss of the property, makes a deposit..."
Even when all means of recovery have failed, the debtor shall never be compelled to pay.
Upon the death of the depositor, that [deposit] must be returned to the immediate successor, such as a son. For this very reason, Manu (8.186) states:
"But he who returns it himself to the immediate successor of the deceased shall not be prosecuted by the king, nor by the relatives of the depositor."

"By himself alone" means without being asked; giving without being asked should be understood to occur when there is no occasion for fear or other such motives, as otherwise a fault would arise. To indicate that the gift should be given in the presence of all the immediate relatives—such as sons—if they are numerous, it is rightly stated that "the depositor or the relatives must not make a claim. If the borrower does not pay voluntarily, then he [Manu] states what should be done by the immediate relative (MDh 8.187): "One should seek that object through friendly means, without any artifice."
Or, having investigated his conduct, one should settle the matter through conciliation alone.

"He should investigate" means he should ascertain [the facts]. By the phrase "having deliberated upon his conduct therein, he should settle the matter through conciliation alone," it is indicated that if the debtor is of evil conduct, he should be made to pay by means of other methods such as the display of intimidation, as described in the section on the recovery of debts (*ṛṇādāna*). Yājñavalkya (2.67) extends this rule to deposits, loans for use, and so forth:
"This same rule applies to articles borrowed, pledged, deposited, or entrusted."

[188] *Yācita* refers to clothing, ornaments, and so forth, requested for the sake of beauty on occasions such as a wedding, which has been brought back after being borrowed from another. *Anvāhita* is that which a depositor has placed in one's hands with the instruction, "This was deposited with me by so-and-so; you must return it to him. Although the rules for *nyāsa* (deposit) and *nikṣepa* (entrustment) have been taught, they were taught by Yājñavalkya specifically in the context of *upanidhi* (sealed deposit) and not elsewhere; therefore, this extension of the rule is appropriate. Bṛhaspati also says:

"In the case of *anvāhita*, borrowed goods (*yācitaka*), artisan deposits (*śilpin-nyāsa*), collateral (*sabandhaka*), and likewise those who have come for refuge (*śaraṇāgata*), this same law is declared to apply."

Regarding "artisans' deposit" (*śilpinnyāsa*), this refers to gold and other materials placed in the hands of a goldsmith or similar craftsman for the purpose of making earrings and other ornaments. Nārada also states (Nikṣepa 14):
"This same rule is seen to apply to borrowed items, those held in trust, and so forth;
it applies likewise to deposits with artisans, open deposits (*upanihi*), sealed deposits (*nyāsa*), and counter-deposits (*pratinyāsa*)."

Regarding artisans, there is the "artisan-deposit" (*śilpinyāsa*). Regarding the "counter-deposit" (*pratinyāsa*), it refers to what is deposited by mutual agreement based on the requirements of the work, such as: "This, which belongs to you, is placed with me; this, which belongs to me, must be placed by you. Since Nārada has provided the rules for the deposit (*nikṣepa*) alone, the rules for the open deposit (*upanidhi*) and the artisan-deposit are extended to it by analogy (*atideśa*). From this extension, one might conclude that when an artisan-deposit—being unsolicited—is destroyed due to an act of God or the king, goldsmiths and others should not be made to pay for it. In response to this, Kātyāyana states an exception in verse 603: "And that deposit which is being refined over a fixed number of days..."
If the artisan leaves it unfinished, he shall be made to pay that amount even after the deity has been installed.

When an old garment or similar item is handed over to a washerman or other artisan for the purpose of cleaning and so forth, if it is destroyed by means of beating and such methods, the artisan shall not be made to pay for it; because the destruction occurred through the beating intended for the sake of cleanliness, there is no fault on the part of the craftsman. However, in the case of a new item or similar object, since the destruction resulting from excessively vigorous beating and so forth is caused by the fault of the artisan, he must be made to pay its value. With this in mind, it was stated by that same author (Kāt. 604): "If the destruction should occur due to a fault of the deposit [other than the artisan's], one should not make the artisan pay for it. One should make him pay for it if it results from the artisan's fault—that which was entrusted for the purpose of restoration."
In response to the question of how much of its value should be recovered when a cloth given by a washerman for the purpose of washing is destroyed by him, Nārada says (Krītā 8–9):
“One-eighth of the value is lost for a garment washed once;
for one washed twice, one-quarter; for one washed thrice, one-third; and for one washed four times, half.”

But beyond the point where half has been destroyed, there is a gradual reduction by one-quarter [of the value]. When that which has been washed once is ruined, its price should be taken as reduced by one-eighth; when it has been washed twice, reduced by one-fourth. This should be applied accordingly for subsequent washings as well. Regarding the punishment for artisans in cases such as the improper use of their tools or materials, Yājñavalkya (2.238) says: "An artisan who wears another's garment is to be fined three *paṇas*."
In cases of sale, lease, pledge, or borrowing, the fine shall be ten paṇas.

A *nejaka* is a washerman. *Avakraya* is the handing over [of an object] for the purpose of its enjoyment by someone after receiving a rental fee and establishing a fixed period of time. *Ādhāna* is making something a pledge. *Yācita* is giving to one's friends on the basis of having been requested. A washerman must not wash clothes on stone; rather, he should do so on a smooth board made of *śālmali* wood. Furthermore, he must not mix their clothes together, nor should they be kept in his house overnight. Thus says Manu (8.396):
A washerman shall wash clothes on a smooth board made of *śālmali* wood.
He shall not exchange clothes for other clothes, nor shall he allow them to be worn [by others].

Regarding the specific case where thread and such materials, entrusted to a weaver or similar artisan for the purpose of making garments, are lost while in the state of a fragmentary cloth or when being delivered by the weaver in their finished state, and are not accepted by the owner but subsequently go missing—the same author states the following concerning that matter (Kāt. 605):
If even a very small amount of work performed by a hired servant is lost,
it will be sufficient to destroy the wealth of one who wishes to give it, provided he does not take hold of it.

If a work such as weaving a garment is defective—due even to a small flaw or a torn edge—and thus ruined, that loss falls upon the hired artisan alone; the meaning is that he must perform the weaving and other tasks again, even without receiving further wages. If the employer does not provide the raw materials such as thread, then even in the absence of further weaving, the employer shall not recover the wages already paid to the artisan. If the employer refuses to accept the finished garment or the like from the hands of the artisan who intends to deliver it in full, the meaning is that the employer loses that completed article. Thus, the final conclusion here is that the hired artisan is not made liable for the loss. Regarding gold and other materials placed in the hands of a goldsmith or similar craftsman for the purpose of making ornaments and the like: the artisan must return an article of gold of the same weight as the gold provided. However, articles made of silver and the like may be returned with some reduction in weight. Blankets and the like, however, may be returned with a slight increase relative to the wool and other raw materials used. If the artisan does not return them in this manner, then he must be compelled by the king to do so and shall be punished. With all this in mind, Yājñavalkya (2.178–180) demonstrates the equality in the case of gold and the specific measures for profit and loss in other cases.
In fire, gold is not diminished; in silver, two palas per hundred;
in tin and lead, eight; and in copper and iron, five per hundred.
In a hundred [palas], the increase for wool, cotton, and silk thread is ten palas;
for medium quality, the increase is five palas; but for fine quality, it is considered to be three palas.
In manufactured cloth and in woolen fabric, a loss of one-thirtieth is considered;
there is neither loss nor increase in silk and in bark-cloth.

The phrase "being heated in fire" is to be supplied [to each case]. When a hundred *pala* of silver is heated, two *pala* are lost; in the case of tin and lead, eight *pala*; in copper, five *pala*; and in iron, ten *pala*—this is the meaning. Since bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) is produced from tin and copper, its loss should be calculated accordingly, and thus it is not mentioned separately. In the case of thick woolen, cotton, or thread fibers weighing a hundred *pala*, ten *pala* increase [in weight]; in those that are not very fine, five *pala*; and in fine ones, three *pala*—this is the meaning. Master Vijñāneśvara states that this refers to unwashed cloth. *Kārmika* means made by variegated work; it refers to a woven cloth on which figures such as the *svastika* are created using multicolored threads. *Romabandha* refers to items such as blankets where animal hairs are woven in. In these two cases, there is a loss of one-thirtieth part relative to the original thread. He states the specific rule regarding borrowed items (Kāt. 606):

If one has been asked for something with a specific purpose in mind, or for a fixed period of time, and that object is not delivered because the purpose was only half-accomplished or the time had not yet arrived, then he is not made to pay it.

When a person has requested an item for a task that is to be accomplished over a long period of time, stipulating, "Let this be given until the end of the year," and having thus fixed the duration; if, while the work is still in progress or within the fixed period, he is asked to return the loan and does not give it back, then he should not be made to pay interest. Rather, the meaning is that once the work is finished or the fixed period has elapsed, he should return only the loaned article itself. However, if he does not return it at the conclusion of the work or after the stated time has passed, then in the event of its destruction by fate or other causes, he must pay its value; so says the same author (Kāt. 607).
If a transaction is completed when the time has arrived, one shall not refuse to deliver it even when requested;
if that object is lost or stolen, the borrower must pay its value.
In some cases, even during the course of a transaction within a fixed period, he (Kātyāyana) speaks of lending on interest:
"If, however, there is a failure of the transaction, that loss shall belong to the owner himself;
even if the fixed time has not yet arrived, he must cause [the borrower] to pay it, even if only half of the work has been done. (Kāt. 609)

The meaning is that if, upon failing to return a borrowed item, its owner’s business is ruined, then one must return it. He himself (Kāt. 610) states what must be done regarding the taking of borrowed items:
"He who, having taken a borrowed item, does not return it when asked;
he should be seized by force and compelled to give it, and he who does not give it shall be fined."
He should be restrained by force and compelled to pay; the meaning is that even so, he who does not pay shall be punished.
Thus ends the exposition of the legal title known as "Deposits" (nikṣepa) in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* of the illustrious Kodaṇḍaparaśurāma. 17.

**Possible reading of the defective text:** In the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "Śrīkodaṇḍa-paraśurāma"— this is the seventeenth [chapter], the exposition of the legal title known as "Deposits" (*nikṣepa*), within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*.
Now follows the determination of the legal title known as "Sale Without Ownership. Nārada defines its essential nature (Asvāmika-vikraya, verse 1):
"Having found, or having seized, property belonging to another that has been deposited, lost, or stolen..."
That which is sold in the absence [of the owner] is to be known as sale without ownership (asvāmivikraya).

The mention of "deposit" (*nikṣepa*) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for items such as those borrowed on request (*yācita*). The phrase "in the absence of the owner" (*asamakṣaṃ svāminaḥ*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. For this very reason, Vyāsa states:

"When a borrowed item, an object held in trust (*anvāhita*), or a deposit (*nyāsa*), or whatever wealth belongs to another, is sold in the absence of the owner, that is to be known as 'sale without ownership' (*asvāmivikraya*)."

[192] "In the absence of ownership" means in the absence of the owner. Here, the mention of "sale" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for both "giving as a gift" and "pledging. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states that these two also are subject to rescission:
"One should rescind a sale, a gift, or a pledge made by one who is not the owner."

*Asvāmi* is a separate word meaning "without an owner," i.e., lacking the presence of an owner. The change in gender is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Alternatively, it means *asvāmivikrayam*, a sale made by one who is not the owner. In this view, by association with that term, the acts of giving and mortgaging (*dāna-adhyau*) should also be understood as being performed by one who is not the owner. For this very reason, Yama says: "Whatever gift or sale is made by one who is not the owner, that should always be known as invalid in legal proceedings."

"Dāya" means "gift. Bṛhaspati demonstrates who is not the owner: one by whom a deposit, a loan for use, a pledge, a borrowed item, or a security has been sold in secret—that person is designated as "not the owner."

The mention of "receiving deposits and the like" is an illustration that includes other forms of another's property, such as lost-and-found items. For this very reason, Manu (8.197) states: "He who, not being the owner and without the consent of the owner, sells what belongs to another... The term *upāṃśu* means "in secret" or "unpublicly. This, too, is an illustration; for even one who sells another's property, such as a deposit, openly is likewise a non-owner. When something sold by a non-owner is seen in someone's possession, it should be recovered from that person by the true owner. And so says Nārada (Asvāmi-vikraya 2):
Having obtained property sold by one who is not its owner, the true owner shall recover it;
Yājñavalkya also states (2.168): "One may recover one's own property sold by another; the fault lies with the purchaser if the sale was not publicly announced."
A thief [is one who takes] from a low person in secret, for a low price, or at an improper time.

If a purchase is made unannounced, concealed, from a person of low character who lacks a legitimate means of acquiring that wealth, in secret or in private, for a low price or with insufficient payment, or at an improper time such as during the night, the purchaser is liable to punishment like a thief; this is the meaning. [193] The owner must recover his property only after having informed the king; otherwise, he may be punished for concealing a thief. Thus, the same author (YDh. 2.172) says:
"He who recovers from the hand of another a stolen or lost article..."
If he does not report [the stolen property] to the king, he shall be fined ninety-six *paṇas*.

Having ascertained the existence of his own property in the presence of the purchaser and having informed the king, he is to be made to recover it by the king’s officers. However, when the king and his officers are at a distance, and there is a suspicion of flight or similar evasion prior to the time of reporting, he himself must seize and hand him over; thus says the same author (YDh. 2.169):
"Having recovered lost or stolen property, one should cause the man who took it to be apprehended."
And if there is a lapse regarding the place or time, one should take it oneself and offer it.

The venerable Vijñāneśvara holds that the word *hartṛ* here intends the purchaser (*kretṛ*). Viṣṇu also states the same meaning as that expressed by Yājñavalkya in the passage beginning with "the fault of the purchaser lies in not making it public" (YDh 2.168–170). "If one should purchase another's property openly and unknowingly, he is without fault; the owner shall recover the property. However, if he purchases it secretly or for a low price, then either the purchaser or the seller is to be punished like a thief. (ViDh 5.159–161)

The meaning is that, due to ignorance—because the seller’s lack of public sale and so forth has not been realized—the purchaser lacks ownership; however, in the case of a non-public sale and the like, because such a sale indicates that the seller is the owner, the purchaser possesses knowledge of that fact and is therefore culpable and subject to punishment. Nārada also [states] (Asvāmi-vikraya 2): "A purchase made publicly is pure; theft results from a secret purchase. Bṛhaspati also [says]:
But there is no fault in that which was purchased for a price and previously reported to the king; one becomes a thief only through the act of secret sale.

The meaning is that even when purchased for a low price, if it has been made manifest prior to the purchase, it does not give rise to a fault. He himself explains the meaning of the term *upavikraya* (fraudulent sale): "That which is purchased inside a house, outside a village, at night, from an unreliable person, or for a low price—this should be known as *upavikraya*."

[194] From an "unworthy person" (*asat*), meaning from a *caṇḍāla* or similar outcaste; the mention of the "unworthy" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for slaves and others. For this very reason, Nārada states: "One who buys at a low price, at an improper time, and in secret, from a slave, from one who is not the owner, or from an unworthy person, shall incur the fault of that [transaction]. (Asvāmi-vikraya 3)

"Without the owner's consent" means without the permission of the owner. The mention of "slave" is an illustration for those who are dependent, such as children and others. The owner whose property has been lost, having brought the purchaser before the royal court, must establish his own ownership over that property through evidence such as inheritance, gift, and so forth, by means of witness testimony. Otherwise, he shall be punished. And thus says Kātyāyana (613):
"The claimant should first establish his own [ownership] through kinsmen";
the word "through kinsmen" implies "acting as witnesses. He himself (Kāt. 620):
If one who denies his kin does not restore the property himself,
he deserves punishment like a thief in order to prevent such occurrences.

The "non-owner" (*nāṣṭika*) is the owner whose property has been lost. "Occasion" (*prasaṅga*) refers to doubt regarding ownership. Yājñavalkya also states (2.171): "If [the property] is not proven [to belong to the claimant] by means of title (*āgama*) or possession (*upabhoga*), then he must pay a fine to the king equal to five times its value, provided it is not established [otherwise]."
A "fivefold fine" (*pañcabandha*) is a penalty equal to one-fifth of the lost property. Vyāsa also states:
"If the plaintiff does not prove the claimed property through witnesses, he shall be made to pay double the fine; the purchaser, however, deserves that property."

The mention of "by witnesses" refers to a dispute concerning sale without ownership (*asvāmivikraya*). It is intended to exclude other means of proof for establishing ownership. In this matter, the distinction in punishment must be determined according to the gravity or lightness of the offense. The grounds for ownership have already been shown in the exposition on inference (*anumāna*). After the claimant of loss (*nāṣṭika*) has established his ownership, he must also prove the absence of any act—such as gift or sale—that would have caused the cessation of that ownership. Thus says Kātyāyana (614): "But the claimant of loss shall establish that wealth as his own through his kinsmen."
Having made something that was not given, not relinquished, or sold one's own, one recovers the wealth.

[195] "Given" means bestowed upon someone who has become a recipient in the manner prescribed by rule. "Relinquished" means given as a reward or similar form of gratuity. Bṛhaspati says that the person from whom the buyer purchased the item—brought there by the king's officers—must be produced, [thinking]: "He from whom it was bought must be shown. However, if the former owner comes and investigates that property, the original source (the seller) must be shown; from that, the buyer shall attain purification.
The "source" is the seller. "Purification" is the cessation of being subject to legal accusation. For this very reason, Vyāsa states:
"Once the source has been produced, the purchaser is not to be accused in any way;
rather, a dispute with the owner of the lost article is ordained to take place regarding that source."

When it has been brought back and pointed out with the words, "This was purchased by me," Yājñavalkya (2.170) also states: "Purification [from the taint] comes from the appearance of the seller; the owner recovers the property, the king receives a fine, and the buyer recovers the price from him who sold it."

In this context, the purpose of the statement "the owner is the [legitimate] possessor of the property" is to indicate that if the seller does not dispute with the claimant (the *nāṣṭika*), or if he loses the dispute once it has been raised, then the ownership of the claimant is established; consequently, the sold goods and so forth must be returned to the claimant and others, and not otherwise. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says: "When the seller is produced but is defeated in the legal proceeding, he shall pay the purchase price and a fine to the king, and the value of the property to the owner."

If the seller resides in another country, then a period of time corresponding to the distance must be granted for the purpose of bringing him; thus says Kātyāyana (615): "In that case, a period for producing the original [seller] should be granted according to the number of stages on the road. However, when he is unable to produce the original even after a lapse of time, then he must prove the purchase by means of witnesses. And so it has been stated by that same author (Kāt. 618):
But one who cannot produce a basis for his possession must clear up the purchase itself;
once the purchase has been cleared up by the king, he should not be held liable for anything at all.

The meaning is that once the purchase has been cleared and the testimony of witnesses has been made public, the king should neither say anything against him nor punish him. As for what was stated by that same author (Kāt.
613): "The plaintiff should first provide his own wealth through his kinsmen;
afterwards, for the sake of his own purification, the purchaser should provide the purchase-price through his own relatives."

It has been stated that once the claimant has established his ownership, the purchaser must subsequently prove the legality of the purchase; however, this requirement is understood from the very same rule to apply only when the source [of the goods] cannot be recovered. Even if the purchaser has proved the purchase, the owner whose property was lost shall not recover the purchased article. And so says Manu (8.202):
"But if the source cannot be recovered and the purchase is cleared by means of a public sale, the purchaser is released by the king without punishment, and the owner recovers his property."

"Unseizable" means not to be brought back [by the owner]. The meaning is that the owner who lost the property does not recover wealth that has been cleared by a public sale; rather, the purchaser, being exempt from punishment, is released from restraint by the king. As for the verse: "That which is situated in a merchant's row, known by the king's officers, and purchased during the day by the buyer—he is pure and recovers the wealth."
And as for the words of Marīci:
"Whatever wealth one might acquire through sale in the presence of the family,
that person indeed acquires the wealth lawfully and it is purified by purchase."

This statement of Manu (8.201) refers to cases where there is an absence of proof for the ownership of the original owner. Kātyāyana (616) states that the proof of purchase must be established by witnesses alone: "One should effect the transaction openly with virtuous kinsmen and one's own people; no other means of proof—neither divine nor human—is prescribed in such a case."
Regarding what the King must do when the seller fails to produce the original object or the means of proof for the purchase, that same author (Kātyāyana, verse 619) says:
"If he does not produce the original object, or if he fails to clear the purchase [by producing the means of proof],
he shall be made to pay the money to the creditor according to the claim, as well as a fine."

The same author (Kātyāyana, verse 617) states that a purchaser, having promised to produce the original source of the goods and then failing to do so, may nevertheless seek to validate the purchase by asserting, "I shall establish the purchase":
"When a litigant, having presented the original source, subsequently speaks of the purchase, he must bring forth the source itself;
there is no need for the purchase."

But when there is no clear evidence establishing the ownership of the claimant, nor any evidence establishing the purchase by the buyer, then, having regard to the integrity and other qualities of the two parties, the king should divide the disputed property equally or in proportionate shares—more or less—and issue a decree stating, "This much is yours; this much is yours. Thus says Bṛhaspati: "In a dispute lacking evidence, the king himself should make a decision based on the character of the individuals, whether by way of equality, deficiency, or excess."

Regarding the phrase "in a lawsuit lacking proof," this also indicates that in a dispute known as *asvāmivikraya* (sale by one who is not the owner), there is an absence of evidence other than witnesses; for it is impossible for there to be a lack of proof when divine ordeals (*divya*) are accepted. Furthermore, he (Kātyāyana, verses 621–622) states that even in some cases where there is proof, the buyer and the original owner may divide the property equally and take possession of it:
"When an item is found in a merchant's stall and recognized by the king's officers, yet was purchased from an unknown person, or where the seller has died."

The owner, having paid half the price, may recover his own property. "Obtained in the merchant's row" means found in the marketplace; by this, the absence of a secret purchase is indicated. "Known by the king’s officers" indicates the absence of clandestine action. "From an unknown source" means from an unknown location. The meaning is that whatever has been purchased without a secret transaction and so forth, from an unknown source, or where the seller is deceased, that may be taken back after paying half the price. He (Kātyāyana, verses 622–23) states the reason for the reduction of the price by half for both parties: Kātyāyana (622): "If a person sells a commodity in the market at a low price, he shall be made to pay the difference between the two prices as a fine. Kātyāyana (623): "If a person purchases a commodity in the market at a high price, he shall likewise be made to pay the difference between the two prices as a fine. The meaning is that when a person sells a good in the market for less than its true value, he must pay the difference between the selling price and the actual value as a fine. Similarly, if one buys a good in the market for more than its true value, he must pay the difference between the purchase price and the actual value as a fine. Thus, in both cases, the fine is equal to the loss incurred by the respective party. Therefore, the owner who recovers his property by paying half the price is effectively compensating for the loss incurred by the seller. This rule applies to all transactions involving stolen goods, whether they are sold openly or secretly. If the seller is dead, the heirs must pay the fine. If the heirs do not acknowledge the theft, the purchaser is liable for the fine. If the purchaser is unable to pay the fine, the king may seize his other property to satisfy the claim. If the purchaser was unaware of the theft, he is exempt from the fine, but the owner still recovers his property upon paying half the price. This law ensures that the thief is punished through the forfeiture of his gains, while the honest buyer is protected from unjust seizure. It also serves to deter theft by making the sale of stolen goods a punishable offense. Thus, the legal system balances the rights of the owner with the protection of innocent buyers in public markets.
In that case, half of the fault shall be assigned to each of the two according to legal procedure:
the fault of purchasing without proper inquiry and likewise the fault of failing to protect [the property].
These two have been declared by the wise to be the causes of the loss of the goods.

"Lost" means destroyed through legal proceedings due to one's own fault. "Purchase from an unknown source" means a purchase made from a place whose identity is not known. "Failure to protect" means a lack of guarding; that is to say, negligence. Marīci also says:
"Because the place of deposit was unknown, where the price cannot be recovered, the loss there should be considered equal between both the buyer and the owner."
Just as the non-owner seller is liable to punishment, so too Nārada declares that the non-owner who enjoys property without the owner's consent is likewise liable to punishment:
"Whether it be a woman, cattle, or even land, one must enjoy only what has been specifically assigned;
however, he who enjoys what has not been assigned shall be made to pay for the enjoyment already consumed."
But one who enjoys by his own power any property not assigned to him— such as clothing, fields, houses, and so forth— deserves punishment like a thief.
One who eats the meat of an ox, a cow, a boat, or likewise a draft animal that has not been specifically designated for slaughter, shall pay a fine of four paṇas.
A female slave, a boat, and likewise a draft animal are not to be used as collateral;
however, the user of such property shall clear the debt by means of the commodity itself.
A female slave is worth two paṇas per day; likewise, a milch cow is eight paṇas;
a draft ox, a horse, and land are thirteen, sixteen, and [twenty] paṇas respectively.
He who enjoys by force a boat, horses, a cow, or the plough of a laborer shall be made to pay eight times the value for each day.
The sage Jaimini declared that the price for a mortar is half a paṇa, for a pestle two paṇas, and for a winnowing basket half a paṇa.

"With merchandise," that is, with a collection of goods. Here, one word "dhenu" denotes a cow, while the other denotes a milch animal such as a buffalo or the like. "Of the artisan" means of one who lives by his craft.

Yājñavalkya (2.173) states that if property whose owner is unknown has been stolen or lost and is somehow recovered by royal officers and presented to the king, its owner, having arrived within the course of a year and established proof of ownership, may take it back from the king:
"Property that has been lost or stolen and recovered by customs officials or local guardians, the owner may take back before one year has passed; after that, the king [takes it]."

[199] Regarding that which establishes the meaning: "The owner who has appeared within three years may take [the property]," the king shall cause property whose owner is lost to be kept for three years.
Before the end of three years, the owner may take it; after that, the king shall take it.

This statement of Manu (8.30) refers to a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct. Gautama (10.36–37) states that property seized by royal officers should be set aside after proclaiming in the presence of many people: "Let him who is its owner come and take it," adding: "Having found property whose owner has disappeared, they shall announce it to the king; it must be guarded by the king for one year. Regarding this, Manu (8.33) says that the owner of the wealth, upon taking it, shall give to the king—by way of wages for its protection—a twelfth, a tenth, or a sixth part of that wealth, respectively, for the first, second, and third years.
"Then the king, remembering the duty of the virtuous, shall take a sixth, a tenth, or even a twelfth part of goods found after being lost.

Here, "sixth part" (*ṣaḍbhāga*) means the sixth portion; for it is stated that in the context of grammatical derivation (*vṛtti*), numeral words are intended to express ordinal completion. Yājñavalkya states an exception regarding specific types of property (2.174):
One should pay five silver paṇas for a single-hoofed animal, four for a human,
two each for a buffalo, a camel, or a cow, and one-quarter each for a goat or a sheep.

Regarding single-hoofed animals such as horses and the like: a *pāda* is one-fourth of a *paṇa*. The meaning is that one should pay one *pāda* for a goat (*aja*) and one should pay one *pāda* for a sheep (*avi*).
Thus ends the exposition of the legal title known as "Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner" in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* of the illustrious Kodaṇḍaparaśurāma. || 18 ||

**Possible reading of the defective text:** In the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "Śrī Kodaṇḍa-Paraśurāma"— this is the eighteenth [section], the exposition of the legal title known as "Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner," within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*.
Now follows the determination of the legal title known as *sambhūya-samutthāna* (joint enterprise).
Regarding its nature, Nārada states (Sambhūya. 1):
"Where merchants and others perform an undertaking jointly..."
That is known as the legal head of joint undertaking.

By the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*), there is the inclusion of priests, farmers, artisans, dancers, and thieves. Bṛhaspati shows who the qualified persons are for performing activities such as trade together:
"One should carry out business with those who are of noble birth, skillful, untiring, wise, knowledgeable in coinage, aware of income and expenditure, pure, and brave."

[200] Regarding activities consisting of trade, sacrifice, agriculture, craftsmanship, music, and theft: those who possess knowledge of coinage have the right to engage in trade; the wise, the noble-born, and the pure have the right to perform sacrifices; those who know income and expenditure have the right to agriculture; the wise have the right to the practice of craftsmanship and music; and the brave have the right to the act of theft. Proficiency and lack of indolence are qualifications for all offices. The mention of "proficient and not indolent" is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of those who are fortunate and not afflicted by disease. The mention of "knowers of coinage" is also an elliptical indication of those who possess capital. For this very reason, by prohibiting those who are proficient yet indolent, unfortunate persons and others are likewise prohibited.
The wise should not undertake activities such as trade and the like with those who are powerless, lazy, afflicted by disease, unfortunate, or without support.
Those who have no support are those devoid of principal capital. Nārada states that profits and so forth should be apportioned according to the share of the principal capital:
"Whether equal, excessive, or deficient, whatever kind of share belongs to anyone therein, loss, expense, and profit shall be of that same kind for him."
Bṛhaspati also says:
"But for those who carry out transactions with gold, grain, liquids, and so forth,
their profit shall be of a corresponding nature, according to whether the shares are equal, deficient, or excessive."
Whatever portion— whether equal, deficient, or excessive— is cast [by a planet], it shall likewise incur expenditure,
perform action, and indeed receive profit.

If an agreement has been made by all [the partners] based on a consideration of the relative importance of their respective contributions—such that "one part belongs to this person" and "two parts belong to that person"—then the gains and losses should be apportioned accordingly; thus says Yājñavalkya (2.259):
"When merchants perform work for the sake of profit through a partnership, the profit and loss shall be according to the capital invested, or as determined by their agreement."
Regarding what must be done by those acting in concert, Nārada says (Sambhūya. 4):
"Established in their own agreement, they should without deviation attend to the merchandise, the capital, the expenses, the profits, the loads, the quality, and the supervision."
Vyāsa also says:
Deceiving one another, whether face-to-face or behind one's back,
they should carry out buying and selling in accordance with various commodities.
Those who do not protect their goods must pay the toll on the road;
otherwise, if they remain outside the toll station, they shall be made to pay double.
Bṛhaspati states that even a single person may perform an act when it has the approval of all:
"If a man, being authorized by many, should give wealth or cause a legal document to be executed, it shall be considered as done by everyone."
The means of proof (*karaṇa*) consists of written documents and so forth. Regarding the method of decision in mutual disputes among these, that same [author] has stated:
"In a doubtful matter or in a case of fraud, those very same persons are declared to be both examiners and witnesses, provided they are not possessed by enmity."
He [Yājñavalkya] himself states that when there is a state of mutual enmity, a determination must be made through oaths:
"If anyone among them is known to be a cheat in buying or selling, he too must be cleared by means of oaths; this rule applies in every legal dispute as well."
Even in the case of all speech, including speech other than that which is deceptive; regarding the certainty of deception, Yājñavalkya (2.265) says:
"They should abandon the crooked person who provides no profit; if unable [to do so], one should have it done by another."

*Jihmam* means deceitful. As for one who, among those acting in partnership, is unable to perform his own work—such as inspecting the merchandise—he may have that work performed by another person appointed by someone; this is the meaning of the phrase "he may have [the work] done by another through a deputy. However, if any one among them causes some loss by performing what is prohibited for others, by doing what was not authorized, or through a lack of attention, then he must pay for that merchandise. But if, out of fear of thieves, kings, or similar threats, one protects the merchandise from among them, the remaining merchandise should be taken by all after giving him a tenth part of the protected merchandise. And so says Yājñavalkya (2.260):

If a deposit is lost through negligence—whether it was forbidden or not specifically instructed—the keeper shall restore it; furthermore, if he protects it from loss, he is entitled to a tenth part as his reward.

[202] That which is neither assigned nor authorized; Bṛhaspati also says: "If one who has not been appointed, while being restrained, should cause loss through negligence, that loss must be made good by him alone to all the partners."
But for one who protects [the property] by his own power from fear of kings or divine calamities,
they should give him a tenth part and take the other portions for themselves.

Bṛhaspati states that when those acting in concert recover common property from debtors and others through means such as petitioning, the profit shall not be given to one who does not recover it along with them:
"That which is given by those acting together must be requested in the same manner;
whoever does not request it is deprived of his share of the profit."

The mention of "requesting" (*yācana*) is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for whatever action must be performed by each person according to their own share. Consequently, it should be understood that even in the failure to perform such an action, there is a loss of profit; this is stated in the *Smṛticandrikā*: "In the event of a loss caused by fate or the king, that [loss] must be apportioned among all [partners] in accordance with their respective shares. And as it has been said by that same author: "When a loss or depletion occurs therein due to fate or the king, it is declared that it shall be apportioned among all of them according to their shares."

*Kṣayahāniḥ* is loss in the form of depletion; it is of the nature of that which is the expenditure for the purpose of increasing that [depletion]. Manu states what must be performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) acting in concert:
"The officiating priests, having assembled as invited at a *sattra*, should perform their respective duties and likewise receive their sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)."

By the word *satra* here, any sacrifice in general is intended, and not specifically that particular type of sacrifice called a *satra* which involves many sacrificers; for in such a case, there would be an absence of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) worthy of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), since the sacrificers themselves would be performing the duties of the *hotṛ* and other priests. Regarding this, Manu himself (8.211) states: "The sacrificial fee is to be received by the priests after being divided among them. Furthermore, he says: "When men here perform their respective duties in combination, the allotment of the portions to be performed must be made according to this sequential method."

"One's own rites" refers to those rites other than that of the sacrificer, such as the duties of the *hotṛ* priest and others. This rule for the conceptual assignment of respective portions applies to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) prescribed merely by its connection to the sacrifice—as in the injunction "its fee is one hundred and twelve"—but not to that which is prescribed specifically in connection with a particular officiant. [203] Otherwise, there would result a contradiction with the Vedic texts establishing that [specific allotment], such as: "One should give a horse at the recitation of the *nivid* during the *śastra*. Therefore, the officiant by whose name the fee is prescribed shall be the one to receive it. For this very reason, Manu and Bṛhaspati stated (Manu 8.209): [text follows].
The Adhvaryu shall take the chariot, and the Brahman the horse at the kindling of the fires;
the Hotṛ shall take the horse that chooses the Nivid, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase [of the Soma].

A *vara* is a boon obtained through petitioning or solicitation. Here, by the word *udgātṛ*, the *subrahmaṇya* is understood as being included within the group of *udgātṛ*s. *Anaḥ* means a cart. Regarding the purchase (*kraya*), that is, the purchase of Soma, Manu and Bṛhaspati state the method for the distribution of shares (Manu 8.210):
"Of all [the priests], the principal ones are entitled to half; others are entitled to half of that [half];
those with a third share receive a third part, while those with a fourth share receive a quarter."

Among all sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the principal ones—the *hotṛ*, *brahmā*, *adhvaryu*, and *udgātṛ*—are the leaders of the group; they are called "half-sharers" (*ardhin*) because they receive a portion slightly less than half of the prescribed sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), for if they were to take the full half, it would result in a contradiction with the distribution of shares to be described hereafter. The others, the second group—the *maitrāvaruṇa*, *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*, *pratiprasthātṛ*, and *prastotṛ*—are "half-holders" (*ardhagrāhin*), receiving half of the share of the principal priests. The third group—the *acchāvāka*, *āgnīdhra*, *neṣṭṛ*, and *pratihartr̥*—partake of a third part of the principal share. The final group, known as the *grāvastotr̥*, *potr̥*, *unnetr̥*, and *subrahmaṇya*, are "quarter-sharers" (*pādin*), meaning they receive a fourth part of the principal share. This applies equally to the mutual distribution among the four groups of the second, third, and fourth ranks. With all this in mind, it is stated in the *Bodhāyanakārikā*: [The text continues with the specific verse from the Bodhāyanakārikā.]
Having divided the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) into twenty-five groups in sequence,
they are twelve, then six, four, and three.

The hundred cows constituting the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must first be divided into four parts. Among these, one part belongs to the group of *hotṛ*s, another to the group of *brahmā*s, another to the group of *adhvaryu*s, and another to the group of *udgātṛ*s. Furthermore, each of these parts must be divided into twenty-five sub-parts. Of these, the first group—the *hotṛ*s and so forth—receives twelve parts; the second group receives six; the third group receives four; and the fourth group receives three. This is the meaning. In the *Kātyāyana-Śrautasūtra* (10.2.24–25) as well, this same method of distribution is stated, based on the position that "the sacrificial fee consists of a hundred cows": "Twelve for the first groups, six for the second groups, four for the third groups, and three for the others. Since an unequal division is not prescribed in the case of animal sacrifices (*paśubandha*) and the like, the division of the fee there is equal, according to the principle: "It should be equal, because there is no scriptural injunction to the contrary" (*Jaiminīya-sūtra* 10.3.53). Manu (8.206) states that if only a portion of the ritual has been performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), then those who worked together should have the remaining work performed by someone else, and the sacrificial fee should be given to both parties in accordance with the portions of the work performed.
If a priest chosen for a sacrifice should fail to perform his own duty,
a share corresponding to the portion of work he has performed must be given to him along with the other performers.

But as for the case where one abandons a portion of the officiating priest’s work after the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has been given, Manu himself says that the remaining part should be caused to be performed by another person present among those engaged in his duties:
"If, however, after the fees have been given, he should abandon his own work, he shall receive his full share and cause it to be performed by another. (Manu 8.207)
Regarding what must be done when a priest dies during the performance of a ritual, Nārada says (Sambhūya, 8):
"In the event of a priest's misfortune, another shall likewise complete that ritual;
he shall receive the portion of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) assigned from it."
By another person who is nearby among those engaged in that group; as for the statement of Bṛhaspati:
"When anyone among those engaged in a ritual action passes away, the rite must be performed by his kinsman or by all the collaborators together."
Thus, regarding the statement of Śaṅkha and Likhita:

"Now, if a priest should die when the time for the sacrifice has arrived, what is to be done? If there is such a desire to know, his own kinsman or a pupil should complete that duty; but if there is no relative, one should choose another priest."

Thus, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* maintains that this refers to sacrifices such as the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, which are performed by officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who do not belong to a subordinate group (*avāntaragaṇa*). Nor should one raise the objection that, because the term *savana* as used by ritualists (*yājñika*) does not apply to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and similar sacrifices, the statement "when the *savana* has arrived" and so forth cannot logically have the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* as its subject; for here too, as in the sentence "one who has finished his studies is a *triṣavaṇasnāyin*" (YDh. 3.48), the word *savana* is employed to denote a point of time. In response to the question of what kind of farmers, acting in concert, should perform agriculture together, Bṛhaspati says:
A wise man should carry out agricultural work together with those who are equal to him in external factors such as laborers, seeds, and other field implements.

The external [animals] are oxen used for pulling plows and the like; by the word "and the like" (ādi), other implements of agriculture are included. That same author shows those to be avoided among the oxen:
"A wise farmer should not take as a draft animal one that is emaciated, excessively old, small, diseased, flighty, one-eyed, or lame."
Fields to be avoided have also been shown by that same [author]:
"One should carefully avoid a field that is on a mountain, near a city, or along a royal road, as well as one that is saline or infested with rats."

"On a mountain" means near a mountain. Regarding the "sacrificial grove," however, having read "in a *vivīta*," it is explained by the word *vivīta* as a protected area of land intended for fodder and the like. The phrase "near the royal highway" is to be supplied [as the location]. The apportionment of shares from the profit and so forth is the same for those who engage in collective commerce as it is for those who engage in collective cultivation. In this regard, that same author states the loss incurred by one person in certain cases:
"If the loss of a field occurs to anyone due to the failure of seed or draft animals, that loss must be made good by that very person for all those who live by agriculture."

The phrase "of those acting in concert" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Demonstrating the nature of artisans, that same author states the method for determining the shares in the distribution of profits among those acting in concert:
"The wise have declared that an artisan is one who knows the craft of processing gold, base metals, thread, wood, stone, and leather."
Where goldsmiths and others perform their craft collectively,
they shall receive wages according to their labor, in proportion to their respective shares.
*Nirveśa* means wages. The meaning of the phrase "according to their shares" has been clarified by Kātyāyana (6.3.2):
"Pupils, those who are experienced, and those who are skilled craftsmen, as well as teachers—these shall receive one, two, three, or four shares, respectively, in ascending order."
In certain primary cases, Bṛhaspati states that there are two shares:
"For those who, acting together, construct a mansion, a temple, or even leather goods and their accessories, the leader deserves two shares. [206]
Extending this principle of sharing two portions even to the dancers, the same author states another distinction:
"This very rule has been proclaimed by the virtuous as the duty of dancers:
the one who knows the rhythm (tāla) receives one and a half shares, while the singers receive equal shares."
"One and a half" means one part plus a half. Kātyāyana describes the method for determining the distribution of gains among thieves acting in concert (vv. 633–34):
"Whatever wealth may have been seized from a foreign kingdom by thieves under the command of their leader, they shall divide it according to rule after setting aside a tenth part for the king."
But the one who is the leader of the thieves shall take four shares from that;
the hero three shares, the capable one two, and the rest only one each.
As for the statement that a sixth part must be given to the king, this is intended to convey that meaning:
"But whatever has been brought from a foreign land by thieves at the command of their master,
they shall, having given a sixth part to the king, divide [the remainder] among themselves according to their shares."
The leader shall receive four shares; the hero shall obtain three shares;
the capable man shall take two shares; but the rest shall have equal shares.

This statement of Bṛhaspati refers to wealth stolen from a fort or difficult terrain protected by a more powerful rival king. Regarding what must be done when any one among these thieves is bound for the sake of his theft, Kātyāyana says:
"If any one among them who have fled should be captured, those [other thieves] shall pay, according to their respective shares, whatever was given for the purpose of his release."

This apportionment of shares for those who act in concert, distinct from the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), should be understood to apply in the absence of an agreement (*samaya*). However, when an agreement is made, the apportionment of shares must follow that very agreement. And so says the same author (Kāt. 637): [207] This is the rule for all—merchants, farmers, thieves, and artisans—who act as contributors of shares without a fixed agreement.
The meaning is: without having established an agreement in such a form as "one part shall belong to him" or "two parts shall belong to him," and so forth.
Thus ends the exposition of the legal title known as *sambhūyasamutthāna* (partnership) in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* by Śrī Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma. || 19 ||

**Possible reading of the defective text:** In the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "Śrī Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma"— this is the nineteenth chapter, the exposition of the legal head titled "Joint Undertaking" (*sambhūyasamutthāna*), within the section on the investigation of legal procedures (*vyavahāraviveka*).

Indeed, that legal heading is known as "Non-delivery of what has been given."

"By resorting to an improper path that is not in accordance with the scriptures. He [Nārada] himself states the fourfold nature of the modes of giving, distinguished by what is not to be given and so forth:
"What is not to be given, what is to be given, what has been given, and what has not been given—this fourfold path of giving is to be understood in legal proceedings. (Nārada, Dattāpradānika 2)

a deposit, one's wife and children, and one's entire property when there is a male heir."
For even when a living being is beset by the most dire calamities,
the teachers declare that there are things which must not be given away, namely, that which has already been promised to another.

"Common property" refers to things such as a street that have many owners, but not gold and the like whose owners are undivided, because those can be given only with the consent of all the undivided owners. Bṛhaspati also says:

"Common property, children, wives, and so forth, one's entire estate, a deposit, what has been borrowed, and what has been promised to another—these eight kinds are traditionally held to be not to be given."

*Samānyam* means common. *Pratiśrutam* means promised by word of mouth. Regarding this, the fact that a son is said to be not subject to being given away refers specifically to an only son; for if he were given away, it would result in the extinction of the lineage. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says (Dharmasūtra 15.1–4): "A person is produced from semen and blood, having his parents as his cause. In the giving away, selling, or abandoning of him, the parents have authority; however, one should neither give away nor accept an only son, for he is for the sake of the continuation of the ancestors."

[208] He himself says that [the gift] should be given by a woman who has been authorized by her husband (15.5): “But a woman shall neither give nor accept a son except with the permission of her husband. Dakṣa also states that even a woman’s property is not to be given (3.19–20):

Even in times of distress, the wise should not give away nine things;
he who gives them is a foolish soul and that man must undergo penance.

"He who takes what is not to be taken and he who gives what is not to be given—both of them are to be punished like thieves and made to pay the highest fine. Thus it is said.

The mention of "taking what is not to be taken" (*adeya-grahaṇa*) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of giving what has not been given. For this very reason, Nārada (Dattā. 12) states: "He who, out of delusion, takes what is not given, and he who gives what is not given—both of these are to be punished by the king who knows the Dharma."
Yājñavalkya states regarding what may be given (2.175):
"One may give from one's own property, provided it does not conflict with the maintenance of one's family, except for one's wife and sons.
"Without conflict with the family" means without causing hardship to the family; the meaning is that one's own property may be given only after what remains following the support of the family.
Nārada also says:
Whatever wealth remains in excess after maintaining one's family should be given away as an offering;
one who gives something other than this incurs fault.

"Having harmed others and having oppressed the family members who must be supported"—the harm to the family consists in the lack of food and clothing, not in the absence of luxuries such as betel-leaf and the like. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says: "That which remains over from the food and clothing for the family should be given. Here, *bhakta* means food and *vasana* means clothing; the grammatical construction is that what remains beyond the food and clothing should be given. [209] Whatever field is given from among the seven types of lands, such as the homestead or the field, whether it be ancestral or acquired by oneself— that which is intended should be bestowed.

"From seven sources" means from the seven types of acquisition previously mentioned. The mention of "fields" is illustrative [of other property]. "Inherited" (pitrya) means obtained through ancestral lineage. "Self-acquired" (svayaṃprāpta) means earned by oneself. The inclusion of both "inherited" and "self-acquired" is also illustrative of [other modes of acquisition] such as purchase and so forth. The meaning is that the scripture has determined that whatever house, field, or similar property is given—whether inherited or self-acquired—it must be given only after extracting it from a house, field, or the like that possesses those seven sources of acquisition. In this context, the expression "from a house or field possessing seven sources" is intended to show that the gift of a house, field, or the like is permissible only when there exists another house, field, or similar property sufficient for the maintenance of one's family that likewise possesses its own sources of acquisition, and not otherwise.
However, that which constitutes one's entire property— excluding the house and the wealth necessary for maintaining the family—

This statement by Kātyāyana (640) refers to cases where there is no other property within the house or elsewhere. He himself states another specific rule regarding property acquired by oneself and so forth: "That which is given at one's own will, that which is acquired by oneself, a pledge according to custom, and [property] obtained through marriage or inherited—there is no gift of these at all times."

"What is received as a dowry, inherited in succession, or obtained through valor, as well as what is given with the permission of the wife, kinsmen, or the owner—such a gift attains validity. Thus it is said.

That which is self-acquired or given at one's own will may be given even without the permission of brothers and others. A pledge (*bandhaka*) may be given by way of a mortgage (*ādhi*) according to the customary practice of pledging. That which was obtained through marriage or inherited through family succession should not be given in its entirety; rather, only a portion of it may be given therein. A gift received from a father-in-law (*saudāyika*) or obtained during a wedding must be given only with the consent of the woman who received it upon her marriage. An inheritance obtained through family succession must be given only with the consent of brothers whose wealth has not been partitioned. That which was acquired in battle by a servant must be given only with the consent of the master—this is the meaning of this collection of statements. As for the previously stated non-transferability of a pledge, that refers to forms other than a mortgage, so there is no contradiction. He [the author] confirms the aforementioned point—that the consent of brothers whose wealth has been partitioned is required for the gift of immovable property inherited through succession—by stating the underlying reason.
Whether divided or undivided, sapinda relatives have equal rights over immovable property;
for no single individual has authority anywhere in regard to its gift, mortgage, or sale.

*Mādhamanam* means pledging as collateral. The mention of "those who are divided" (*vibhaktāḥ*) is intended to demonstrate the *kaimutikanyāya* (the logic of "how much more so"), implying: "If even those who are divided are equal regarding immovable property, how much more so those who are undivided? It is not, however, intended to establish that divided sons possess ownership over such property, for that would render the act of division itself meaningless. Furthermore, even immovable property acquired by oneself, as well as slaves and the like, must be given to sons who have attained legal capacity only with their consent. Thus says Vyāsa: "Even immovable property and bipeds, though acquired by oneself..."
Without having assembled all the sons, there shall be neither gift nor sale.
Those who are born, those yet unborn, and those situated in the womb— all these desire their livelihood, but not through giving or selling.

The verse beginning with "those who are born and those yet unborn" is intended to strengthen the meaning stated in the preceding verse by demonstrating the *kaimutika* (how much more so) principle. In times of distress, for the sake of maintaining one's family, or for necessary religious duties such as ancestral *śrāddha*, the maintenance of a daughter, or her marriage, one may perform the gift of immovable property inherited through succession even without the consent of sons, brothers, and others. Thus says Nārada: "Even a single person may perform the giving, mortgaging, or selling of immovable property in times of distress for the sake of the family, and especially for the sake of dharma."
Yājñavalkya says (2.176): "If one has promised to him, 'I shall give this to you,' that must necessarily be given to him.
Furthermore: "What has been promised must indeed be given, and once given, it must not be taken back again.
Hārīta states the fault of one who does not deliver what was promised or who takes back what has been given: [The text continues with Hārīta's description of the consequences for such a person.]
By failing to give what was promised and by seizing what has been given,
one goes to various hells and is born among the animal species.
Whatever has been promised by word alone but not fulfilled through action is a debt bound to dharma, both in this world and in the next.

The application of these two fines is determined by the relative gravity of the offense. And those who know the law of gifts understand that what is given for the purpose of favoring the bride-price is a valid gift.

The price of merchandise is the value of a purchased commodity. Wages are remuneration. "Out of satisfaction" means given with full contentment; the phrase "to bards and the like" is understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Out of affection" means given out of love to daughters and others. "In return for a service" means given by way of recompense to one who has rendered a favor.
