"For the sake of favor" means given for the purpose of helping another, that is to say, for the sake of merit (*dharma*). These are the seven kinds of gifts. The meaning is that after they have been given, they must not be taken back. The things that are not to be returned have been shown by that same author (Nārada, *Dattāpa-neya* 9–11).

That which is performed by one who is a child, deluded, lacking independence, afflicted, intoxicated, or insane; and that which is done with the desire for gain, thinking, "This person is my agent" and "this is my deed."
If that which is an unworthy recipient is called a worthy recipient, or if an act is designated as unrighteous,

**A possible reading of the defective text:** In the Madanaratnapradīpa composed by Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "Śrīkodaṇḍaparaśurāma"— this is the twenty-second [section], the exposition of the legal title known as "Non-delivery of what was given," within the Vyavahāravivekoddyota.
Now follows the determination of the legal title known as *abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā* (failure to serve after having agreed), as spoken by Nārada.
Regarding that, Nārada demonstrates its essential nature (*svarūpa*) [in *Abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā* 1]:
"But he who, having agreed to service, does not perform it..."
This title of law is called "Failure to Serve" after having entered into such an agreement.

Service (*śuśrūṣā*) consists in obeying orders. A servant (*śuśrūṣaka*) is of five kinds: a student (*śiṣya*), a resident pupil (*antevāsī*), a hired laborer (*bhṛtaka*), an overseer (*adhikarmakṛt*), and a slave (*dāsa*). Among these, the four excluding the slave are called "laborers" (*karmakara*); they perform auspicious work. Slaves are of fifteen types, distinguished by being born in the house and so forth; they, however, perform inauspicious work. Nārada himself has stated all of this (Abhyudayaprakaraṇa 2–7): "In the treatise, the wise have observed five types of servants. Four of them are laborers (*karmakara*); the slaves (*dāsa*) are fifteen."
The pupil, the resident student, the hired servant, and fourthly, the laborer for extra work—these are to be known as laborers; whereas slaves are those born in the house and so forth.
The wise have declared their common characteristic to be dependence;
however, the specific distinctions among them are said to arise from birth, action, and likewise from their mode of livelihood.
Action should also be known to be of two kinds: indeed, the inauspicious and the auspicious.
The inauspicious is said to be the work of a servant, while the auspicious is remembered as that of those who perform [righteous] deeds.
The cleansing of house doors, impure places, roads, and refuse heaps; the touching of private parts, and the handling and discarding of food remnants, feces, and urine.
Service to one's master with one's limbs according to his desire, and even beyond that, is to be known as inauspicious karma; other than this is auspicious.

The genitive case in *teṣām* is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). "Tri-pañcakāḥ" means fifteen. A *śiṣya* is one who seeks the knowledge of the Vedas; an *antevāsī* is one who seeks the knowledge of crafts (*śilpa*). One who performs work after receiving wages is a *bhṛtaka*. An *adhikarmakṛt* is a supervisor over those performing work. "By way of livelihood" (*vṛttitaḥ*) means by way of a means of subsistence. *Avaskara* is a place for heaps of swept dust. The word "cleaning" (*śodhana*) is connected with the four items beginning with "the door of the house. "Discarding" (*ujjhana*) means abandonment. "Finally, at the master's pleasure" (*antataḥ svāmina iṣṭataḥ*) means approaching with one's limbs or offering one's hands and so forth for the purpose of sweeping places where urine, excrement, and the like have been deposited, according to the master's command. There exists a distinction among *śiṣyas*, *antevāsīs*, and *dāsas* based on caste and other factors. Among them, the distinction based on caste is clear, because only those who are Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas are entitled to the study of the Vedas. Bṛhaspati, however, demonstrates the distinction based on function (*karman*).
The triple Vidyā is declared to be characterized by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
for its purpose, one should perform service to the teacher as enjoined by the scriptures.

Nārada also says (Abhyudaya 8.15): "Until he has acquired knowledge, the disciple should serve his guru with self-restraint; he should behave toward the guru’s wives and likewise toward the guru’s son in the same manner."
Having completed his studies and having presented the teacher’s fee to the guru, he should return to his own home; this is declared to be the conduct of a student.

Conduct (*vṛtti*) is here what constitutes *dharma*. Since the specific duties of students have been described in the *Ācāravivekoddyota*, they are not elaborated upon here. Manu shows the particularities established by the author of the *Vṛtti* (Manu 2.48–49):
"Having received his desired staff and having worshipped the sun, he should circumambulate the fire from left to right and go about for alms according to the rule."
"A twice-born man who has been initiated should beg for food with the word 'bhavat' at the beginning;
a Kṣatriya, however, with 'bhavat' in the middle; and a Vaiśya, with 'bhavat' at the end. Thus Bṛhaspati shows the distinction among students based on their caste and occupation.
Skill is said to be the mastery of arts such as the crafting of gold and base metals, as well as dancing and so forth; to acquire this, one should perform service in the house of a teacher.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), activities such as the making of pots and other crafts of the potter are included. "Art" (*śilpa*) refers to knowledge concerning the making of bracelets, crowns, and so forth; the meaning is that for the sake of attaining that [skill], one should perform work such as the making of bracelets while in the house of a teacher. By this, it is stated that there is a distinction among apprentices based on their caste—such as being a goldsmith—and based on the specific craft they perform, such as the making of bracelets. Nārada (Abhyudaya 16–17) demonstrates the distinctions among them based on their work and their livelihood:
Desiring to acquire his own craft with the permission of his kinsmen,
he shall dwell in the presence of a teacher for a well-determined period of time.
The teacher should instruct him in his own home, providing him with food;
he should not make him perform any other work and should treat him like a son.

*Ante* means "nearby. *Anyat* refers to work other than [the teaching of] the craft. By this, it is shown that his service consists precisely in performing the tasks that result in the completion of the bracelet and so forth. The phrase "food provided in his own house" indicates his livelihood. Regarding the punishment if the pupil is made to perform work other than the instruction in the craft by the teacher, Kātyāyana says (713): "But he who does not cause [the pupil] to learn the craft, yet causes him to perform other tasks, shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine; from that, the pupil withdraws."

The "pupil" (*antevāsī*) here refers to a resident student. For as long as the period has been stipulated—thinking, "I shall remain in your house for this much time for the purpose of learning a craft"—for that long must he remain in the teacher's house even after he has acquired the knowledge. And so says Nārada (Abhyudaya 19):
"Even when instructed, the resident student should complete the full term;
whatever work he performs there, the fruit thereof belongs to the teacher alone."

Yājñavalkya also (2.184): Even one who has mastered a craft shall dwell in the house of his teacher for a fixed period as a resident pupil; he shall receive his food from the teacher and offer him the fruits of his labor.
Regarding the misconduct of a resident pupil, Nārada states (Abhyu. 18):
"He who abandons a teacher who is instructing him and is not at fault should be forced to stay by means of restraint; he deserves both corporal punishment and imprisonment."

"He should be made to dwell" means he should be established in the presence of the teacher; this is the remainder [of the sense]. "Killing" here refers to beating and not execution, because the offense is minor. He states what must be done after the craft has been acquired by the same author (Nārada, *Abhyudaya* 20):
"Having mastered the craft at the agreed time, the apprentice, having circumambulated the teacher from left to right and having honored him according to his ability, departs."

[217] However, for a hired laborer (*bhṛtaka*) or a supervisor (*adhikarmakṛt*), there is no distinction based on caste (*jāti*) and so forth. Bṛhaspati states the different types of hired laborers according to the differences in their wages:
"One who enjoys the master's female slave is to be known as a 'slave for concubines' (*vanitābhr̥ta*);
he shall perform that work for his master just like any other man hired for wages."
The *arthabhṛta* has been described as one who is supported by a large amount of wealth, while another is the *bhāgabhṛta*.

He who performs work for his master in exchange for the enjoyment of another's wife is the *vanitābhṛta*. He who performs work in exchange for the receipt of money is the *arthabhṛta*. He who performs work in exchange for the receipt of a stipulated share is the *bhāgabhṛta*. That same author states that the *bhāgabhṛta* is of two kinds:
"The *bhāgabhṛta* is recorded as being of two types among those who live by agriculture and cattle-rearing."
Likewise, he would obtain it from grain that has grown and from milk; of this there is no doubt.

The genitive case in the phrase *kr̥ṣigojīvinām* is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). The meaning is that the cultivator shall receive a share from the harvested grain, and the cowherd a share from the milk. That same author further states that there is a twofold division among laborers (*bhr̥takāḥ*) based on their being superior, middling, or inferior:
"Inferiority, mediocrity, and superiority are prescribed for all;
however, the soldier is declared to be the best, while the cultivator is middling."
The carrier of burdens is declared the lowest, as is the house-servant;
the cultivator is the farmer. Nārada states (Abhyudaya 22) that their wages should be determined according to their capacity and devotion:
"A hired servant is to be known as threefold: superior, middling, and inferior."
Their maintenance, based on their work, should be in accordance with their capacity and devotion.
Bṛhaspati states the duties of a hired servant: "A servant hired for a day, half a month, six months, or three months shall perform the work agreed upon and receive the stipulated wage."

One should perform for that duration the work promised, thinking, "I shall do this work for this length of time. The meaning is that when it has been thus arranged, one receives that wage. Nārada (Abhyudaya 24) shows the nature of the *adhikarmakṛt* (manager): "He who is appointed over all [the servants] and likewise over the household is to be known as the *adhikarmakṛt*; he is remembered as the *kauṭumbika* (household supervisor)."

"Appointed over all laborers" means one who has been made their supervisor; "likewise appointed over the household"—this is the connection. He who is appointed as a supervisor over all laborers is to be known as the *adhikarmakṛta* (manager). But he who is established for the purpose of protecting the household by authorizing expenditures is the *kauṭumbika* (household steward); this is the meaning. By means of demonstrating the etymology of the word "slave," Kātyāyana shows the true nature of a slave:
"Bhṛgu [declares] that slavery arises from the gift of oneself while one is independent, just like [the gift of] a wife."

The meaning is that Bhṛgu stated that just as a wife possesses the status of a *dāra* (wife) through the surrender of her own body for the sake of her husband’s enjoyment, so too does one possess the status of a slave (*dāsatva*) through the act of giving oneself away—which consists of making an independent self completely subject to another. By this, the essential nature of slaves is shown: they are those who serve while being entirely dependent on others. He [Bhṛgu] himself shows the distinctions among slaves based on caste (Kāt. 715): "Slavery is to be recognized among the three [lower] castes, but never for a Brāhmaṇa.
Regarding even those [three castes], he says that slavery must be performed only in accordance with the natural order (*ānulomyena*) (Kāt. 716).
Slavery is permitted for the castes in the direct order of succession, but not in the inverse order;
for the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras lose their independence when they do so.
And this [rule] refers to cases other than those who have abandoned their own *dharma*. Thus says Nārada (Abhyudaya 39):
"The state of slavery is not ordained for the castes through the inverse order (*prātilomya*).
Except for those who have abandoned their own *dharma*, slavery is considered to be like [the taking of] a wife."

And this statement—that one who has fallen from the religious life (*pravrajyāvasita*) becomes even a slave to a person of inferior caste—refers specifically to those who have fallen from the religious life among the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, but not to those who have fallen from the religious life among Brāhmaṇas; for it is stated that the latter are to be banished, and thus they do not incur slavery. That he is to be banished has been declared by Kātyāyana:
"Where the three twice-born castes have fallen from the religious life, one should cause the Brāhmaṇa to be banished; Bhr̥gu says that the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya shall become slaves."

The king should cause [this] to be done—this is the remainder [of the sense]. "Kṣatriya and Vaiśya" is *kṣatraviṭ*; the singular form is used because of the rule stating that "every *dvandva* compound may optionally be treated as a singular. Dakṣa and Nārada state that banishment must be carried out after branding [the person] with the mark of a dog's foot: "But he who, having taken up the life of a wandering mendicant, does not abide by his own duty—the king should quickly banish him after branding him with the mark of a dog's foot."
If this were so,
a man who has fallen from the renunciant life would become a slave to the king himself;
for him there would be no liberation from that state, nor any purification whatsoever.

Thus, because Nārada (Abhyudaya 35) states that one who has fallen from the life of renunciation becomes the slave of the king alone and no other, it must not be argued that his statement—that one who abandons their own duty becomes [the slave] of another—is without scope. This is because the word "king" (*rājan*) here refers to the protector of subjects (*prajāpālaka*), and the status of being a protector of subjects is possible even for Vaiśyas and others appointed by the king. Therefore, the purpose is to demonstrate that a Kṣatriya who has fallen from renunciation becomes the slave of even a Vaiśya who protects subjects, even if that Vaiśya is of a lower caste. Furthermore, according to Nārada’s statement that "slavery is like marriage," just as a wife may be of the same or a lower caste, so too may a slave be of the same or a lower caste; thus, since it would follow that a Brāhmaṇa could be the slave of a Brāhmaṇa, Kātyāyana (717) provides an exception to that.
"Even one of the same caste must never cause a Brahmin to perform servitude.
He (Kātyāyana, verse 719) further states that a Brahmin, even if he engages in service to another Brahmin out of his own free will, must not perform any impure work:
"In the case of one endowed with good character and Vedic study, [the master] may, at his pleasure, have him perform work inferior to that [of the master]."
Even there, the best of the twice-born should not perform any unwholesome act.

Because there is an injunction that one must perform service for others, for that reason, even a lowly or inferior task—such as carrying loads and the like—one should perform out of one’s own will for the sake of helping others, even without receiving wages; this is the meaning of the first half-verse. Furthermore, among those very lowly tasks, one should not perform such unwholesome work as cleaning the door of a house; this is the meaning. Alternatively, *tadūnam* may be taken as a single compound meaning "deficient in Vedic study. In this interpretation, the verb *kārayet* ("should cause to do") from the preceding sentence is supplied as an ellipsis. A Brāhmaṇa should support a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya who are distressed for a livelihood out of compassion, making them perform their own respective duties.

"By *ānr̥śaṃsya* [means] by non-cruelty. By the phrase 'those emaciated by their livelihood,' it is indicated that for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, since no other means of subsistence is possible, they must accept servitude; however, it is not indicated that this is a viable alternative path (*gati*). Regarding the punishment for forcibly making someone a slave, Manu himself (8.412) says: 'If a Brāhmaṇa, out of greed, forces initiated twice-born men to perform servitude against their will because of his superior power, he shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.'"

"Because of power" means because of lordship (*prabhutvāt*). The suffix *añ* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) according to the rule stating that it is prescribed after words such as *sādhāraṇa*. By the mention of the "twice-born" (*dvijāti*), it is shown that there is no punishment for the forcible enslavement of a Śūdra. For this very reason, it was stated by that same author (Manu 8.413):
"But one may compel a Śūdra to perform servitude, whether he has been purchased or not;
for he was created by the Self-existent One himself solely for the purpose of servitude."
Kātyāyana states the punishment for reducing Brahmin women and others to the status of slaves (verses 726–728):
"Whoever should seize a Brahmin woman, or likewise sell her, that act must be undone by the king;
all of them shall be punished."

But he who, out of lust, should make a woman of good family who has sought refuge with him a slave, or should transfer her to another, shall be punished; and that [marriage] shall be as if it had never been performed.
He who enjoys a nurse, whether she be a wet-nurse or not, as if she were a slave-girl,
or the wife of an attendant, shall incur the first amercement.

[221] The meaning is that the work which has not been performed must be made good. The syntactical connection is: "those [offenders] shall be punished by the king. Viṣṇu (5.151) states: "But he who employs a woman of the highest caste as a slave shall receive the highest amercement. Regarding the sale of a female slave in certain cases, Kātyāyana (729) declares the punishment:
"He who, being capable and not in a state of distress, desires to sell a female slave who is devoted to him and is crying out [in protest], shall incur a fine of two hundred [paṇas]."

"Two hundred *paṇas*" is the understood remainder. By the word "of food," it is shown that there is no punishment for selling a wicked woman. Nārada shows the different types of slaves (*abhyu. 26–28*):
"One born in the house, one purchased, one obtained, one received as an inheritance, one maintained during a famine, and likewise one who has been placed [with him] by his master."
I have been released from a great debt; I have been won as a prize in battle;
I have approached you saying, "I am yours"; and I have been made one who has completed his term of exile.
The slave by gift, as well as the one acquired from a mare (a captive),
and the one who sells himself— these are recorded in the treatise as the fifteen types of slaves.
"Born in the house" means born of a female slave of the household. "Bought" means acquired from a former owner for a price.

"Obtained" means acquired through acceptance of a gift (*pratigraha*) and the like. "Inherited" means received from ancestors such as a father by sons and others as their legal portion (*riktha*). "Supported during a famine" means one who was nourished for the purpose of being made a slave during a time of scarcity. "Entrusted" means one who has been made a pledge (*bandhaka*) by a debtor to his master. "Released from debt" refers to one who, having promised, "If I am released from this debt, then I shall become your slave," has his own debt cleared by the creditor after he has paid the money; thus, his status as a slave is voluntarily accepted as a reciprocal service for that release from debt. "Captured in battle" means seized after being defeated in war. "Won at a wager" means one who, having agreed to the condition, "If I am defeated by you in this dispute, then I shall become your slave," is subsequently defeated. "Approached saying 'I am yours'" means one who has come of his own accord, having consented, "I am your slave. "Fallen from renunciation" means one who has lapsed from the life of a wandering ascetic (*pravrajyā*). "Made" means one who has been made to accept, "For this long a period of time, I am your slave. "Slave for food" means one who, having agreed, "As long as I give you the value of my food, I am your slave," is obtained through the medium of the price of food consumed. "Brought by a female slave" (*vaḍavāhr̥ta*) means one brought by a female slave (*vaḍavā*); out of greed for her, having married her, he enters into the state of slavery for the sake of obtaining the permission of her owner. "Seller of himself" means one who sells himself for the sake of wealth. Such are the fifteen types of slaves recorded in the *Dharmaśāstra*. This is the meaning.

Regarding those [eight types of slaves], the liberation from slavery for the first four—those born in the house and so forth—occurs only through the favor of the master and not by any other means; thus he (Nārada, *Abhyudaya* 29.3) says:
"In that regard, the former group of four is not released from slavery except by the grace of the master; their servitude is hereditary."
That lowest of men who, being independent, sells himself—
he is the most despicable of them all, and even he is not released from servitude.

By stating "in another case, through the master's favor," it is shown that for all types of slaves—beginning with those born in the house (*gṛhajātādi*)—except for those who have renounced their vows (*pravrajyāvasita*), liberation from slavery occurs through the master’s favor. He himself (Nārada, *Abhyudaya* 30) states that for all [slaves], beginning with those born in the house and those maintained out of season (*akālabhr̥tādi*), liberation from slavery occurs by saving the master's life:
"Whosoever among them should rescue the master from a danger to his life, he shall be released from slavery and shall receive a share equal to that of a son."

The genitive case in *eṣām* is used for selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). The meaning is: "among these fifteen types of slaves. This refers to cases other than those who have fallen from the religious life (*pravrajyāvasita*). However, for the latter, there is never any release from slavery. The compound *caurāpahṛtāś ca te vikrītāś ca* is a *karmadhāraya*. With the intention that one who, being the slave of someone, desires to become the slave of another should not be accepted, it was stated by that same author (*Nārada*, *Abhyupagamana* 40):

The meaning is that the former owner may take back that slave girl who was desired as a wife by another. "Seed" refers to the conception resulting from one's own act. "Having considered," meaning having determined, that she should be made a slave or a female slave along with her offspring—this is the sense. Nārada states the method for releasing one from slavery (Abhyudaya 42–43):

From the harvest of a field cultivated by a laborer who receives food and clothing, one should take a fifth part;

[226] One who is supported by food and clothing is one nourished by the gift of food and raiment; one other than this is "unsupported. Alternatively, where there is no prior agreement stating "I shall give this much," there the mediator shall determine whatever wage is appropriate, and that much should be paid. Thus says Vṛddha-Manu:
"Those skilled in sea-voyages, who perceive the requirements of place, time, and purpose, shall fix the wage which should be paid, provided it has not been previously settled."
In some cases, even when a fixed agreement exists, Yājñavalkya (2.195) states that payment may be made according to whether the wages are deficient or excessive:
"If one exceeds the [agreed] place and time, or effects a profit otherwise than [stipulated], in those cases it shall be at the will of the master; if more has been done, more must be paid."

If one, out of pride, laziness, or other such reasons, fails to perform the sale or other transactions at a place or time suitable for them without the master’s permission, or if he realizes a profit that is smaller than expected due to excessive expenditure, the master shall give him wages according to his own discretion, but not the payment of the entire stipulated wage. However, for one who, through knowledge of the conditions of place, time, and circumstance, produces a greater profit, more must be given even beyond the stipulated wage; this is the meaning. The method for the distribution of wages when a task is to be accomplished by many has been stated by that same author (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.196): "Among those who have completed the work, the wages should be distributed in proportion to their respective efforts. But among those who have not completed it, they should be made to complete it, or else they should receive wages in proportion to the work actually done. Thus, the rule regarding the payment of wages in cases where a task is to be performed by several people has been explained.
Whatever amount of work one performs, that much indeed is his wages;
if the task is impossible for both, [the fee is waived], but if it is possible, he should perform it according to what was heard [in the agreement].

The word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "of both also" (*ubhayor api*) implies the inclusion of many [workers]. When a wage has been stipulated for those performing a task such as digging a well, with the agreement: "I shall give this much to the performers of this work," if that work undertaken by two or more persons is not completed due to illness or other causes, then among them, whatever portion of the work each performs, to him a wage determined by an intermediary (*madhyastha*) in accordance with that specific work must be given; however, the payment is neither made equally nor withheld entirely on account of the lack of completion. If the work is completed by them, then it must be paid exactly as stipulated. The meaning is that the entire wage should not be paid to each individual, nor should it be distributed after being calculated according to the amount of work performed. Regarding one who, having accepted wages, fails to perform the agreed-upon work despite being capable—whether out of pride or other motives—Bṛhaspati states that he shall pay double the wages received to the employer and a fine to the king.
[227] When a hired laborer who has received his wages does not perform the work,
provided he is capable, he shall be compelled to pay a fine and twice that amount as wages.
Yājñavalkya also (2.193): "One who, having received wages, abandons his work, shall pay double."

The meaning is that if one who has not received wages fails to perform the work he undertook, he must pay the master an amount of wealth equal to what was stipulated as wages, but no fine to the king. Thus, since Bṛhaspati states regarding the taking of wages, "And that wage [shall be] taken," prescribing the delivery of the wages doubled for what was received, the payment of an amount equal to the wages—caused by the laborer's own fault—is required even when there is no taking of wages; for Yājñavalkya also states, "If not taken, it is equal," prescribing the payment of an amount equal to the stipulated wages. The distinction, however, is that in one case there is a royal fine, while in the other there is none. This is the position favored by the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* and others. But the teacher Vijñāneśvara says that upon the taking of wages, there is the payment of twice that amount, whereas upon its non-taking, there is the payment of an amount equal to it, and not the payment of twice the amount. Nārada states another view (*Vetana* 5): "If one who has not received wages promises and then does not perform the work, he should be made to do it by force after being given his wages."

Having promised to perform work, one who does not do it after receiving wages by force shall pay double the wages; likewise, one who has received wages but does not perform the work shall forfeit double the wages.
Regarding this very subject, Kātyāyana (657) also states that after the commencement [of work], even one who is being forced [to continue] shall be liable to punishment if he does not perform it:
"But he who, having made an agreement for the commencement of work, does not have it completed, must be forced to do so;
if he does not do it, he deserves punishment."
In response to the question of how much property one should be fined, Vriddha-Manu says:
"He who, having made a promise, does not fulfill it, should be compelled by force to do so;
if he still does not perform that work, he shall incur double the fine."

"Having promised" means having commenced; for Kātyāyana prescribes the penalty at the very moment of commencement. As for that which was stated by Manu [228]: "If one who has been hired, being neither ill, should not perform the work as prescribed out of pride, he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas*, and his wages shall not be paid."

Thus, a small fine has been prescribed; that is to be understood as applying when one performs less than half of the work. However, if one performs slightly less than the full amount of work, there is neither a fine nor the receipt of wages. And so it has been stated by Manu himself (8.217): "Whether afflicted or healthy, he who does not perform the work as stipulated shall not be paid his wages, even if the work is only slightly incomplete."

By the phrase "one should cause [the work] to be done here," it is shown that there is no fault even for a healthy person when the performance of the task is undertaken by another individual. However, if one who was previously afflicted performs the work undertaken by himself after his recovery from illness, then—even if there is a delay—there is no fault on his part; thus, he receives his wages, as stated by that same author (Manu 8.216): "But if one who was afflicted, having become healthy, performs the work exactly as agreed from the beginning, he shall indeed receive his wages, even after a very long period of time."

The meaning is that one should act exactly as was stated and as was promised from the very beginning; the phrase "even after the lapse of a very long time" is to be understood as the ellipsis. However, if someone, having agreed that he will perform the work for such a length of time, abandons the work before that period is completed, he does not receive his wages due to the fault of the employer. But if he abandons it [by choice], Nārada says that he receives wages calculated according to the amount of time for which the work was actually performed: "If he abandons the work before the time is complete, he shall suffer the loss of his wages."
If he departs due to a fault of his master, he shall receive whatever has been earned up to that point.

The fault of the master consists of harsh speech and the like. Viṣṇu also states the punishment for dismissal without such a fault of the master (Viṣṇu 5.152–153): “A hired servant who leaves before the term is complete shall forfeit his entire wages and pay a fine of one hundred *paṇas* to the king. *Mūlya* means wages. Viṣṇu says that if the master dismisses the servant before the term is complete without any fault on the part of the servant, the servant shall receive the full wages as calculated and the fine shall be paid (Viṣṇu 5.155–156): “If the master dismisses the hired servant before the term is complete, he shall pay him his entire wages and a fine of one hundred *paṇas* to the king, except in the case of a fault of the servant. Regarding the loss of the master’s property due to the fault of the servant, the same author says that the value of that property must be paid to the master (Viṣṇu 5.154): “Whatever is destroyed through his fault must be restored to the master, except in the case of damage caused by fate (*daiva*). The mention of *daiva* is also indicative of damage caused by the king. For this very reason, Nārada says (Vetana 9):
If the merchandise should suffer loss due to the fault of the carrier,
he shall be made to pay for whatever has been lost, except in cases caused by fate or the king.

*Bhāṇḍa* refers to goods to be transported; *vyasana* means loss. Here, the mention of "goods" (*bhāṇḍa*) is an elliptical expression for oxen and the like [used for transport], and the mention of "carriers" (*vāhaka*) is likewise an elliptical expression for farmers and others. This rule applies to cases where the loss occurs through negligence. However, if the master’s property is destroyed through malice, Vṛddha-Manu states that twice the value must be paid:
"One who causes loss through negligence shall be made to pay an amount equal [to the loss]; one who causes loss through malice shall pay double.
But he shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by thieves, or burnt, or carried away by water."

"Twice to be made to pay" means he is to be made to pay double. "Carried away" (*ūḍha*) means taken away. However, if a hired laborer, when the master is setting out at an auspicious moment for a marriage or similar occasion, creates an obstacle to the departure by failing to perform the work he has undertaken—because there is no time to secure another servant—he must be made to pay double wages to the master. Thus says Yājñavalkya (2.197–198): "And one who causes an obstacle to the departure shall be made to pay double wages; likewise, one who abandons [the service] after it has begun shall be made to pay a seventh part, and one who abandons it on the road, a fourth part."

The one who causes abandonment shall also be made to pay the entire wages up to the halfway point; this refers to when the act of setting out has already commenced. The meaning of the phrase "the one who causes abandonment" (*tyājaka*) is that if the master causes the servant to abandon the journey after it has begun, then he must cause the servant to be paid the seventh part and so forth, according to the previously stated sequence. As for the payment of a fourth part mentioned regarding the master’s causing of abandonment, that refers to the case of a master of goods not yet sold; however, by a master of goods that have been sold, half of the wages must be given. For this very reason, Vṛddha-Manu says:
If, having sold that merchandise on the road, he should abandon the merchant's servant, then a half-share of the profit must be given to him as well; he shall receive half of the gain from the sale.
Regarding what must be paid by the owner when there is an obstruction of the goods on the road by customs officials and others, or when they are seized by the king and others, Kātyāyana says:
"When those goods are lost or stolen on the way, the [carrier] shall receive as much wages as correspond to the portion of the journey that has been completed. (661)
Regarding the punishment for a master who abandons a sick servant on the road, that same author (Kātyāyana, verse 660) says:

"He who abandons a companion on the road who is exhausted or afflicted by disease shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine; likewise, he who fails to provide care for three days in a village [shall incur the same]."
Bṛhaspati says that when an offense is committed by a servant acting with the master's permission, that offense belongs to the master alone:
"If a hired servant performs an inauspicious act for the sake of his master while being directed by him, the master incurs the guilt therein."
Regarding the non-payment of wages by an employer to a laborer who has performed his work, that same author states:
"If an employer does not pay the wages to a laborer after the work has been completed, he shall be compelled by the king to pay the wages in accordance with the nature of the work. Thus it is said.

If one hires another's vehicle or similar property for a fee in order to transport goods, and after agreeing that "this shall be mine until the completion of such-and-such a task," such as the delivery of the goods, fails to proceed with it, he must pay a fourth part of the rental fee agreed upon to the owner of the vehicle. However, if, having taken it, he abandons it halfway, then he must pay the entire hire. Thus says Nārada (Vetana 7):
"But one who, having hired a vehicle or beast of burden to carry goods, does not take them..."
If he abandons [the work] halfway, he must be made to pay the entire wages plus a fourth part.

A "vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to a cart and the like; a "conveyance" (*vāhana*) refers to a horse and the like. Regarding one who, having hired a vehicle or the like, takes his goods and carries them to another region while leaving the vehicle behind and failing to pay the hire, Vriddha-Manu states that he must certainly be made to pay the hire:
"He who, having hired a cart, takes it and goes elsewhere, yet does not pay the hire, shall be compelled to pay the hire even for the portion [of the journey] not yet completed."

Even in the case of one who has not married [the woman] or provided assistance, if one does not return the carriage or other means of transport for which it was hired once that specific purpose has been accomplished, then he must be made to pay the hire until its return; thus says Kātyāyana (662–663):
"Whoever, having taken elephants, horses, cattle, donkeys, camels, and so forth on hire, does not return them after his business is done, shall be made to pay the hire together with interest."
He who, having taken houses, shops, and so forth on lease,
does not return them to the owner, shall be made to pay [the value] together with the rent for as long as he has retained them.

Here, by the word *vāri*, a water-vessel is understood. The phrase "having completed his task, he shall not return it to the owner" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Regarding the specific rules for the breaking or loss of water-vessels and other items taken on lease, Nārada states (Vetana 22):
"One should return the vessels that carry the hire-charge full at the end of the stipulated time.
If they are broken or lost, the liability falls upon the taker, except in the case of an accident."

The first half of the verse means that those [houses] which carry praise and have been taken on lease should be restored to their owner once the period for which the lease was stipulated has expired. "Damaged" (*bhagna*) means partially disfigured; "lost" (*naṣṭa*) means entirely disfigured. "Collision" (*saṃplava*) refers to mutual friction or impact. Whatever is damaged or lost by a mode other than such collision belongs to the lessee; however, as for what is lost or damaged through collision, the meaning is that the lessor must restore it as before or compensate the owner for its value. Regarding one who builds a house on another's land at his own expense, pays rent to the landowner, and dwells there, Nārada says the following (Nārada, Vyetanādhyāya 20):
[232] But he who, having built a house on another's land and offered praise, should dwell there, must take with him that house— its grass, wood, bricks, and so forth— and depart.
*Stoma* means rent. Regarding one who dwells without paying rent, Nārada says (Vetana 21):
"But one who has lived on another's land without a settled agreement and without paying rent shall by no means take away grass or wood when he departs."
Whatever grass or wood has been placed there as bricks, all that which is removed shall be reported to the owner of the land.

"Unrestricted" means free from any agreement (*paribhāṣā*) such as "one must depart taking grass, wood, and so forth at the time of leaving," or "one must not depart in this manner. He should inform or announce [this]. However, if an agreement has been made, one must act according to that agreement. Regarding the case of a prostitute and her client, Nārada (Vetana 18) says: "Having accepted the fee, if a courtesan does not wish to go, she shall pay double.
Even if the payer of the fee does not wish to go, he shall suffer the loss of the fee."
However, Bṛhaspati states that there is no fault for a woman who does not go to the presence of the giver of the bride-price due to being overcome by illness or similar circumstances:
"One who is diseased, exhausted, distressed, or occupied with royal business,
and who does not come when invited, is declared to be a blameless mare."

"Summoned" means invited. "Vaḍavā" refers to a female slave; this term is also indicative of a courtesan. Regarding the specific case of the man who enjoys her, Nārada states (Vetana 18–19): "If a man, having enjoyed a woman, does not pay the fee, yet she has intercourse with him in an improper manner by injuring him with teeth, nails, and so forth..."
He who approaches a woman in an improper place, or causes her to dwell with many men,
shall be made to pay eightfold the bride-price and an equal fine as a penalty.

[233] Regarding the abandonment of the bride-price (*śulka*) paid by a man and his subsequent going to another man, the fine and other penalties are stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa* (227.145): "If a courtesan, having received her fee (*vetana*), goes elsewhere out of greed, one should cause her to pay a fine; the other [man] shall also receive his hire (*bhāṭaka*)."
Regarding the other [type], one for whom the bride-price has been paid; another distinction is also stated in that very same place (*Matsyapurāṇa* 227.146–148):
"He who, for the sake of another, leads a courtesan intending her for someone else..."
The king's punishment for that shall be one māṣaka of gold.
He who, having taken up work, does not provide the labor, shall be made to pay double wages;
he shall also pay a fine of double that amount to the king, so that justice is not violated.
If many men go together to abduct a single woman, they shall all give her double that amount as compensation,
and each shall separately pay a further double amount as a fine to the king.
Nārada speaks of those who are the adjudicators in disputes concerning courtesans:
"Those courtesans who are the principal ones there, and the lovers who have resided in their houses—
they are known to provide the decision in cases of doubt regarding matters arising from them."
Thus ends the twenty-second section, the determination of the legal title known as "Non-payment of Wages," in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* by Śrī Kodaṇḍaparaśurāma.

Now follows the determination of the legal head of dispute known as the transgression of conventions (*saṃvid-vyatikrama*).
Regarding that, Nārada states its essential nature (*svarūpa*) [in *Sama* 1]:
"The established practice of heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*), guilds (*naigama*), and so forth, is called a convention (*samaya*)."
The non-fulfillment of an agreement is recorded as that point of dispute.

*Pāṣaṇḍas* are those who oppose the Vedic path, such as the Kṣapaṇakas and others. *Naigamas* are merchants or members of a caravan; however, the teacher Vijñāneśvara maintains that *naigamas* are those who accept the authority of the Vedas, such as the Pāśupatas and others. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), groups such as the *traividyabrāhmaṇas* are included. Their *sthiti*—the establishment of them as possessing specific conventional duties—is called *samaya* (convention). The non-neglect (*anapākarma*) of that convention, which consists of its observance and non-transgression, is recorded in the Smṛti as a title of dispute (*vivādapada*) known as "non-neglect of convention" (*samayasyānapākarma*). The phrase "if it is not being performed" (*akriyamāṇam*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. Alternatively, by the word *anapākarma*, which denotes non-transgression, transgression is here indicated through *viparītalakṣaṇā* (indirect indication), as in the expression "eat poison. Thus, the meaning is that the transgression of that convention is a title of dispute. Yājñavalkya (2.185) demonstrates a certain point relevant to this: [The text continues with the verse: "Those who do not follow the conventions established by their own group, nor those of other castes, regions, guilds, or families, shall be punished with a fine of one *māṣaka*. Having established his residence in the city and entrusted the status of the Brahmin there to those possessing the threefold knowledge (traividya), the king should say: "Let your livelihood be maintained; let your own duty (svadharma) be protected."

*Brāhmaṇyam* refers to the community of Brahmins. The suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule *brāhmaṇamāṇavavāḍavād yat* (Pā. 4.2.42). *Vidyā* means the Vedas; the collection of the three *vidyās* is *trividyam*. One who knows these three kinds is called *traividyam*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tad adhīte tad veda* (Pā. 4.2.59). Here, because the *aṇ* is not caused by a *dvigu* compound, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by *dvigor lug-anapatye* (Pā. 4.1.88) does not apply. The mention of *traividyam* is for the purpose of ensuring that not only the Rigvedins, Yajurvedins, or Sāmavedins are appointed individually, but rather that all three must necessarily be appointed so that the performance of Vedic rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma—which is accomplished through the three Vedas known as Ṛk, Yajus, and Sāman—may be successfully carried out in the absence of those proficient in all three. Bṛhaspati also says:
Having summoned Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, well-versed in the scriptures, and maintainers of the sacred fire-offering,
he should establish them there and provide for their livelihood.
He himself describes the manner of allotting the means of subsistence:
"The king should grant them lands for their houses with the right to an unseizable tax, having recorded them as 'to be enjoyed without obstruction' in his own edict."

They are those who impose taxes that cannot be revoked and whose own hands cannot be seized. They are to be maintained by the king; "maintainable" means they are to be supported by future kings, being free from such [harsh] taxes. He himself states what must be performed by the established Brāhmaṇas:
"They shall perform the daily rites, the occasional rites, the optional rites, as well as those for peace and prosperity;
likewise, they shall provide a decision in matters of doubt."
[Regarding] the ancient inhabitants of the city, Yājñavalkya also states (2.186):
"That which is conventional and does not conflict with one's own duty,
as well as that which is established by the king— that too must be protected with effort as dharma."

A conventional duty (*sāmayiko dharmaḥ*)—one that arises from custom—is that which does not conflict with one's own specific duty (*nijadharma*), meaning it does not subvert the duties prescribed by the *Śruti* and the *Smṛti*. Such duties consist of things like tending cattle, protecting water sources, or maintaining the household, and these too must be diligently upheld. Likewise, whatever duty is established by the king without subverting one's own specific duty—such as the rule that "as many travelers as arrive must all be fed"—that too must be maintained. However, that which contradicts one's own specific duty, such as the rule that "at the time of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and other rites, everyone must abandon their own work and come to the royal palace, and whoever does not come shall be punished," is not to be maintained; this is the meaning. Yājñavalkya (2.192) extends the requirement to maintain both conventional and royal duties to guilds (*śreṇi*) and other such groups.
This same rule applies to guilds, merchant associations, heretical sects, and assemblies;
the king should protect them from internal dissension and preserve their traditional livelihoods.

Guilds (*śreṇi*) are those who subsist by a single craft, such as weavers and the like. The mention of "companies" (*gaṇa*) is also indicative of *pūgas* and *vrātas*. A *pūga* is a collection of those who subsist by the same occupation, such as elephant-riders, horsemen, and so forth. The terms *gaṇa* and *vrāta* have been explained by Kātyāyana (678): "Those who bear various weapons assembled together are called *vrātas*; indeed, a collection of families is proclaimed to be a *gaṇa*."

The meaning is that the king should protect the distinctions and the legal regulations of these guilds and so forth, and he should maintain their traditional way of life as it has been handed down from generation to generation. Bṛhaspati indicates a certain occasion for the making of such an agreement (*samaya*): "In a village, there may be a convention or the making of an agreement among guilds and assemblies;
however, that [agreement] should be made only in times of distress, and never regarding matters of dharma."

The meaning is that if a calamity is difficult to avoid or a religious duty is difficult to accomplish without establishing a convention (*samaya*) for villages and the like, then a formal agreement in the form of a convention must be made. This is also an illustration; therefore, even in the absence of such [specific causes], a convention may be established by the will of all. The avoidance of calamities must be performed by all those who have entered the convention (*samayin*) acting together, not by one alone. And thus, that same [text] states: "In the face of danger from robbers and thieves, afflictions are considered common to all."
In that regard, the pacification must be performed by all together, not by any single individual.

A rogue is like a wolf. This is also an illustration; for when there is fear from rogues, thieves, and the like, the resulting afflictions are considered common to all. Therefore, whatever agreement has been made—such as "for the sake of averting drought and calamities, and for the successful performance of planetary sacrifices (*grahayajña*) and so forth, this much must be given by each house and field"—the alleviation [of the distress] must be carried out by everyone in accordance with that agreement. He states the same regarding religious duties (*dharmakārya*) which must also be performed collectively by all:
"The restoration of assembly halls, water-stations (*prapā*), temples, houses, ponds, gardens, and groves..."
Likewise, for those who are destitute and poor, the performance of purificatory rites and sacrificial acts [is prescribed].
We must also partially accomplish the cessation of the nest of worldly existence;
that which is written here on this leaf is a righteous formal agreement.
This must be observed by all of them; he who is capable of violating it shall be punished with the confiscation of his entire property and banishment from the city.

A *sabhā* is an assembly hall; an *ārāma* is a grove or garden. The consecration (*saṃskṛti*) of these refers to their restoration when they have fallen into decay. *Saṃskāra* includes rites such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and the cremation of the deceased (*pretadāha*). The performance of sacrifice (*yajanakriyā*) refers to giving gifts to those who perform rituals such as the *Soma-yāga*. The "blocking of the family-canal" (*kulāyananirodha*) means the prevention of the arrival of a herd of people afflicted by famine and other calamities at a family settlement, and the maintenance of that blockade until the famine has passed. In the *Kalpataru*, however, the reading is *kulyānayanarodham* (the blocking of the bringing of irrigation channels); this refers to the obstruction of the flow or the diversion of an irrigation channel (*kulyā*). He [the author] states that members of a community should carry out communal tasks after establishing mutual trust so as not to violate their agreements.
"Having first established mutual trust through an ordeal, by means of a written document, or by intermediaries, they should thereafter carry out their business.

Here, "by an ordeal" means by drinking the water used for bathing a deity; "by means of a written document" means by a formal agreement (*samayapatra*); and "by intermediaries" means by guarantors (*pratibhū*). Nārada (Sama. 2) states that even a king must uphold such an agreement.
The king should likewise protect the established conventions among heretics, guilds, corporations, associations, bands, and assemblies, as well as within fortresses and the countryside.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the great multitude residing in the city of Brahmā is intended. The convention (*samaya*) of heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*) and others is well known. In a fortress (*durga*), however, the convention is such as: "Having taken grain and other goods, one who is going to another country must not sell them [on the way]," and so forth. In a district (*janapada*), however, the convention is such as: "In some places, a toll is collected from the seller; in others, from the buyer," and so forth. Explaining the previously stated point—that the religious duty (*dharma*) and other matters established by convention for heretics and others are not to be revoked—the same author (Nārada, *Sama.* 3) says:
Whatever the duty, whatever the action, and whatever the method of service for these [monks],
as well as whatever their means of livelihood may be— one should approve of that accordingly.

Dharma consists of the worship of shrines and similar acts; ritual action (*karman*) consists of wandering for alms in the morning and so forth; the rule for attendance (*upasthānavidhi*) refers to gathering in a pavilion or similar place upon hearing the sound of a drum or other signals for communal business; and the adoption of a livelihood (*vṛttyupādāna*) means assuming the garb of an ascetic for the sake of subsistence. He himself (Nārada, *Sama.* 4) indicates that which must be avoided by the king: "Whatever is contrary to the king, whatever is despised by the subjects, and whatever is detrimental to one's interests—that he should cause them to desist from."

The meaning is that he should turn them away from those things which are unfavorable to the king—such as the judicial administration of justice performed by a *śūdra*; those things which are inherently or by their very nature despised and disregarded, such as the chewing of betel among heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*) and others; and those things which are detrimental to wealth and cause the loss of property, such as alchemy (*rasavāda*) and the like. He should act in such a way that they do not perform these acts. Regarding the unfavorability of the judicial administration of justice performed by a *śūdra*, it is stated in another *smṛti*:
"That king for whom a *śūdra* performs the judicial administration of justice..."
His kingdom becomes agitated, and his army and treasury perish.

"In whose king's realm"—the word "realm" (*rāṣṭra*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. He himself (Nārada, *Sama.* 7) shows another thing that ought to be revoked: "[238] Whatever practice should be defective, not established by the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), even if it has been introduced, a king who desires his own welfare should cause it to be revoked."

The meaning is that even if it has been practiced for a long time, a king must suppress such things as the practice of prostitution among widows and others—things invented by heretics and the like, which have greed and other vices as their cause and which contradict the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. Regarding quarrels and the like, he (Nārada, *Sama.* 5) states that the king must not tolerate these: their forming mutual associations for the purpose of war, their bearing of weapons, and their seizing one another’s property, and so forth: "The king shall not condone their forming mutual associations, their bearing of weapons against [the state], or their mutual harassment."

Because it is impossible for many members of a collective, who possess diverse opinions, to carry out a task with unanimity, Bṛhaspati states that they should appoint two, three, or five persons to deliberate on the affairs of the group, and whatever those [officers] declare must be accepted by all the members of the collective:
"Two, three, or five should be appointed as speakers for the welfare of the assembly;
their word must be carried out by the village, guild, corporation, and other such groups."
In response to the inquiry as to what kind of people should be appointed as counselors of affairs and what kind should not, he [the same author] says:
"Those who are hostile, those who are addicted to vices, the modest, the lazy, and the timid; the greedy, the very aged, and children—these should not be appointed as counselors of affairs."
Those who are pure, knowers of the Vedic dharma, skillful, self-controlled, of noble birth,
and proficient in all tasks— such persons of the highest caliber should be appointed.

The *śālīnas* are those who are unassailable; they are the "considerers of affairs," meaning those who deliberate upon what promotes or obstructs the accomplishment of the collective work. Regarding one who does not do what is stated by the considerers of affairs, Yājñavalkya (2.188) declares the following punishment:
"All must carry out the command of one who speaks for the welfare of the assembly.
He who acts contrary to that [command] shall be made to pay the first fine."

First is the *pūrvasāhasa* (lowest fine). Intending to show that there is no punishment for transgressing what has been stated by the judge (*kāryacintaka*) if it is contradicted by reason, Kātyāyana says (671):
"He who destroys what is consistent with reason, he who gives no opportunity to the speaker, and he who speaks what is unreasonable—such a person shall be made to pay the *pūrvasāhasa*."
Bṛhaspati also points out another who deserves punishment:
"But he who injures what is common property, or insults those learned in the three Vedas,
or obstructs the performance of a treaty, shall be banished from that city."

One who would injure a common object belonging to a group, such as a staff or other communal property—by providing assistance to those who strike with it or by destroying it; one who would insult or revile another; one who is a wounder of vital parts, a slanderer, a creator of dissension, or likewise a perpetrator of violence; and one who is hostile toward guilds, corporations, or the king—he shall be swiftly banished from there.

An *aruntuda* is one who strikes at the vital points (*marmodghātaka*), a slanderer, and a backbiter; an *apiśuna* is one who creates dissension among those living together and incites discord. Nārada (Sama. 6) states:
"Those who cause divisions among various groups should be especially punished;
for if they are neglected, they will bring about terrible danger, like a disease."

Regarding groups (gaṇas) such as guilds and other associations: "If any man there causes division or shows indifference toward them, a fine of four suvarṇas and six niṣkas is ordained for him. Bṛhaspati [states this].

The determination between four *niṣkas* of gold and six *niṣkas* depends on the relative capacity [of the offender] and other factors. Regarding a collective fine, the authority belongs to the group itself; for this very reason, it has been stated by that same author:
"The heads of families, guilds, and assemblies, as well as those residing in cities and fortresses, shall impose the punishments of verbal censure, social ostracism, and expulsion upon evildoers."

Whatever punishment or favor toward men is carried out by them in accordance with their own duty must also be approved by the king, for they are traditionally considered to have been delegated full authority.

The punishment of speech (*vāg-daṇḍa*) consists of saying, "You are a sinner. The punishment of reproach (*dhig-daṇḍa*) consists of saying, "Fie upon you! Abandonment (*parityāga*) means making one unfit for social intercourse or banishing them; this also serves as an illustration for punishments involving the forfeiture of wealth and so forth. At the end, the terms "restraint and favor" (*nigrahānugraha*) are mentioned again in a general sense. Regarding those who have been given full authority (*nisṛṣṭārtha*), meaning those authorized to carry out a task: he states that if, under the influence of hatred or other such motives, they collectively inflict restraint upon a single individual, then all of them must be punished by the king.
"When those joined by hatred together cause harm to one person... [240]
But the king must restrain them and punish them for their persistence.

"According to the consequence" means in accordance with the degree of severity of the punishment. If the community is unable to punish the offender, then he must be punished by the king. For this very reason, Manu (8.219–221) says:
"A man who, having made a covenant in good faith with a village, a district, or an assembly, should break it out of greed—that person the king shall banish."
Having apprehended him, one should compel that violator of the agreement to pay four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and a silver śatamāna.
In this manner, a righteous lord of the earth should administer the rule of punishment toward those who violate their agreements within villages, castes, and assemblies.

The application of these four punishments—banishment, four *suvarṇas*, six *niṣkas*, and one hundred *mānas*—should be determined in accordance with considerations such as caste, learning, and personal merit. Bṛhaspati states that when there is opposition from a collective body against those who deliberate on affairs, it is the duty of the king to resolve it:
"When a conflict arises between the leaders and the collective bodies, the king shall then investigate the matter and establish them upon their own proper course."
Yājñavalkya (2.187) states the specific punishment for specific offenses committed by leading members:
"He who misappropriates the property of a corporation (*gaṇa*) or violates its agreement,
having been deprived of all his possessions, shall be banished from the kingdom."

Even in the case of the primary punishment, the authority belongs to the corporation itself; in the event of the corporation's incapacity therein, it belongs to the king. For this very reason, Kātyāyana (672) states:
"The perpetrator of violence, the sower of dissension, and the destroyer of the corporation's property—all these must be executed after being publicly proclaimed by the king," so says Bhṛgu.

The meaning is that they are to be destroyed by the *gaṇa* after having been proclaimed before the king. Regarding the penalty for one who does not deliver to the *samūha* what was given by the king to the chief who had come for the sake of the *samūha*'s business—for the purpose of honoring the *samūha*—Yājñavalkya says (2.189–190):
"The lord of the earth, having honored those who have come for the business of the *samūha* with gifts, respect, and hospitality, should dismiss them once their business has been accomplished."
One who has been dispatched for the business of a corporation shall hand over whatever he may obtain;
if he does not hand it over himself, he shall be made to pay eleven times that amount.

The phrase "whatever one might obtain" implies for the purpose of honoring the group as a whole. Bṛhaspati states that whatever is given by the king belongs in common to all the members of the assembly; therefore, it should be taken after being divided according to shares, or else given to those who are destitute and so forth: "Whatever may be obtained from that [gift] shall belong equally to all;
it should be divided according to shares every month or every six months."
One should give to the destitute, the aged, the blind, women, children, the sick, and the diseased, as well as to those seeking offspring and others; this is the eternal law.

"Six-monthly" means sufficient for the maintenance of one person or one family for six months; likewise "monthly. This is merely an illustration. That same author shows that other things as well are common to all:

"Whatever they have acquired or preserved, or whatever debt has been contracted for the sake of the community, or whatever is obtained through the favor of the king—all that belongs equally to everyone."

The meaning is this: whatever additional land, groves, and so forth have been acquired by those leaders through legal proceedings in the court of justice regarding boundary disputes and the like; whatever has been protected from being seized by others; whatever has been done for the sake of the community's business (*gaṇakārya*); and whatever has been obtained through the favor of the king—all that belongs equally to all the members of the assembly. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states (674): "Whatever debt may have been incurred or consumed on account of the community..."
Or if it was assigned for their own personal use, that [gift] should be returned by them alone.

Regarding those who have attained inclusion within a group by virtue of favoring the collective, and those who have attained exclusion from it due to disturbances in the group and so forth— among them, he (Kātyāyana, verses 675–676) states a specific distinction:
"Even those who have reached the status of mediators among corporations (*gaṇas*), guilds (*śreṇis*), and classes (*vargas*),
all of them shall indeed receive equal shares of the previous wealth and debts."
Likewise, in matters of eating, sharing, giving gifts, and performing religious duties, one who remains within the group shall receive a share; however, one who has departed does not receive a share.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Determination of the Legal Head of Dispute Known as Transgression of Consciousness," within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* concerning the venerable Paraśurāma, the Wielder of the Bow.

**A possible reading of the defective text:** In the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "Śrīkodaṇḍaparaśurāma"— this concludes the twenty-third section, the exposition of the legal title known as "Breach of Contract" (*saṃvidvyatikrama*), within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*.
Now follows the determination of the legal head of dispute known as "Repentance after Purchase.
Regarding its nature, Nārada states (Krītānuśaya 1):
"When a purchaser, having bought a commodity for a price, does not regard it highly..."
The legal ground known as "repentance regarding what has been purchased" is thus described.
"He does not hold it in high regard" means he thinks, "This was not acquired with due deliberation. Bṛhaspati states that one must examine what has been purchased:
"One should personally examine what has been bought and show it to others;
once it has been examined and approved, the purchaser shall not relinquish it again."

Regarding that, Vyāsa states that hides and other such items are to be examined immediately: "The examination of hides, wood, bricks, thread, grain, liquor, juices, wealth, base metals, and gold must be conducted at once."
In this context, the word *vasu* refers to silver. Nārada (Krītānuśaya 5–6) states the different times for the examination of milch cows and other such items:
"One should examine a milch cow within three days, but a draft animal within five;
for pearls, diamonds, and corals, the period of examination shall be seven days."
For bipeds, the period is half a month for males and double that for females;
for all seeds it is ten days, and for metals and clothes, one day.

In this context, it should be understood that the counting of three days and so forth begins from the day of purchase. "Dohya" refers to milch cattle and the like; "vāhya" refers to draft animals such as horses and the like. "Muktā" (pearl) is also an indicative term for gems. "Of bipeds" means of male slaves. "Twice that for a month" is the meaning. "Of a woman" means of a female slave. By "all seeds" here, grains and other crops taken for the purpose of sowing are intended, because items taken for consumption and other purposes are stated by the previously cited verse of Vyāsa to be subject to immediate examination. Kātyāyana says:
The period of rescission (*anuśaya*) for land is ten days, and this applies to both the buyer and the seller.

"Land" refers to such things as houses and fields. "Period of rescission" means the time during which a reversal of the sale is possible; that is to say, the period of examination. During this period of examination, such as the three-day period and so forth, if a defect in the purchased item is discovered, it must be returned to the seller. Thus, after specifying the periods of examination such as "milkable [cattle] within three days," Bṛhaspati stated:
"If, however, a defect in the commodity should arise at any time before this [period], [it may be returned]."
That must be returned by the seller; the buyer shall receive his purchase price.

"It is produced" means "it is recognized. Kātyāyana states (688) that once the period for examination has elapsed, even if defects are subsequently discovered, the item need not be returned: "But that which was purchased without being recognized and later found to be defective must be returned to the owner at the proper time; otherwise, it need not be returned."

"Subsequently found to be defective" means determined to be possessed of a flaw. "At the time" means at the time of examination. By the phrase "that which was purchased without being recognized [as defective]," it is shown that only that which was purchased without prior examination may be returned when a defect is discovered at the time of inspection; however, that which was taken after examination may not be returned. On this point, Nārada also says (Krītānuśaya 16.4):
"A merchant who is skilled in commodities should not exercise regret after purchasing;
he should understand the depreciation and appreciation of goods, as well as their provenance."
The buyer should personally examine the merchandise beforehand for its qualities and defects;
once it has been examined, approved, and purchased, it shall not be returned to the seller.

*Anuśaya* means regret. *Kṣaya* and *vr̥ddhi* refer to the decrease in value and the increase in price, respectively, of commodities such as horses in this or that region. The meaning is that one should understand even before purchase whether a commodity originates from this particular place—that is, its provenance (*āgama*). Regarding the specific rule for returning a purchased item when no defect was observed at the time of inspection, Kātyāyana says:
[244] Having purchased a commodity, a person may relinquish it due to regret, provided there is no defect;
however, if he returns it within the [stipulated] time while it is still unsatisfactory, he shall pay a tenth part of the price.
If a buyer, having purchased [an item] and while departing, develops regret once it has come into his hand,
he may relinquish the purchased object by paying one-sixth of its value.

"Unenjoyed" means not yet used. "At the proper time" refers to the time for inspection. Here, the rule is that the payment of one-tenth of the value applies to objects such as land which do not perish through use, whereas the payment of one-sixth applies to seeds and other items that do perish through use. Regarding items that perish through use but are distinct from seeds and the like, Nārada states a specific rule (Krītānuśaya 2–3): "If, after purchasing a commodity for its price, the buyer considers it a bad purchase, it must be returned to the seller on that very same day, provided it is undamaged."
If the purchaser returns it on the second day, he shall pay a thirtieth part of the price as a fine;
on the third day, that fine shall be double; after that, the loss falls upon the purchaser alone.

By stating "it is thought here," the absence of fault in reality is expressed. Regarding the penalty for returning or re-accepting what has been bought or sold without having observed faults such as an increase or decrease in value at the time of purchase, Yājñavalkya (2.258) says:
"Having purchased goods from a merchant without knowing their profit or loss, one must not exercise regret; if one does so, he shall be liable to a fine of one-sixth."

The meaning is: by the buyer who does not recognize the increase in price, or by the seller who does not recognize the decrease in price; the mention of "the merchant" (*vaṇik*) is merely an illustration for any buyer or seller. A "sixth part of the price" means the sixth portion of the value. From the use of the term "not recognizing" here, it is understood that if the increase or decrease in price is discovered after the purchase has already taken place, a rescission (*anuśaya*) must be effected according to the circumstances (or according to the scripture). Manu states the penalty for returning goods after the period for examination has elapsed (8.222–223): MDh 8.222: *paribhuktam avikhyāpya rūpaṃ yad vikrīṇīte | tad apy anyena mārgeṇa na rājñaḥ pratipadyate ||* MDh 8.223: *anyahaste ca vikrītaṃ duṣṭaṃ vā duṣṭavādinā | avijñātaṃ vijñātaṃ vā vikretur na tv ato ’nyathā ||* [He who sells what has been used without disclosing its condition, or what is defective while claiming it is sound, or what was purchased from another's hand—whether it was known to be defective or not—is not released from liability to the king.]
If, after having purchased or sold anything, one should have cause for regret in this matter,
he may return that object or take it back within ten days.
But after ten days, one should neither give nor cause to be given;
both he who takes it and he who gives it shall be fined six hundred by the king.

In this context, *anuśaya* refers to remorse preceded by the perception of a defect. The mention of "ten days" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the period for examination mentioned previously. Even if an item is defective, if it has undergone a change through use, then it need not be returned even within the period of examination. For this very reason, Nārada says (Krītānuśaya 7):
"But a garment that has been worn, which has turned black and soiled—even if it was purchased with a defect—it shall not be returned to the seller."

The mention of "clothing" (*vāsa*) is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*). All of this pertains to cases where no specific rule has been stated. However, where a specific rule (*paribhāṣaṇa*) exists, one must understand the matters of returning the goods or not doing so, and so forth, in accordance with that very rule.
Thus ends the determination of the legal title known as "Repentance after Purchase" (*krītānuśaya*) in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* by the illustrious Kodaṇḍaparaśurāma. 24.

**Possible reading of the defective text:** In the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "Śrīkodaṇḍaparaśurāma"— this concludes the twenty-fourth section, the determination of the legal title known as "Repentance after Purchase" (*krītānuśaya*), within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*.
Now follows the exposition of the legal title known as "Non-delivery after Sale.
Regarding that, Nārada demonstrates its essential nature (Vikrī. 1):
"When, having sold a commodity for a price, it is not delivered to the purchaser..."
The failure to deliver after having sold is called that title of dispute.
He (Nārada, *Vikraya* 2–3) states that there are two kinds and six types based on the different categories of goods to be sold:
"In this world, merchandise is of two kinds: movable and immovable.
However, the procedure for its giving and taking is understood by the wise to be of six types."
That which is to be counted, weighed, measured, or [appraised] by action, form, or beauty;

Selling (*vikraya*) is giving; buying (*ādāna*) is purchasing. That which is subject to purchase and sale after being counted is "countable" (*gaṇima*), such as mangoes and the like. Similarly, there are "weighable" (*tulima*) items, such as saffron, gold, and sandalwood; "measurable" (*meyam*), such as rice and the like. Or, it refers to that which is associated with action in the form of carrying, milking, and so forth—this is the remainder of the sense. An object endowed with form (*rūpa*) is that which possesses beauty. An object possessed of splendor (*śrī*) or luster is such as topaz (*puṣparāga*) and the like. [246] Regarding what must be done when a seller, having accepted the price, fails to deliver the sold item to the buyer who requests it, the same author (Nārada, *Vikrīta-anuśaya* 4) says:
If one who has sold a commodity does not deliver it to the purchaser for the price,
he shall be made to pay the loss of value in the case of immovable property, and the fruit of its use in the case of movable property.

If immovable property has been sold, the seller should be made to deliver it along with its loss; however, in the case of movable property, he should deliver it together with the fruit of its use—this is the meaning. Here, "loss" refers to the enjoyment [of the property] that occurred after the sale. "Fruit of use" refers to the result of actions such as milking, namely milk and so forth. This should be understood to apply when, at the time of delivery, the value is greater than it was at the time of sale. But regarding a decrease in value, the same author (Nārada, *Vikrīta*, 5) says: "If the price should fall by half, he must deliver the commodity together with its profit."

In the *Kalpataru*, however, the reading is: “*arvāk ced apacīyeta*. This means: if, prior to the delivery to the purchaser after it has been sold, the price should decrease (*apacīyeta*), that is, become lower in value, one should deliver the commodity along with its interest (*sodayam*). The meaning is that at the time of delivery, one should give whatever amount is obtained—including the increase—corresponding to the value actually received at the time of sale, even if that value has diminished due to a fall in prices. But when there is equality of price, since an increase in the form of the commodity’s appreciation is impossible, [the rule applies] to deposits, the remainder of interest, and indeed to buying and selling itself.
If that which was requested is not given, it increases by five percent per month.
Thus, he shall be made to pay the merchandise together with the interest specified by the aforementioned rule (Kātyāyana 506). Likewise, Yājñavalkya (2.254) states:
"He who, having received the price, does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer, shall be made to pay it with interest;
or, if the buyer has come from another region, he shall pay the profit derived from that region."
