However, for one who comes from another region for the purpose of purchasing and then buys [the goods], he should be made to deliver that merchandise together with whatever profit was gained from the value of those goods in that other region; this is the meaning of the rule "or the regional profit, if he has come from a distant region. This requirement to deliver the merchandise along with the profit from another region applies not only when prices are equal, but also when the price increases or even decreases. For this very reason, Nārada (Vyavahāra 5) states: "This rule applies to local residents; for those who travel to distant regions, there is the regional profit."

"Of those who remain"—meaning those who remain in the place of the seller. This rule refers to the regulation stated in such passages as "he shall be made to pay for the loss of immovable property. Viṣṇu states regarding the punishment for the seller (5.126–7): "If one who has received the price does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer, he shall be made by the king to pay that [price] along with interest, and shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*. This applies to the case of a haughty seller who is free from any right of rescission (*anuśaya*). Regarding the seller who, due to a desire for rescission, does not hand over the goods after having sold them, and the buyer who, due to a desire for rescission, does not take back the merchandise after having paid its price, Kātyāyana says (683):
He who, having purchased and received an article, does not accept it, or he who does not return an undamaged item,
shall recover his own property by paying one-tenth of the price as a fine.
If the time for performing the purposeful act has not yet arrived, one should certainly not cause it to be performed once it has been completed;
such is the law, but after ten days, there shall be no rescission.

"Unspoiled by water and so forth" is the implied remainder [of the verse]. "The time for the purposeful action" refers to the time for milking, carrying, and so on, regarding merchandise in the form of things to be milked or carried. Nārada (Vikraya 6) states that if the seller fails to deliver the goods after being requested by the buyer, and those goods are damaged by the king, fate, or other causes, the loss belongs to the seller alone and not to the buyer: "If the merchandise is damaged, burnt, or stolen, that loss belongs to the seller alone who, having sold it, does not deliver it."
Yājñavalkya also (2.256):
"If a commodity is damaged by an act of the king or by fate,
the loss belongs solely to the seller who, having been asked for it, does not deliver it."

In this context, because of the qualification "of that which has been requested," there is no loss for the seller in the absence of such a request. Nārada (Vikrīyāsaṃpradānika 9) states that if the buyer does not take possession of the commodity being offered by the seller due to subsequent regret, the loss falls upon the buyer alone: "If the buyer does not accept the purchased commodity while it is being offered, that fault shall belong to him; [otherwise], it belongs to the seller who does not deliver it."
Yājñavalkya also states (2.255):
"If there is a loss due to a defect in the purchaser, that loss shall indeed belong to the purchaser alone."

[248] The fault of the purchaser (*kretṛdoṣa*) consists in the non-acceptance of what is being given; the meaning is that the loss falls upon the purchaser because there is no payment for the price of the object. Regarding a case where, immediately after the purchase, the purchaser has not requested [the return] and the seller has not delivered [the item], and a seizure by the king or others has occurred, Devaṇabhaṭṭa states in the *Smṛticandrikā* that since both parties are equally at fault due to their negligence in requesting and delivering, an equal loss should be assigned. Nārada (Vikrī. 9), however, states that when an item is not accepted because of a subsequent change of mind (*anuśaya*), or when the sold item is sold elsewhere, there is no fault on the part of the seller.
If a buyer does not accept a commodity being offered,
or if a seller sells it elsewhere after having already sold it, neither shall be held at fault.
Yājñavalkya (2.255) also states: "Even if it has been sold, the article may be reclaimed by the original buyer if he has not accepted it.

Regarding one who sells a defective thing claiming it is non-defective, or one who sells elsewhere what has already been sold to someone else even without that buyer's consent, Nārada says (Vikrīta 7–8): [text follows].
But he who, having shown a faultless [article], delivers one that is defective,
shall be made to pay double its value as a fine, and an equal amount as a judicial penalty.
Likewise, he who sells an item into the hand of one person and then delivers it to another shall be made to pay double that amount as a fine, and the same amount as a disciplinary penalty.
Yājñavalkya also (2.257): "If one sells what has been sold into another's hand, or what is defective as if it were non-defective,
the fine in that case shall be twice the value."

This provision for the payment of double the value and the imposition of a corresponding fine for selling what is defective as if it were non-defective applies specifically to cases of intentional sale. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati states:
"If an unwise person, knowing a commodity to be defective, sells it, he shall be made to pay double that amount, as well as a fine equal to it."

In the case of a sale made without prior deliberation, however, there is merely an exchange. In another instance, that same author (Kātyāyana, verse 692) speaks of the reversal of a purchase elsewhere: "What has been sold by one who is intoxicated, insane, or out of fear, or by one who is not independent, foolish, or deluded—this must be relinquished; it shall belong to him again."

This entire rule is to be understood as applying when the price for the commodity has been paid. However, where the purchase has been made by the buyer through mere word alone without payment of the price, or where no such stipulation has been made as that "the rescission of the sale must not be effected," then there is no fault whatsoever in either proceeding with or withdrawing from the transaction. And so says Nārada (Vikrī. 10):
"This rule has been proclaimed regarding a commodity for which the price has been paid;
in other cases, if the price has not been paid, there is no violation on the part of the seller, provided there is an agreement [to the contrary]."

However, where this purchase is merely verbal and something is given by the buyer into the hand of the seller so that it may not be [merely] words, there, if the purchase fails due to a defect in the seller, the seller must give that object back to the buyer twofold. And thus says Yājñavalkya (2.61):
"He who has made a *satyaṅkāra* (earnest-money agreement) shall restore the object twofold."

*Satyaṅkāraḥ* means the act of making true, that is to say, the confirmation of a completed purchase. As Amarasimha states in his lexicon: "The word *satyāpana* is neuter, while *satyaṅkāraḥ* and *satyākr̥tiḥ* are feminine. The term *satyaṅkārakr̥tam* means that which has been made or delivered for the purpose of such confirmation. Regarding the case where a purchase fails due to a defect in the buyer, Vyāsa says:

"If one who has given a *satyaṅkāra* does not appear at the appointed time, the merchandise shall be considered relinquished; likewise, [the price] must be paid by him who refuses to accept it when it is being offered."

"Released" (*nisṛṣṭa*) means "given up" (*utsṛṣṭa*); this is the meaning. It should be understood that here there is not merely the relinquishing of the commodity itself, but rather the relinquishing of it together with the substance constituting the earnest-money (*satyaṅkāra*) that has been paid. Otherwise, since the one who paid the earnest-money would be equivalent to a mere verbal purchaser, the seller’s obligation to return double the earnest-money—arising from offenses such as selling the item elsewhere after having accepted the earnest-money from him—would not apply.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth [section], the exposition of the legal title known as "Non-delivery after Sale," in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* by the illustrious Kodaṇḍaparaśurāma.

**Possible reading of the defective text:** In the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "Śrī Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma"— this is the twenty-fifth [chapter], the exposition of the legal title known as "Non-delivery after Sale" (*vikrīyāsaṃpradāna*), within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*.
[250] Now follows the determination of the legal title known as "Disputes between Owners and Herdsmen.
Manu (8.229) announces its exposition:
I shall now fully declare, according to the true principles of dharma, the legal procedure regarding disputes arising from the transgressions of both owners and herdsmen in relation to livestock.
Nārada (Vetana 10) indicates the measure of wages for a cowherd and other livestock keepers:
"For every hundred cows, a heifer shall be the wage; for two hundred, a milch-cow. This is the annual fee for the cowherd, and a milk-gathering shall take place on the eighth day."

A *vatsatarī* is a two-year-old cow whose calf has already passed its [first] stage; that is to say, a heifer. A *dhenu* is a milch cow together with her calf; that is to say, a cow that yields milk. *Saṃdoha* is the milking of all the cows. The meaning is that when one hundred cows are being tended, a *vatsatarī* is to be given to the cowherd as his annual wage, and when two hundred are being tended, a *dhenu* is to be given; furthermore, on the eighth day, the *saṃdoha* (the entire yield) is also to be given. The *saṃdoha* is to be combined with the *dhenu*, not with the *vatsatarī*. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"Likewise, one who is supported by a *dhenu* shall receive the entire milk on the eighth day."

*Dhenubhr̥taḥ* means "supported by a cow," that is, one who protects two hundred [cows]. Kalpatarukāra has explained *dhenubhr̥taḥ* as "a cowherd"; according to his view, it is understood that the milking of even a heifer is included. The mention of "cows" (*go*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for buffaloes and other animals as well. Following this, the amount of wages should be determined according to the protection of a smaller or larger number of cows and so forth. Furthermore, this specification of the amount of wages applies to cases where no specific contractual wage has been stipulated; however, if there is a specific agreement, payment must be made without exceeding it. Manu (8.231) states the measure of wages in another manner:
A servant who subsists on the milk of cows may, with the consent of the cow-owner, milk the best cow from among ten; this shall be the wages for a herdsman who receives no other pay.

From among ten cows that yield milk, one should milk the best and most excellent cow for the sake of wages; the cowherd, who is the servant supported by that milk, milks her as his remuneration. This constitutes his wage provided he has not been hired for other forms of compensation. However, if he has been hired with another form of payment, then that alone is his wage—this is the meaning. Following this principle, the wages should be determined according to the protection of a smaller or larger number of cattle and so forth. Nārada (Vyavahāra 11) states what the daily duties of the master’s cattle-keeper are:
The cowherd should bring back the cows every day at the end of the night;
having grazed and drunk, he should bring them back in the evening.

"Consumed" means they have eaten grass and so forth; "drunk" means they have drunk [water]. The mention of "cows" is an illustration for all livestock. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya (2.164) states:
"The cowherd should return the animals in the evening exactly as they were entrusted.

This means that however many animals were handed over to him by the owner in the morning, that many must be returned by the keeper to him. He further states (YDh 2.164) that if the death or similar misfortune of a cow or other animal occurs through the fault of the keeper, he must compensate for it.
Having caused those [animals] lost through negligence to be recovered, he shall pay the agreed wage;
"lost" means taken away. Negligence as a cause of loss has been made explicit by Manu (8.232):
"That which is bitten, lost to worms, killed by dogs, or died in a dangerous place..."
But the guardian alone may give away what is inferior in terms of human effort.

"Killed by a dog" means killed by a dog. "In a difficult place" means in an inaccessible region. "Human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) means human exertion. The meaning is that whatever has been lost or destroyed through a lack of human effort must be restored. And this human effort has been demonstrated by Bṛhaspati:
"One should protect [the property] from the fear of worms, thieves, and tigers, as well as from caves and pits;
one should strive to the best of one's ability, cry out for help, or inform the owner."

"Should exert himself" means he should strive to eliminate the calamity. Nārada also states that there is liability to punishment for failing to exercise human effort (NSm 12.13): "If a cattle-calamity occurs, the cowherd should exert himself therein according to his ability;
if he is unable, he should quickly come and report it to the owner."
If he does not exert himself, nor raise an outcry, nor inform his master,
the cowherd must bear the loss and pay a fine to the king.

That refers to cattle and the like. Furthermore, the gift of lost cattle and so forth should be understood as being by way of their value. For this very reason, Viṣṇu (5.137–138) states: "If cattle are harmed by wolves or other predators during the day while the herdsman does not come to their aid, it is the fault of the keeper; he shall pay the value of the lost animal to the owner. "Does not come" means does not arrive. Regarding the amount of the fine for the substance, Yājñavalkya (2.165) says: "But when destruction occurs through the fault of the keeper, a fine is prescribed for the keeper:
twelve and a half *paṇas*, and the value of the substance itself must be paid to the owner."

"Thirteen-and-a-half paṇas" means thirteen paṇas less half a paṇa, that is to say, twelve-and-a-half paṇas. This is a *karmadhāraya* compound with elision of the second member (*uttarapadalopa*), based on the statement of the Vārttikakāra: "Words ending in *kta* preceded by a third [member] are compounded with a word in apposition, provided there is elision of the second member. As for what some have said—that the fine is "thirteen paṇas plus a half"—that is to be disregarded, because we observe the usage of terms such as *ardhatrimātra* ("two and a half morae") by the author of the Mahābhāṣya and others in cases like *sārdhadvimātra*. In certain instances, Manu (8.233) states the absence of fault on the part of the cattle-herder:
If cattle have been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the herdsman is not liable to pay,
provided he informs his master of it at the proper place and time.

Having made a proclamation by means of horns, trumpets, flutes, and so forth, creating a loud noise; in the place, meaning the location where the owner is stationed; at the time, meaning at a time not separated from the moment of the theft. That very [rule] is stated in Manu (8.235–36): "But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the keeper does not come to their aid, whatever wolf may forcibly kill shall be the fault of the keeper."

If, among those cows that have been penned and are grazing together in the forest, a wolf should spring upon and kill one, the herdsman is not at fault. The meaning of the first verse is that when individual animals are situated on easy ground, the herdsman is culpable for the injury caused by wolves and other predators if he fails to exercise human effort [to prevent it]. However, the meaning of the second verse is that when they are situated in difficult terrain, he is not at fault because it is impossible for him to exercise human effort [in such a place]. Vyāsa also says:
In the event of the seizure of cattle, the destruction of a village, or the upheaval of a kingdom,
whatever has been lost or stolen therein, the herdsman is not at fault.

[253] Regarding a cattle-herder who has received his wages but, having abandoned the cattle in a difficult forest, remains at home through negligence, a punishment is prescribed in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"A cowherd who has received his fee, having abandoned the cattle in a desolate forest,
if he wanders about in the village or acts as a forest-dweller, is to be executed by the kings."
The term *śalākī* is explained as "barber" in the *Kalpataru*. In that same work, it is stated in one place that even a master may be subject to punishment:
"If a cow under the care of a cowherd dies due to his negligence, then he alone shall be punished, but the owner of the cow shall be made to pay the fee."
When a cow dies anywhere in the house due to a defect such as disease, then the owner of the cattle shall be fined, after paying the wages of the cowherd.

The phrase "due to a defect such as disease" implies that the fault lies with the owner for failing to provide medical treatment. Here, the mention of "cattle" (*go*) is to be understood as an illustration for all animals whatsoever. For this very reason, Nārada extends (*atidiśati*) the rule prescribed for the cowherd to all animal-keepers (Vet.
17). By this, the legal dispute concerning all keepers has been illustrated.
Furthermore, he states the means by which the keeper remains blameless when animals die through an act of fate (Vet. 17).
And there would be purification when [the parts] are dead, because of the observation of the hair, horn, and so forth.

Regarding "and when dead," the word *bahiḥ* ("outside" or "externally") is the understood remainder. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the ears and other such parts are included. For this very reason, Manu (8.234) says:
"The two ears, the hide, the hair, the bladder, the sinew, and the *rocanā*..."
But one should give [the animals] to the owners of the cattle when they have died, upon the appearance of the marks.

In some places, the reading is "he should show the marks and so forth" (*aṅkādi darśayet*). A "mark" (*aṅka*) is a sign such as a horn or an ear; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), witnesses are included. The meaning is that when the animals have died, he should show the marks and so forth to the owner, and he should give him that which was useful, such as the yellow pigment (*rocana*) and the like. Yājñavalkya (2.166) states that for the purpose of grazing cattle and other livestock in villages and similar areas, a certain uncultivated portion [of land] should be set aside:
"Pasture for cattle shall be according to the will of the village, or according to the authority of the king."

[254] By the will of the village—that is, by the will of the villagers—or by the nature of the land, having regard for its smallness or greatness; or by the power of the king—that is, by the king’s will—the pasture for cattle (*gopracāra*) should be designated so as to facilitate the coming and going of cows and other livestock. This is the meaning. For the sake of facilitating the standing and sitting of the cows, he (the same author, Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.167) states that another place, unplowed and situated between the field and the village, should be designated around the village: "The distance between a village and a field should be one hundred *dhanus* in circumference."
There should be two hundred for a market town, and four hundred for a city.

By the term *parīṇāha* (circumference), what is meant here is ground upon which no crops have been sown in any direction. Such a space measuring one hundred *dhanus* should be made as the interval between a village and a field; that is to say, two hundred for a *kharvaṭa* and four hundred for a *nagara*. A *kharvaṭa* is a village endowed with many artisans and cultivators; some say a *kharvaṭa* is a village abounding in thorny growths. Since it is stated that herdsmen are not to be punished when fields near pasture lands are damaged by cattle and other animals due to a lack of enclosure, the field must be covered with thorns and the like. For this very reason, Manu says (8.237, 238): [text omitted].
There shall be a pasture-land of one hundred bows all around a village.
If cattle should damage the uncultivated grain there,
the king shall not inflict punishment upon the cattle-herders.

A *parīhāra* is an unplanted area. By this, it is stated that there shall be punishment for cattle-herders when they damage an enclosed field. Furthermore, the enclosure must be constructed quite densely even before the crops have begun to grow. And so says Kātyāyana (6.66):
"One should construct a large enclosure while the crops have not yet sprouted;
for once the wild animals have tasted their flavor, they are difficult to turn away."

The mention of "wild animals" is illustrative. Nārada (Sīmā, 41) states: "A fence should be constructed around a field on the road such that a camel cannot look over it, nor can a beast, a dog, or a boar break through it."

*Vṛti* means a fence or enclosure. It refers to a field situated on a path or near a road; this is also an elliptical designation for a field located in the vicinity of a village and the like. Any opening that has somehow formed in the enclosure must be filled again with thorns and other such materials. And so Manu (8.239) says:
"One should construct a fence there such that a camel cannot look over it, or one should fill every gap through which the snout of a dog or a pig might pass."

Regarding what must be done when damage to crops is caused by animals even after they have bypassed a protective fence, that same author (Manu 8.240) says: "In the case of a field enclosed along a path or near a village, the herdsman is liable to a fine of one hundred [paṇas]; however, he should drive away the animal if it is unherded."

"In the vicinity of a village" means near a village. "An animal with its keeper" means that the keeper of such an animal is liable to a fine of one hundred *paṇas*; this is the meaning. "An animal without a keeper" means it should be driven away by striking it with a staff or the like, or by seizing it by the ear or other parts; this is the meaning. For this very reason, Kātyāyana (664) states: "In fields, groves, pastures, houses, and cattle-pens, Bṛhaspati [prescribes] the seizing and the beating of those who have entered them."

By the word *vivīta*, an area of grass or wood not enclosed by another person's property is meant. "In pens" refers to cow-pens and the like; "seizing" refers to calves and similar animals, while "beating" refers to large bulls and the like. Furthermore, beating must not be done beyond what is necessary for the purpose of restraint. For this very reason, it has been stated by that same author (Kātyāyana, 665):
"In cases where there is a dispute between the owner and [the keeper] regarding the beating of animals—whether they be of low, high, or middle quality—the king shall determine the punishment."

The meaning is that where a master disputes an unjust beating, the king shall punish the one who administered the beating. When damage to crops and the like is caused by an animal, whether with its keeper or without its keeper, the owner of the animal must pay the value of the crops and such things eaten by the animal to the owner of the field; this will be stated further ahead. Furthermore, the punishment prescribed for a herdsman when a crop is destroyed by an animal crossing a boundary fence is to be understood as applying when the animal was not being restrained by him. And so says Nārada (Sīmā, 28):
If, however, cattle or other animals should break through the enclosure and destroy the standing crop,
the keeper shall be punished therein, provided he is not capable of preventing it.

Even when there is unavoidable damage to the crop due to the absence of a fence, the herdsman is not subject to punishment; for there is the previously cited traditional verse (Manu 8.238): "In that case, the grain is considered unfenced. Nārada also states this same point (Sīmā 40): "If a field located near a village, at the edge of a pasture, or on a great highway is unfenced, there is no transgression on the part of the herdsman if it is destroyed."
The distinction is that [the offense applies] to the keeper who is unaware of that destruction. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya (2.162) states:
"There is no fault regarding a field located on a path or at the edge of a village pasture;
however, if one acts intentionally, he deserves punishment like a thief."

"On the path" means at the edge of a village pasture or in close proximity to a road and the like. This refers to cases where the grazing lasts for a short period of time. In the case of long-term grazing, even if the keeper is unaware of it, he is liable to punishment because of his lack of vigilance in protecting the cattle; thus, a penalty certainly applies. For this very reason, Viṣṇu (5.146, 148) states: "There is no fault [if grazing occurs] on a path or at the edge of a village pasture for a short time. Just as there is no punishment for the herdsman when grazing occurs unintentionally for a short time, so too the owner of the cattle—whether with or without a keeper—is not required to pay compensation for the value of the crops and such, since there is no fault in that grazing being unavoidable. As for that which...

"But in all cases, it is the settled rule that the owner of the field shall pay the damage" (Manu 8.241). This refers to cases other than those [previously mentioned]. "In all cases"—that is, whether the cattle are attended by a keeper or unattended—the "damage" (*sada*) refers to the value of the crop. Manu (8.241) states the penalty for cases other than those where immunity from fault was declared regarding uncultivated fields:
"But in other fields, the animal deserves a fine of one *paṇa* and a quarter."

“In other [fields]” means in fields other than those adjacent to the previously mentioned enclosed paths and so forth, such as those described by the phrase “in a field enclosed by a path. While it would have been necessary to state that the keeper or the owner is to be punished, the fact that the animal itself is declared to be the one to be punished is for the purpose of ensuring that the prescribed fine applies to each individual animal when there are many animals. Here, the word *paśu* (animal) refers to either the keeper or the owner. In this regard, the rule is established that if the animal has a keeper, the keeper is to be punished; but if it is without a keeper, the owner is to be punished. For this very reason, Gautama (12.16–17) states: “In the case of injury to cattle, the fault lies with the owner; but if the animal is under the charge of a keeper, the fault lies with him. Nārada also says (Sīmā, 35): [text follows].
If a cow that has strayed due to the fault of its keeper should destroy a field, there is no punishment for the owner; the keeper alone deserves that punishment.
Whether the keeper is absent or present, the compensation for the crop damage belongs to the owner alone. And so says that same authority (Nārada, Sīmā 38):
"If a man demands compensation for grain eaten by cattle, the grain that was sown there should be given with the consent of the neighbors."
As for that which establishes the owner's liability to punishment even when the animal is with its keeper:
"One should ward off the cows from the crops; if they have fed there, the fault shall belong to both.
The owner should be made to pay the prescribed fine, while the keeper deserves a beating."
Thus says Bṛhaspati: "Goodness and self-restraint constitute 'sadadama'; as much of the crop as may be destroyed, that much shall be the fruit for the owner of the field.
The herdsman is to be beaten, but the owner of the cow deserves the previously mentioned fine."

Thus, regarding the statement of Yājñavalkya (2.161), the remainder of the sense is that the owner of the cattle (*gomī*) must pay the fruit [of the crop] to the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*). *Gomī* means the owner of the livestock. Both of these two statements refer to the case of the destruction of standing crops along with their roots. And so says Nārada (Vetana 29):
"But upon the destruction of standing crops along with their roots, the owner of those [crops] shall receive compensation;
the herdsman is released from blame by [the payment of] slaughter [as atonement], and he shall inflict the fine upon the owner."

The owner of that [crop] is the owner of the grain. "He shall obtain a fine" refers to the owner of the animal; this is the ellipsis. "Killing" here means striking with a whip or similar instrument. "As previously stated" indicates that the punishment concerning specific types of animals has been shown by Yājñavalkya himself (2.159–160):
"A buffalo that causes damage to the crop shall be fined eight māṣas;
a cow, half of that; and goats or sheep, half of that."

[258] For those who sit down after having eaten, the fine shall be double that which was stated. In the case of a forest preserve (*vivīta*), the fine for these [animals] is equal; for a donkey or a camel, it is the same as for a buffalo.

The owner of a buffalo shall be fined eight *māṣas*; the owner of a cow, four; the owner of a goat, two; and the owner of a sheep, two. If these animals graze without being restrained and then lie down right there, the owner shall be made to pay double the aforementioned fine. Even in the case of damage to grass and other vegetation in a pasture (*vivīta*), they are to be punished in the same manner as for damage to standing crops. The owner of a donkey and the owner of a camel are to be punished like the owner of a buffalo. When the punishment for animal owners is to be stated, the specific mention of the "buffalo" and so forth—just as with the mention of the word "man" in the *Mānava* code—is for the purpose of indicating that the fine is to be assessed per head of animal. If buffaloes and other such animals graze and then remain lying down, their owner shall pay a fine four times the standard amount.

"Double for those who live [there], and fourfold for those with their calves"—from this statement, since the punishment must be appropriate according to the offense, it is stated in the *Smṛticandrikā* that only a copper *māṣa* is to be taken, and not a gold or silver one. A *māṣa* is the sixteenth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*, which is measured by a *karṣa*. This same [unit] is the twentieth part of a *paṇa*—which consists of twenty *māṣas*—in the view that a *pala* is measured by five *suvarṇas*, as it is the fourth part of a *pala*.
Thus, the *māṣa* is proclaimed to be the twentieth part of a *paṇa*.

Thus addressed by Nārada (Parishishta 58), even a twentieth part [of a *māṣa*] becomes [the unit]. Since there is no difference in meaning in either case, that which was stated by some—“The number [of units] cited by Manu is rooted in rays (*raśmi*), dust (*rajas*), and [atoms];
it should be employed in ordeals (*divya*) and likewise in legal proceedings (*vinaya*), ending with the *kārṣāpaṇa*”—[is refuted].

Thus, because it contradicts the statement of Bṛhaspati, the twentieth part mentioned by Nārada is not to be adopted; rather, the sixteenth part mentioned by Manu alone is to be adopted—this [position] is refuted. As for the fine of one *paṇa* and a quarter mentioned by Manu (8.241), "he deserves a *paṇa* and a quarter," that refers to intentional cases, whereas the fine mentioned by Yājñavalkya refers to unintentional cases; thus there is no contradiction. As for the statement of Viṣṇu (5.140–141) establishing the liability of the keeper to be fined—"If a she-buffalo should destroy the crops, the keeper shall be fined eight *māṣas*, but if she is unattended, the owner"—that also refers to the destruction of crops with their roots, since it is appropriate that the fine for either of them be imposed only in the case of a minor offense. As for another Smṛti text...
For two quarters of a *paṇa* [is the fine for stealing] a cow; for a buffalo, it is double that;
likewise, for goats, sheep, and calves, a quarter *paṇa* is proclaimed as the punishment.

Thus, having consumed that [grass], those animals such as cows and others sit down; this refers to their case. As for the penalty: "One should cause a cow to pay a fine of one *māṣa*, and likewise a buffalo two *māṣas*; similarly, the fine for goats, sheep, and calves shall be half a *māṣa*."

Thus, the statement of Nārada (Sīmā. 31) refers specifically to the case of grazing for only a *muhūrta*. For this very reason, Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated: "A cow grazing at night [incurs a fine of] five *māṣas*, during the day three [māṣas], and for a *muhūrta* one *māṣa*; however, there is no punishment for a single mouthful (*grāsa*). Here, "mouthful" refers to the consumption of a single morsel. In this context, the mention of fines of five or three [māṣas]—which differ from the fines prescribed by Yājñavalkya—should be regulated according to the relative gravity of the offense. This applies to cases where the herdsman is not present; however, for those who graze under direct supervision, Nārada’s statement—"The wise declare that the punishment shall be the same as for a thief"—applies. Regarding animals, Nārada (Sīmā. 36–37) states in some instances that they are subject to punishment.
Whether seized by a king’s malady, or struck by a thunderbolt,
or bitten by a serpent, or fallen from a tree;
Even if [the animal] is killed by tigers and the like, or afflicted by diseases,
there is no fault on the part of the herdsman, nor is there any fault on the part of the owners.

Yājñavalkya (2.163): Bulls set at liberty, sacrificial animals, those that have recently calved, newcomers, and others of this kind— those for which there is no keeper— are not to be held liable [for damage], even when overwhelmed by divine forces or royal authority.

A "great bull" (*mahokṣa*) is a proud ox. "Animals set free" (*utsr̥ṣṭapaśavaḥ*) refers to those released according to the ritual injunctions for the *vṛṣotsarga* (the rite of releasing a bull) or other rites of dedication to the deities. A "recently calved cow" (*sūtikā*) is one that has given birth within the ten-day period. An "intruder" (*āgantukaḥ*) is one who has strayed from its own herd and arrived from another region. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), elephants and other such animals are included. The meaning is that even those for whom there is no keeper—such as those destroyed by fate or the king, or those that cause the destruction of crops—are not to be punished. Manu (8.242): "A cow that has recently calved within ten days, a bull, and likewise animals dedicated to the gods..."
Manu has declared that neither those with their owners nor those without owners are exempt from punishment.
"Devapaśavaḥ" refers to animals established in temples for the enjoyment of the deity. Nārada (Sīmā. 30) states:
"A cow that has recently calved, as well as bulls, horses, and elephants, should be kept away [from the crops] with great effort for ten days; their owner shall not be subject to punishment."

In this context, the mention of the "owner" (*svāmin*) is also indicative of the "keeper" (*pāla*). By the word "horse" (*vājin*), the royal horses stationed for the protection of the subjects are intended here. For this very reason, Uśanas states: "Horses and elephants are not to be punished, for they are remembered as protectors of the subjects.
One-eyed animals, those with false marks, bulls, and those bearing official insignia are also exempt from punishment."

"A stray cow, one that has recently calved, and one that is in heat are not to be punished. "Hornless" means those with a single horn. "Branded" means marked with a sign made by heated iron. "Abhisāriṇī" is one who, having strayed from her own herd, returns again to it. As for the rule:

"If a buffalo causes the destruction of crops, the keeper shall be fined eight *māṣas*; if she is unattended, the owner [shall be fined]. For a horse, a camel, or a donkey, the fine is half of that; if it is a cow, half of that again; and if it is a goat or sheep, if they remain after grazing, the fine is double."

Thus, the statement of Viṣṇu (5.140–145) establishing the punishability of horses refers specifically to those horses kept by merchants and others for the purpose of sale and so forth. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “Mules, elephants, and horses are not to be punished, but must necessarily be turned aside gently. Āpastamba declares that all cows are exempt from punishment during festivals and on the day of a *śrāddha* ceremony: “Cows are not to be punished during an festival, and likewise at the time of a *śrāddha*. Vyāsa says this with the intention that what is consumed by cows at the time of a *śrāddha* and similar occasions becomes exceedingly auspicious.
O tiger among men, that which is eaten by Brahmins after they have been invited, and when one's kinsmen are impoverished,
as well as by cows, is superior even to the Vājapeya sacrifice.
If grain has been eaten by cows at the time of a *śrāddha* or similar occasion, and the owner demands it back, Uśanas says there is a fault:
"The ancestors of that man who demands back grain destroyed by cows do not eat [the offerings], nor do the inhabitants of heaven eat them."
Manu summarizes this head of legal procedure (8.244):
"A righteous lord of the earth should observe this rule regarding transgressions involving owners of cattle, the cattle themselves, and the herders."
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section, the determination of the legal title known as "Disputes between Master and Herdsman," in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* by Śrī Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma.

**A possible reading of the defective text:** In the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "Śrīkodaṇḍaparaśurāma"— this is the twenty-sixth section, the determination of the legal title known as "Disputes between Master and Herdsman," within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*.
Now follows the determination of the legal title known as "Disputes over Boundaries.

In this regard, intending the term *sīmā* (boundary) as used by Manu and others to be illustrative, Nārada has demonstrated its essential nature by designating it as "disputes concerning fields" (*kṣetraja-vivāda*) [Nārada, Sīmā 1]:
"The determination of embankments, field-marks, boundaries, and land that is ploughed or unploughed..."
Where there is a dispute concerning ownership of a field, that is a "dispute over land" (kṣetraja).

A *setu* is a dam that binds the flow of water. A *kedāra* is a field; its boundary or limit is the *sīmā*. A *vikr̥ṣṭa* is a place tilled by the plow; *akr̥ṣṭa* means devoid of that, which is to say, fallow land (*khila*). Where there is a dispute regarding the determination of these things, that is "pertaining to fields" (*kṣetrādhikāra*), meaning a dispute concerning a field is called "born of fields" (*kṣetraja*). This dispute is of six kinds, as Kātyāyana says (732): "Excess or deficiency in the portion, existence or non-existence [of ownership], possession without enjoyment, and the boundary—these are the six causes of dispute."

When it is said, "I have more land than this," and the dispute is "No," it is a dispute concerning excess (*adhikyavivāda*). When it is said, "Your land is only this much," and the dispute is "Mine is this much," it is a dispute concerning deficiency (*nyūnatāvivāda*). Here, when it is said, "I have a share," and the dispute is "No," it is a dispute concerning existence (*astitvavivāda*). Here, when it is said, "You have no share," and the dispute is "It does exist," such a dispute is a dispute concerning non-existence (*nāstitvavivāda*). When it is said, "This land was not enjoyed by you before, yet it is being enjoyed now," and the dispute is "I too have enjoyed this land before," such a dispute is a dispute concerning enjoyment (*bhogabhuktivivāda*). When it is said, "This boundary belongs to my land," and the dispute is "No," it is a dispute concerning boundaries (*sīmāvivāda*). Such is the meaning of the sixfold dispute. Boundaries are fourfold: the boundary of a country (*deśasīmā*), the boundary of a village (*grāmasīmā*), the boundary of a field (*kṣetrasīmā*), and the boundary of a house (*gṛhasīmā*). Regarding these four types as well, Nārada states that they possess five modes according to their respective applicability.
The boundary is recorded as being of five kinds: that marked by a banner, that marked by fish, that established by fire, that free from fear, and that determined by royal decree.

The *dhvajinī* (flag-marked) boundary is characterized by trees and other such signs; the *matsyinī* (fish-marked) is marked by water-signs; the *naidhānī* (buried-marked) is indicated by buried husks, charcoal, and so forth; the *bhayavarjitā* (fear-free) is established through mutual agreement between the plaintiff and the defendant; and the *rājaśāsananītā* (king’s decree-bound) is a boundary established by the king in the absence of boundary markers or those who know the boundaries. The nature of the *dhvajinī* and others, as well as other divisions of boundaries, have been shown by Vyāsa:
"The *dhvajinī*, the *naidhānī*, and that made by the king—these five kinds of boundaries are considered stable; however, the *matsyinī* is recorded as unstable."
Where there is a depression between two villages that marks the boundary,
that is declared by those learned in the scriptures to be characterized as a "low-lying" boundary marker.
Where reeds, hunchbacks, anthills, temples,
and heaps of stones are seen, that [ground] should be known as "elevated" (samunnatā).
Where trees stand high and tall along the boundary of both villages,
rising up like banners, that is proclaimed as the *dhvajinī* boundary.
That place where bricks, charcoal, sand, gravel, bones, and potsherds are seen deposited is proclaimed as *naidhānī*.
[263] Where there is an absence of witnesses, a boundary that has been determined by the lord with the consent of the neighbors is to be known as one established by the king.
That which flows according to its own will, possesses abundant water, is inhabited by fish and tortoises,
and has a constant current, is considered to be the Matsyinī boundary.
Bṛhaspati states that boundary markers must be established at the time of entering a village or similar settlement:
"At the time of settling [the land], the determination of the boundary enclosure must be made;
it should be characterized by both manifest and secret signs, thereby removing all doubt."

That by which one is bound is a "bond" (*bandha*); a bond at a boundary is a "boundary-bond" (*sīmābandha*). That by which something is determined is a "determination" (*viniścaya*); thus, a "boundary-bond determination" (*sīmābandhaviniścaya*) refers to a boundary-marker stone (*sthalaguḍaka*) that serves as the cause for deciding a boundary, being accompanied by both manifest and concealed signs. This is the meaning: such a stone should be placed at the boundary. He himself shows the manifest and concealed signs: "Ponds, wells, and tanks; shrines, groves, and temples; high ground, depressions, river currents, reed-beds, thickets, mountains, and so forth."
One should always cause these signs of demarcation to be made at the boundary:
stones, bones, cow-hairs, as well as ashes and potsherds.
Dried cow dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel, and likewise sand—
whatever things of this kind exist, the earth shall not consume them over time.
He should cause these to be made unobvious at the junctions of the boundary.
A *caitya* is a structure built of bricks and the like, such as a quadrangle; a *sthala* is an elevated portion of ground; a *nimna* is a ditch; and *naga*s are trees such as the *aśvattha*.
Regarding boundary trees, he should plant *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, and *kiṃśuka* trees.
And [he saw] śālmalī, śāla, and tāla trees, as well as milky trees.

"Various thickets, bamboos, *śamī* trees, creepers, and open grounds"—thus from the *Manusmṛti* (8.246–247). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), paths and so forth are included. "Bones" refers to the bones of animals and the like. He himself [the author of the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti*] states the method for placing concealed signs:
"Cow-dung, bones, husks, charcoal, gravel, stones, and potsherds..."
Sand, bricks, cow-hair, cotton, bones, and ashes.
Having thrown these into jars, one should have them deposited at the boundaries.
"Cotton seeds" means cotton fibers and cotton seeds. He himself stated that these signs, which are associated with discernment and emergence, should be made known to children by the elders:
"Then, one should carefully show them to children who are not yet of age."
And likewise, they should show those children to them when they have grown old.
In this way, when there is knowledge through tradition, no confusion regarding the boundary arises.
The word "pradarśayet" (he should show) is a Vedic singular used for the plural. Nārada states the means of determination when these boundary marks are somehow absent (Sīmā. 6):
"In lands where rivers have carried away, or where marks have been abandoned or destroyed..."
And by means of those inferential cognitions based on specific locations, as well as through the observation of experiences.

Those whose marks have been carried away—meaning removed by the flow of a river, displaced from their original positions, or destroyed—are described as such. By means of measurements, such as witnesses and neighboring landowners; for even when such marks exist, if there is distrust regarding them, Manu states that the king must resolve the boundary dispute by means of the aforementioned marks:
"By these marks the king shall determine the boundary between two disputing parties" (Manu 8.252).

Even when there are signs present, if there is disagreement regarding them, or if they are absent, the decision is based on the testimony of witnesses. And so it is said by that same author (Manu 8.253):
"If there should still be doubt even upon seeing the signs, the determination of the boundary dispute must rely solely on the testimony of witnesses."

"Based on witnesses" means having witnesses as the cause. The word "api" (also) is intended to include the alternative case where there is an absence of marks (*liṅga*). Those witnesses are concerned with the marks of the boundary or the boundary itself. Regarding the specific requirements for witnesses of the boundary, Bṛhaspati says:

[265] "Those who know the title-deed (*āgama*), the legal proof (*pramāṇa*), the possession (*bhoga*), the time (*kāla*), the name, and the characteristics of the plot of land—they are the witnesses in this matter."

The measure is the extent [of the boundary]. In the absence of witnesses for both parties, the decision is based on the neighbors. Thus says Manu (8.258): "In the absence of witnesses, however, four inhabitants of the village boundaries, being purified, shall determine the boundary in the presence of the king."

Yājñavalkya also states (2.152): "Or four, eight, or even ten neighbors from the entire village"—meaning neighbors who are residents of the entire village, numbering equally as four, eight, and so forth, and who are users of the adjacent villages, fields, and other properties. And likewise Kātyāyana (736):
A village is declared to be the neighbor of a village, a field the neighbor of a field,
and a house is specified as the neighbor of a house, for they encircle one another on all sides.

A *sāmanta* is a village situated surrounding and bordering a village on all four sides; the same applies to fields and other such properties. Regarding the determination of boundaries when the *sāmantas* are found to be manifestly corrupt, the same author (Kātyāyana, verse 739) states: "When the *sāmantas* are corrupted in establishing the truth of the matter, because of the gravity of the issue, the settlement must be made by those associated with them; there is no doubt in this regard."
Regarding the fact that even these [witnesses] may be possessed of manifest defects, the determination [of their testimony] is based on their neighbors; thus he says (Kāt. 740):
"In cases where those who are closely connected or attached [to the parties] are found to have faults, those who are connected to them are declared [to be the witnesses].
But when even these are found to be openly corrupt, then the determination is based on the *maula* and other [classes of witnesses]; thus he says (Kāt. 740, 742): [the same].
A king who understands the Dharma should not punish those who are not corrupt;
rather, having set aside the corrupt vassals, he should act together with other ministers, such as the hereditary ones and so forth.
Those who know the Dharma understand that one should establish the boundary by assembling them in this manner.

This means: other than the immediate neighbors (*sāmanta*), their neighbors (*tatsāmanta*), and those beyond them, one should assemble citizens (*nāgara*) and others who are familiar with the boundary markers. By "the original ones and so forth" (*maulādibhiḥ*), it is meant the original, the aged, and those who have been removed. Having assembled (*saṃmiśraya*) them—that is, having brought them together—the citizens and others are indicated by Nārada (Sīmā, verse 2): "The citizens, the members of the village community, and those men who are the most senior."
The nature of the *maula* witnesses and others has been shown by Kātyāyana (vv. 743–745):
"Those who were neighbors there previously but later went to another country are called *maula* by the sages because they are rooted in that [original location]."
Those endowed with human virtues who have witnessed a task being accomplished—
whether they be old or not old— are proclaimed as "the experienced" (vṛddha).
Because they extract [the essence] from that which consists of listening, enjoyment, activity, narration, and reflection,
they are therefore known as "extracted" (uddhṛta).

The meaning is that those who, endowed with the qualities of men and the qualities of heroes, have known the facts through tradition, are "extracted" [as witnesses]. However, when the neighbors (*sāmanta*) are not manifestly possessed of defects, yet some defect is alleged by the opponent, then a distinction has been stated by that very same author (Kāt. 746):
"The neighbors are the primary means of proof when they are endowed with good qualities and no undesirable [defects] are alleged;
but the subsequent ones should be known as being twice as many, and others beyond them are considered to be three times as many."

When the opponent states an undesirable point and names a fault, twice as much [of the fine] as that fault's value shall be taken from him. If they also name a fault, twice as much as those [faults] shall be taken from them. If the same occurs there as well, then the original elders and others shall be made to pay three times the value of the neighbors; this is the meaning. When these witnesses and others are absent, Manu says (8.259–260):
"But in the absence of neighbors who are original witnesses to the boundary, one should also interrogate these men who frequent the forest:"
He [should employ] hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers,
snake-catchers, gleaners, and others who dwell in the forest.

[267] And this inclusion of those whose range is the forest is to be understood as applying when there are no farmers in the areas adjacent to the boundary. For this very reason, Nārada says (Sīmā. 3):
"And those who live outside the village boundaries and subsist on farming—cowherds, fowlers, hunters, and others whose range is the forest."

The author of the *Smṛticandrikā* states that the order of recitation is intended here: these neighbors and others are the arbiters in all disputes concerning immovable property and disputes concerning embankments and the like. And so says Kātyāyana (737, 734, 735):

"In their absence, the neighbors—the original inhabitants (*maula*), the elders (*vr̥ddha*), those who have been uprooted (*uddhr̥ta*), and so forth—are the authorities even in the sixfold case of immovable property; no further deliberation is required in this matter."
Regarding fields, buildings, ponds, wells, groves, and embankments,
one should reach a definitive decision here through the testimony of neighbors based on their comprehensive knowledge of the area.
And likewise at village boundaries, as well as for cities and districts—of those witnesses; Bṛhaspati also states:
"In every case concerning immovable property, this rule is proclaimed."
Yājñavalkya also (2.154): "In the case of groves, temples, villages, water-stations, gardens, and houses,
as well as in the case of rainwater, flowing streams, and the like, this same rule is to be understood."

A *āyatana* is a site prepared for the purpose of storing straw and other materials. A *nipāna* is a watering place, such as a well or the like. A *varṣāmbupravaha* is a flow of water produced by rain. Kātyāyana further states:
"In the case of fields, wells, and tanks, as well as in the case of irrigated plots, groves, houses, palaces, dwellings, and likewise temples."

*Kedāra* is a specific type of field characterized by small embankments; it is mentioned separately from "field" (*kṣetra*) according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*). Here, *prasāda* refers to a palace or temple. Manu (8.254–55) states that the king should question the witnesses, the neighbors, and others in the presence of the villagers, as well as the plaintiff and the defendant, and what they declare must be recorded in writing:
"In the presence of the village assemblies, the boundary witnesses should be questioned regarding the boundary markers, as well as those two litigants."
In whatever manner those questioned together should deliver a decision regarding the boundary,
he shall record that decision as well as their names, all together.

Regarding the phrase "boundary markers," this refers to the witnesses to the boundary. As for the boundary witnesses, they shall declare the boundary. Bṛhaspati states that those witnesses and others, having been sworn by the oaths prescribed in the section on witnesses—beginning with, "One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth" (Manu 8.113)—shall speak;
"Sworn by their respective oaths, they shall declare the determination of the boundary and point out the markers; that is the authority; such is the settled rule."

In response to the question of how those witnesses, such as neighbors and others, who are unable to point out the specific boundary marks but know the boundary itself, should speak, Manu says (8.256): "Having grasped the earth with their heads, wearing garlands and red garments,
and having been sworn by their respective meritorious deeds, they shall determine that boundary correctly."

They should lead [the boundary] along the broad earth—this is the ellipsis; they should reach a decision. They should do so correctly and properly (*samañjasam*). Even the garland must be worn red, as Yājñavalkya (2.152) has stated:
"Or four, eight, or even ten neighbors from all the villages, wearing red garlands and garments and carrying earth, should lead the boundary."
By the expression "the entire village," the exclusion of a single individual is indicated; Nārada clarifies this [in Sīmā-vivāda 9]:
"A man, even if he be trustworthy, should not determine the boundary alone;
because of the gravity of this matter, this procedure is established among many."
The determination of the boundary must be carried out even by a single person approved by both parties. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"Even a single virtuous man, approved by both sides, who is free from [conflicting] witnesses and marks, wearing red garlands and garments and carrying earth upon his head..."
A man, firm in his vows and having observed a fast, should point out the boundary.
In the absence of witnesses to the boundary or of marks indicating it, Nārada (Sīmā 10) also states:
"If there is only one person who may determine the boundary, he should determine it while fasting,
wearing red garlands and garments, and placing earth upon his head."

For witnesses, neighbors, and others, the determination [of the boundary] occurs within three fortnights from the day of traversing the boundary, provided there has been no affliction by divine or royal calamities such as disease; it does not occur immediately after the traversal. For this very reason, Kātyāyana (751) states:

"In the case of traversing the boundary, in the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa), and likewise in touching the foot, a period of three fortnights, one fortnight, and seven days is prescribed for divine and royal [calamities]."

The phrase "in due order" is to be understood as the ellipsis. When, within the three fortnights, it is determined through the observation of witnesses suffering from illness or other divine or royal calamities, or by some other means, that they have spoken falsely, then Manu states the punishment (8.257):
"Those who lead [the case] according to what was stated are purified as truthful witnesses;
but those who lead it otherwise shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas]."

"In the manner described"—that is, by the method stated in the verse beginning with "Having grasped the earth with their heads" and so forth. "Leading" means reaching a decision; the phrase "in accordance with reality" is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Two hundred" means two hundred *paṇas*. The meaning is that each individual should be made to pay a fine of two hundred *paṇas*. Regarding the punishment for neighbors who speak falsely, Nārada says (Sīmā-vivāda, 7):
"If the neighbors should speak falsely in the determination of a boundary, all of them shall be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement."
The same author states the punishment for those other than the neighbors—namely, the immediate neighbors (*saṃsaktas*) and so forth—if they speak falsely:

"If the remaining persons, having been appointed to the task of examining the land, should speak falsely, each of those lowest-ranking individuals is to be punished with the first amercement. (NSM 1.270)
Furthermore, other persons such as the chief elders and so forth, who persist in falsehood, are each to be punished separately and disciplined with the first amercement.
(Nārada, Boundary Disputes 8)

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), those such as the *uddhṛtagaṇa* (members of a guild who have been removed from their office) are included. Those "deserving punishment" (*daṇḍanīyāḥ*)—namely, the elders of the community (*maulavṛddha*) and others who are worthy of being punished for speaking falsely—are to be disciplined or fined with the first *sāhasa* (lowest fine) individually; this is the meaning. In this matter, one should not suspect any fault on the grounds that the increase in punishment for neighbors (*sāmanta*) and others relative to witnesses is merely a textual prescription (*vācanika*). Alternatively, by relying on the fact that the word "witness" (*sākṣin*) as used by Manu refers to one who knows the truth of the matter, Manu’s statement should be applied to forest-dwellers such as cowherds and the like. Furthermore, although Viṣṇu’s statement (5.175)—that "for false witnesses, the confiscation of all property shall be carried out"—is heard as a general rule, it should be applied here to the dispute over land because of the severity of the punishment. Kātyāyana (750, 741) states the punishment for witnesses and others who have been summoned for the purpose of a decision if they fail to speak or if they speak falsely: "If, having been summoned, a witness does not speak, he shall be fined one hundred [paṇas] and shall be compelled to give testimony by force. If he speaks falsely, he shall be fined eight hundred [paṇas]. If he remains silent, he shall be punished with the same penalty. If he speaks the truth, he is purified; otherwise, he incurs sin. And: "If a witness, having been summoned, does not appear, he shall be fined one hundred [paṇas] and compelled to testify. If he speaks falsely, he shall be fined eight hundred [paṇas]. [End of excerpt]
But if, among many who have been summoned, they do not all reach a verdict—
whether out of fear or greed— they shall be made to pay the highest fine.
For neighbors are indeed released from liability regarding a decision on a boundary if they acted through ignorance;
however, if they declare it out of ignorance, the king should fine them and then re-examine the boundary.

If a dispute should arise when [the boundary] has been proclaimed, those [witnesses] should be punished with the highest fine. The mention of "neighboring landowners" (*sāmanta*) is illustrative; in cases where all [witnesses], such as witnesses and others, fail to recognize [the boundary] or provide conflicting testimony, a re-examination must be conducted by means of documentary evidence (*lekhyapramāṇa*). For this very reason, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In case of conflict among neighbors, documentary evidence is the authority. Nārada (Sīmā, 11) says that in the absence of both boundary markers and those who know them, the king may make a decision according to his own discretion:
"But when there are no knowers of the boundary and no marks..."
Then the king himself may, as he desires, establish the boundary between the two.
Yājñavalkya also (2.153) states:

"In the absence of knowers and marks, the king is the *pravartitā* of the boundary. *Pravartitā* means the one who causes it to proceed; here the verbal root *vṛt* (in *pravartita*) functions in the sense of the activity of an instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*).

[The determination of] the boundary (dhātu): If a piece of land that has become the subject of dispute is of extreme benefit to one person’s village, field, or the like, then the king should assign that entire land to him alone—specifically to where the excellence of benefit lies—and not to both parties. And so Manu (8.265) says: "When a boundary is impossible to determine, the king himself, knowing the dharma, shall assign the land to those for whom it provides greater benefit; such is the settled rule."

In a case that is difficult to resolve and devoid of marks known by witnesses, the determination of the boundary should not be made by the king immediately after the petition, as in other types of cases; rather, it should be done when boundary markers such as embankments are clearly visible due to the absence of obstructions. To this effect, Manu (8.245) says: "When a dispute has arisen regarding a boundary between two villages, he should determine the boundary in the month of Jyeṣṭha, when the embankments are clearly visible."

The mention of "in the month of Jyeṣṭha" is merely illustrative. Bṛhaspati provides a reasoned decision regarding a doubt as to how a determination should be made in cases where a river—having been designated as the boundary between villages and so forth by being situated on the right side of one village or the left side of another—sometimes flows across land belonging to a different village, thereby shifting a certain plot previously situated on the right side to the left side; and likewise, where land belonging to one village is joined with another by a king. He states that in such a case, the land belongs to that very village to whose side it was originally assigned and with which it was subsequently joined by the king. *Bṛhaspati says:* "In the month of Jyeṣṭha, when the river overflows its banks due to the rains, the land situated on the right bank [belongs to one] and that on the left bank [to another]; yet, when the river shifts its course, the land remains with the village to whose side it was formerly attached. This establishes that the ownership of the land follows its original designation by the sovereign, even if the physical flow of the river changes. Thus, the determination is based on the historical assignment rather than the current hydrological state.
When land has been brought from another village and given to someone else by a great river or by the king, how can there be a legal dispute in that case?
Land that has been abandoned by a river or granted by a king belongs to him alone;
otherwise, men shall have no gain resulting from royal or divine causes.
The decline, rise, and life of men are subject to fate and the king;
therefore, in all undertakings, one should not disturb what has been ordained by them.
Since the word *daiva* signifies "fate" (*bhāgya*), even that which is caused by a river is considered "caused by fate"; thus, the same author says:
"Wherever a river is established as the boundary between two villages, it effects the giving and taking [of land] for men according to their fortune and misfortune."
Whether it causes a collapse of the bank in one place or establishes stability in another on the riverbank, one should not disturb that [action] of his.

For that person who has acquired the land due to the course of a river, [the king] shall not displace him from that acquired land nor cause it to be otherwise; the meaning is that the former owner shall not confiscate it. However, if a river overflows and washes away the land upon which the former owner had sown crops, then the fruit of those sown crops must be taken by the former owner. And so says the same authority: "When a field containing standing crops is submerged by the flow of a river's current and the land becomes covered, the former owner shall regain it."

"Land bearing crops"—this refers to the period ending with the harvest of the sown grain. It should be understood that after the harvest of that fruit, the former owner shall not regain possession of that land; for such is the intended meaning, as determined by the force of the previously cited scriptural statement. Regarding the general rule stated there—"the former owner shall not dispossess land granted by the king"—the same author clarifies the specific distinction between which grants may be revoked and which may not:
"That which was taken away by the king through anger, greed, or through fraudulent means."
If these have been given by a wicked person, she shall not attain success.
If land that was seized from someone who enjoyed it without legal title is given to one of superior merit, that gift shall not be revoked from him.

"Devoid of proof" means lacking proof such as acceptance, which is the cause for ownership. He himself states that the existing prior arrangement in houses and so forth, beginning from the time of entry, must be maintained by neighbors and others exactly as it is and not altered otherwise:

"Beginning from the time of entry, whatever has been used by whomsoever, to what extent, and in what manner—namely, the house, the enclosure, the shop, and so forth—that should not be disturbed. (NSM 1.273)

The meaning is that one should not displace from its owner that which was used by him—whether it be a courtyard, a piece of land for cultivation, or the like—and in whatever manner, such as being equipped with doors facing the east or other directions; this is because it is stated here "starting from the time of construction," which demonstrates that an arrangement made in the interim is subject to reversal. Furthermore, it has been stated by that same author that windows and the like, established starting from the time of construction, must not be removed even if they cause inconvenience to neighbors:
"One should not remove the window, the water-channel, nor likewise the turret or the terrace."
One should not move a four-sided chariot-pit that has been previously established.

A *vātāyana* is a window. A *praṇālī* is a means for the exit of water, such as a conduit made of stone and the like. Regarding a *niryūha*, the *Smṛticandrikā* states it is the corner of a house, while the *Kṛtyakalpataru* defines it as the wooden structure projecting from a door. A *vedikā* is a raised, prepared ground in areas such as a carriage road. A *catuḥśāla* is the collection of four halls; from that comes the *syandanikā*, which is the falling of rainwater. The term *catuḥśāla* is indicative of a grass hut. Kātyāyana also says: "One should not obstruct the girdle, the drain, the outlet, or the window."
One who obstructs a water-channel or a house-site shall be liable to punishment.

The *mekhalā* is the foundation at the base of the wall. The *bhrama* is the water outlet. The *niṣkāsa* is a seating area constructed of wood and other materials projecting from a palace or similar structure, not touching the ground. The *gṛhavāstu* is the site of the dwelling. Regarding these, the same author (Kāt. 753) states that they should not be made if they did not previously exist or if they cause harm to others: "After the time of settling [the house], these should never be added;
one should not construct a drainage channel (*praṇālī*) or a watercourse (*dr̥ṣṭipāta*) directed toward the houses of others."
The "falling of the gaze" refers to looking through a window. Bṛhaspati states that one should not perform acts such as voiding excrement near another's wall while facing the house of another:
"One must never, under any circumstances, perform the act of defecation, the building of a fire-pit, or the disposal of waste water too close to another's wall."

The *varcaḥsthāna* is the place for the evacuation of waste. "Atyārāt" means too near; the meaning is in a space measured at two *aratnis*. For this very reason, Kātyāyana (754) states: "One should construct the placement of fire and pits for urine, feces, and water, leaving a distance of two *aratnis* from the neighboring wall."
Bṛhaspati states that it must not be obstructed, following an explanation of the etymological meaning of the word *saṃsaraṇa* (transmigration):
"That by which people and even animals go forth and come back without being hindered is called *saṃsaraṇa*; it must not be blocked by anyone."
Nārada also states that even crossroads and similar places must not be obstructed (*Kṣetrajavi.* 15):
"One should not block crossroads, shrines of the gods, or royal roads with refuse heaps, mounds, pits, ditches, drains, and the like."
The nature of the crossroads (*catuṣpatha*) and the royal highway (*rājamārga*) has been shown by Kātyāyana (7.55): "That by which all people always travel is the crossroads;
that which is not obstructed at the proper times is called the royal highway."

The phrase "not prohibited" connects with what precedes it. The meaning is that where movement is forbidden by royal authorities at improper times, that is a "royal road" (*rājamārga*). One must not obstruct such a road where a path exists either through the middle or in the vicinity of a field. Accordingly, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "On a field-path, one should clear the way; on a royal road, one should allow a chariot to turn. "Clearing the way on a path" means that on a royal road, one should relinquish as much space as is required for a chariot to turn. Bṛhaspati states the punishment for those who cause obstructions on such thoroughfares and the like.
Whoever there, out of desire, should create a mixture [of waste], a pit, or even plant trees,
and should void excrement, his fine shall be one māṣaka.

"Confusion" (*saṅkara*) refers to the state of being cluttered with carts and the like. The mention of "trees" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes creepers and so forth as well. Here, a "māṣa" should be understood as a copper coin, since it is appropriate to determine the fine according to the nature of the offense. Regarding the excretion of feces on the royal highway, Manu states (9.282):
"But he who, when not in distress, should void impure matter on the royal highway, shall pay two *kārṣāpaṇas* and must immediately clean away the impurity."
Regarding those who have committed offenses and so forth, it has been stated by that same author (Manu 9.283):
"One who is in distress, as well as an elderly person, a pregnant woman, and a child, deserve only verbal censure; and that [offense] must be expiated—this is the settled rule."
Reproach means harsh speech. Regarding excessive punishment for [defiling] tanks and the like, Kātyāyana states:
(758) "He who defiles tanks, gardens, or sacred bathing places with impure matter shall, after having that impurity cleared away, be fined the first *sāhasa*."
He who defiles sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*) by washing dirty clothes and the like is likewise to be punished; thus he [Kātyāyana] says (Kāt. 759):
"One who defiles established sacred bathing places—those which are meritorious, purifying, and founded by great souls—shall incur the first amercement."
Yājñavalkya (2.155) states the punishment for the breaking of boundaries and similar offenses:
"For the breaking of a boundary, for the transgression of a limit,
and for the seizure of a field, the punishments are the lowest, the highest, and the middle."

For breaking a boundary mark or destroying a boundary sign, the punishment is the first amercement (*pūrvasāhasa*). For crossing a boundary—that is, for plowing across a boundary—the punishment is the highest amercement (*uttamasāhasa*); for the seizure of a field, the meaning is that the middle amercement (*madhyamasāhasa*) applies. As for the statement of Viṣṇu (5.172): “Having punished the breaker of a boundary with the highest amercement, he shall have the boundary re-established,” there the term ‘breaker of a boundary’ refers to a cultivator who has overstepped the boundary; ‘re-establishing the boundary’ should be explained as the cessation of cultivation there once again. Thus, there is no contradiction with the preceding statement. Furthermore, this mention of the highest amercement is to be understood as applying when half of the boundary is crossed. However, for the crossing of an entire boundary, a specific punishment is stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita: “In the case of crossing a boundary, however, [the fine is] eight thousand. Regarding the crossing of a small portion of the boundary, Vṛddha-Manu states a lesser fine: *“Ardhasīmāyās tu haraṇe dāpyaḥ prathamasāhasam | sīmātikramaṇe caiva hiṃsāyāṃ ca tathā naraḥ ||”* [“But in the case of seizing half of a boundary, a man should be made to pay the first amercement; likewise for the transgression of a boundary and for causing injury. *“Sīmāyām aviṣahyāyāṃ svagrāmīṇaiḥ parair api | ardhatṛtīyapaṇas tāvad dāpyāḥ kṣetrasaṃskṛtiḥ ||”* [“When a boundary is impassable, the inhabitants of one's own village, as well as those of others, should be made to pay two and a half paṇas each, and the improvement of the field must be carried out. *“Kṣetraṃ sīmāntare yasya grāmasya syāt tadgrāmyaiḥ | kāryā saṃskṛtis tasya sarvaiḥ sāmantavāsibhiḥ ||”* [“The improvement of a field belonging to a village within the boundary should be performed by all the inhabitants of that village, as well as by the neighboring residents. *“Sīmāyāṃ vivāde cotpanne grāmayor dvayoḥ | jyeṣṭhe māsi nayen maryādāṃ saprakāśeṣu setuṣu ||”* [“When a dispute regarding a boundary has arisen between two villages, one should establish the boundary in the month of Jyeṣṭha, where the landmarks are clearly visible. *“Sarvān pārśvagatān grāmān vijñāpayet tathaiva ca | ete doṣā mayoktā ye syur maryādāvilopane ||”* [“He should likewise inform all the neighboring villages: ‘These evils have been declared by me which would arise from the destruction of the boundary. *“Evaṃ ca saṃśaye chinnāṃ bhūmiṃ rājā vibhajya tu | dadyād dvayoḥ sāmantebhyaḥ svakarmakaraṇād ṛte ||”* [“And thus, when the matter is in doubt, the king, having divided the disputed land, should give it to both parties from among the neighbors, except for those who fail to perform their duty. *“Sāmantāś cen mṛṣā brūyuḥ setau vivādatāṃ gate | sarve pṛthak pṛthag daṇḍyā rājñā madhyamasāhasam ||”* [“If the neighbors should speak falsely when a dispute regarding a boundary has arisen, they shall all be individually fined by the king the middle amercement. *“Grāmasīmāntare ye ca kṣetrārāmādikāriṇaḥ | teṣāṃ daṇḍaḥ pṛthak kāryo deśadrohasamo nṛpaiḥ ||”* [“And those who construct fields, gardens, and so forth within the boundary of a village, a punishment equal to treason against the state should be separately inflicted upon them by the kings. *“Sīmāyāṃ samavetānāṃ na ced dadyāt kathaṃcana | mukhyānāṃ caiva sarveṣāṃ rājā daṇḍaṃ prakalpayet ||”* [“If, in the case of those assembled at the boundary, the king should not grant [a settlement] in any way, he should impose a punishment on all the leaders. *“Sīmāyāṃ ca vihanyante setavo ye parasparam | sarveṣāṃ pṛthak teṣāṃ daṇḍaḥ kārṣāpaṇaśatatrayam ||”* [“And when embankments are mutually destroyed at a boundary, the punishment for each of them shall be three hundred kārṣāpaṇas. *“Kṣetrasya haraṇe daṇḍaḥ prathamaḥ parikīrtitaḥ | maryādāyāś ca bhedane dviguṇaḥ parikīrtitaḥ ||”* [“For the seizure of a field, the first amercement is proclaimed as the punishment; for the breaking of a boundary mark, double that is proclaimed. *“Vināśane ca setūnāṃ prathamaḥ sāhasadaṇḍaḥ syāt | saṃrodhe ca tathānyeṣāṃ grāmakṣetrādyupadrave ||”* [“For the destruction of embankments, there shall be the first amercement; likewise for the obstruction of others and for the harassment of villages, fields, and so forth. *“Mārgāṇāṃ ca vināśe ca prathamaḥ sāhasadaṇḍaḥ syāt | tathā ca dharmasaṃsthānāṃ devāgārādikarmaṇām ||”* [“And for the destruction of roads, there shall be the first amercement; likewise for religious institutions and works such as temples. *“Kūpārāmasabhādīnāṃ vināśe dviguṇo damaḥ | devāgāradvārāṇāṃ ca vināśe dviguṇo damaḥ ||”* [“For the destruction of wells, gardens, assembly halls, and so forth, the fine is double; and for the destruction of the doors of temples, the fine is double. *“Prathamaḥ sāhasadaṇḍaḥ syāt kūpabhedane tathā | dviguṇaḥ setubhedane tathā caivāvakartane ||”* [“There shall be the first amercement for the breaking of a well; likewise for the breaking of an embankment and for its cutting away, the fine is double. *“Vināśane ca setūnāṃ prathamaḥ sāhasadaṇḍaḥ syāt | saṃrodhe ca tathānyeṣāṃ grāmakṣetrādyupadrave ||”* [“And for the destruction of embankments, there shall be the first amercement; likewise for the obstruction of others and for the harassment of villages, fields, and so forth. *“Mārgāṇāṃ ca vināśe ca prathamaḥ sāhasadaṇḍaḥ syāt | tathā ca dharmasaṃsthānāṃ devāgārādikarmaṇ
[276] And boundaries have indeed been established between the two villages forever;
those wicked ones who transgress them shall be punished with a fine of two hundred.

The punishment prescribed by Yājñavalkya for the destruction of boundary marks should be understood to apply to the destruction of boundary marks of a house, because it is a minor penalty. However, for the destruction of boundary marks of a field, a heavier punishment has been stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita: "In the case of breaking a field boundary, the fine is eight hundred [paṇas].
