For the destruction of boundary marks of a village or similar entities, an even greater punishment than this should be inferred. As for the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*) mentioned by Yājñavalkya regarding the seizure of a field, that is to be understood as applying to seizure by force; however, for seizure by other means, a different punishment has been stated by Manu (8.264).
One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done through ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred.

As for the statement of Śaṅkha and Likhita, “In the case of seizing fields or water, the fine is eight hundred,” that should be understood to apply to the forcible seizure of fields such as those sown with rice and requiring irrigation. However, when the fields or other property being seized are extensive, a higher penalty should be inferred in accordance with their magnitude. Regarding boundary trees, since they belong to both parties, one person alone should not take their fruit and so forth; thus Kātyāyana says:
“Trees grown in the middle of a boundary between two fields—their fruit and flowers shall be declared common to the owners of both fields.”

"In the case of two fields, [the term] *kṣetrasvāmiṣu* means among the owners of the fields. By this it is indicated that when one person takes all the fruits and other produce belonging to this tree, the punishment should be determined accordingly. Now, in response to the inquiry as to who is the owner of a tree or similar growth when it has arisen on land belonging to one owner while its branches extend over land belonging to another owner, he says (Kātyāyana 761): 'But for those grown in another's field whose branches rest upon another [plot], one should know him to be the owner in whose field they are supported.'"

"Dependent" (*saṃśritāḥ*) means "resorted to" (*āśritāḥ*), that is to say, "grown. Regarding the construction of embankments, wells, and so forth on another's field, Yājñavalkya (2.157) states that it must be done only after obtaining the permission of the owner and others: "He who constructs an embankment on a field only after having informed the owner—if [the water] has been produced, the enjoyment belongs to the owner; in his absence, to the king."

"In the absence of that [owner], and in the absence of one belonging to his lineage"—meaning, he who constructs a water-channel (*setu*) or similar work on another's field without the consent of the owner, or in the absence of the owner, without the consent of one of his lineage, or in the absence of such a person, without the consent of the king, does not partake of the fruit produced from that channel and so forth; rather, the owner and others are the ones who partake of the fruit. Therefore, the meaning is that one should construct a channel or similar work only after obtaining their permission. Regarding this, the same author (Yājñavalkya, 2.156) states: "A water-channel that causes little harm and brings about welfare should not be prohibited."
A well that draws water from another's land has little soil of its own but much water.

"Causing little trouble" means causing little affliction. "Beneficial" means providing great assistance. By these two qualifiers, it is shown that a boundary which, by being situated in the middle of a field, causes much trouble, or which, by being situated in a field adjacent to a river or similar feature, provides little benefit, should be prohibited. Nārada also says (Kṣetrajavivāda 17): "A boundary embankment in the middle of another's field is not prohibited if it has great merit and little defect, provided that an increase [of land] is desired when there is a decrease."

Even when there is a loss of a small portion of one's own field, if an increase [of yield] is observed from that [repair], then it possesses great merit; the meaning is that if it brings benefit even to one's own field and involves little harm, it should not be prohibited. Furthermore, the restoration of dilapidated embankments and other structures belonging to others must also be carried out after obtaining the permission of their owners and so forth. And thus says Nārada (Sīmā, 20–22): "But he who should construct a new embankment without seeing the owner or [finding that] the previously established one has fallen into disuse, shall not partake in its fruit."
When the owner of that [land] has died, and even when a descendant of his lineage is no longer a human being,
one should then consult the king and proceed with the construction of the embankment.
Otherwise, one would be subject to afflictions, as illustrated by the example of the hunter.
The analogy of the hunter has been made clear by that very same author (*Nārada*, *Kṣetrajavi.* 22):
"The arrows of him who pierces again what has already been pierced go astray"—that is, of that hunter. Kātyāyana also (762–763):
But he who performs a consecration for a house, a garden, or a pond without the consent of the owner does not obtain [the property].
If the master has arrived and the king has not been informed, the gift should not be given;
however, if it is employed after being reported, one recovers that expenditure from him.

If one undertakes the repair of a tank or similar structure without informing the king, even if the owner returns from another village, he does not recover the expenses incurred; however, if the repair is carried out after informing the king, he recovers those expenses. But the meaning is that if he fails to obtain the owner's consent, he does not receive the fruit [of the work]. Nārada (Kṣetrajavyavahāra 18) states that there are two kinds of embankments (*setu*):
"An embankment should be known to be of two types: *kheya* (dug-out) and likewise *bandhya* (built-up).
A *kheya* is for the purpose of directing water, while a *bandhya* is for the purpose of stopping it."

*Pravartana* is the flowing out; *nirgamana* is the exit; *nivartana* is the turning back; and *nirodha* is the obstruction. That which is constructed by digging for the purpose of draining excess water situated in a field is called *kheya*. That which must be blocked with earth and other materials for the purpose of retaining incoming water—the flow of water—is called *bandhya*; such is the meaning. He himself (Nārada, *Kṣetrajavivāda*, verse 19) states their purpose: "Without water there is no crop, yet when there is excessive water, there is destruction.
Whatever fault exists in the absence of water, that very same fault occurs when there is excessive water."

If someone, having made a formal agreement before the owner of a field stating, "I shall perform all activities such as plowing and so forth that are conducive to the production of the field's fruit," performs only the plowing but not the sowing of seeds and other such tasks, he must be compelled by the king to give the fruit of that field to the field-owner, and the field itself should be given to another cultivator. Thus says Yājñavalkya (2.158):

"Even if a field has been struck by the plow, if one neither cultivates it nor causes it to be cultivated, the king should compel him to pay the value of the crop from the unplowed land and have the field cultivated by another."

"Phālāhatam" means split by the ploughshare, that is to say, tilled. "Akr̥ṣṭasadam" refers to the cultivation; having agreed upon the tilling, the meaning is that whatever fruit arises from the untilled land shall be given to its owner. "Pradāpya" means having caused [the person] to give. However, he who, having promised to cultivate and so forth, does not even perform the tilling and lets the entire period for the production of fruit pass by, should also pay to the king a fine equal to the produce of the field. Thus say Vyāsa and Bṛhaspati: "He who, having taken a field, neither cultivates it nor causes it to be cultivated..."
He shall be made to pay the owner the full amount, and a fine equal to that to the king.

In response to the inquiry as to how much of the field's produce should be taken by the owner, Bṛhaspati says: "If the land has been neglected for a long time, one-tenth [of the produce] shall be taken; likewise, if it is being cultivated, one-eighth;
but if it is well-prepared, one-sixth shall be taken, after determining the established custom."

Regarding a field that has long been neglected—that is, one left uncultivated for a long time—if a person promises to cultivate it but then neglects it, the neighbors, according to the established custom of the field, shall determine what amount ought to be produced there and pay a tenth part of that to the owner of the field; however, if the field has been uncultivated for a short time, an eighth part is due, and if it was well-prepared, a sixth part is due—this is the meaning. But if a field has reached a state such as being half-waste due to the owner's lack of capacity or other reasons, and someone else, unforbidden by the owner, personally performs the cultivation and so forth, he need not be made to give the fruit to the field-owner; rather, he should take that fruit himself. Thus says Nārada (Kṣetrajavyavahāra 23).
If someone should cultivate a field that has been abandoned by its owner due to incapacity, death, or disappearance, he shall enjoy the fruit thereof without being hindered.

"Preta" means deceased; "naṣṭa" means lost or gone away, such that they have been unknown for a long time. "Kṣetrikas" are the owners of the field. He himself (Nārada, *Kṣetravivāda* 24) states that the owner of the field, or his son or other heir, must take back his own field only after providing the cultivator—who has come before him—with expenses for the purpose of breaking up fallow land: "But when the field is being cultivated, if the owner returns, he shall recover the field after being given all those expenses incurred for the treatment of the fallow land."
[280] To explain when a field reaches the state of being half-waste or completely waste, the same author (Nārada, *Kṣetrajavyavahāra* 26) says:
"In one year it becomes half-waste; in three years it becomes waste;
but a field neglected for five years becomes equal to a wilderness."

The meaning is as follows: after one year of being uncultivated, it is called "half-waste" (*ardhakhila*); after three years of being uncultivated, it is "waste" (*khila*); and after five years of being uncultivated, it is "equal to a forest. When the owner of the field is unable to pay the expenses for the purpose of reclaiming the field, the cultivator shall give an eighth part of the field's produce to the owner for eight years; he may take all the remaining produce himself. After the eight years, the field must be returned to its owner. Thus says Kātyāyana (764):
If, due to incapacity, he does not pay the expenses incurred for the purpose of clearing fallow land,
the cultivator shall receive the fruit of his labor reduced by one-eighth.
He shall enjoy it for eight years; thereafter, however, it belongs to the owner.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh section, the determination of the legal title known as boundary disputes, within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* concerning the illustrious Paraśurāma, the wielder of the bow.

**Possible reading of the defective text:** In the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with “Śrīkodaṇḍaparaśurāma”— this concludes the twenty-seventh section, the determination of the legal title known as “Disputes over Boundaries,” within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*.
Now follows the determination of the legal title known as verbal abuse (*vāk-pāruṣya*).
Regarding that, Nārada defines its nature (Pāruṣya 1):
"That which consists of insults and slanders directed at a person's country, caste, family, and so forth..."
Speech whose meaning is offensive is called verbal abuse.

"Abuse" (*ākrośa*) means reviling or threatening. "Defamation" (*nyaṅga*) means a blemish. He (Nārada, *Pāruṣya* 2) states that it is of three kinds: "That too is recorded as being threefold—harsh, vulgar, and severe. According to the sequence of their gravity, the punishment shall also be progressively heavier."
The nature of *niṣṭhura* and the other [forms of verbal abuse] has been shown by that very same authority (*Nārada*, *Pāruṣya* 3):

"Harsh speech (*niṣṭhura*) should be known as that which is accompanied by reproach; vulgar speech (*aślīla*) is that which is joined with the mention of private parts (*nyaṅga*); and the wise say that intense abuse (*tīvra*) consists of insults involving acts leading to loss of caste (*patanīya*)."

Harsh speech consists of insults such as "you fool," "you idiot," and so forth; it is accompanied by physical defects (*nyaṅga*) and is indecent (*avadya*), involving references to sexual intercourse with one's sister or others. It is "abusive" (*aślīla*), meaning a severe verbal assault involving "causing to fall" (*patanīya*) acts such as drinking liquor and the like. Bṛhaspati, however, describes its first three varieties:
"Insulting regions, villages, families, and so forth, by associating them with sin, but without reference to wealth—that is called the first type of verbal abuse."
Speaking ill of one's sister or mother,
or proclaiming their faults, is declared by those learned in the Vedas to be middling verbal violence.

"The discussion of forbidden foods and drinks, the defilement by mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), and harshness that strikes at the vital points (*marmābhighaṭṭana*)—this is declared to be the highest [degree of] verbal abuse. Here, "without substance" means without the excellence of substance; "striking" means exposing. Regarding verbal abuse among those of equal caste or equal qualities, the same author states the punishment:
In the case of mutual verbal abuse between those of equal caste and qualities,
the fine prescribed in the treatise for discipline is twelve and a half panas.

"Those who are thirteen and a half" means *ardhatrayodaśāḥ*, which signifies twelve and a half. Regarding the equality of status among castes, Viṣṇu states (5.35): "In the case of insulting someone of the same caste, one should be fined twelve *paṇas*. The word "mutually" (*parasparam*) is to be supplied. When no distinction can be discerned between the two—such as who was first or last—the fine shall be equal. Thus it is said in another Smṛti: "When two persons, both obscured by the fault of harshness, engage in abuse simultaneously, and no distinction is perceived, the punishment for both shall be equal."

The sense is that, however, when a distinction is observed, the punishment shall be unequal according to the degree of fault. Regarding the distinction created by priority and posteriority, Nārada (Pāruṣya 9) states: "He who first utters an insult shall certainly bear the guilt; he who does so afterwards is also at fault, but the penalty for the former is more severe."
The teacher is superior. Bṛhaspati states that there shall be inequality in punishment based on distinctions of caste and qualities:
"In cases of mutual verbal abuse between equals, the punishment is equal; for an inferior, it is double; and for a superior, it is declared to be greater."

[282] When a person of lower status insults one of higher status, the fine is doubled; when a person of higher status insults one of lower status, the meaning is that the punishment shall be half-measured. Yājñavalkya (2.206):

"In the case of those of lower status, the fine is half; in the case of the wives of others and those of higher status, it is double. Punishment should be administered according to the relative superiority or inferiority of caste and class."

The *varṇas* are the Brāhmaṇas and so forth; the *jātis* are the Mūrdhāvasiktas and so forth. These, together with their respective superior and inferior ranks, constitute the "superior and inferior castes and classes. When they engage in mutual abuse, the application of punishment—the infliction of a fine—is to be understood [as follows]: the punishment must be determined after considering their relative status of superiority and inferiority. This is what Manu demonstrates (8.267–268): "A Kṣatriya, having abused a Brāhmaṇa, deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas];
a Vaiśya, one hundred and fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment."
A Brahmin shall be fined fifty [paṇas] for defaming a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya, the fine shall be twenty-five; and for a Śūdra, the punishment is twelve.
Bṛhaspati says: For a Brahmin, the fine for slandering a learned man is fifty; for a Kṣatriya, it is half of that;
for a Vaiśya, half of that again, which is fifty; and for a Śūdra, it is twelve and a half.
This discipline has been declared for a true Śūdra who is innocent;
a Brāhmaṇa shall not incur guilt by using harsh words against one who is devoid of virtue.
A Vaiśya, however, should be fined one hundred [paṇas] for insulting a Kṣatriya;
a Kṣatriya, by insulting a Vaiśya, deserves half of that as a disciplinary fine.
For insulting a Śūdra, the fine for a Kṣatriya shall be twenty-five [paṇas].
For a Vaiśya, this same [penance] is declared by those learned in the scriptures to be double.

"A Śūdra who slanders a Vaiśya should be made to pay the first fine; [if he slanders] a Kṣatriya, the middle fine; and [if he slanders] a Brāhmaṇa, the highest amercement. In this context, the "highest amercement" should be understood as consisting of the cutting off of the tongue. For this very reason, it was stated by that same author:
One who provides instruction in the Dharma accompanied by citations from the Vedas,
as well as one who reviles Brahmins, shall be punished by having his tongue cut out.

[283] The term "Śūdra" is to be supplied [to the preceding verse]. Manu states the punishment for the verbal abuse of mothers and others by their sons and others (MDh 8.275): "One who reviles his mother, father, wife, brother, father-in-law, or teacher shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], as well as one who does not yield the path to his teacher."

"Brother" means an elder brother. And this [penalty] is to be understood as applying when the mother and others have committed an offense, whereas it applies to a wife who is innocent, according to the teacher Vijñāneśvara. Yājñavalkya states the punishment for harsh verbal abuse (YDh 2.208):
"For verbal threats involving the destruction of the arms, neck, eyes, or thighs, the fine is one hundred [paṇas];
for those involving the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth, it is half of that."

The meaning is as follows: if one verbally threatens, "I shall destroy his arms and so forth," the fine is one hundred *paṇas*; if one makes an insult such as, "I shall break his feet and so forth," the fine is fifty *paṇas*. Regarding one who speaks thus while being incapable [of carrying out the threat], that same author states a small fine:
"But one who is incapable yet speaks in this manner should be fined ten *paṇas*. (YDh. 2.209)

He who is capable of inflicting a fracture of the arms or other limbs upon one who is incapable [of retaliation] shall, after being punished by the king with a fine of one hundred *paṇas* or more, be made to provide a surety for the safety of the incapacitated person; so says that very same author (YDh. 2.209):
"Likewise, the capable [offender] shall be made to provide a surety for the safety of that [victim]."
Regarding the punishment for offensive abuse, that same author (Yajnavalkya, YDh. 2.205) says:
"If one swears, 'I shall violate your sister or your mother,' the king should cause him to pay a fine of twenty-five [paṇas]."

The same author (Yājñavalkya) states the punishment for insulting those learned in the three Vedas and so forth (YDh. 2.211): "The punishment for insulting those learned in the three Vedas, a king, or a deity is the highest amercement.
He also states the punishment for insulting [a person] with harsh words (YDh. 2.210):
When an accusation is made involving an offense causing loss of caste (pātaniya), the punishment is the middle amercement;
however, if it involves a minor offense (upapātaka), he shall be made to pay the first amercement.

By "patanīyas" is meant those causes of loss of caste, such as the killing of a Brahmin; "upapātakas" refers to minor offenses, such as the killing of a cow. [284] Even when one speaks of a fault that is not true, the punishment for verbal abuse still applies. For this very reason, Nārada (on Verbal Abuse 21) states:
"If one says of an outcast, 'You are an outcast,' or of a thief, 'You are a thief,' one incurs an equal fault by that statement;
if it is false, one incurs double the fault."
Manu also says (8.274):
"Even if one speaks the truth regarding someone who is one-eyed, or lame, or otherwise similarly deformed, he shall be made to pay a fine of at least one kārṣāpaṇa."
One who insults another by means of an indirect reference, whether for the purpose of censure or praise, shall be punished. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya (2.204) states:
"If one insults those who are deficient in limbs, senses, or afflicted by disease, by means of true, false, or distorted praises, he shall be fined twelve and a half paṇas."

Those with deficient limbs are those lacking hands and so forth; those with deficient sense organs are those lacking eyes and so forth; the diseased are those such as lepers and the like. "Otherwise" refers to praise that is actually censure. Nārada also says: "But he who proclaims the faults of a wicked person for the sake of provoking anger, speaking under some other pretext—him they know as a man of corrupt speech."

By the phrase "on account of anger," it is indicated that there is no fault in proclaiming a defect for the purpose of abandoning a corrupt person. And this has been stated by Kātyāyana (776): "Where there is a proclamation of one who has fallen [from caste] by that very person for the sake of avoidance, there is no fault arising from such speech, provided he can prove his case."

"By his own statement" means by the confession of the fault. Even in cases such as a formal accusation where one might otherwise establish grounds for loss of caste (*pātitya*) and so forth, there shall be no fault due to that statement; this is the meaning of the phrase "where he should manifest [the truth]," as stated in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Regarding someone who has committed verbal abuse, Uśanas says:
"If one says, 'I spoke thus out of delusion, negligence, rivalry, or affection,' and adds, 'I will not speak like this again,' the king should impose upon him half the prescribed punishment."

In the phrase "I shall speak" (*vakṣye*), the word "speaks" (*vakti*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Thus ends the exposition of the legal category known as verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*) within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* [of] the illustrious Kodaṇḍaparaśurāma. || 28 ||

**Possible reading of the defective text:** In the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "Śrī Kodaṇḍa-Paraśurāma"— this is the twenty-eighth [chapter], the determination of the legal title known as "Harshness of Speech" (*vākpāruṣya*), within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*.
Now follows the determination of the legal title known as *daṇḍapāruṣya* (assault).
Regarding its nature, Nārada states (*Pāruṣya* 4):
"Assault against the limbs of another with hands, feet, weapons, and so forth..."
And injury by means of ashes and so forth is called "assault with violence."

Regarding the limbs of others, consisting of both the stationary and the moving—the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes stones and the like—*abhidroha* means injury or killing. By the word "etc. in the phrase "with ashes and so forth," dust and similar substances are included. *Upaghāta* means the production of pain. Its threefold nature has been stated by that same author (Nārada, *Pāruṣya* 5):
"Its visible [manifestation] is also threefold, according to the sequence of low, middling, and high.

And its status as low and so forth is understood respectively from its form, such as threatening and the like, and from its object being low-grade property and so forth"; thus says he himself (Nārada, *Pāruṣya* 5–6).
Through acts such as threatening, causing a fall without hesitation, or witnessing an injury,
and by the transgression of low, middling, or superior objects.
Threatening is the preparation for striking and so forth. Other sub-varieties of this have also been shown by Vyāsa:
"Throwing with the hand or other limbs, striking with the hand or other limbs, and binding with garments and the like—this is called *daṇḍapāruṣya* (assault)."
The author of the *Pariśiṣṭa* also states:
"Causing pain, bloodshed, a wound, a fracture, or likewise cutting or piercing of living beings— this indeed is called violence (*daṇḍapāruṣya*)."

In this case as well, as in the matter of verbal abuse, the punishment is equal for two who act simultaneously. For those who do not act simultaneously, the one who acted first receives a heavier punishment. As it is said: "A man who, having been reviled, reviles in return; or, having been struck, strikes back;
or, having killed an assailant—shall not be considered guilty."

This statement of Bṛhaspati means that the equal punishment previously established does not apply to one who acts later; it does not mean there is an absence of punishment altogether. Regarding both forms of verbal and physical assault, Nārada says that he who practices forbearance is to be honored:
"When an assault has occurred and arisen from passion between two agitated parties, he who shows forbearance is honored; the one who persists in the offense deserves punishment. [286]

Regarding doubts concerning the specific nature of assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*), Yājñavalkya states (2.212) that which determines it: "In a case where [the crime] has been committed without witnesses, the legal proceeding must be examined by means of physical marks, circumstantial evidence, and testimony,
for fear that false marks might have been fabricated."

When someone reports in secret, "I have been struck by this person," then an investigation must be conducted out of fear that false marks might have been made—by means of signs consisting of the nature of the wounds and so forth, by logical reasoning (*yukti*) consisting of an examination of the causes, by tradition (*āgama*), by public rumor (the word *ca* implying also by divine proof). Regarding the punishment in certain cases, Manu (8.284) says: "One who breaks the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas];
one who draws blood, six niṣkas; one who cuts the flesh, shall be banished; but one who breaks a bone [shall be punished with death]."
One who cuts flesh is a wound-maker. Kātyāyana (781) states:
"For the cutting off of the ear, lip, nose, foot, eye, tongue, penis, or hand, the highest fine is prescribed; for piercing them, the middle fine, according to Bhṛgu."
Yājñavalkya (2.213–14):
For touching ashes, mud, or dust, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed;
for touching impure substances, saliva from the hand, or spittle, double that amount is prescribed.
In the case of other men's wives who are of equal status, the punishment is double; for those of superior status, it is likewise doubled.
For women of inferior status, the punishment is half; however, there is no punishment if the act was committed through delusion, intoxication, or similar conditions.

Impure substances refer to tears, phlegm, and the like. Delusion (*moha*) is a state of mental derangement; intoxication (*mada*) is a specific condition produced by the drinking of liquor. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), possession by spirits (*grahāveśa*) and similar states are included. Regarding the specific penalty for touching feces and other such impurities, Kātyāyana says:
"If one causes [the body] to be defiled by vomit, urine, feces, and the like, the penance is fourfold;
it is sixfold if it occurs on the middle part of the body, but it is traditionally held to be eightfold if it occurs on the head."
Regarding the punishment for making a gesture with the hand, foot, or other limbs for the purpose of striking, Yājñavalkya (2.216) says:
"If one merely raises the hand or foot, the fines shall be ten and twenty [paṇas] respectively; but if they strike one another with a weapon, it is the middle amercement for all."

The meaning is that when weapons are raised against one another for the purpose of killing, the punishment for all castes (*varṇas*) is the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*). He (Yājñavalkya) states the punishment elsewhere as well (YDh. 2.217–218): "For pulling at the feet, hair, clothes, or hands, the fine is ten *paṇas*;
for causing pain, dragging, wrapping with a cloth, or treading upon [another's foot], the fine is one hundred."
A man who causes pain with wood or other materials without drawing blood shall be fined thirty-two paṇas; if blood is seen, the fine shall be double.

"He who, having wrapped [the limb] with a cloth, squeezes it firmly, pulls it, and strikes it with his foot, shall be fined one hundred [paṇas]"—this is the meaning of the phrase "squeezing, pulling," and so forth. That same [text, Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.219–220, states]: "In the case of breaking or piercing the hand, foot, or tooth, or the ears and nose, the middle amercement is the fine; likewise for causing a wound or striking someone until he is nearly dead."
In cases of obstructing movement, food, or speech; piercing the eyes or other [senses];
and breaking the neck, arms, or thighs, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
The punishment for an offense committed against the inverse order has been stated by that same author (Yājñavalkya 2.215):
"But in the case of a non-Brāhmaṇa who causes pain to a Brāhmaṇa, the offending limb shall be cut off;
if he merely raises his hand, the first amercement is the penalty, but if there is physical contact, it is half of that."

"Of a non-Brahmin" refers to a Kṣatriya or others. "Upon contact" means upon contact with a weapon or similar object; the meaning is that the fine shall be half of that, namely half of the first *sāhasa*. The mention of the first *sāhasa* for raising a weapon with the intent to kill a Brahmin applies to cases other than those involving a Śūdra. Thus says Manu (8.279–280): "If a low-caste person should injure a superior with any limb whatsoever, that very limb of his shall be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu."
Raising his hand or his staff, he deserves the amputation of his hand.

Since the term "superior" (*śreyāṃsam*) is mentioned here in general terms, this same punishment applies by parity of reasoning even to a Śūdra who has offended a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya. Furthermore, the punishment for a Vaiśya who has offended a Kṣatriya is that stated by Yājñavalkya. Regarding this, Kātyāyana extends by analogy those punishments previously declared in the context of verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*) concerning the inverse and natural orders of castes: "Just as the punishments have been declared in cases of verbal abuse according to the inverse and natural orders of castes..."
In the same way, punishments for assault with a staff should be inflicted in their respective order.

Viṣṇu (5.73) states that when many people join together to kill one person, double the prescribed punishment for each individual shall be imposed: "For many who strike one person, the punishment declared for each individually is doubled. He further states (5.74) that for those standing nearby who join together to beat someone while ignoring him as he cries out loudly, double the punishment applies: "Double [the penalty] for those standing nearby who do not run toward one crying out, and for those passing by. Regarding the case where unbearable wounds or similar injuries arise from the beating, Kātyāyana (787) says:

In the event of injury to the body or the senses, however, the wise should prescribe a punishment according to the severity of the offense, as well as provide for the restoration of health and the means for recovery.

Wealth that provides satisfaction—that is, wealth sufficient to satisfy the pain of a difficult wound—should be given. "Expenses for recovery" (*samutthāna*) refers to the costs incurred for the physician, medicine, diet, and so forth; the ellipsis to be supplied is that these are determined by the learned according to the severity of the wound. He [the same author] states the limit for the payment of expenses for recovery (Kāt.
787): "And he shall pay the expenses for recovery until the wound is healed.
Bṛhaspati states that whatever was taken at the time of the quarrel must be returned to the owner.
In cases of crushing a limb, as well as in breaking or cutting it,
the offender shall be made to pay the expenses for recovery, as well as whatever was seized during the quarrel.

Viṣṇu (5.75–76) states that the expenses for recovery must be paid even when there is injury to domestic animals: "All those who cause injury to persons and those who cause injury to domestic animals shall be made to pay the expenses for recovery. Regarding the fine for injury to animals, Yājñavalkya (2.225–26) says: "For causing pain, for drawing blood, and likewise for cutting off a branch or a limb, the fine for small animals shall be two *paṇas* and so forth, in successive order."
[289] In the case of cutting off the male organ or causing death, the middle amercement shall be the fine;
for these acts involving large animals, the punishment is double.

Regarding small animals such as goats, sheep, deer, and the like: causing pain by beating them, drawing their blood, cutting off a limb—here meaning the horns and so forth—and amputating a member—meaning the cutting off of hands, feet, and so on—for these four acts, the fines shall be two *paṇas* and upwards, namely two *paṇas*, four *paṇas*, six *paṇas*, and eight *paṇas* respectively. For the cutting off of a generative organ or for killing, the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*) is the fine; furthermore, the value of the animal must be paid to its owner. Regarding large animals such as cows, elephants, horses, and so forth: the meaning is that for these four causes, such as causing pain and the rest, double the previously stated fine is to be taken. Manu states the fine for injuring immobile living beings (verse 8.285): "Whatever stationary being a man intentionally injures, by that very [being] he shall be afflicted in the next world, and he shall also pay a fine to the king."
The degree of punishment for the injury of all forest trees should be determined according to their utility; such is the established rule.

The mention of "trees" (*vanaspati*) is an indicative term for all stationary living beings (*sthāvara-prāṇin*). By the phrase "according as the enjoyment [is]," it is shown that for those trees such as mangoes whose fruit is enjoyed, the punishment for injuring them is greater; for those such as *campaka* trees whose flowers are enjoyed, the punishment is less than that; and for those whose leaves are enjoyed, the punishment is even less than that. This has been explained by Viṣṇu (5.55–59):

One who cuts down a tree that provides fruit shall be punished with the highest amercement; one who cuts down a tree that provides flowers, with the middle amercement; one who cuts down a creeper, shrub, or climbing vine, with one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*; and one who cuts down grass, with one *kārṣāpaṇa*. In all these cases, [the offender] must restore the produce to its owners. Thus it is said.

The ellipsis is that all [those liable for] cutting fruit-bearing trees and so forth must pay the owners of those trees—the owners of the felled trees and such—to produce them again; that is, they must provide the production of fruit-bearing trees and so forth sufficient for the period of enjoyment until the replanted trees and such have reached maturity. Although other specific punishments for verbal abuse and physical assault have been taught by the authors of the legal codes (*smṛtikāra*) due to differences in the subject matter, nevertheless, because such punishments cannot be carried out by contemporary kings for fear of causing unrest among the subjects, and because they lack great utility, we have not included them here for fear of an unnecessarily prolix text.
Thus ends the exposition of the legal title known as *daṇḍapāruṣya* (assault) in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* by the illustrious Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma. 29.

**Possible reading of the defective text:** In the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by the illustrious Madana Siṃha Deva— the son of the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Śaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "the Illustrious Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma"— this is the twenty-ninth [section], the determination of the legal title known as "Assault" (*daṇḍapāruṣya*), within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*.
[290] Now follows the determination of the legal category known as theft (steya).
In this regard, Nārada shows its nature (Sāhasa 14–17):
"Earthenware, seats, beds, bones, wood, leather, grass, and so forth;
pulses and grains, as well as prepared food—these are declared to be minor objects."
Clothing other than silk, livestock other than cattle,
metals other than gold, and grains such as rice and barley constitute the middling [gift].
Gold, gems, silk, women, men, cattle, elephants, and horses—
these are to be known as the most excellent property belonging to the gods, the brahmins, and the kings.
The wise declare that theft consists in the removal of these [goods] after deceiving them by various means, while they are asleep, intoxicated, or heedless.

Of these—low, middling, and high—their "removal by deception" means taking away after having deceived them, that is, carrying off by way of fraud while the owner and others are not present; in other words, taking without the use of force. Manu and others say that this is *steya* (theft), distinct from *sāhasa* (violence). However, an act of taking carried out by force is included within *sāhasa*. As it has been stated by that same author (*Nārada*, *Sāhasa* 12):
"Theft is a variety of that very [crime]; the distinction therein is now stated:
*sāhasa* is taking by force, whereas *steya* is taking by deception."

The *ādhi* of that very *sāhasa* is *pīḍā* (affliction). It is an affliction inflicted upon another by means of seizing and forcibly taking away wealth; this constitutes theft in the form of *sāhasa*. However, when it is performed through deception (*chala*), the *ādhi* is merely theft—this is the meaning. Nārada himself (Sāhasa 13) states that there is a threefold division of theft, consisting of the removal of inferior, middling, and superior objects:
"That [theft] should also be known as threefold by the wise, depending on the object, due to the removal of inferior, middling, and superior goods."

Manu states that there are two kinds of thieves who steal the property of others: "The king, whose eyes are his spies, should know that there are two kinds of thieves who carry off the wealth of others: those who are open and those who are secret" (9.256).
[291] Bṛhaspati also says:
"Thieves are recorded as being of two kinds: those who act openly and those who act in secret;
through their intelligence, skill, and guile, they are divided into a thousand varieties."
That same [text] points out the thieves of light:
"Merchants, physicians, gamblers, members of an assembly, bribe-takers, deceivers,
those who predict divine portents, fortune-tellers, craftsmen, and counterfeiters."
Those who fail to perform their duties, those who remain indifferent, false witnesses, open thieves, and those who live by deceit— these indeed are the manifest robbers.
Nārada also says (Parisiṣṭa 2–3): "In that [assembly],
there are those who deceive by means of open fraud,
those who rely on false measures and scales, those who take bribes, those who use trickery, deceivers, and courtesans."
Those who produce counterfeits and those who subsist on the practice of giving auspicious instructions—
such as these are to be known as open thieves on this earth.

Those who seize the property of others under the pretext of being *naigama*s (guildsmen) and so forth are *naigama*s and the like; the meaning is that they are open thieves. Vyāsa states their liability to punishment:
"In this world, ignoble men who assume the marks of the noble, living by the profession of offering auspicious blessings and instructions, deceive women and men and take wealth through fraud."
Guilds and other wealthy groups shall be fined in proportion to their offense,
so that they do not transgress and remain steadfast in their agreement.

The meaning is that they should be punished according to the nature of the offense, and not according to the amount of wealth involved. Bṛhaspati states the punishment for certain types of open thieves: "A merchant who sells a commodity after concealing its defects, adulterating it, or processing it again, shall be made to pay double the value of the merchandise and a fine equal to that amount."
But that physician who, being ignorant of medicines and mantras and lacking knowledge of the true nature of diseases, takes wealth from the sick, shall be punished like a thief.
Those who play with false dice, the base, those who misappropriate royal revenues,
fraudulent accountants, and gamblers— all these are declared to be punishable cheats.
Those members of the assembly who speak unjustly, as well as those who live on bribes and those who betray the trustful— all of them must be banished.
Those who, out of greed for wealth, proclaim to men knowledge of astrology and portents without actually knowing them, should be carefully avoided.
Those who display themselves as being endowed with the staff, the deerskin, and other such signs,
yet secretly harm men, should be executed by the king's officers.
Those who, by means of processing, turn an item of small value into one of great value and thus deceive women and children, shall be punished according to the extent of the loss.
Those who manufacture artificial gold, gems, coral, and the like,
shall be made by the king to pay the purchaser the price and a fine double that amount.
When neutral witnesses deceive one another out of affection, greed, or other such motives,
and when witnesses speak falsely, they shall be made to pay a fine double the amount in dispute.
The specific nature [of the punishment] must be determined. Manu (9.292):
"But the king shall cause a goldsmith who is most wicked among all thorns and who practices injustice to be cut into pieces with razors."

Viṣṇu (5.134): "In gambling, those who play with fraudulent dice shall have their hands cut off. Vyāsa describes the nature of secret thieves: "Those who move about at night equipped with tools and the like, remaining unobserved and whose place of residence is unknown, are to be known as concealed thieves."

The phrase "at night" is intended as a general rule; for there is the possibility of thieves—such as highwaymen and those who plunder travelers—who roam even during the day in forests and other secluded places while remaining concealed. He (Yājñavalkya) himself states the classifications of these non-public thieves: "The one who picks pockets, the housebreaker, the highwayman, the one who cuts through bundles, the thief of women, men, horses, or cattle—the thief is declared to be of nine kinds. [293]

One who, having ascertained the negligence of the owner of wealth, takes the wealth placed nearby, is an *utkṣepaka* (one who picks up). One who, staying at the junction of two houses, breaks through the wall therein, is a *sandhibhettā* (wall-breaker). One who steals the wealth of travelers in the wilderness and similar places is a *pānthamuṭ* (robber of travelers). One who unties a knot in order to seize wealth tied within a garment or the like is a *granthibhedaka* (knot-cutter). It is stated that there are nine types [of thieves], because the word *steya* (theft), which is heard at the end of the *dvandva* compound, is connected with each member—namely, the thief of women, men, cattle, horses, and livestock. In response to the inquiry as to what punishment applies to whom among these, such as the *utkṣepaka* and others, Bṛhaspati says:
The thumb and forefinger of the one who picks up [goods] should be cut off by the king’s officers;
here, "saṃdaṃśa" refers to the hand. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya (2.274) states:
"The pickpocket and the cutter of knots shall be deprived of their hands and thumbs."
For a second offense, they should be deprived of one hand and one foot.

In this context, "tongs" refers to the index finger and the thumb, because these two are the most effective instruments for untying knots. The meaning is that for the first offense, those two [hands] should be deprived of their fingers one by one; for the second offense, both hands should be deprived of one hand and one foot respectively. Manu (9.276) states: "Those thieves who commit robbery at night by breaking into a house—the king, having cut off their hands, shall impale them on a sharp stake."
The word "them" (*tān*) is to be supplied as the object. Bṛhaspati [states]:
"Likewise, one should have highway robbers tied by the neck and suspended from a tree.
"Highway robbers" (*pānthamuṣaḥ*) refers to those who plunder travelers. Manu (9.277) [says]:
In the first seizure of one who cuts the knots of fingers, the king should cause the fingers to be amputated;
in the second, both hands and feet; in the third, he deserves the death penalty.
The fingers refer to the index finger and the thumb. Nārada (Parishishta 32) [294]:
"In the first case of breaking a knot, there shall be the amputation of the fingers and the thumb. Vyāsa:
The abductor of a woman shall be burned on a bed of iron with a fire of straw;
the abductor of a man shall have his hands and feet cut off and be stationed at a crossroads.
Bṛhaspati: Having cut off the nose of one who steals a cow, one should bind him and submerge him in water.
Nārada (Parisiṣṭa 28).
For one who seizes all one's property, the punishment is the seizure of a woman; for one who seizes a maiden, however, it is death.
Bṛhaspati says that for horses, elephants, and metals, one should take restitution of the value.
The phrase "his entire property" is to be supplied [to the previous rule]. Vyāsa states: "One who steals an animal should have half a foot cut off with a sharp weapon.
Nārada says that the thief of an animal is to be punished according to the value of the animal (Parishishta 29).
For one who steals large animals, the punishment is the highest amercement;
for stealing medium-sized animals, the middle amercement; and for stealing small animals, the first amercement.
The word *hr̥ta* is in the genitive case. Manu (8.320) states the punishment for the theft of grain and other such goods:
"For one who steals more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, the penalty is death;
for stealing less than that, he shall be made to pay eleven times the value, and that property shall be returned to its owner."
A *kumbha* consists of twenty *prasthas*. In the remaining cases, it refers to amounts less than ten *kumbhas*. For the owner of that grain, he alone [is liable]—(Manu 8.323):
"For the theft of the most excellent gems, one deserves the death penalty.
Nārada (Parishishta 27).
For gold, silver, and the like, as well as for the finest garments and all kinds of gems, if the value exceeds one hundred [paṇas], there shall be the death penalty.
"In the case of gold, silver, and other such items, as well as the finest garments,
when the value exceeds fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of the hand is prescribed."
But in other cases, one should prescribe a fine eleven times the value.

Regarding this, the elders say that the calculation of gold, silver, and so forth is based on the *karṣa*. Other punishments as well should be understood from the treatises of Manu and others; they are not included here for fear of excessive prolixity. In this context, punishments such as the amputation of limbs apply to those other than Brāhmaṇas. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya (2.270) states: "Having branded a Brāhmaṇa, he should banish him from his own kingdom. The "brand" (*cihna*) refers to marking the forehead with the shape of a dog's foot. This branding and so forth should be understood to apply to one who is unwilling to perform penance (*prāyaścitta*). And thus says Manu (9.240): [text follows]
But when members of the higher castes perform the prescribed penance as declared, they shall not be branded on the forehead by the king; rather, they shall be made to pay the highest fine.

Even for those other than Brāhmaṇas, punishments such as the amputation of limbs apply when there is the theft of property of the highest value, because they constitute the highest degree of violence (uttamasāhasa).
"The same punishment which has been declared by the wise for the three degrees of violence applies also in cases of theft, according to the order of the three types of property."

Thus, because Nārada has established this rule regarding the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*) in the case of high-value property (*Nārada, Sāhasa* 21), the punishment for those who steal small or medium-value goods and the like should be proportionate to that [offense], and not such things as the cutting off of hands. Furthermore, the punishment for a thief must be carried out after making him restore the stolen property to its owner. And so says Bṛhaspati: "Having restored the stolen property, he is to be punished with penalties prescribed by the scriptures."
Yājñavalkya (2.270) also states: "Having compelled the thief to restore what was stolen, one should have him executed by various forms of capital punishment.
Since the punishment of a thief is contingent upon prior knowledge of the thief, Vyāsa speaks in response to the inquiry as to how they are to be identified:
Thieves are recorded as being of two kinds: those who act openly and those who act in secret;
they are to be identified by their own characteristic marks, by spies, and by those knowledgeable about thieves.
[296] Bṛhaspati states: "Or he may be identified by the king's officers through signs of association or stolen goods.
Here, "association" (*saṃsarga*) refers to association with thieves and the like; "stolen goods" (*loptra*) refers to wealth obtained through theft. Yājñavalkya also says (2.266–68):
A thief is apprehended by the pursuers through his stolen goods, his footprints,
his prior criminal record, his offenses, and likewise through his residence with those of impure character.
Others also should be apprehended on suspicion through the concealment of their caste, name, and so forth,
as well as those addicted to gambling, women, and intoxicants, and those whose faces and voices appear parched and altered.

Those who inquire about the property and houses of others while moving about in secret, those who have no income yet possess great expenditures, and those who sell goods that do not exist— these are [thieves].

"By royal apprehenders" means by the king's officers. "One guilty of prior acts" refers to one previously notorious for theft. "One of impure residence" is one whose place of dwelling is unknown. "Denial" means concealment. "With parched faces and broken voices": when the thief-apprehenders ask, "Where are you from?", those who have faces that have become dry and voices that are broken [are suspected]. "Sellers of lost property" are sellers of goods whose owners are unknown. Regarding this, the same author (Yājñavalkya, 2.269) states that those seized on suspicion of being thieves must necessarily clear themselves through ordeals and other such means.
If one seized on suspicion of theft does not clear himself,
he shall be made to restore the stolen property and be punished with the penalty for a thief.
Regarding those who assist thieves, Manu (9.271) says:
"Those in the villages who provide food to thieves, as well as those who give them shelter for their goods— all of them he should cause to be executed."
"Bhāṇḍa" refers to the implements used for theft. Nārada (Sāhasa 19) states:
"Those who provide food and lodging to thieves as they move about, and those who, though capable, neglect them—they too share in the guilt of that crime."
Those who summon, those who carry out the orders, as well as those who provide intermediaries—
these are declared by the legal codes to be subject to equal punishment, as are those who conceal them.
"Carrying out instructions" means those who execute orders.
Thus ends the exposition of the legal head titled "Theft" in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* [composed by] the illustrious Kodaṇḍaparaśurāma. || 30 ||

**Possible reading of the defective text:** In the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "Śrīkodaṇḍa-Paraśurāma"— this is the thirty-first [chapter], the determination of the legal title known as theft (*steya*), within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*.
Now follows the determination of the legal title known as *sāhasa* (violence).
In this regard, Nārada (Sāhasa 1) shows its essential nature:
"Whatever action is performed impulsively by those arrogant of their strength, that is declared to be *sāhasa*; here, *saha* is said to mean strength."

Whatever involves the killing of a human being, the theft of another's property, and so forth; for this very reason, Bṛhaspati says: "Killing a human, theft, violating another's wife, and the two kinds of harshness—this constitutes the fourfold *sāhasa* (heinous crime)."
Both [types] constitute verbal and physical assault. Regarding its threefold nature, Nārada says (Sāhasa 3–6):
"Furthermore, it should be known as threefold—first, middling, and likewise highest—and their respective definitions have been stated separately in the treatises."

The first degree of violence (sāhasa) is declared to consist of the breaking, throwing down, or trampling of fruits, roots, water, and other such things belonging to a field, as well as its implements.
In this same manner, the seizure of clothing, cattle, food, drink, and household utensils is declared to be the middle amercement (madhyama-sāhasa).
Malice, the use of poison, weapons, and the like, violating another's wife,
and whatever else obstructs life— these are declared to be the highest amercement (uttama-sāhasa).

*Bhaṅga* is the destruction of the very nature of the fruit and so forth; *ākṣepa* means reviling or, in other words, contemptuous treatment by speech; *avamarda* is the infliction of pain while leaving the essential form intact. In this very manner—by the methods described as *bhaṅga*, *ākṣepa*, and so on—Bṛhaspati states the means of knowledge for identifying a perpetrator of the violent crime known as human murder: "Where the victim is seen to have been carried off but the slayer is not seen, he should be identified by the king through inference based on prior enmity."
His neighbors— both those living next door and those further away— as well as his friends, enemies, and kinsmen,
should be questioned by the king’s officers using conciliation and other such means.
He is to be identified by men through association with the virtuous, or by signs, or by means of stolen goods;
thus has been declared the method for discerning murderers and thieves.
But he who, having been apprehended on suspicion, does not admit the charge, must be made to confess by means of an oath; this is the rule in all legal disputes.

A "mark" (*cihna*) refers to the application of blood and the like; "spoils" (*hoḍha*) refers to wealth and so forth found in the hand of a dead person. Regarding what must be done after knowing such [evidence], Yājñavalkya (2.273) says: "Those who capture prisoners, as well as those who steal horses and elephants, and those who kill by force—these men he shall impale upon stakes."
As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati: "Those who are open assassins as well as those who are secret assassins,
having been properly identified and their wealth confiscated, they should be executed by various means of death."

Thus, the confiscation of property has also been mentioned; that refers to the case of Kṣatriyas and others who have committed the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. For this very reason, Baudhāyana (1.10.20–21) states: “In the case of the killing of a Brāhmaṇa by Kṣatriyas and others, there shall be corporal punishment and the confiscation of all property. Regarding these—Kṣatriyas and others—in the case of killing an equal or an inferior, meaning the killing of one of the same or a lower caste, the punishment is corporal. If many should kill one, then they are to be punished in accordance with their respective guilt. And so says Bṛhaspati:
[299] Where many people, filled with rage, strike at one person,
he who delivers the blow to the vital organ is declared to be the slayer.
But he who strikes a vital point among them shall receive the punishment as prescribed;
the one who provides the means and the one who assists share half of that penalty.
Having carefully ascertained the smallness or greatness of the wound, the location of the vital point (marmasthāna), the patient's capacity, and the complications, one should treat the symptoms.
Kātyāyana also says (832–834):
"The instigator, the accomplice, likewise the one who points out the way,
the shelterer, the provider of weapons, and the provider of food for those committing forbidden acts [are all liable]."
One who instructs in war, one who incites its destruction, one who remains indifferent to what ought to be done, one who points out faults, and one who approves of them.
Those who do not obstruct and are capable [of assisting] shall all perform their duties;
one should assign them punishment according to their capacity and in accordance with the circumstances.
Nārada states (Sāhasa 9–10) that even though a Brāhmaṇa may be the perpetrator of human murder, there is no corporal punishment for him:
"This rule of punishment is ordained for all without distinction;
except for death, a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve death."
Shaving the head is his punishment, as is banishment from the city;
furthermore, he shall have a mark branded on his forehead and be made to travel upon a donkey.
Yama also says: No corporal punishment whatsoever shall be inflicted upon a Brahmin;
rather, having bound him in a secure prison, the king should cause him to be provided with food.
In some cases, Manu states that there is no punishment by way of declaring the absence of fault for one who kills a human being (8.348–49):
"The twice-born may take up arms when their dharma is obstructed."
And when there is a disruption among the twice-born castes caused by the force of time.
One who kills in self-defense, in a conflict over sacrificial fees, or in order to protect a woman or a Brahmin, does not incur sin if he acts according to dharma.

In a place or at a time where *dharma*—in the form of tanks, gardens, and so forth—is obstructed by means of breaking or cutting them down; likewise, in cases involving the intermixture of castes other than the Śūdra, such as violating another’s wife, when caused by the absence of a king; likewise, when there is a danger to one's own life from oneself or others; likewise, in a battle for the sake of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) or a war caused by the seizure of cattle; and likewise, in the protection of women and Brahmins, or in warding off the injury of the weak—one who kills does not incur sin for the sake of *dharma*. Therefore, the logical connection is that even those of the twice-born (*dvijāti*), provided they are capable, should take up arms even if they do not rely on the duties of a Kṣatriya. Since the taking up of arms by a Kṣatriya for the purpose of protecting the subjects is already established by another scriptural statement, the mention of "the twice-born" here refers specifically to Brāhmaṇas and Vaiśyas. For this very reason, Baudhāyana (2.2.80) says: [text follows].
For the sake of a Brahmin, for the sake of a cow, or to prevent the intermixture of the social orders,

Viṣṇu also states: “In self-defense, or when there is a threat of intermixture of castes, a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya may take up arms. Gautama likewise says (7.25, 21.19): “Even a Brāhmaṇa may take up arms when his life is in danger, and if he is capable, for the sake of liberating one who is being harmed by the weak. As for the statement of Āpastamba (1.10.29.6) that “a Brāhmaṇa should not take up a weapon even for the purpose of testing,” and that “a Brāhmaṇa should not take up a weapon even for the purpose of jesting,” [these apply to other circumstances].

The statement of Baudhāyana refers to matters other than those involving the obstruction of dharma and so forth. Bṛhaspati declares the absence of punishment by way of stating that there is no fault in killing an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor):
"In the killing of an *ātatāyin*, the slayer shall never incur guilt. Manu also says (8.351): [the same].

“There is no fault whatsoever for the slayer in killing an *ātatāyin* (one who comes with intent to kill), whether openly or in secret; fury recoils upon that fury. Kātyāyana also states the same.

Even when an assailant who has raised a weapon is slain, there shall be no destruction of the merit born of austerity and Vedic study; however, Bhrigu maintains that there is no sin in killing one who is devoid of virtue.
But as for the statement:
"One should indeed kill, without hesitation, an assailant who approaches, whether he be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a learned Brāhmaṇa."
Thus says the statement of Manu (8.350):
"Even one who has mastered the Vedāntas, if he approaches as an assailant with the intent to kill, one may kill him; by that act, one does not become a killer of an embryo."

Thus, the statement of Vasiṣṭha (3.17) is intended to establish the *kaimutika* principle—that there is no fault even in killing *ātatāyins* who are otherwise absolutely exempt from being slain, such as preceptors and the like, much less so in the case of killing other *ātatāyins*. Regarding this, Medhātithi states in his commentary on the verse of Manu that the word "approaching" (*āyāntam*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); therefore, he asserts that an *ātatāyin*, even if he has previously committed an offense, must certainly be killed, based on the passage: "And because he is an *ātatāyin*, he is slain; for the status of being an *ātatāyin* does not depart from one who has performed [the act]. The abandonment of oneself is worse than the abandonment of others, even more so than a sin;

He who, though endowed with intelligence, abandons himself amidst all successful undertakings, is cooked in the Raurava hell which consists of the suffering of toil.
Even having slain an assailant who approaches with a weapon raised, even if he be an embryo, one does not become a slayer of an embryo; by not slaying him, one becomes a slayer of an embryo.

Bṛhaspati describes the nature of the violent offense consisting of sexual intercourse with a woman: "That which is done in secret by force against one who does not desire it, or who is asleep, insane, intoxicated, or even raving—that is [the offense of] *strīsaṃgrahaṇa*."

[The phrase] "with one who does not desire it" implies [intercourse] with another man; Saṃvarta shows the marks of such a woman who does not desire it, as well as the duties to be performed by her and the duties to be performed by the king: "Hear those marks of women which occur in their associations with other men, whether they are unwilling or produced by force."
A woman who is emaciated by nail-marks, teeth-bites, and scratches, whose hair has been seized and torn, and who has been instantly ravished— she is defiled by force.
Crying out loudly and weeping in the presence of the people,
she spoke by his name, saying, "Just as I have been defiled by him."
One whose breasts have been wounded, whose eyes are agitated by the marks of ornaments and hair, may indeed grieve with such signs;
having been led into the assembly hall by the king and his courtiers, she was searched for by him himself at that very moment.
Whatever spontaneous word he may speak, that should be carried out with diligent effort.
In this dispute, one should take the testimony of witnesses;
because of the request of the accused, one ought not to administer an ordeal.
Regarding this, Manu states the punishment (8.378): "A Brāhmaṇa who approaches a protected Brāhmaṇa woman by force shall be fined one thousand [paṇas];
'protected' means guarded by her own vows. Regarding the case of women of the same caste, such as Kṣatriyas and others, Bṛhaspati states the punishment:
But he who lusts after her by force shall forfeit his entire wealth;
having had his penis and testicles cut off, he shall be paraded about on a donkey.

One who desires and approaches another's wife shall be punished as follows: this same penalty applies for approaching the wives of others belonging to either the *anuloma* (natural order) or *pratiloma* (inverse order) castes, provided they are of the same caste [as the offender]. However, for approaching women of lower castes among all classes, including Brāhmaṇas and others, the punishment shall be half of this amount. But for approaching a woman of a higher caste, he himself states that this punishment must be accompanied by execution: "In the case of a woman of equal caste, the fine should be imposed; in the case of a woman of lower caste, it should be half of that. But in the case of approaching a woman of higher caste, the man must be put to death. (NSm 12.70–71)
It has been stated in the legal texts that one should desire to subdue [the offender] by force. He is to be led away, meaning he is to be brought [to justice]. As for what Kātyāyana said:
"When a man should enjoy women by force, he should proceed to inflict death upon him, for that constitutes a transgression of the law."

Thus, what has been stated refers solely to the case of killing when the wife of one devoid of merit has been enjoyed. And here, although no punishment is mentioned for the woman because she is without fault, nevertheless, since she is tainted by having been enjoyed by another man, he [Yājñavalkya] himself says that in some cases she may be restored to social intercourse after performing penance, while in others she may not:

"But a woman who was enjoyed against her will, if she is protected, the king should cause her to dwell in the house, with her eyes smeared with soot, sleeping on the ground, and subsisting on mere alms."
If she has had intercourse with a man of equal caste, she should perform a Kr̥cchra or a Parāka penance as an expiation;
however, if she has been enjoyed by a man of lower caste, she should be abandoned or even put to death.

"Concealed" (*guptā*) means one who is deprived of sexual enjoyment; "he shall cause her to dwell [there]" until purification is reached—this is the remainder of the sense. Regarding "equal" (*same*), meaning of the same caste (*savarṇa*): Nārada (Sāhasa, 7–9) states the threefold punishment for *sāhasa* (violence), which consists of verbal and physical cruelty and so forth, and is categorized as first, middle, and highest, involving fruits, roots, water, and the like, as expressed in the verse:
[306] "The punishment for the first degree depends on the act committed; it begins at one hundred [paṇas].
For the middle degree, however, the experts in the scriptures have determined that it begins at five hundred."
In the case of the highest degree of violence, a fine of at least one thousand [paṇas] is prescribed;
[the punishments may include] execution, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, or branding.
In the case of the highest assault, the punishment prescribed is the cutting off of that limb.

The punishment depends on the act; that is to say, it must be determined in accordance with the nature of the offense committed. Regarding the first degree of violence (*sāhasa*), which consists of verbal and physical assault, the fine is "not less than one hundred," meaning it cannot be below one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. The same principle should be understood for the phrases "not less than five hundred" and "not less than one thousand. As for the punishments prescribed for the highest degree of violence (*uttama-sāhasa*), these should be applied either individually or collectively according to the specific circumstances of the offense. Nārada (Sāhasa 11) states that even one who has been punished for committing the highest degree of violence remains unfit for social intercourse (*asaṃvyavahārya*).
In the two preceding cases, both may be treated as fit for social intercourse once they have paid the fine;
however, in the case of the highest violence (uttama-sāhasa), one who has paid the fine is to be known as unfit for social intercourse.
Thus ends the determination of the legal head titled "Sāhasa" (Violent Crime) within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* of the illustrious Kodaṇḍaparaśurāma. || 31 ||

Now follows the determination of the legal title known as *strīsaṃgrahaṇa* (adultery).
Regarding that, Bṛhaspati says it is threefold:
"Understand that adultery, which is rooted in evil, is of three types:
two are committed through force or fraud, while the third arises from passion."
The nature of all three types of violation has been shown by that same [author]:
"That which is done in secret by force against a woman who does not consent, being intoxicated, insane, or deranged, or while she is prattling, is indeed a violation committed by compulsion."
When, having brought her to the house by means of deception and given her an intoxicant,
a union is effected, that they know to be "brought about by fraud" (upādhikṛta).
[307] That which is produced by mutual passion for the eyes, or by the dispatching of female messengers,
or by greed for beauty and wealth, should be known as arising from passion (*anurāgaja*).

Intoxicants are substances that cause intoxication, such as the seeds of the *dhattūra* plant and others. Regarding sexual intercourse with a woman by force, since it is included within the category of *sāhasa* (violence), it has just now been shown in that section. He states the punishment for one who acts through deception (*upādhi*): "He who should desire [a woman] through fraud shall be fined the forfeiture of all his property;
having branded him with the mark of a female organ, he shall then be banished from the city."

"He shall take all [the man's] property; he shall take all his possessions. This refers to the case of approaching the wife of another who belongs to the same caste (*sajātīya*); in the case of approaching one of a lower caste, the punishment consists of taking half of that, namely, the seizure of all his property. However, in the case of approaching one of a higher caste, this punishment is accompanied by death. And so says that very same [author]: "The fine should be imposed for [approaching] an equal woman, but half of that for a lower one; however, in the case of approaching a woman of superior caste, the man must be put to death."

In this case, since the fault lies solely with the man and not with the woman, punishment is prescribed for him alone and not for her. Therefore, it should be understood that even in the case of a deceptive act (*chadmakṛta*), if she was enjoyed by one of equal caste, she remains fit for social intercourse after performing penance; however, if she was enjoyed by one of lower caste, she is not. Vyāsa states that there are three types of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct) arising from passion: "It should be known that *saṃgraha* is of three kinds—the first, the middle, and the highest—and their definitions are stated separately in the scriptures."

Bṛhaspati demonstrates their essential nature: "Glancing from the corner of the eye, laughter, sending a female messenger, as well as touching ornaments and garments— this is remembered as the first stage of courtship."
The sending of perfumes, garlands, fruits, food, wine, and garments,
as well as private conversation, they know to be the middling form of seduction.
Sharing a bed and a seat, as well as play, kissing, and embracing—
this is declared by those who know the scriptures to be the highest form of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct).
Regarding these three, he himself stated the punishments in sequence:
"For all three of these, the first, middle, and highest forms of discipline should be prescribed; for one with greater wealth, the punishment should be more severe."

"Greater than" means greater than the first *sāhasa* and the others. Manu states the punishment for one who engages in conversation with another's wife (8.354): "A man who, having been previously accused of such offenses, should engage in conversation with another's wife, shall incur the first *sāhasa*."

"Accused" means charged with faults such as the desire for various enjoyments and the like. However, for one who is free from evil intent and converses for another reason, there is no punishment; thus it has been stated by that same [author] (Manu 8.355):
"But he who, previously unaccused, speaks for a reason, shall not incur any fault, for there is no transgression on his part."

She who engages in conversation with another man despite being forbidden by her father or others shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*; a man who converses despite being forbidden by his father or others shall be fined two hundred *paṇas*. In the case of a prohibition, a woman shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], but a man shall be fined two hundred as a penalty. In the case of their prohibition, the punishment is the same as that for adultery (*saṃgrahaṇa*). "Prohibition" (*niṣedha*) means that which is prohibited; it is derived with the suffix *ghañ* according to Pāṇini 3.3.121 (*halaś ca*). This refers to women other than those such as female performers (*cāraṇa*). Thus says Manu (8.362):
This rule does not apply to the wives of wandering performers nor to those who live off their own labor;
for they entice women and keep them hidden away.

[309] *Cāraṇas* are actors; *ātmopajīvins* are those who live by their own means, and *veśopajīvins* are those who live by the brothel. This rule regarding their wives concerns the penalty for addressing them and so forth. The meaning is that these men "appropriate" women—that is, they unite them with other men and cause them to circulate while keeping them concealed. Regarding the penalty for sexual intercourse, Yājñavalkya (2.286) states: "In the case of a woman of equal caste (*sajātī*), the highest fine; in the case of a woman of a lower caste (*ānulomya*), the middle fine;

Since a punishment is prescribed for the woman here as well, it is understood that this statement refers specifically to the case of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse) arising from passion (*anurāgaja*), because in cases of force or under duress (*upādhikṛta*), the woman is not at fault and thus there is no punishment for her. However, the meaning is as follows: in approaching a woman of equal caste (*sajātīya*), the punishment is the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*); in approaching one of lower caste, the middle fine (*madhyamasāhasa*); and in approaching one of higher caste, the man is subject to death while she is to have her ears and so forth cut off. Precisely because, having ordained death for the man in the case of approaching [a woman] in the reverse order of castes (*prātilomya*), the ordinance prescribes half of that—namely, the cutting of the ears and so forth—for the woman, it is indicated that whatever punishments of the highest or middle fines are stated for the man in the case of approaching women of equal caste and so on, half of those shall be the punishment for the woman. For this very reason, Kātyāyana (verse 487) says:
In all offenses, whatever monetary fine is prescribed for a man, women shall pay half of that; however, in the case of killing, the man's limb shall be amputated.

The phrase "women who have committed an offense" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. A Brāhmaṇa who approaches an unguarded Vaiśya woman, a Kṣatriya woman, or a Śūdra woman shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; however, if he approaches a woman of the lowest castes (antyaja), he shall be fined one thousand.

If he approaches a woman who does not desire it, the traditional law prescribes the *ardhadaṇḍa* (half-penalty) for him as he departs. (But if she desires it and comes to him...)
