A woman who, having come to a man's house, entices him with touching and other such acts and desires him there, shall be punished; for the man, half the fine is prescribed. [313] The meaning is that whatever fine is to be imposed upon a man who approaches a woman after enticing her with words, half of that fine shall be taken from the woman; thus the man shall receive half of her punishment. Regarding certain cases of approaching female slaves and others, Yājñavalkya also states a fine (2.290):
A man who has sexual intercourse with female slaves, female servants, or likewise with women who are not forbidden [to him],
shall be made to pay a fine of fifty paṇas.

Those women who must remain in the house for the sake of service to their master are *avaruddhāḥ* (confined women); those who, having been confined by another man, are enjoyed by him are *bhujiṣyāḥ* (servile women). Whether they are female slaves (*dāsyaḥ*), *bhujiṣyāḥ*, or *avaruddhāḥ*, since they are accessible to all men by virtue of being common property, one who approaches them is to be fined fifty *paṇas*, because, being held by another, they are equivalent to the wives of others. Because of the inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*), it should be understood that this same fine applies to approaching a prostitute (*veśyā*) or a wanton woman (*svairiṇī*) who has been taken by another. This has been clarified by Nārada (Strīpuṃsa 78–79): "A man who approaches a woman who has been confined by another, or a *bhujiṣyā*, or a female slave, shall be fined fifty *paṇas*. Likewise, he who approaches a prostitute or a wanton woman who has been taken by another shall be punished in the same manner."

A woman who is self-willed, a non-Brāhmaṇa woman, a courtesan, a female slave, and one who has left her husband— all these may be approached in the direct order of castes, but never in the inverse order. However, even with these women who are at their own disposal, there would be the same fault as in the case of another's wife.
For even among those women who are permissible, one should not approach them, since they are already under the protection of another.

The term *abrāhmaṇī* is a qualification of the *svairiṇī*. A *svairiṇī* is an independent unchaste woman (*puṃścalī*). A *niṣkāsinī* is an unchaste woman who has departed from her family circle. The connection is that this applies specifically to *bhujiṣyās*. Vyāsa also says: "For approaching a woman who is restrained by another, the fine is fifty *paṇas*;
for approaching a prostitute by force, the punishment is ordained as ten *paṇas*."

"By force" means the giving of a fee without [the owner's] consent. In this context, the statement that prostitutes and the like—who are not restricted by another man—are "to be approached" is intended merely to indicate that there is no punishment for those who have intercourse with them; it does not imply freedom from sin, for a *prājāpatya* penance is prescribed for approaching animals or prostitutes.

Because of the instruction regarding penance for approaching her in such passages as these, Yājñavalkya (2.294) states that after the fine of one thousand paṇas prescribed by Manu for approaching a woman of the lowest caste (antyajā), the three higher castes who do not intend to undergo penance shall be branded on the genitals and banished from the kingdom; furthermore, a Śūdra who performs such an act becomes a Caṇḍāla himself: "But upon approaching a woman of the lowest caste, one should brand him with the mark of a eunuch and banish him; likewise, a Śūdra becomes a person of the lowest caste. In the case of a person of the lowest caste approaching an Ārya woman, there is death."

"Having marked" means having branded. "By a foul bond" means by a contemptible bond in the form of the *bhaga* (vulva). Regarding sexual intercourse with a woman of superior caste (*āryāgama*), Yājñavalkya (2.283) states the means for determining such an act, since adultery with a woman is the cause for punishment:
"A man shall be apprehended for adultery when he is caught *keśākeśi* (by the hair) with another's wife, or immediately by signs born of passion, or likewise when both parties admit it."

The term *keśākeśi* is a compound with the third case ending elided due to its being an indeclinable (*avyaya*). The meaning is that one should be known as a "seizer" (*saṃgrahaṇavat*) when, together with another's wife, there is either the act of playing "hair-to-hair" (*keśākeśika*), or the presence of fresh marks such as nail-scratches, or mutual consent. He (Yājñavalkya) states another means [of proof] (YDh. 2.284):
"Grasping the waist-knot (*nīvī*), the breasts, the upper garment, or the thighs; touching the hair; conversing at an improper place or time; and staying in the same location together."

The word "acting" (*kurvāṇa*) is to be supplied [as the subject]. *Sakthi* means the thigh. Manu (8.358) states that he who, being touched by another's wife, endures it, is also to be apprehended for the offense of adultery (*strīsaṅgrahaṇa*):
"He who touches a woman in an improper place, or who, being touched by her, endures it—with mutual consent, all this is recorded in tradition as adultery."

Furthermore, regarding one who says out of pride or similar motives, "This woman has been enjoyed by me," Nārada states (Strīpuṃsa 69) that such a person is also to be understood as being in that same category:
"Whether out of pride, or delusion, or even out of self-praise, if one should say of his own accord,
'I have previously enjoyed this woman,' that is recorded in tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery)."
Thus ends the thirty-second section, the determination of the legal title known as "Adultery," in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* by the illustrious Kodaṇḍa Paraśurāma.

Regarding that, Nārada demonstrates its essential nature (strīpuṃsa. 1):
That legal subject in which the rites of marriage and so forth for women and men are proclaimed is called the title of law known as "Union of Man and Woman."

The ritual procedures for marriage and other such matters have been explained by us at length in the *Ācāravivekoddyota*. Here, by the word "and others" (*ādi*), the duties of husband and wife are intended. For this very reason, at the time of enumerating the titles of law (*vyavahārapada*), Manu first announced them and then defined them [in verse 9.1], having mentioned the duties of husband and wife and the rules for partition:

Women must be kept under control by their own men day and night;
even when they are attached to sensual objects, they should be established under one's own authority.

By such statements [as these]: in *saṃyoga*, meaning mutual union; in *viprayoga*, meaning the absence thereof; and regarding those things that are eternal and necessarily to be performed (*śāśvatān avaśyakaraṇīyān*); and regarding objects (*viṣaye*) which are causes for punishment, such as the object of fickleness and the like. Hārīta says that a wife must necessarily be protected by a man from misconduct, lest she be born in a noble family (*satkula*).

Because they have failed in their singular vow and because they are afflicted by the senses of others, such women become corruptors of the lineage. While the husband lives, the son born of a paramour is a *kuṇḍa*; when the husband is dead, he is a *golaka*. Therefore, one should protect the wife from the corruption of the seed. With the destruction of the wife comes the destruction of the family; with the destruction of the family comes the destruction of the lineage; with the destruction of the lineage comes the destruction of sacrifices to the gods and ancestors; with the destruction of sacrifices to the gods and ancestors comes the destruction of Dharma; with the destruction of Dharma comes the destruction of the self; and with the destruction of the self comes the destruction of everything. Thus it is said.

"Because of the failure of her single vow" means because of the transgression of the vow consisting of having only one husband. "Lineage" (*tantu*) refers to sons, grandsons, and so forth. Manu says (9.5–6) that women must be protected even from looking at other men and similar acts.

*Viniyoga* means application to a task; *bhartṛ* means a supporter. Demonstrating a certain inherent nature of women, Dakṣa says (4.8–10, 2):

The leech alone takes away the blood, for she is a poor creature;

Full of apprehension during her childhood, she becomes forward in her youth;

"Unprotected, though confined at home by men who are *āptakārin*—that is, those who are both trustworthy (*āpta*) and capable of acting (*kārin*). He [Manu] stated this very point (9.22–23) to show that even the husband’s devotion to his duty is a means of protecting women:
'With whatever qualities a husband is endowed, according to the rule, with such qualities shall the wife be united.'"
She comes to possess such qualities as those of the river by the ocean.
Akṣamālā, though born of a low womb, attained a state worthy of honor through her union with Vasiṣṭha;
and Śārṅgī likewise attained a state of venerability through Mandapāla.
The same author (Manu 9.95) states that the maintenance of the wife is also an obligatory duty:
"A husband obtains his wife as a gift from the gods; he cannot obtain her by his own will.
He should always support her with care, performing what is pleasing to the gods."

By the statement "she does not obtain [a husband] by her own will, but rather [one] given by the gods," it is shown that the relationship between a man and a woman characterized by marriage is not under one's own control, but rather is created by the gods. Regarding the fact that women are given by the gods, [the Vedic text states]:
"Soma gave her to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave her to Agni;
Agni gave her to me, along with wealth and sons—and indeed, this [woman]."

This is understood from such Vedic passages as *Rigveda* 10.85.41. Consequently, the explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) implies that by failing to support a woman given by the gods, one commits an offense against those very gods who gave her. Regarding this, Nārada states (*Strīpuṃsa* 91): "Even for a wicked woman, maintenance with coarse food and the like must be provided; [as punishment for] infidelity, however, she shall undergo shaving of the head and sleeping on the ground."
Bad food, poor clothing, and work that involves throwing away refuse.
Disposal of waste refers to the removal of impurities. Whatever is desired by a pregnant woman must necessarily be given to her. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya (3.79) states:
"By the non-granting of what she desires during pregnancy, the fetus may incur defects;
it may result in deformity or even death. Therefore, one should do what is pleasing to the woman."
Manu says (9.74):
"A man who intends to go to another village should depart after providing for the maintenance of his wife;
for a woman, even one of steadfast character, may fall into corruption when distressed by a lack of livelihood."
"Steadfast" means established on the path of righteousness. Bṛhaspati says that even ornaments and such should be given to the wife according to one's ability:
"The husband should honor his wife with garments, ornaments, and food, as well as during festivals and by her paternal relatives, brothers, fathers-in-law, and other kinsmen. [319]

Intending to show that one must not abandon a wife who is free from fault, Devala says: "For a man who, out of delusion, abandons his own wife, who is unrighteous and who causes the abandonment of dharma and lineage, no atonement is prescribed."

Regarding his punishment, Viṣṇu states (5.162–163): "Having abandoned a faultless wife... The phrase "he shall be punished like a thief" is to be supplied as a continuation. "Faultless" means free from those defects that would otherwise justify abandonment. If he wishes to abandon her while she possesses good qualities, then Nārada says (Strīpuṃsa 95): "If he abandons a wife who is compliant, not corrupt in speech, skillful, virtuous, and has borne children, he shall be punished by the king according to the law."

The meaning is that a man who abandons a virtuous wife should be made to accept punishment from the king and then be compelled to maintain her. However, if she does not remain even when he has been compelled to do so, then Yājñavalkya (1.76) says: "One who abandons a wife who obeys his commands, is skillful, bears him heroic sons, and speaks kindly, shall be made to pay a third of his property; if he possesses no wealth, he must provide maintenance for her."

The king shall cause the wife to receive a third part of that property—that is, a third part of his wealth; however, if he possesses little wealth, she shall be made to receive only what is sufficient for her maintenance—this is the meaning. Manu (5.151, 156) states that a husband must necessarily be served by a wife: "To whomsoever the father gives the daughter, or the brother with the father's consent, she shall serve him while he lives and must not disregard him when he has passed away."
A virtuous wife, desiring the world of her husband, should not do anything displeasing to him who took her hand, whether he be living or dead.
Yājñavalkya (1.77): Women must carry out the word of their husbands; this is the highest duty of a woman.
For one who is defiled by a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) must be awaited until purification.
Manu says that even a husband devoid of virtues is to be served: (5.153–154) "A husband who has performed the sacramental rites with mantras, whether out of season or during the fertile period,
always bestows happiness upon his wife in this world and in the next."
Whether he be lacking in virtue, addicted to sensual pleasures, or devoid of good qualities,
a husband must always be served by a virtuous wife like a god.
Kātyāyana states that she must also necessarily perform the service of the fires according to the Śrauta and Smārta rites:
"The fire is ordained to be served by a wife who is not separated from her husband,
out of devotion to her lord and with the desire for good fortune and freedom from widowhood."

Viṣṇu states certain duties of women (25.2–13): equality of conduct with the husband; honoring the father-in-law, elders, deities, and guests; keeping household utensils well-maintained; being unstinting with resources; keeping stores well-concealed; lack of interest in worldly amusements; devotion to auspicious customs; performing personal adornment only when the husband is pleased (or, even when he is away); not visiting the houses of others; not lingering at doorways or windows; dependence in all matters; and subordination to the father, the husband, and the son during childhood, youth, and old age, respectively. Thus it is said.
R̥ṣyaśr̥ṅga also said:
"One should always be a householder and worship ornaments;
one should always worship the braid of those who have bathed with a garland of flowers."
One should first go into seclusion before anyone else awakens;
there, one should perform the propitiation of the deity with incense, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings.

*Gṛhamedhā* means one who is devoted to domestic duties. "She should honor the ornaments" means she should refine them through cleaning and so forth. "Refined by bathing" means purified by a bath. "From a secluded place" means from a private location; the meaning is "another husband. "Worship of the deities" refers to the worship of the deities of the doorway and so on. Other duties of women have been shown in the *Ācāraviveka-uddyota*, and thus they are not elaborated upon here. Yājñavalkya (1.74) states that when there is mutual affection between husband and wife, there is an increase in spiritual welfare (*śreyaḥ*).
Where there is harmony between husband and wife, there the threefold aim (*trivarga*) flourishes.
The threefold aim consists of dharma, pleasure, and wealth. Manu also says (3.60, 9.101): "The husband is satisfied with his wife, and likewise the wife with her husband."
In whatever family there is constant goodness, in that one it is indeed certain.
[321] Mutual fidelity until death—
this should be known as the supreme duty of husband and wife in brief.

Although a dispute between a man and a woman in the capacity of plaintiff and defendant before the king is prohibited, nevertheless, if their transgression of their own duties is somehow discovered, they must be established in their respective duties through punishment and other means; for this purpose, the duties of men and women are set forth among the heads of legal procedure (*vyavahārapada*).

**Possible reading of the defective text:** In the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with "Śrī Kodaṇḍa-Paraśurāma"— this is the thirty-third [chapter], the exposition of the legal title known as "Union of Man and Woman" (*strīpuṃyoga*), within the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota*.
Now follows the exposition of the legal title known as the Partition of Inheritance.
In this regard, Nārada (Dāyabhāga 1) shows its essential nature:
"That wherein the division of property belonging to a father and others is determined by the sons is declared by the wise to be the legal title known as Dāyabhāga."

"Belonging to the parents" (*pitrya*) means "this belongs to the parents. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of [property belonging to] the grandfather and others is intended. The mention of "sons" (*putra*) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for grandsons and so forth. By this, it is shown that this term is used in the context of legal procedure (*vyavahārapada*) through its etymological connection as "the division of inheritance" (*dāyabhāga*), where a portion of the inheritance is determined. "Inheritance" (*dāya*) refers to property related to the father and others that is fit for partition. Thus says the author of the *Nighaṇṭu*: "The wise call the ancestral property that is to be divided 'inheritance' (*dāya*). The author of the *Smṛtisaṃgraha* also states:
That property which comes through the father and that which comes through the mother is designated by the term *dāya* (inheritance); its partition is now being described.

The mention of "father and mother" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes the grandfather and others as well. Furthermore, this inheritance (*dāya*) is of two kinds: with restriction (*sapratibandha*) and without restriction (*apratibandha*). That property which becomes the own right of the owner's sons and others even in the absence of the owner himself is inheritance with restriction; for example, the wealth of sons and others belonging to their father and so forth. That property which belongs to a son or grandson by virtue of birth—namely, the wealth of the father or grandfather—is inheritance without restriction, because in that case the existence of the owner or his son does not constitute a restriction on ownership. Manu states the time for partition [at 9.104]:
After the father and mother have passed away, the brothers, having assembled, shall divide the paternal inheritance equally; for they have no authority over it while the two are alive.

"This belongs to the parents" means *paitṛka*. Since previously, while their mother and father were living, they were powerless and lacked independence regarding the acquisition of that property, the meaning is that after those two [die], they should divide that wealth equally. Here, "after the father" indicates the time for the division of the father's wealth; "after the mother" indicates the time for the division of the mother's wealth. The word *ca* (and), however, serves to aggregate other times of division that will be mentioned later. By this, even while the mother is living, if the father is absent, the division of the father's wealth is appropriate; and even while the father is present, if the mother is absent, the division of the mother's wealth is appropriate. For this very reason, the author of the *Smṛtisaṃgraha* says:
The division of the paternal estate shall take place even while the mother is living;
for she possesses no independent ownership in the absence of her husband.
Likewise, even when the father is alive, there is a division of the mother's property among the children;
for as long as sons exist, the husband is not the master of the woman's wealth.

Since a mother has no independent ownership over her husband’s wealth even in the absence of her husband, the division of the father’s wealth may take place while she is still living. Since the husband has no ownership over his wife’s wealth while his offspring remain, the division of the mother’s wealth may take place even while he is alive; this is the meaning. Although sons possess ownership in their paternal wealth from the moment of birth, nevertheless, as long as the father is alive and free from defects such as illness, the sons are not entitled to a division of that wealth without his consent. Thus says Śaṅkha:

"While the father is alive, the sons may divide the inheritance, even if it has been acquired by them later; yet those sons are indeed unworthy [of independent action], because they lack autonomy in matters of wealth and dharma. Thus [it is said].

The meaning is that even in regard to religious acts (*dharma*) such as sacrifices, which involve the enjoyment of wealth, one is not entitled to proceed without the father’s permission; the phrase "after birth" is to be supplied [as the time when this applies], and "ownership has been acquired" is also to be supplied. Harīta has explained the lack of independence regarding wealth: "While the father lives, sons have no independence in the taking, giving away, or pledging of wealth. Here, "taking and giving away of wealth" refers to the enjoyment and expenditure of property; "pledging" refers to the threatening of servants and others for offenses and the like. The meaning is that they lack independence in these matters, and they must not act according to their own will without the father’s permission. Furthermore, as for...
[323] When the father has passed away, the sons shall divide the father's wealth;
for they would have no ownership while the faultless father remains alive.

Thus, regarding the statement of Devala, the meaning of "lack of ownership" (*asvāmya*) and "lack of independence" (*asvātantrya*) therein should be understood as follows: even when the father is faultless, the ownership of sons and grandsons over the property of the father and grandfather is established by worldly consensus from the very moment of their birth; and this is because Gautama stated: "By the very fact of birth, one acquires ownership of wealth, so say the Teachers.

Now, how can it be said that ownership is established by worldly consensus, given that the author of the *Saṃgraha* has argued that the relationship between owner and owned is to be known solely through the scriptures?
Whatever is in someone's hand belongs to that person alone;
for what other's property, held in the hands of others, is not seen as stolen through theft?
Therefore, ownership must arise solely from scripture and not from experience;
it is not proper to say otherwise, for this [scriptural authority] has been taken away by him.
The acquisition of wealth is understood in the treatise according to its various specific descriptions;
however, that which is expended according to one's own whim is not called "one's own."

"The application (*viniyoga*) of all this is regulated by the scripture alone. This is its meaning: for it is not the case that whatever wealth is seen near someone belongs to him as his own property and he is its owner; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a relationship of ownership existing even in the case of wealth obtained through theft and the like. Furthermore, the common legal usage—"My property has been stolen by him"—would not be consistent, because according to your view, ownership in that instance would belong solely to the person near whom the wealth is found. Moreover...

Ownership arises through inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, or finding; among these, what is obtained is the specific property of a Brāhmaṇa, what is conquered is that of a Kṣatriya, and what is received as a gift is that of a Vaiśya and a Śūdra. (Gautama Dharmasūtra 10.39–42)

In such statements by Gautama and others, the teaching regarding the common causes of ownership—such as inheritance (*riktha*) and so forth—and the teaching regarding the specific causes of ownership for each caste, such as acceptance of gifts (*pratigraha*) and so forth, would otherwise be rendered meaningless. "Inheritance" (*riktha*) refers to an unobstructed legacy (*dāya*). "Purchase" (*kraya*) is well known. "Partition" (*saṃvibhāga*) refers to a partitioned legacy. "Acquisition" (*parigraha*) is the taking possession of wood, grass, water, and the like belonging to common areas such as forests, which were not previously claimed by another. "Discovery" (*adhigama*) is the finding of buried treasure and the like. When these causes of ownership exist, one becomes the owner. Here, it should be understood that an unobstructed legacy is a cause of ownership by birth alone, whereas a partitioned legacy becomes a cause of ownership once the obstruction has been removed. For a Brāhmaṇa, what is "obtained" (*labdha*)—acquired through acceptance of gifts and so forth—is his exclusive, non-common property. For a Kṣatriya, what is "conquered" (*vijita*)—acquired through victory, fines, and so forth—is his exclusive property. For Vaiśyas and Śūdras, what is "earned" (*nirviṣṭa*)—acquired in the form of wages—is their exclusive property. In this context, the term "earned" includes everything mentioned in Manu (10.47), such as "for Sūtas, charioteering," which is the exclusive wage-earning activity for others, including those born in the *anuloma* and *pratiloma* orders; for the Vaiśya, it is earned through agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so forth, while for the Śūdra, it is earned through service to the twice-born. That the prefix *niḥ-* in the root *viś-* signifies "wages" is understood from Amarasimha’s definition: "earnings (*nirveśa*) mean wages or enjoyment. This is the meaning of Gautama’s statement. Nor should it be argued that whoever can employ something as he pleases is its owner, and that what is obtained through theft and the like is not so; for even in the case of all wealth acquired through lawful means, its employment for the maintenance of the family and so forth is regulated by scripture, and thus it cannot be the object of employment according to one's own will. This opinion of the author of the *Saṃgraha* was also adopted by Bhaṭṭa Dhāreśvara. Therefore, since the relationship between owner and owned is cognizable solely through scripture, how can it be said to be established by worldly convention?

To this, it is replied: Even among commoners (*pāmaras*) who lack knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures, we observe the worldly transaction of ownership (*svatva*) regarding wealth acquired through purchase and other means by a buyer and so forth; and this would not be possible if ownership were cognizable solely through the scriptures. Nor should it be argued that if ownership were merely a worldly matter, then even what is obtained through theft and the like would result in ownership; for in the world, the usage of "ownership" applies only to things acquired through means such as acceptance of gifts (*pratigraha*). Furthermore, it does not follow that scriptural texts such as "The owner [is he who is] the heir... would become purposeless; for that text serves to establish the causes of ownership already established in the world, just as the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*) does. This has been stated by Bhavanātha, the illuminator of the lotus-like Prābhākara doctrine in his *Nayaviveka*: "Acquisition (*arjana*), such as birth and so forth, is established in the world; therefore, since these are objects of worldly cognition from time immemorial (*anidampathamata*), the Smṛti text is intended to provide a formal basis (*nibandhana*), just like the Smṛti on grammar and other sciences. Here, acquisition is the cause of ownership. "Birth and so forth" means that the birth of a son is the cause of ownership over the wealth of the father and grandfather; by the word "and so forth," purchase and other means are included. "From time immemorial" (*anidampathamata*) means beginningless. "Just like the Smṛti on grammar and so forth" means: just as in the science of grammar, words already established in usage are enumerated for the sake of knowing their correctness, so it is here. That the science of grammar explains words already established in the world is stated in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "Because the scripture explains what is existent" (*sadanvākhyānāt*); that is to say, because it explains words that are already established. Nor do we say that ownership is the state of being capable of being employed according to one's will. Rather, it is the capacity for such employment. And that capacity exists precisely due to the fact of having been acquired, even for one who is not currently employing it in another way because the scripture restricts its use to maintaining the family and so forth. It is just as a seed situated in a granary, though not currently producing a sprout due to some cause, still possesses the capacity to produce a sprout inherent in its nature as a seed. As stated in the *Nayaviveka*: "And that belongs to him which has been acquired by him"—meaning that it is fit for such [use], i.e., fit for employment according to one's will. In the *Tantraratna*, following the Bhaṭṭa school, it is also said: "Ownership is indeed the state of being capable of being employed according to one's will; for if it were intended solely for the sake of a sacrifice (*kratu*), there would be an absence of employment according to one's will due to the lack of application elsewhere. Here, "employable" (*viniyojya*) means "fit for employment" (*viniyogārha*), according to Pāṇini’s rule: "The kṛtya and tr̥c suffixes are used in the sense of fitness" (*arhe kṛtyatṛcaś ca*, Pā. 3.3.169). As for the claim made by some who, having established the worldly nature of ownership, state its purpose: that whatever is obtained by a Brāhmaṇa through the acceptance of improper gifts or through trade and the like—[this would not constitute ownership if ownership were cognizable solely through the scriptures].
When Brahmins acquire wealth through a censurable occupation,
they become pure by relinquishing it, as well as by the recitation of sacred texts and by austerity.

Because this statement declares that [the property] must be relinquished, it would follow that it does not belong to him at all, and thus it would be indivisible among his sons. However, if ownership (*svatva*) is considered worldly (*laukika*), even such [property] indeed becomes one's own; therefore, it is certainly divisible among his sons. The penance (*prāyaścitta*), however, belongs only to the one who committed the offense, and not to his sons and others, because they receive it as an inheritance (*dāya*), and an inheritance, being a righteous acquisition (*dharmyāgama*), does not entail moral fault. Regarding its status as a righteous acquisition, it is said: "There are seven righteous ways of acquiring wealth: inheritance, finding, purchase, conquest..."
Application, the yoga of action, or even the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous.

Because of this statement by Manu (Manu 10.115): "The application [of wealth] is for the purpose of interest, namely the lending of goods; the application [of labor] is the performance of priestly duties and the like. This, however, does not seem quite right. Just as in the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*), which is intended to teach the established forms of words, all words already established in common usage are taught either generally or specifically—such that whatever is not explicitly taught there, or whatever is taught to be incorrect by such rules as "not in the *ṅi* case or the vocative" (*Pāṇini* 8.2.8), meaning that a word with its *n* elided in the vocative is ungrammatical—that very thing is not established in common usage and is therefore unfit for use. Similarly, in the treatises of Gautama and others, which are intended to establish the grounds for ownership (*svatva*) based on worldly practice, every ground for ownership is indeed taught. Therefore, whatever is not taught therein, or whatever is stated to be incapable of establishing ownership—such as theft—is not a worldly ground for ownership. Consequently, if the scripture prohibits ownership acquired through improper gifts, trade, and so forth, then even in the world, such ownership must not be recognized, just like property obtained through theft. Therefore, the phrase "by what is censurable" (*garhitena*) implies that although improper acceptance of gifts, self-performed agriculture, trade, and the like may serve as grounds for ownership, they are forbidden for a Brāhmaṇa.
Even when fallen into distress, a Brahmin who accepts gifts and eats whatever may be available from anywhere is not defiled by sin, for he is equal to fire and the sun.
He may engage in money-lending, agriculture, and trade, provided these are not performed by himself.
In times of distress, a twice-born man may act on his own initiative; he is not tainted by sin.

On account of such statements by Yājñavalkya, Bṛhaspati, and others, which describe these [means of livelihood] as applicable only in times of distress (*āpad-vṛtti*), one must conclude that since there is a connection with fault (*doṣa*) in resorting to them when not in distress, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) consists of renouncing the wealth obtained through those means and performing penance (*japa-tapas*); however, it does not negate the ownership (*svatva*) of what was acquired by those means. For this very reason, no specific punishment like that for thieves is prescribed in the Smṛtis for one who acquires property through improper acceptance of gifts (*asat-pratigraha*) and the like. Thus, even in the absence of distress, the ownership of what is acquired through improper acceptance of gifts and so forth certainly exists, and therefore it is indeed to be divided among the sons. Since the fault attaches only to the acquirer, he alone must perform the expiation; whereas that which is obtained through theft and the like does not possess such [legitimate] status and is therefore not to be divided. Furthermore, if the sons were to divide and take it, they would be subject to punishment. Enough of this incidental discussion. From the statement, "While the father remains faultless," it follows that even while a father with faults is alive, his sons do not remain under his subjection; thus, they have the right to effect a partition according to their own will. For this very reason, Nārada (Dāyabhāga 16) says:
A father who is diseased, angry, whose mind is attached to sensual objects,
or who acts contrary to the scriptures, is not competent to make a partition.

[327] Otherwise, one who acts contrary to the treatises follows a path devoid of the conduct prescribed by the *smṛtis*. Śaṅkha also states: “The division of the inheritance occurs even while the father is unwilling, provided he is aged, of perverted mind, or afflicted by a chronic illness. “Unwilling” means lacking the desire for partition; “aged” means incapable of managing the household affairs due to being disabled by infirmity and other such defects. When the father lacks the desire for partition, the eldest son is authorized to exercise independence, while the younger brothers must remain subject to his authority. Accordingly, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “When the father is incapacitated, the eldest son, or the next brother who understands the business, shall manage the household affairs with his consent. Here, “next brother” means the younger brother; “with his consent” means with the consent of the eldest. Hārīta also says: “If the father is distressed, away from home, or fallen into affliction, the eldest may at will consider the matter of the shares. While the father is living and free from defect, the division of the paternal estate among the sons occurs according to his wish. However, when the mother has ceased her menstrual flow (i.e., she is past childbearing age), the division of that wealth among the sons may take place by their own wish even in the absence of the father’s consent. Thus says Gautama (28.1–2): “After the father’s death, the sons shall divide the inheritance; or, while the father is living, after the mother has ceased her menstrual flow, if he so desires. Bṛhaspati also says:
The partition among brothers in the absence of both parents has been demonstrated;
it is also recommended when the mother’s menses have ceased, even while both parents are still living.

And when the father lacks the capacity for sexual pleasure, or his desire for wealth has ceased, the division of that wealth occurs by the son's own wish. Thus says Nārada (Dāyabhāga 2–3): "After this, the sons shall divide the father’s wealth equally, once the mother’s menses have ceased and her daughters have been given away in marriage."
And when the father’s pleasure had ceased and his desire had subsided, [the son]...

Here, by the statement "the sons shall divide," partition is declared to take place even in the absence of the father’s desire. Regarding the term *prattāsu*, it means "those for whom marriage has been performed. Regarding *ramaṇe*, it means "in the capacity for sexual pleasure. Regarding *uparataspr̥he*, it means "one whose longing for wealth has not ceased. The phrase "and when the sisters have been given away in marriage" (*prattāsu bhaginīṣu ca*) is connected to both parts like the eye of a crow (i.e., it applies to both preceding and following clauses). By this, the following is stated: when there is certainty that the mother lacks the capacity to produce offspring due to the cessation of her menses, and the father lacks the capacity for sexual pleasure, and the father has no desire for wealth, then the sons may divide the property according to their own will, provided the sisters have already been married. However, some authorities accept the passage from "when the mother’s menses have ceased" up to "whose longing has ceased" as a single sentence, asserting that the cessation of menses and the other conditions constitute three combined grounds for partition. Vyāsa states that while the brothers should live together while both parents are alive, this is the primary rule.

While the parents are alive, the co-residence of brothers is ordained. Śaṅkha and Likhita state that even after the parents have passed away, they should live together for the sake of increasing the estate: "They may, if they so desire, live together in one place; united, they shall attain prosperity. Nārada also says (Dāyabhāga 5): "The eldest brother may support them all in one place, just as a father does."
Whether it be an elder or a younger brother who is capable, the stability of the family depends upon capability.
"Those who desire the increase of dharma should divide [the estate] because of the separate performance of rites for the gods and the ancestors," so said Manu and Prajāpati (Manu 9.111):
"Thus they may live together or separately out of a desire for dharma;
dharma increases when they are separate; therefore, separation is consistent with dharma."

After partition, Bṛhaspati states that the performance of rites for the gods and ancestors is separate: "For those living together under a single cooking fire, the worship of the ancestors, gods, and twice-born shall be one; for those who are divided, that same worship shall be performed in each individual household."

Āpastamba (2.6.14.1) states the manner of that partition which occurs by the father’s wish: “Having satisfied the eldest son with one principal object, he should divide the inheritance among his sons equally while he is still living. The meaning is that, having gratified the eldest son with a single item—such as a cow or a horse—extracted from the middle mass of property, he should divide the remaining wealth in equal shares. Baudhāyana also [states this] (2.2.2–5).

"Manu divided his inheritance among his sons; the share is equal for all because there is no distinction," and "the eldest shall take one additional portion of wealth; therefore, they cause the eldest son to depart with the wealth"—so says the Śruti. Because there is no distinction—that is, because no specific difference is heard in the text stating that "Manu divided his inheritance among his sons"—[it follows that the shares are equal]. Nārada states that when a father divides his inheritance among his sons, he himself should take two shares:
"When dividing [the estate], the father should receive two shares for himself. (Dāyabhāga 12)
Bṛhaspati also says:
"In the division of property while the father is still living, the father himself shall take two shares."

[329] Śaṅkha and Likhita state that the taking of two shares from the father applies only to the case of an only son: "If he should be an only son, he shall take two shares for himself. Regarding this, the author of the *Pārijāta* holds that the word "only" (*eka*) here signifies "preeminent" (*śreṣṭha*). According to his view, the meaning of this statement is that if a son is capable of acquiring wealth due to his virtuous qualities, then, upon partition with him, the father should take two shares. Kātyāyana, however, maintains that an equal share must be given by the father to all sons alike; he says this intending that no single superior object should be given to the eldest, and that the father himself should take a share equal to theirs, rather than two shares.
"When the father and the brothers divide the entire collection of property into equal shares, that division is said to be righteous.
Yājñavalkya shows both of these two positions in verse 2.114.
If the father should make a partition, he may divide the sons according to his will;
he may give the eldest a superior share, or all may be equal sharers.

The meaning of the first half-verse is that, in resorting to either of these two alternatives—namely, the "best portion" (*śreṣṭhabhāga*) consisting of the most excellent object, or the "extra portion" (*uttamavastusahitena bhāgena*)—the father's own will alone is the determining factor. Nārada states (Dāyabhāga 15) that the younger brothers should not harbor resentment when the eldest receives an extra portion of superior goods from the parents, nor should the eldest harbor resentment when equal shares are distributed, thinking, "An extra share was not given to me. Furthermore: "But those who have been divided by the father himself with wealth that is equal, deficient, or excessive—for them, that very division shall be lawful; for the father is the master of everything."

If a father, by his own will and by deviating from the path prescribed in the scriptures, makes an unequal division, then that [division] must certainly be set aside; with this intention, Yājñavalkya says (2.116): "For those who have been divided unequally, a division made by the father is recorded in tradition as being consistent with dharma."

If it is *dharmya*—that is, prescribed by the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*)—then that which was made by the father must indeed remain as it was and cannot be revoked. Otherwise, however, it may be revoked; this is the meaning. When he himself takes an equal share and gives equal shares to the sons, including the eldest and the others, then the same author states that the wives shall have a share equal to that of their respective sons (YDh. 2.115):

"If he should make the shares equal, the wives are to be made sharers of equal portions, provided that no separate property (*strīdhana*) has been given to them by the husband or by the father-in-law."

[330] Because of the use of the plural form "wives" (*patnyaḥ*), each wife should take a share equal to her own portion, but no separate share should be given to them individually; for that would contradict the statement of Hārīta: "No partition exists between husband and wife" (*ĀpDh* 2.6.14.16). He (Yājñavalkya) states that if a son, being capable of earning wealth, does not wish to take his own share, then a partition must still be made by giving him something so that his sons have no desire to claim the inheritance (*YDh* 2.116).
When one who is capable does not desire [partition], a separate division is made after giving something [to him].
As for that partition which occurs by the son's own wish while the father is still living, since no other method is heard of [in the scriptures],
they take the entire collection of property in equal shares.

According to the statement of Kātyāyana (838), and because of the phrase "when the mother's menses have ceased" and the connection with the word "equally," the partition must be made equally. The division for those whose father has died must be performed with equality. And so says Yājñavalkya (2.117):
"After the death of both parents, the sons shall divide the inheritance and the debt equally.

Hārīta also says: "The division of the inheritance is equal when the father has died. Paiṭhīnasi also says: "When the paternal estate is being divided, the division among the brothers is equal. As for those [texts] which...
The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as his preferential share, and whatever is the best among all the goods;
half of that shall be the share of the middle son, while the youngest shall receive a fourth.
But if their shares have not been extracted, this distribution of portions shall apply:
the eldest son shall take one share in excess, and the next younger brother shall take half a share more than that.
"Established in the Dharma, [Manu] stated: 'The younger brother shall take share after share'";

such statements by Manu and others (9.112, 116–117) which prescribe an unequal distribution apply to periods other than the Kali Yuga. For this very reason, the prohibition of unequal distribution in the Kali age is found in the Ādi Purāṇa:
"Remarrying a wife who has already been wedded, taking a preferential share for the eldest, and likewise the killing of a cow..."
In the Kali age, one should not perform these five: [the killing of] a brother's wife, [carrying] a water-pot, ...
[331] "The senior share (jyeṣṭhāṃśa) is based on seniority established by birth, learning, and so forth; as it is stated even in the *Smṛtisaṃgraha*:

'Just as the practice of mandatory appointment (*niyoga*) or the rule regarding the *anūbandhyā* cow no longer exists today, so too the distribution of the extra share (*uddhāra-vibhāga*) does not exist at all nowadays.'"

Now, regarding partition after the father's death in the Kali age, Yājñavalkya (2.123) states that the mother shall receive an equal share with her sons: "When they divide [the estate] after the father's death, the mother also shall take an equal share.

Viṣṇu also says: "Mothers are entitled to shares corresponding to the shares of their sons" (18.34). It should be understood that the mother’s entitlement to an equal share applies when she is without *strīdhana* (woman’s property). For this very reason, it is stated in another *smṛti*:

A mother who possesses no property shall take an equal share upon partition with her sons; "possessing no property" means being devoid of her own specific woman's property (*strīdhana*). However, according to the teacher Vijñāneśvara, a mother who possesses woman's property is entitled to a half-share, whether the partition occurs during his lifetime or after his death. The mention of the "mother" is an elliptical expression intended to include stepmothers and paternal grandmothers who likewise have no sons. For this very reason, Vyāsa states: "The childless wives of one's father are declared to be entitled to equal shares."
And all those paternal grandmothers are proclaimed to be equal to one's own mothers.

As for what has been stated by some—that the mother and others receive only that portion of wealth necessary for their subsistence—one must consider how, according to their view, the word *sama* (equal) would not be untenable; this should be investigated by the learned. Furthermore, the claim made in the *Smṛticandrikā* regarding the meaningfulness of the word *sama*—that its purpose is such that when the divisible property is large, they take only what is necessary for subsistence, but when it is small, they take equal shares and do not take more on account of the necessity of subsistence—is unsatisfactory. This is because it would result in a discrepancy between injunctions (*vidhi-vairūpya*), leading to a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) where in one case there is an injunction to take only what is necessary for subsistence, and in another case an injunction to take equal shares. Nor can it be argued that this injunction applies only to cases where the divisible property is small, for it is improper to arbitrarily restrict the scope of an injunction. Bṛhaspati describes the method of division for those born of different mothers who are of the same caste and equal in number: * *Savarṇāsu tu jātānāṃ nānāmātṝṇāṃ dāyakramaḥ |* * *mātṛbhāgaṃ pṛthagbhūtaṃ labheraṃs te yathāṃśataḥ ||* * "But for those born of wives of the same caste from different mothers, the order of inheritance is as follows: they shall receive their respective shares of the maternal portion separately."* * *Yady ekajātā bahavaḥ pṛthakkṣetrāḥ pṛthagdhanāḥ |* * *sakṛjjātāḥ pṛthagjātāḥ pṛthakkṣetrāḥ samāṃśinaḥ ||* * "If many sons, born of one [father], have separate wives [mothers] and separate properties, whether born at the same time or at different times, they are entitled to equal shares if they have separate wives."* * *Samaṃśāḥ sarve jñeyā bhrātaro ye ca sahodarāḥ |* * *ye cāpy anyatra jātās te 'py ūrdhvaṃ pituḥ samāṃśinaḥ ||* * "All brothers who are uterine shall be known to have equal shares; and even those born of other [mothers] shall likewise have equal shares after the father's death."* * *Mātṛto bhāgakalpanā ||* * "The calculation of shares is according to the mother."* * *Aniyuktāsutaś caiva putriṇyā putro yaḥ smṛtaḥ |* * *ubhau tau rikthayor bhāginau samāṃśau nirbharisyataḥ ||* * "The son of a woman not authorized [to bear a child] and the son of a woman already having a son—both of these are declared to be sharers of the inheritance, each receiving an equal share."* * *Niyuktāyām api jātas tu naivāṃśaṃ pitur arhati |* * *yad evāsya pitā dadyāt tad evāsya dhanaṃ bhavet ||* * "But one born even of an authorized wife does not deserve a share of the father's [estate]; whatever his father may give him, that alone shall be his wealth."* * *Aputreṇa parakṣetre niyogotpāditaḥ sutaḥ |* * *ubhayor apy asau rikthī piṇḍadātā ca dharmataḥ ||* * "A son procreated through *niyoga* in the field of another by one who is childless is, according to the law, the heir to the estate and the giver of the funeral oblation (*piṇḍa*) to both [the biological father and the owner of the field]."* * *Haret tatra niyuktāyāṃ jātaḥ putro yathaurasaḥ |* * *kṣetrikaś caiva dadyāt tāv uddhāraṃ yathā pitā ||* * "In that case, the son born of the authorized wife shall take [the estate] just like a legitimate son (*aurasa*); and the owner of the field (*kṣetrika*) shall give them the preferential share (*uddhāra*) just as a father would."* * *Dattaurasetareṣāṃ tu putratvena parigrahaḥ |* * *savarṇānām amavarṇānāṃ ca vidhivat parigrahītavyāḥ ||* * "The formal adoption of sons other than the *datta* and *aurasa* types—whether of the same caste or of a different caste—must be performed according to the prescribed rules."* * *Sajātīyeṣv ayaṃ proktas tanayeṣu mayā vidhiḥ |* * *jātānām anyajātebhyo nihnave jyeṣṭha eva hi ||* * "This rule has been declared by me regarding sons of the same caste; however, among those born of different castes, the eldest indeed prevails in the matter of concealment [of status]."* * *Uttamavarṇā jātās tu hīnavarṇais tu yad dhanam |* * *tad dhanam aṃśato grāhyaṃ śeṣāṇāṃ tu svayaṃgrahaḥ ||* * "But as for the wealth belonging to those born of lower-caste men from women of higher caste, that wealth should be taken in shares; the remainder, however, is to be seized by themselves [the higher-caste heirs]."* * *Jyeṣṭhena jātamātreṇa putrī bhavati mānavaḥ |* * *pitṝṇām anṛṇaś caiva sa tasmāt sarvam arhati ||* * "By the mere birth of the eldest, a man becomes a father of a son and is freed from his debt to the ancestors; therefore, he deserves everything."* * *Yady api syāt tu satputro 'py asatputro 'pi vā bhavet |* * *nādhikaṃ daśamād dadyād auraso 'rthasya bhāgavit ||* * "Even if he has a legitimate son or even an illegitimate son, the *aurasa* son, knowing the nature of the property, shall not give more than a tenth part [to others]."* * *Kṣetrajaḥ putrikāputraḥ svayaṃdattaḥ kṛtakaḥ sutaḥ |* * *apaviddho 'paviddhaś ca dāyādā bāndhavāś ca ṣaṭ ||* * "The *kṣetraja*, the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*), the self-given, the adopted, the discarded, and the foundling—these six are heirs and kinsmen."* * *Paunarbhavaś ca kānīnaḥ svairiṇyāṃ yac ca dattakaḥ |* * *svayaṃ copāgatā ye ca klība-viṣṭādayaḥ sutāḥ ||* * "The son of a remarried woman, the maiden-born, the son of an unchaste woman, the one given away, and those who have come of their own accord, as well as the impotent, the outcast, and so forth—"* * *Amī gotrabhājaḥ syur arikthā bāndhavā
If many sons are born of one mother and are equal in their number of births,
they must divide the inheritance according to the law, based on the share of the mother due to their status as half-brothers.
Vyāsa also says:
"When sons of the same caste and number are born from one father but different mothers,
the division according to the mothers is recommended for them."
Bṛhaspati states the method of partition for those of the same caste who are unequal in number:
"When there are [sons] of the same caste who are unequal in number, the division of the male share among them is prescribed.

Even by many [sons] who have remained undivided with their father, when they eventually divide together with paternal uncles, their sons, and others, that single share which belonged to their own father must be taken. And so says Yājñavalkya (2.120):
But for those who have multiple fathers, the allotment of shares is according to the father;
Kātyāyana also says:
"If a younger brother dies while the estate is undivided, his son shall be the heir to the inheritance."
One should make one's livelihood by means other than what has been received from one's grandfather.
He shall indeed receive his paternal share from his paternal uncle or from that uncle’s son;
for according to the law, that very share belongs equally to all the brothers.

Or his son may receive it, and thereafter there shall be cessation [of succession]. The mention of the younger [son] is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for the elder. This is the meaning: when the father has died, the grandson should take that share of his own father which belongs to him in the grandfather’s wealth from the paternal uncle and others. Likewise, when his father has died, the grandson’s son should also take the share of his great-grandfather. However, the great-grandson’s son has no right to a share in the wealth of the great-great-grandfather. Devala also says: "Of kinsmen who live together, whether undivided or divided..."
The rule is that there may be a further division of the inheritance up to the fourth generation.

In the word *avibhaktānām*, the elision (*luk*) of the genitive plural ending is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). The meaning is that the division of inheritance (*dāyavibhāga*) occurs again—whether among those who were previously undivided, or even those who were divided, living together, or reunited—only up to the great-grandson (*prapautra*); from the fourth generation onwards, however, it ceases. As for the statement:
"Whether he be the third, the fifth, or even the seventh [in descent], if the births [of his ancestors] are unknown, he shall receive the share descended in due order."

[333] That statement of Bṛhaspati concerns the great-grandson, the son, and others residing in a distant or inaccessible region, because it is recited in that context. However, the statement "up to the fourth" refers to those residing in the same locality; thus, there is no contradiction between these two. Regarding the question of how the division of the grandfather’s property is to be made with the father when a grandson is present, Bṛhaspati says: "In property acquired by the grandfather, whether immovable or movable, equal ownership is declared for both the father and the son."

The meaning is that an equal share must be taken from the father, and not two shares by resorting to the option of unequal division as in the case of self-acquired property. Yājñavalkya also states (2.121): "Regarding land acquired by the grandfather, a fixed endowment, or even wealth, the ownership there is indeed equal for both the father and the son."
Vyāsa states that the partition of the grandfather’s wealth occurs even if the father does not desire it:

"In regard to a house and field acquired by succession, the sons have equal shares with the father; they are not entitled to a partition of the paternal estate as long as the father does not wish it."
In some cases, Manu and Viṣṇu state that the division of the paternal estate occurs solely by the father’s will (Manu 9.209;
Viṣṇu 18.43):
"But whatever property of the father a son may acquire without having received [his share] from him..."
One who is without desire should not share with his sons that which was acquired by himself.

The meaning is this: if something belonging to the grandfather has been taken away by someone else or by the grandfather himself and cannot be recovered by the father, yet the father recovers it, that is considered as if it were acquired by his own effort; being free from any desire to divide it, he should not share it with his sons. Bṛhaspati also says: "Regarding property belonging to the grandfather which was seized and subsequently acquired by the father through his own power—whether obtained by means of learning, valor, or other such means—it is recorded in tradition that the father’s ownership over it is absolute."
One may make a gift at one's own will and likewise take a share from that wealth;
in the absence of such [a gift], the sons are declared to have equal shares.
Yājñavalkya states the method of partition for those of different castes (2.125):
"The sons born of a Brāhmaṇa shall have shares of four, three, two, and one according to their respective castes;
those born of a Kṣatriya shall have shares of three, two, and one; but those born of a Vaiśya shall have shares of two and one."

The sons born of a Brāhmaṇa from the four women beginning with the Brāhmaṇī—the Brāhmaṇa, the Mūrdhāvasikta, the Ambaṣṭha, and the Pāraśava—inherit shares in the order of four, three, two, and one respectively. Those born of a Kṣatriya from women beginning with the Kṣatriyā—the Kṣatriya, the Māhiṣya, and the Ugra—inherit three, two, and one shares respectively. Those born of a Vaiśya from a Vaiśyā and a Śūdrā—the Vaiśya and the Karaṇa—inherit two and one shares; this is the meaning. Bṛhaspati states that land acquired through gift should not be given to the Mūrdhāvasikta and the others: "Land obtained as a gift must not be given to a son of a Kṣatriya woman or similar status."
Even if their father should give [the property], when he has died, the son born of a Brahmin woman shall take it.

In this context, because of the specific qualification "received as a gift" (*pratigraha*), the inheritance of even those such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others who have acquired land through purchase and other means certainly occurs. However, one born of a *śūdra* woman by men of the three higher castes, such as Brāhmaṇas, is not entitled to receive land even if it was acquired through purchase and other means. Thus says Devala:
"One born of a *śūdra* woman by twice-born men does not deserve a share of land;
he may obtain everything [only] from a co-uterine brother (*sajātīya*)—such is the settled rule of Dharma."
And as for the son of a Śūdra born to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas, he does not inherit the estate;
whatever his father may give him, that alone shall be his wealth.

Regarding this statement of Manu (9.155), the Southerners (*dākṣiṇātyāḥ*) maintain that it refers to a case where there exists wealth given out of affection by the father. The Easterners (*paurastyāḥ*), however, say it refers to the son of a Śūdra woman who was married without [proper] qualities. Regarding the son of a Śūdra woman married to a man of good qualities, Bṛhaspati states:
"The virtuous son born of a Śūdra womb, who is intent on service for one who has no offspring, shall receive a livelihood;
the remainder, the kinsmen (*sapiṇḍāḥ*) shall obtain."

In the context of the phrase "among those not taken as wives," Gautama also states (28.37): "Even the son of a Śūdra woman, if he is obedient, shall receive the means of subsistence from one who has no other offspring, according to the rule for a pupil (*antevāsividhinā*). "Means of subsistence" (*vṛttimūla*) refers to the basis of livelihood. He (Gautama) himself states (28.43)—regarding those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*)—that they share only in the means of livelihood, just like the son of an unmarried Śūdra woman: "As in the case of the son of a Śūdra woman, so among those born of inverse unions. This means that those born of women of superior caste by men of inferior caste share only in the means of subsistence, just like the son of an unmarried Śūdra woman. As for the distinction among sons of different castes based on their possession or lack of qualities and so forth, that is...

"Marriage with girls of a different caste by the twice-born"— since this prohibition against marrying those of a different caste is stated in the *Ādipurāṇa* within the section on what is to be avoided in the Kali age, and since the practices of the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others are no longer current today, they have not been elaborated upon here. Furthermore, regarding the acceptance of sons other than the *datta* and *aurasa* types as one's own offspring, we have already cited [the relevant authority] in the section on what is to be avoided in the Kali age within our *Samayanirṇayodyota*.

By this statement, since secondary sons (*gauṇaputra*) such as the *kṣetraja* and others—excluding the biological son (*aurasa*) and the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*)—are prohibited in the Kali age, and since they are currently not in practice, no specific details regarding their partition are set forth here. In that statement, the mention of the "biological son" is as follows:
"The biological son is one born of the lawful wife; equal to him is the son of an appointed daughter" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.128).

Thus, the term "son of an appointed daughter" (*putrikāputra*)—which is mentioned in the statements of Yājñavalkya and others as being equal to a biological son (*aurasa*), primary even in relation to the "given son" (*datta*), and embraced by contemporary worldly usage—is also included here by way of illustration. The nature of the primary and secondary sons, beginning with the biological son, has been defined in the section on *śrāddha* in the *Ācāravivekoddyota*.
[The formula for appointing a daughter is: "I shall give this sisterless maiden, adorned, to you;
whatever son is born of her shall be my son."

Regarding the question of how the distribution of shares is determined when a legitimate son (*aurasa*) is born after the appointment of a daughter as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) according to the methods stated by Vasiṣṭha and others, Manu says (9.134):
"But if, after an appointed daughter has been designated, a son is subsequently born..."
In that case, the division shall be equal, for there is no seniority for a woman.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"The legitimate son alone is declared the sole owner of the paternal wealth;
the appointed daughter is said to be equal to him, while the other sons are to be maintained."
As for those [texts] which prescribe a smaller share for the son of an appointed daughter:
"Even the legitimate son born later shall be the enjoyer of the entire estate;
the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) enjoys one-third, and the son of the appointed daughter (*putrikāsuta*) enjoys one-fourth."

These and other such statements from the *Brahma Purāṇa* and other texts are to be understood as referring to cases where the legitimate son (*aurasa*) is extremely virtuous, while the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) is of a different caste or is utterly devoid of merit. Manu (9.141–42) states that in the absence of a legitimate son, the adopted son inherits the estate: "If a man has an adopted son who is endowed with all good qualities, he shall inherit that estate, even though he has come from another lineage."
An adopted son shall never inherit the family name or the estate of his biological father;
for the funeral cake follows the family name and the estate, and the ancestral offering (svadhā) ceases for one who gives [the son away].

By the use of the word "api" (also), it is implied [the son] is from one's own lineage (*svagotra*). *Svadhā* is the cause of satisfaction. Vasiṣṭha (15.9) states that if a legitimate son (*aurasa*) is born after the adoption of a given son (*dattaputra*), the latter is entitled to a fourth share: "If a legitimate son is born after that adopted son has been received, the adopted son shall be a sharer of a fourth part. Kātyāyana also says (857): "But when a legitimate son is born, the other sons take a fourth share; however, those of different caste (*asavarṇa*) are entitled only to food and clothing."

Those of the same caste (*savarṇa*) are the adopted sons (*dattaka*) and others; those of a different caste (*asavarṇa*) are the maiden-born sons (*kānīna*) and others. In the *Kalpataru*, however, it is read that "the sons take a third share. This should be understood to apply when the adopted son possesses superior qualities relative to the legitimate son (*aurasa*). As for the verse: "The legitimate son alone is the master of the paternal wealth; he should grant a mere livelihood to the rest for the sake of kindness" (YDh 2.132).

This statement of Manu is intended as praise for the *aurasa* (legitimate) son. However, the view of the sage Vijñāneśvara is that it is intended to prohibit the [heir’s] entitlement to a fourth share when the *dattaka* (adopted) and other sons are either opposed to the *aurasa* son or lack merit. *Vasunaḥ* means of wealth. As for the verse: "Manu has declared that if among brothers born of the same father even one should have a son, they all become possessed of a son through that son" (9.182).

This statement of Manu is intended to mean that in the absence of the paternal uncle’s sons and others, the *śrāddha* must necessarily be performed for him just as for one's own father; it does not, however, establish their status as actual sons. For if that were the case, [the following verse would be contradicted]:
"For one who has gone to heaven without a son, the heirs to the wealth are, in successive order:
the wife, the daughters, the parents, and likewise the brothers."

In the statement of Yājñavalkya (2.135–136), "His son, a kinsman born of the same lineage," the designation of one as "sonless" despite the existence of a brother's son is not contradictory. Regarding the specific rules for the division of a Śūdra’s wealth, Yājñavalkya says (2.133–34):
"Even a son born to a Śūdra by a female slave shall, if born of [the father’s] desire, be entitled to a share."
If the father has died, the brothers should make him a recipient of half a share.

A son begotten by a Śūdra on an unmarried woman through lust, with the father’s consent, becomes a sharer of a portion [of the estate]. If the father dies and there are sons of the married wife, then those brothers shall make the slave-girl’s son a recipient of half a share relative to their own shares. If there are no sons of the married wife, nor daughters, nor their sons, then the slave-girl’s son shall take the entire wealth of the progenitor. If there are daughters or grandsons (daughters’ sons), then he receives only a half; such is the meaning. Here, by the specific mention of "by a Śūdra," it is indicated that one begotten by twice-born men on a slave-girl does not receive a share even with the father’s consent, nor a half when he has died, nor the whole in the absence of sons and others. However, it has already been shown by us that if he possesses qualities such as serviceability, he receives merely a means of subsistence. When dividing, the previously initiated brothers must perform, from their middle wealth, the initiatory rites up to marriage for the uninitiated brothers and sisters. And so says Bṛhaspati:
But those brothers who are uninitiated and younger than others should indeed be initiated by their elder brothers from the paternal wealth remaining after the middle portion has been set aside.

[338] Regarding the term *yavīyasaḥ* (younger ones), the absence of the *mum* and *dīrgha* [augmentations] is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). Here, the mention of "brothers" (*bhrātṛ*) is also indicative of sisters (*bhaginī*). For this very reason, Vyāsa states: "Those who have not been consecrated there [at the time of partition] should be consecrated by their elder brothers from that paternal wealth itself, as well as the unmarried daughters, according to the prescribed rule."
Regarding sisters, Yājñavalkya states a specific rule (2.124):
"But those [brothers] who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by those brothers who have already been consecrated;
and the sisters, having been given a fourth part from their own share."

In this context, the ablative case in the phrase "from his own share" (*nijād aṃśāt*) is not used in the sense of an *apādāna* (point of departure); rather, it is used with the elision of the suffix *-lyap*, meaning "having taken into account his own share, [he should give] a fourth share that has been apportioned. This is the meaning: having extracted from the common property a share equal to a fourth part of the portion belonging to a son of the same caste as the daughter, and having given that to each sister, they are to be married. By this, it is understood that daughters also have a right to a share in the partition after the father's death. And Manu likewise demonstrates this (9.118):
"From their own respective shares, the brothers shall give to the unmarried daughters a fourth part each from their own portions; those who are unwilling to give shall become outcasts."

This is the meaning: by such statements as “the brothers, beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, shall give to their sisters, beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, four, three, two, and one shares,” they shall each give a fourth part from their own respective shares out of those portions prescribed for their own caste. For example: if someone has only a Brāhmaṇa wife, one son, and one daughter, he should divide the paternal estate into two parts; then, dividing one of those parts into four, he gives a fourth share to the daughter, and the son takes all the remainder. If there are two sons and one daughter, he divides the paternal wealth into three parts; then, dividing one of those parts into four, he gives a fourth share to the daughter, and the remainder is to be divided and taken by the two sons. If there is one son and two daughters, then he divides the whole into two parts; then, dividing one of those parts into four, he gives two shares of that to the two daughters, and the remainder is to be taken by the son. If there is one son of a Brāhmaṇa wife and one daughter of a Kṣatriya wife, then he divides the paternal property into seven parts; then, dividing the three shares belonging to the Kṣatriya son into four, he gives a fourth share to the Kṣatriya daughter, and the son takes the remainder. This should be applied in all cases. As for what some have said—that here the intention is only to provide enough wealth for the performance of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) and not the giving of a fourth share, because otherwise there would be the consequence of excessive wealth for a girl with many brothers, or the consequence of poverty for a man with many sisters—that too is refuted by the aforementioned explanation. For it is not stated here that a fourth part must be given after extracting it from one’s own share. Therefore, Vijñāneśvara, Asahāya, and Medhātithi hold the view that upon the father’s death, during partition, the daughter is entitled to a share according to the stated method; but while the father is alive, she receives only what her father gives her, since there is no specific rule to the contrary. Nārada (Dāyabhāga 33–34) states that in the absence of paternal wealth, the elder brothers must perform the necessary sacraments using their own earned property.
But for those for whom the rules of consecration have not been performed in due order,
they must be performed by their brothers from that very paternal wealth.
If the paternal wealth is not available,
the sacraments that must necessarily be performed for the brothers should be carried out by those who have already been consecrated, having extracted the funds from their own shares.

The mention of "brothers" is also an elliptical indication for sisters. When a father has divided his estate with his sons while his mother or a co-wife is pregnant but not yet clearly showing her condition, those who have already divided shall set aside a portion from their respective shares equal to one's own share and give it to the child born after the partition. Thus says Viṣṇu (17.3): "Those divided by the father shall give a share to the one born after the division. And the father, having taken that share given by the divided sons, shall live together with him, because he must be protected due to the child’s lack of legal capacity (*aprāptavyavahāra*). If the father dies before the distribution of the share, no share need be given by the divided sons; rather, the son born after partition shall take only the father’s share. Thus says Gautama (28.27): "The son born after partition takes only the paternal [share]. Furthermore, one who was conceived in the womb after the partition and is born subsequently shall take only the paternal share. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
Those who have been divided from their father, whether they be stepbrothers or uterine brothers,
those born later shall indeed take the paternal share of those [who were divided].

The reason for this has been stated by that very same author: "A son born before partition has no authority over his paternal share; one born after partition has no authority over his brother's share.
He himself also states something else: "[340]"

Whatever has been acquired by the father himself after he has divided [the estate] with his sons, all that belongs to the son born after the partition; the earlier-born sons are declared to have no right to it.
Just as with wealth, so it is with debt, and in matters of giving, pledging, and buying;
they have no mutual authority over one another, except regarding impurity and the water-libation rite.

If some [sons] were reunited with the father, then even after the father's death, one born after the partition should not receive a share of the paternal estate from those [reunited sons]. Thus says Manu (9.216):
"But one born after partition shall take only the paternal wealth;
or he shall divide it with those who may have been reunited with him."

Yājñavalkya (2.122) states that a son born after his father’s death, while the mother is not yet manifestly pregnant and the brothers have already divided the estate, shall receive from those brothers a share equal to their own portions, drawn from the divided wealth—whether visible or invisible.
"A son born after the partition from a wife of equal caste is entitled to a share."

By the mention of "a woman of the same caste" (*savarṇā*), it is shown that for one born after partition from a woman of a different caste, the previously stated rule—that he receives his own share—applies; he does not receive a share equal to the portion of the divided brothers. By this very logic, it should be understood that even in the case of partition during the father's lifetime, a son born of a woman of a different caste who is born after partition is not entitled to a share of the entire paternal estate. Alternatively, regarding the wealth consisting of visible assets such as houses, household utensils, draught animals, milch cattle, ornaments, and so forth, which have been determined through increase or decrease, he receives the share extracted from the documents and the like, but not from what is hidden. Or rather, its distinction [from the seen] would arise from the visible object itself once it has been purified by the subtraction of income and expenditure.

Halāyudha has established that this position refers to the case where, among divided brothers, one possesses fewer merits. Thus, at the time of the division of the brothers' inheritance, a son born later to a brother who died while his wife—who was pregnant with a manifest fetus—was childless, receives his own paternal share from them. When a brother’s wife is manifestly pregnant, the division must not be carried out until the birth. Accordingly, Vasiṣṭha (17.40–41) states: "Now, regarding the division of the inheritance among brothers: those women who are childless, [the division for] them [is postponed] until the acquisition of a son. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "an expectation must be maintained until the acquisition of a son. Furthermore, what was previously given by the father out of affection to the divided brothers, such as ornaments and so forth, need not be recovered by one born after the division. And thus says Yājñavalkya (2.123): [text omitted].
Whatever has been given by the parents to someone shall belong to that person alone as their wealth.

This same principle is to be understood regarding gifts made out of affection and so forth even prior to partition. As for property that is common to brothers, their sons, and others—thinking, "I too have a share in this substance"—one obtains one's own share from that wealth after it has been set aside from those who have already divided, even if the formal division has not yet occurred. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"Whether the division has been made or not, wherever an heir presents himself..."
If one contemplates the universal, he is indeed the recipient of a share.

Regarding the time of partition, the same author states that a brother, his son, or others who were residing in another country at the time of division, even if they arrive later after a long time, shall receive their own shares from those who have already divided:
"The debt, the document, the house, and the field which belong to the grandfather..."
Although he had been away for a long time, that sharer of portions has now returned.
Having abandoned his common lineage and resorted to another country, a share must undoubtedly be given to him when he returns to that family.
