Whether it be the third, the fifth, the sixth, or even the seventh [in the line],
if the names of the ancestors are unknown, one shall receive the share that has descended in due order.
"Land that has been known for generations by the primary and neighboring lords as belonging to their master must be given to one who has come from that lineage by the kinsmen.
Thus Kātyāyana states what property is fit for partition: (840) [text follows].
That which was inherited from the grandfather, that which was inherited from the father, and whatever else was acquired by oneself—
all this is to be divided among the heirs in their respective shares.

"Self-acquired" means acquired by oneself through the use of property not partitioned from the father or others. Otherwise, it would not be subject to partition as "self-acquired," according to the forthcoming statement: "But that which is self-acquired is not to be divided, provided it does not conflict with the paternal estate. [342] Even for this threefold wealth, if there should be a debt incurred by the grandfather or others, then the partition must be carried out after repaying that debt. And so he (Kātyāyana, 850) says: "Having paid a debt or a gift made out of affection, one should divide the remainder. Likewise:

"Debt contracted by a brother, a paternal uncle, or a maternal uncle for the sake of the family must be paid in its entirety by the heirs at the time of partition. Thus also says Nārada (Dāyabhāga 32).
Whatever remains after the paternal inheritance has been given, as well as any debt incurred by the father, shall be divided among the brothers; otherwise, the father would remain a debtor.

And this refers to cases where the divisible property is abundant; however, when it is small, the debt must also be divided and taken by all like the inheritance, according to the previously cited verse: "After the death of their parents, the sons shall divide the inheritance and the debt equally" (YDh 2.117). At the time of partition, he [Kātyāyana] states what kind of debt should be examined and paid (Kāt. 849):

"Debt pertaining to the father, debt related to the paternal estate, or one's own personal debt—in this manner, such incurred debt must be cleared by the kinsmen together during the partition. Thus [it is said].

That debt connected with the father's debt is that incurred for the purpose of clearing the father's obligations. That which is one's own is that incurred by another for the sake of necessary tasks such as maintaining one's own family; the remainder implies that what is incurred by oneself is likewise for the maintenance of one's own family. When among undivided co-sharers, something has been given from the common paternal wealth—whether for the sake of religious duty (*dharma*), out of affection, or as a loan—without the consent of all, it must be recovered from the giver after being divided among all, provided it is known to them all. For it is not proper to give away a portion of the common paternal wealth as if it were one's own exclusive property; thus says the same author (Kāt. 848).

A debt contracted by oneself for the sake of dharma, or given out of affection, or that which was personally incurred—that should be divided when it is evident; however, there is no distribution of gifts from ancestral wealth.

When house, field, or other property is being divided while known to all, they shall divide and take possession of it. However, when it is not known, one should have that person—who is suspected of having a connection with that property—purified by means of the ordeal known as the *kośa* (the water-vessel). And so says the same author (Kāt. 841–42):
"A visible house, field, or quadruped may be divided;
but when there is suspicion of hidden property, an ordeal is declared to be required therein."
Household utensils, draft animals, milch cattle, ornaments, and servants are divided while being visible; regarding hidden property, Manu has declared that it goes to the treasury.

The "pledge" (pratyaya) refers to divine [evidence]. Household utensils such as mortars and the like, as well as servants and others belonging to the debtor, constitute the pledge. Regarding this, it is said:

"In matters of doubt, establishing trust, making a compact, the partitioning of inheritance, and when one must act as the agent for a series of transactions, one should always cause the pledge itself to be delivered."
Thus, for the purpose of reminding one of the rule regarding the ordeal by oath (*kośa*) stated by himself in the section on divine ordeals (Kāt. 415), Manu shows what is indivisible (9.206):
"But whatever is the wealth acquired through learning, that shall belong to that person alone;
as also [wealth] from a friend, [wealth] received at marriage, and likewise [wealth] received during the honey-mixture offering (*mādhuparkika*)."

That which is obtained from a friend is *maitra*; that which is obtained as an object of honor at the time of the *madhuparka* offering is *mādhuparkika*. Vyāsa says: "Whatever is acquired through learning, wealth gained by valor, and that which is a wedding gift (*saudāyika*), these shall not be sought back from him by his heirs at the time of partition."

The nature of *saudāyika* (gift received at marriage) has been stated by that same [author]: "That which is obtained by a married woman or even by an unmarried girl from her husband, from the father's house, from a brother, or from her parents, is known as *saudāyika*. Thus it is said.

And this [property] is not subject to partition if it was acquired without expending undivided ancestral wealth; otherwise, it is certainly subject to partition. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya (2.118–119) states:
"What else has been acquired by oneself without detriment to the paternal estate, as well as what is received from a friend or obtained through marriage—that shall not belong to the heirs."
He who recovers property that was held by him after it had been lost over time need not give it to his heirs; the same applies to what has been acquired through learning.

The phrase "one should set aside" refers to property inherited through the paternal line; the remainder of the sentence is that this is done with the consent of the others. This is a prohibition against dividing property that has been recovered from others after being lost, intended to mean that the recoverer shall receive an equal share while the others do not. For this very reason, Śaṅkha says:
"But if one person alone recovers land that was previously lost according to the order of succession, the others obtain their shares by giving him a fourth part."

The meaning is that after giving a fourth part of what has been acquired, the others shall take the remainder according to their respective shares. Manu also states (9.208) that all this is indivisible only when the acquisition was made without relying on the undivided property of the father and others, and not otherwise: "What one may acquire by labor without using the paternal property, as well as what is obtained through learning, he need not give to his heirs."

"By labor," such as service, agriculture, and so forth. Vyāsa also says: "Whatever wealth one acquires by one's own effort without depending on paternal property, that wealth—and likewise wealth obtained through learning—one need not give to the heirs."

Kātyāyana defines the nature of what is acquired through learning (vidyā): "That wealth which is obtained through learning that was acquired from another by means of the use of food provided by someone else is called 'obtained through learning'. (867)

In this context, the words "other" (*para*) and "another" (*anya*) are used with reference to those who are not divided [by birth]. Regarding what has been explained concerning the acquisition of learning, it is stated by that same authority (Kāt. 868–873):

"But that which is obtained through learning on the basis of a prior agreement as a prize, one should know that to be 'wealth acquired through learning' (*vidyādhana*); it is not to be divided during partition."

That which is obtained from a disciple, from officiating as a priest, from answering questions, from resolving doubts through inquiry, from praising one's own knowledge, from debate, and from extensive study;
[345] They say that the wealth of knowledge is not to be divided at the time of partition;
for this same rule applies even among craftsmen regarding whatever may exceed their wages.

That which is acquired through the power of learning, as well as from officiating at sacrifices or from teaching a pupil—this they call the property of learning; anything other than this is common property.
Bṛhaspati declares that what is obtained by learning after excluding others, having previously made a wager, is "learning-wealth" (vidyādhanam); he states that this is not to be divided.

"That which is obtained through a pledge of learning, that which is received from a disciple, and that which is obtained according to the rule of the officiating priest (r̥tvij)—Bhṛgu declares this to be 'wealth acquired through learning' (vidyādhana). Thus it is said.

"Having been presented"—meaning having been set forth in the form of *krama*, *jaṭā*, and so on, and recited by compiling them; "having been presented for a wager," such is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). From a student: through teaching. From officiating as a priest (*ārtvijya*): through performing the duties of the *hotṛ* and other priests. From questioning: from questioning difficult points of meaning. From resolving doubtful questions: from providing answers to difficult inquiries. From proclaiming one's own knowledge: from making one's own learning known in an assembly, in the form of debate (*vāda*), sophistry (*jalpa*), cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), and so forth. From superior study (*prādhyayana*): from excellent study. The phrase "even among artisans" and so on means that this law regarding the division of the wealth of learning exists even among those who subsist on the science of crafts. That which is obtained in excess of the customary fee (*ucitamūlya*) due to a person's standing; that which is produced by the power of learning, obtained through the superiority of one's learning in matters such as honor in an assembly; that which is obtained from being a patron (*yājya*), obtained in the form of hospitality apart from the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); that which is obtained by a claim to learning, obtained by the claim "I am a man of great learning"; from a student, in the form of a teacher's fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*) received; and according to the rule of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), by way of acting as an observer (*upadraṣṭṛ*) and so forth. Nārada (Dāyabhāga 10) states that someone may also have a share in the wealth of another's learning: *Yas tatra vidyādhikārī syāt prāptam artham sa eva ca | vidyādhanaṃ tu tad bhāvyam anyathā na vibhajyate ||* "He alone who has authority over that learning shall take the wealth acquired therein; that is to be considered the property of learning, otherwise it is not to be divided."* *(Note: The Sanskrit provided in the source was a mix of commentary and verse. The above is a translation of the core commentary and the cited verse.)*
He who maintains the household of a brother who is acquiring knowledge shall receive a share from that wealth acquired through learning, even if he himself has not studied.

Even if one has not studied and is ignorant, if wealth has been acquired through knowledge obtained from a father or other relative who did not partition their own inheritance, that is "wealth acquired through learning" (*vidyādhanam*), and it must be divided by all. Thus says Kātyāyana (874): "Bṛhaspati declares that wealth acquired through valor by brothers who have been trained in learning within the family, or even by a father, is subject to division."

Wealth acquired through valor, or that which is acquired by means of learning or valor, is to be divided. Even in that case, the acquirer shall indeed receive two shares, because Vasiṣṭha states: “He among them who has himself acquired [property] shall take two shares” (17.51). Regarding even non-divisible wealth acquired through learning (*vidyādhanam*), Gautama (28.28) declares that it may be given at the wish of the acquirer: “A learned man (*vaidya*) may, at his pleasure, give his own acquired property to those who are not learned (*avaidya*). By the word "learning" (*vidyā*), a branch of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) is meant; a "learned man" (*vaidya*) is one who knows such learning. Nārada (Dāyabhāga 11) states that in the absence of the acquirer's wish, there is no giving of a share.
A physician shall not, against his will, give a share from his own wealth to one who is unqualified,
unless that person has acquired it by means of the paternal estate.
One should not give [the property] to one who is unlearned, even if there is a desire [to do so]. And thus Kātyāyana says (875):
"The wealth of learning must never be given by a learned man to those who are unlearned;
however, that wealth may be given by a learned man to those who are equal or superior in learning."

"Knowledge should not be given to the ignorant at any time; even by one who desires [to give], it should not be given"—this is the meaning. And this prohibition is to be understood to apply when those devoid of knowledge possess wealth. However, if they lack wealth, then even to them it should be given at will by one who possesses knowledge. He (Kātyāyana, verse 877) states that things acquired through valor and so forth are not subject to partition: "What is acquired through valor, what is acquired through learning, and that which is known as a woman's property—all this is not to be divided by the heirs at the time of partition."
The nature of indivisible wealth acquired through valor has been shown by that same author (Kāt. 876):
"When one performs an act with boldness after having entered into danger, and the master, being pleased with that act, bestows a favor..."
Whatever wealth is obtained there through valor shall belong to him.
Its nature as something not to be divided has been stated by that very same author (Kāt. 878):
"That which is acquired by means of a banner (in battle) is declared by tradition never to be subject to partition;
for it is that which is brought back from the field of battle after putting to flight the enemy's forces."
Having sacrificed one’s life for the sake of the master, that is called "acquired under the banner" (*dhvajāhṛta*).

Vyāsa states that when something is obtained through valor or similar means by relying on common property, ancestral wealth, and so forth, the acquirer is entitled to two shares because of his role as the earner:
"Whatever vehicle or other property has been acquired by relying upon common property..."
If one acquires wealth through valor or other such means, his brothers are entitled to a share therein.
Two shares of that [property] shall be given to him, while the remainder are to be divided equally. Regarding other indivisible items, Bṛhaspati says:
"And what may have been given by the grandfather, by the father, or even by the mother..."
That [wealth] of his must not be taken away, as it is with the wealth acquired through valor or from a wife.

Nārada also says (Dāyabhāga 6–7): "Both the wealth acquired by valor and the wealth from a wife, as well as that which may be the wealth of learning— these three are indivisible, as is a gift from a father."
And for one to whom his mother has given her own property out of affection, this same rule is seen to apply; the mother is as much a beloved object of worship as the father.
Intending that property received from a daughter is likewise indivisible—just like what is received at marriage—Kātyāyana describes the nature of those two types of wealth (verses 879–880):

"That which is obtained by a woman of her own caste together with a daughter at the time of receiving [a bride] is known as 'daughter-acquired' (kanyāgata) wealth; it is declared to be pure and productive of interest."
One should know that wealth which has come together with one's wife is matrimonial;
all such wealth is to be understood as conducive to the performance of dharma.

In the case of these two as well, when wealth is acquired by relying on common property, the acquirer’s share is to be understood as two portions, based on the previously cited texts; and it should be known that the other [co-heirs] also have a share. Even when not relying on common property, if the younger brothers are devoted to the study of knowledge (*vidyā*), then whatever is acquired by the eldest brother while the father is deceased and they remain undivided must be shared with them as well, because of his status as the acquirer; however, he himself shall take two shares. For this very reason, Manu (9.204) says:
"Whatever wealth the eldest brother acquires after the father has died..."
In that case, there shall be a share for the younger brothers, provided they are observers of sacred knowledge.

He (Manu, 9.205) states that even if all the brothers, being without [paternal] property, acquire wealth through agriculture and other means, the division there shall be equal for all; an unequal division should not be devised by considering the greater or lesser amount of wealth acquired:
"But if all those who are unlearned should acquire wealth through their own exertion, the division therein shall be equal, as it is not ancestral—this is the settled rule."

"From effort" means from activities such as agriculture and the like. "Even when not inherited from the father" (*apitrye*) means even in the absence of reliance upon paternal property. Manu states another thing that cannot be divided (9.219):
"Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women, security of possession (*yogakṣema*), and pasture grounds—they declare these to be indivisible."

The garment that was worn is for him by whom it was worn; however, the garment worn by the father should be given to the recipient of the *śrāddha* after the father's death. Whatever garments, ornaments, beds, and so forth, as well as the father’s vehicles and other belongings, one should offer those to the recipient of the *śrāddha* after honoring them with perfumes and garlands.

Thus, according to the statement of Bṛhaspati: new garments must indeed be divided. "Vehicles" (*patra*) refers to conveyances such as horses, palanquins, and the like; these belong to the one who was mounted upon them. However, ancestral property (*pitrya*) is treated exactly like the garments. Alternatively, "vehicle" (*patra*) may mean the wealth deposited in a document as a debt, since Kātyāyana states: "wealth deposited in a document" (882). When there is a large number of horses and so forth, they must be divided by those who subsist on their sale. In the case of goats and the like, if an equal division is impossible due to inequality, a larger share should be given to the eldest.
One should never divide goats, sheep, and single-hoofed animals unequally;
goats, sheep, and single-hoofed animals are ordained for the eldest alone.

Because of this statement by Manu (9.119): even an ornament, if it was worn by someone, belongs to him alone; if it was not worn, it is common property and must be divided. Prepared food—such as rice, sweetmeats (*modaka*), and so forth—is also indivisible and should be consumed according to necessity. Water refers to water-reservoirs such as wells and the like; these, if they are of unequal number, should be used in turn rather than being divided by means of their monetary value. Female slaves who are unequal in number should be made to perform work in turn; however, those women kept by the father (*pitrāvaruddhā*) are indivisible even if they are equal in number, because Gautama stated: "There is no division among women who are united [with others]" (28.45). By the word *yoga* is meant the cause for obtaining what has not yet been obtained, and by the word *kṣema* is understood the construction of tanks and other works of public utility (*pūrta-karman*). These two, even if acquired by relying upon paternal wealth, are not to be divided.
Those who perceive the truth say that security, charitable works, yoga, and sacrifice are [the fruits of] these;
yet they declare that these, as well as beds and seats, are indivisible [among co-heirs].

Thus it is stated by Laugākṣi. The authors of the *Kalpataru* and others maintain that the term "yogakṣema" includes ministers, domestic priests, and so forth, because they are the causes of acquisition (*yoga*) and security (*kṣema*). "Pasture" (*pracāra*) refers to the paths for entering and exiting houses and gardens, as well as the paths for the roaming of cattle and other animals. Vyāsa and Uśanas state another thing that is indivisible:
"What is indivisible belongs to those of the same lineage even up to a thousand families:
the officiating priest, the field, the document, cooked food, water, and women."

The *yājya* (the person for whom one performs sacrifices) is the disciple (*śiṣya*). Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "There is no division of the dwelling, nor of water-vessels, ornaments, and used garments. Here, "dwelling" (*vāstu*) refers to a house. This statement regarding the indivisibility of fields and houses should be understood to apply to a single house, field, or the like that is so small that it cannot be divided among many. In such a case, however, it must be given to one person by all the others through means such as exchange. Alternatively, this prohibition against dividing fields and the like may refer to the fact that land and property obtained through inheritance (*pratigraha*) is not to be divided between the son of a Brāhmaṇa wife and the sons of Kṣatriya wives and others. Thus is the prohibition of the divisibility of fields and other assets.
A Kṣatriya bride should certainly not be given to the son of a Kṣatriya or other [lower caste];
even if their father should give her away, upon his death, the son of a Brāhmaṇa wife shall take her.

Because of this statement, Bṛhaspati— intending that this prohibition against the partition of clothes and such items refers specifically to those already being worn and not to clothes in general— describes the method of partitioning clothes and other items when there is a disparity caused by differences in number or value: "Those who stated that clothes and such are indivisible did not consider that wealth belonging to the affluent may consist of clothes and ornaments."
That which stands in the middle and cannot sustain life cannot be given to a single person;
it must be distributed with skill, for otherwise it would become useless.
Having sold clothing and ornaments, having recovered a debt by means of a written bond,
and having exchanged prepared food for unprepared food, the property is then divided.
Having drawn water from wells and tanks, it is used according to one's own need;
so too, one woman should perform work in every house according to her respective share.
Many [wives] should be given equal shares; this same rule applies even to female slaves.
"The boundary and the field are divided according to their respective shares;
the heirs must always carry out the cultivation according to their portions.

This means that the specific scope of the prohibition against partition has not been considered, nor has it been explained with analytical distinction. "Having recovered the debt" (*ṛṇam udgrāhya*) means that the debt recorded in the document must be extracted from the debtor and then divided; it does not mean that the debt as it stands in the document itself is to be divided. Kātyāyana also [states this] at verses 882–884.
But wealth recorded in writing that has been designated for the sake of Dharma,
as well as water-rights, wives, and property inherited through succession;
A garment or ornament that is not suitable should not be worn;
rather, kinsmen should provide those things that are appropriate for the specific occasion.

Bṛhaspati has declared that a cow-pasture, a carriage-road, and whatever is fixed to these two [a house or a field] shall not be divided when put to use, nor that which is for the purpose of an artisan's craft.

[351] That which has been determined for the sake of Dharma, such as items like bells and the like dedicated for the purpose of worshiping the gods and so forth, established as common property; "bond" (*nibandha*) refers to wealth fixed by kings and others in the form of a decree that "this much must be given here"; "worn" (*dhṛta*) clothing refers here to that which is of great value; "that which may be inappropriate" refers to that which cannot be directly divided; "clothing applied to the body" refers here to that which is of little value. According to the Easterners, the word *prayojya* includes books and the like. It should be understood that books and the like, as well as tools for crafts, are not to be divided with fools or those unacquainted with the craft, respectively; otherwise, since they serve as means of livelihood, they are to be divided by all—this is the meaning. He (Yājñavalkya) himself states that the division should be carried out in accordance with the laws of the region (884a).
"The law of a country, of a caste, of a corporation, or of a village, as declared by Bhṛgu—that very one shall determine the law of inheritance. Thus it is said.
Whatever was set aside at the time of partition by someone through deception, and is discovered after the partition, that must be divided equally among all and taken. And so Manu (9.218):
When all debts and assets have been distributed according to the prescribed rule,
whatever may be discovered afterwards, all of that should be divided equally.
Yājñavalkya also states (2.126): "If any property that was mutually concealed is discovered after partition, it should be divided again by equal shares; such is the settled rule."

That which was concealed at the time of partition but later discovered, as well as that which was forgotten at the time of division and subsequently recovered, must also be divided equally. Thus states Kātyāyana (885–886): "But whatever was concealed by one [co-heir] and later discovered, that shall be divided equally with the brothers; indeed, in the absence of the father, the sons [shall divide it]."
Bhṛgu has declared that whatever has been withheld from one another, or whatever may have been improperly divided, should be divided with equal shares when it is subsequently discovered.

[351] The previous rule regarding the method of partition is intended to establish that even in this case of unequal division, the shares must indeed be equal. Furthermore, whatever has been seized or lost by anyone and subsequently recovered after the partition has already taken place, that too must be divided and received by all. And so says the same author (Kāt 887): "Whatever wealth is obtained by one who has already partitioned shall belong to him alone; however, what was seized, what was lost, and what was recovered, as well as what was previously mentioned, shall be shared again."

"Previously stated" refers to what was said in the passage beginning with "concealed," and so forth; the meaning is that it "should be divided again. In this context, since the rule for division applies only to property and such that were previously withheld but later seen, there is no further division of anything that had already been divided before.
However, if after a division has been made, some commonality is perceived, that should not be understood as a [valid] division; indeed, it must be divided once more.

Thus, Manu’s statement prescribing the method for the division of all property should be understood as applying only when property such as embezzled goods is discovered *before* the expenditure and income of the divided property have occurred; otherwise, the previously cited statements—which prescribe the division of only embezzled property and the like—would result in being rendered meaningless. Regarding the punishment for one who embezzles common property, Manu (9.213) says:
"If an eldest brother, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers, he shall lose his status as the eldest, receive no share, and be restrained by the kings."

The mention of the "eldest" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes the younger brothers as well. The term "without a share" (*abhāga*) is intended to demonstrate their wickedness (*duṣṭatva*), and not to indicate that they are entirely unworthy of receiving a share, in accordance with the statements previously cited. Regarding the means of proof for determining a partition when someone among those already divided denies the partition, Yājñavalkya (2.149) says: "When a partition is denied, the determination of the partition is to be known through kinsmen, relatives, witnesses, and documents, as well as by means of houses and fields held separately."

Relatives (*jñātayaḥ*) are those on the father’s side; kinsmen (*bandhavaḥ*) are those on the mother’s side; witnesses (*sākṣiṇaḥ*) are those whose characteristics have been previously described; and the written document is the deed of partition (*vibhāgapatram*). The connection between the terms is one of qualifier and qualified: "by means of separate houses and fields that have been divided as *yautaka* (separate property). Nārada also says (Dāya-vyavahāra 36): "In a dispute regarding the law of partition, the determination of the heirs' shares is made by the relatives, by the document of division, and by the commencement of separate activities."

"Because they engage in separate activities and because they perform separate religious duties such as the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, he (Nārada, Dāyabhāga 37) states that the religious duties such as the Vaiśvadeva must be performed separately by those who are divided:
'For brothers who are undivided, a single religious duty prevails;
when division has occurred, their religious duty shall also be separate for each.'"

Other signs of partition have also been shown by that same author (Nārada, Dāyabhāga 38–40): "Brothers who are divided may act as witnesses, sureties, or in matters of giving and receiving; those who are undivided may not do so with one another."
The giving away, receiving, and acceptance of cattle, food, houses, and fields,
as well as the religious duties, income, and expenditures of those who have been partitioned, are to be understood as distinct for each individual.
One should recognize those among whom these transactions regarding their own inheritance take place in the world as divided, even in the absence of a written document.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"Those who separately manage income and expenditure, lend money to one another, and engage in trade, are divided; of this there is no doubt."

Trade refers to commerce. Mutual lending of money and so forth is forbidden for those who have not divided their property; therefore, such activity is a sign of having divided. This prohibition was established by Yājñavalkya (2.52): "Indeed, among brothers, between husband and wife, and between father and son, acting as a surety, contracting debt, and serving as a witness are not recorded as permissible when they have not divided."
Bṛhaspati has stated that, in the absence of evidence such as witnesses, the determination of partition must be made by these signs of partition:
"Violent acts, ownership of immovable property, and prior partition among heirs are to be known through inference when there are no witnesses."

Vriddha-Yajnavalkya prohibits the divine ordeal—which would otherwise be applicable by virtue of the general rule stating that "if a decision cannot be made even by means of signs, and if arguments are insufficient, one should distress the defendant with oaths"—by adding the following: [354] When it is impossible to reach a determination even by means of indicative marks (*liṅga*), and when logical arguments (*yukti*) are also inadequate, one should afflict him with oaths (*śapatha*). Thus, by this general statement, he prohibits the divine ordeal (*divya*).
"In a dispute regarding the law of partition, the determination of partition should be made by means of relatives, witnesses, and written documents; there shall be no recourse to divine proof.
Manu further states that if it is somehow impossible to reach a decision, the partition must be performed again.
Where there is mutual doubt among heirs regarding a partition,
a re-partition must be made even by those who are situated in separate places.
The ellipsis is that where doubt does not depart in any way whatsoever. Furthermore:
"The portion [of the gift] falls once; the maiden is given once;
he says 'I give' once—these three things happen only once each."

This was stated by that very [author] (Manu 9.47); it should be understood as applicable when a decision can somehow be reached through logical reasoning. Nārada (Dāyabhāga 42–43) has stated what must be done by those who have divided their property: "If there are many born of one [father] who follow separate religious duties, perform separate activities, possess separate qualities and occupations, and are not in agreement regarding their affairs..."
If they should give or even sell by their own will,
they may do all that as they please, for they are indeed masters of their own property.

This is the meaning: if many [sons] born of one [father] are divided, then they shall have separate duties; that is, they may perform religious rites such as the *agnihotra*—which require wealth—without mutual consent. Likewise, they may perform worldly activities such as agriculture, which require material resources. Similarly, they may maintain their own distinct households and perform all other tasks according to their own will. They shall possess the houses, utensils, and other materials required for their respective occupations. Furthermore, if brothers or others are not in agreement regarding a task, they may carry it out regardless of them. Likewise, being divided, they may perform everything—including the taking, giving, selling, or mortgaging of their own shares—according to their own will, because, by virtue of being divided, they are independent masters over their own property. As for that which...
Whether divided or undivided, heirs have equal rights over immovable property;
for no single person has authority anywhere to give, mortgage, or sell it.

This is the statement of Bṛhaspati. Having divided and taken the movable property, those who—considering the division of immovable property to be difficult—take only its fruits at the time they yield fruit, have no independence regarding the immovable property even though it has been divided; therefore, without mutual consent, acts such as its gift and so forth must not be performed. Vijñāneśvara and others, however, say: "Since the property is common among those who are undivided, one individual lacks independent authority, and thus the consent of all must necessarily be obtained. But in the case of those who are divided, the consent of all is required later on—not because of a lack of independence in one person, but for the sake of facilitating legal transactions by removing doubts as to whether they are divided or undivided. Therefore, even without the consent of those who are divided, legal transactions are indeed valid. Another duty of those who are divided has been stated by Bṛhaspati:
One should not disturb the share of whichever portion has been enjoyed by whomsoever.

Among those who have divided their property, whoever transgresses the allotment of shares must be restored to his own share by the king; furthermore, he should be punished for such misconduct. And so says that same [author]:
"He who, having made a division according to his own will, should again act inconsistently with it..."
Having established him in his own share of the kingdom, he should be punished for having committed such an offense.
*Anubandha* means persistence. Manu (9.201) shows those who are unworthy of a share of the inheritance:
"The impotent and the outcast, those born blind and deaf, as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and all others who lack [vital] faculties, are entitled to no share."

The "insane" (*unmatta*) is one overcome by madness. The "imbecile" (*jaḍa*) is one whose internal organ is impaired and who is devoid of the knowledge of what is beneficial and harmful. The "devoid of sense organs" (*nirindriya*) are those whose life-force and organs—such as hands and feet—are lost due to disease and the like, and thus are ineligible for the performance of rites prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. Yājñavalkya (2.140) states: "The impotent, the outcaste, his offspring, the lame, the insane, the imbecile, the blind, and those afflicted with incurable diseases and the like, shall be maintained [by the family] but are entitled to no share."

"Born of that" means born from one who has fallen from caste. "Incurable diseases" refers to those afflicted with diseases such as consumption (*kṣaya*) that cannot be cured. If, after the partition has taken place, a disease is somehow removed through medicine or other means, there is certainly a right to a share, just as in the case of one born after the partition has already occurred. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), those who hate their father and others are included. For this very reason, Nārada says (Dāyabhāga 21–22): "A hater of his father, one who has fallen from caste, a eunuch, and one who has been excluded from the community—even these, though legitimate sons (*aurasa*), shall not receive a share; how much less so those born of the wife (*kṣetraja*)?"

Those who are seized by long-lasting or severe illness, as well as the dull-witted, the insane, and the lame—these must be maintained by the family; however, their sons shall be entitled to a share of the inheritance.

One who has been "excluded from the vessel" (*apapātrita*) is one who has been cast out by his kinsmen through the ritual of breaking the water-pot (*ghaṭāpavarjana*) due to a great offense such as treason against the king. Śaṅkha and Likhita also state: "In the case of one excluded from the vessel, inheritance, the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), and the water libation cease. Vasiṣṭha also says (17.52): "Those who have entered other stages of life (*āśrama*) are non-sharers [of the estate]. The other stages of life are those of the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*), the forest-dweller (*vanastha*), and the renunciant (*yati*). Kātyāyana (862) states:
"The son of a woman married out of order, one born of a woman of the same lineage (*sagotra*), and one who has fallen away from the life of a renunciant—among these, there is never any inheritance."

And one who is born from a man of the same *gotra* is produced in a woman of the same *gotra* by a husband of the same *gotra*. Regarding the son of a woman married out of order (*akramoḍhā*), he [Kātyāyana] himself states that even if he is of the same caste as the father, he is entitled to a share of the inheritance: "But the son of a woman married out of order is an heir if he is of the same caste as his father; so too is the son born of a woman of a different caste who was married in the proper order. (Kāt. 863)
The same author (Kāt. 864) states that one born of an inverse union is unworthy of inheritance:
"The son of a woman born of an inverse union does not share in the estate;
it is held that food and clothing must be provided for her by her relatives for as long as they live."

Bṛhaspati states that among virtuous sons, a son who lacks the qualities necessary for performing the ancestral rites—both seen and unseen—is unworthy of his father’s inheritance: "Even one born of a wife of the same caste is not entitled to his father’s wealth if he is devoid of virtue;
rather, that [wealth] is ordained for those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) who offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) for him."
A son protects his father from creditors;
however, there is no purpose served by one who acts in the opposite manner.
What is done with that cow which is neither a milch-cow nor pregnant?
What is the purpose of a son being born who is neither learned nor righteous?
A son who lacks the strength of learning, wealth, and purpose, who is devoid of austerity and wisdom,
and who is bereft of proper conduct, is considered equal to urine and excrement.
A debt to ṛṣis, gods, and ancestors is a *uttamarṇa* (creditor-debt); a worldly debt is an *adhamarṇa* (debtor-debt). Manu also states (9.214):
"All those who persist in improper occupations do not deserve to receive wealth from their brothers.

These individuals excluded from inheritance—such as the impotent and others—must be maintained for life by those who take the estate, according to the previously cited statement of Yājñavalkya: "They are to be supported, though they have no share. In the event of non-maintenance, [punishment follows].
However, it is right for the wise to give to all of them food and clothing according to their ability;
for one who does not give becomes fallen.

And because the fault has been declared by Manu (9.202): "absolutely," meaning for as long as one lives. Devala states that one who has fallen [from his caste] is not to be supported: "When the father has died, the impotent, the leper, the insane, the idiot, the blind, the outcast, his offspring, and those wearing [ascetic] marks do not share in the inheritance."
To them, food and clothing are given, with the exception of meat.

A *liṅgin* is one who wears the dress of a religious mendicant through deceit and the like. The mention of "the outcast" (*patita*) is also an elliptical designation for the offspring of an outcast. For this very reason, Baudhāyana (2.2.43–46) states: “They shall support those whose legal capacity has passed [due to age], as well as the blind, the mentally dull, the impotent, those addicted to vices, and the diseased who are incapable of performing rites—excluding the outcast and his offspring—with food and clothing. Those whose legal capacity has passed are the mute and others. Those incapable of performing rites are those unable to perform the Vedic and Smārta rituals that produce merit. Furthermore, those who have entered other stages of life (*āśrama*) are not to be supported. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha (17.52–54) says: “Those who have entered another stage of life, as well as the impotent, the insane, and the outcast, do not receive a share; however, maintenance shall be provided for the impotent and the insane. Since this passage specifies that only the impotent and the insane are to be maintained, the prohibition of others follows by implication. One who has fallen from the life of renunciation (*pravrajyāvasita*) is also not to be nourished because, due to extreme depravity, he stands on the same footing as an outcast. Devala states that sons who lack shares, provided they are free from impotence and other conditions that render them unworthy of inheritance, are entitled to receive their father’s portion.

[358] Their sons, being free from defects, shall receive their father’s inheritance. Yājñavalkya also (2.141): "Among them, the legitimate (*aurasa*) and the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), if they are without defect, are entitled to a share."

Viṣṇu (15.34–38): “Only those sons who are born of the legitimate wives (*aurasa*) of these [men] are entitled to inherit, but not the sons of one who has become an outcast (*patita*) after he has committed an act causing loss of caste (*patanīya*). Furthermore, those born subsequently to such a man, as well as those born of women in the inverse order of castes (*pratiloma*), are non-participators; their sons likewise have no share even in the grandfather’s property. Like the son of an outcast, the son of one who has abandoned the world for asceticism (*pravrajyāvasita*) is also not entitled to a share. The daughters of those who are without shares must be maintained and undergo the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) until their marriage. Likewise, their wives, provided they are of good conduct and lack faultless sons, must be maintained for as long as they live. And so says Yājñavalkya (2.141–142):
And their daughters must be maintained until they have been given away to husbands.
Among these, childless women who are of virtuous conduct must be maintained;
however, those who are unfaithful or likewise hostile should be banished.

However, those who have violated their prescribed conduct (*kṣatavr̥tta*) should be expelled from the house and not supported; yet the elders maintain that they should indeed be expelled only upon mere hostility toward their supporter, whereas support must still be provided. Likewise, it should be understood that the wife and others—who will be mentioned as heirs in the absence of a son—as well as those such as reunited coparceners (*saṃsṛṣṭin*), do not receive inheritance if they possess qualities that render them unworthy of a share, since Yājñavalkya, after stating "the wife, the daughters," etc., mentions as an exception to that rule: "the impotent, the outcast, and his offspring."

Regarding the succession for the inheritance of the property of one who has died separated from his brothers and others, and who is devoid of a legitimate son (*aurasa*), a son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), an adopted son (*dattaka*), or a son made by appointment (*kṛtaka*), Yājñavalkya states the following order (2.135–136): "The wife, the daughters, the parents, the brothers,
as well as their sons, the *gotraja* kinsmen, the relatives (*bandhu*), the pupil (*śiṣya*), and those who have studied under the same teacher (*sabrahmacārin*)."
In the absence of these, each subsequent one among them becomes the heir to the wealth of the deceased who left no son; for this rule applies to all castes.

The "wife" is one who has been consecrated by a lawful marriage (*dharmyavivāha*). By the word *ca* ("and"), which serves the purpose of including those not explicitly mentioned, the daughters and grandsons (*dauhitra*) are included. "Their sons" refers to the brothers' sons. "Kinsmen of the same lineage" (*gotraja*) includes both *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas*. The genitive case in the word *eṣām* ("of these") is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). Among these—starting with the wife and so forth—in the absence of each preceding one, each succeeding one inherits the wealth of the deceased (*svaryāta*) who was partitioned and left without a son. The meaning is that this rule is common to all those born in the natural order (*anuloma*), those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), and across the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. Although the term "son" (*putra*) here generally applies to all primary and secondary sons, nevertheless, because in the Kali age the *kṣetraja* and other such sons are prohibited, the term effectively refers only to the three types of sons beginning with the legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*). Bṛhaspati also states that the wife is the first to take the inheritance.
In the sacred scriptures, in the treatises of tradition, and in worldly custom,
the wise have declared that a wife is half of one’s own body, sharing equally in the fruits of both merit and demerit.
For one whose wife has not passed away, half of his body still lives;
while half of the body lives, how could another take her place?
When paternal kinsmen— such as a father or brothers who are uterine relatives— are present,
the wife of one who has died without a son shall take his share.
In the *Āmnāya*, the Veda: “The wife is indeed half of one’s own self,” and so forth (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 6.1.8.5). In the *Smṛtitantra*, the Dharmaśāstra:
“He whose wife drinks liquor falls from his status in this world.”
No expiation is prescribed for one whose body is half-fallen [into a degraded state].

(VaDh 21.15); (Parāśara Smṛti 10.26), and so forth. Bṛhaspati states that only a wife who is devoted to her husband is entitled to inherit his wealth, and no other: "A sonless widow, remaining faithful to her vows, protecting her husband’s bed," [is entitled to his estate].
The wife alone shall offer that funeral cake (piṇḍa) and receive the entire share.
Prajāpati also said:
"If she has died previously, or if her husband dies while the Agnihotra is being maintained, a woman devoted to her husband shall obtain that wealth; this is the eternal law."

By the term *agnihotra*, the means for that [rite], such as the sacred fires and so forth, are understood. His wealth consists of both the stationary and the moving. For this very reason, it was stated by that same author:
"Having taken the moving, the stationary, gold, base metals, grain, liquids, and clothing, one should cause the *śrāddha* to be given for a month, six months, and so forth."

"One should honor with *kavya* and *pūrta* offerings one's paternal uncles, preceptors, daughters' sons, the brother-in-law (husband's sister's son), maternal uncles, elders, and guests, as well as women.

*Kupya* refers to base metals such as tin, lead, and so forth. *Kavya* refers to food and other items offered with the ancestors in mind. Here, *pūrta* refers to gifts and the like that constitute part of rites such as the digging of tanks. As for the prohibition against the gift of immovable property (*sthāvara*) which is recorded in the *Smṛticandrikā* as being of Bārhaspatya origin:
Whatever various property, such as inherited wealth and so forth, is recorded as having been divided,
the wife whose husband has died shall receive it, with the exception of immovable property.
Even if she has remained faithful and even if she has contributed to the estate, a woman does not deserve immovable property.

This statement [of Smṛticandrikākāra] appears to be unworthy of regard, because it is not cited in numerous authoritative digests such as the *Vijñāneśvara*, *Kṛtyakalpataru*, *Ratnākara*, *Pārijāta*, and *Halāyudha*; on the contrary, in works like the *Kalpataru*, the verse beginning with "movable property, immovable property, and gold" is recorded as a statement of Bṛhaspati. Even if one were to accept it out of deference to the authority of the author of the *Candrikā*, since the word *patnī* (wife) is not used here, whereas in the previously cited passage—"she shall obtain the entire estate"—which establishes that the wife is entitled to the whole wealth consisting of both movable and immovable assets, the word *patnī* is indeed employed, this statement must be restricted to wives obtained through forms of marriage other than *pāṇigrahaṇa* (such as *āsura* and others). However, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* establishes a distinction: he holds that the statement "the woman is entitled to the immovable property" refers to a wife who has no daughter, thereby indicating her entitlement to the immovable, while the verse beginning with "movable property, immovable property, and gold" refers to a wife who does have a daughter. In this arrangement, we see no conclusion whatsoever other than mere personal conjecture. In the *Mādhavīya*, the venerable feet of Vidyāraṇya maintain that the expression "excepting immovable property" is intended to prohibit the sale of immovable property without the consent of the heirs. As for that which prescribes that even for women whose husbands are divided or unseparated, they are entitled only to subsistence—

One should set aside what is not to be given— namely, property destined for the king, that belonging to women, that belonging to servants, and funeral offerings— and having excluded the property of a *śrotriya*, one should deliver it to other *śrotriyas*.

Thus is the statement of Kātyāyana (931), and that which [is stated in verse 361]: "Whatever [property] other than that of a Brāhmaṇa the king, devoted to righteousness, [possesses], he should grant as a livelihood for women; this is recorded as the rule for inheritance."

Thus, both of these statements by Nārada (Dāyabhāga 52) should be understood as referring to women who have not been formally wedded (*avaruddha*). As for that which indicates the wife’s lack of independence regarding giving and so forth—namely: "A woman who protects her family shall receive a share from her husband when he has died;
for as long as she lives, she has no ownership [right] over giving, mortgaging, or selling"—[this applies to such women].

This statement by Kātyāyana (924) is intended solely to prohibit independence regarding gifts to actors, dancers, and the like, which serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). However, she certainly possesses independence in giving for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), as well as in pledging or selling property used for that purpose:
"Devoted to vows and fasting, established in celibacy, and constantly delighting in self-restraint and charity, even a woman without sons shall go to heaven."

This is because his constant devotion to giving is expressed by this very [verse] (Kāt. 925), and also because of the previously cited statement: “movable property, immovable property, gold,” etc. However, as for those [verses]: “If among brothers some one should become a renunciant or die childless, his remaining brothers shall divide his wealth, excluding the woman’s property.”
And they should provide for his maintenance until the end of their lives, provided they preserve the bed of their husband; in other cases, they may take that property away.

And such statements as those of Nārada and others (Dāya-bhāga 25–26) are to be understood, as the case may be, as referring either to women whose husbands have not divided the estate or to women whose husbands were reunited, because they are recited in connection with that very subject. Nārada states that women whose husbands have not divided the estate and those whose husbands were reunited must be maintained by the one who takes their husband’s wealth: "As many widowed women as there are, they must be maintained with clothing and food by the eldest [son], by the father-in-law, by a kinsman of the same lineage, or by any other [relative]."
Regarding this very subject, Kātyāyana states another view (922):
"But when the husband has died, the wife is entitled to food and clothing;
however, if [the estate] is undivided, she receives a share of the wealth until her death."

[362] The mention of "undivided" (*avibhakta*) is also indicative of that which is "mixed" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*). Here, the word *tu* has the sense of the word *vā*, because particles have multiple meanings. A woman becomes an heir to food and clothing until her death. The meaning is that she receives a share from her husband's wealth equal to whatever amount of wealth is required for her livelihood—which is free from hardship—to perform the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites suitable for women, as well as optional (*kāmya*) rites such as those directed toward the east, and so forth. Regarding this, the first position concerns wives other than the legal wife (*patnī*), since it states they are entitled only to property sufficient for their subsistence. The second position concerns the legal wife; such is the settled rule. Even the legal wife, if she does not perform service to her father-in-law and others, is entitled only to food and clothing. And thus says the same author (Kāt. 923):
One devoted to service for the teacher deserves to eat the allotted portion;
if she does not perform service, one should employ her in tasks such as gathering rags or collecting alms.
The phrase "having cut off the allotted share" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. He states that in some other cases as well, the removal of the allotted share must be performed (Kāt. 928–929):
"A woman who is intent on doing harm, shameless, one who destroys wealth, and she who is devoted to adultery—such a woman does not deserve the property."
Nārada states that even the entitlement to food and clothing does not belong to unfaithful women (Dāyabhāga 26):
"They shall provide maintenance for these women until the end of their lives, provided they preserve the bed of their husband; otherwise, they shall forfeit that [right]."

Regarding the other [wives] who are unfaithful: "One should perform this very same rite even for women who have fallen from their status; however, food and clothing must be given to them, and they should dwell near the house. As for the injunction that one should provide food and clothing even to those who are unfaithful, it is exactly as stated: "One should perform this very same rite even for women who have fallen from their status; however, food and clothing must be given to them, and they should dwell near the house."

The elders maintain that this statement refers to the husband. A wife who has been separated from her husband or whose husband is missing, and who is suspected of misconduct, is entitled only to subsistence. Thus says Hārīta:
"If a widow remains in the prime of youth and is harsh [in disposition], the wise should provide her with a livelihood merely for the sake of sustaining her life."

"Harsh" means one whose internal disposition is cruel, that is to say, one who is suspected of infidelity. Thus, it is established that a wife who remains steadfast in her conduct and is not adulterous is entitled to a share of the entire estate of the husband, consisting of both movable and immovable property. When there are many wives, those wives of the same caste shall divide and take the property equally. Prajāpati states that those who obstruct a wife from taking her husband’s property should be punished by the king:
"Those sapindas or kinsmen who act as obstacles to her..."
The king should punish those who destroy property with the same punishment meted out to thieves.
[They] would harm [her] or obstruct [her]. Regarding the point that "in the absence of a wife, the daughter is the heir to the father's wealth," Bṛhaspati says:
"From every limb of men a daughter is born, just like a son;
she is equal [to him], married to one of equal status, virtuous, and devoted to service."

Therefore, how could another man take the paternal wealth? "Another" means one other than the son or the wife; the meaning is: while she remains, how could anyone else take the paternal wealth? Manu also says (9.130): "As one's own self, so is the son; by the son, the daughter is equal."
While she remains within oneself, how could another take away one's wealth?
Nārada also says:
"Even in the absence of a son, the daughter [is entitled to the inheritance] because she is seen to produce an equal lineage;
both the son and the daughter are the continuators of the father's lineage."

The mention of "sons" (*putra*) is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for daughters. Some say that these statements, which indicate a daughter's right to inherit, refer specifically to the *putrikā* (appointed daughter). That is incorrect. Because of Vasiṣṭha’s statement (17.15–16), "The third son is known as the *putrikā*," the *putrikā* is included within the category of sons; thus, like an *aurasa* (legitimate) son, she inherits the father's estate even when a wife exists. Furthermore, it is improper to include her under the word "daughter" in such texts as "the wife and the daughters" (*patnī duhitaraś ca*), which establish the daughter's right to take the inheritance in the absence of a wife. If there are many daughters, the inheritance should be taken by them after dividing it equally. If some are married, then it must be taken by those who are unmarried alone. If there are many unmarried daughters, it should be taken by them after dividing it. For this very reason, Kātyāyana (926) states: [text follows].
The wife who is unfaithful to her husband shall be the taker of his wealth;
in her absence, however, it shall be the daughter, provided she be unmarried.

Even though all [the daughters] have been married, if some are established and others are unestablished due to poverty, then it should be taken by the unestablished one alone. If there are many who are poor, it should be divided among them. For this very reason, Gautama (28.22) states: "The woman’s property belongs to the daughters who are unmarried and unestablished. "Woman’s property" (*strīdhana*) refers to the mother’s wealth; and this is also an indicative term for the father’s wealth, as the principle is the same. In the absence of even a daughter, the son of a daughter (*dauhitra*) is the inheritor of the wealth. And so says Viṣṇu:
In the absence of sons and grandsons in the lineage, daughters' sons shall obtain the wealth;
for in the ancestral offering (svadhākāra) to the ancestors, grandsons and daughters' sons are considered equal.

In the absence of a daughter's son, the father is the inheritor of the wealth; in his absence, the mother is the taker of the inheritance; in her absence, the brothers; in their absence, the brother's son. Thus says Bṛhad-Viṣṇu (17.4–9, 11): "The wealth of one who has no son goes to the wife; in her absence, it goes to the daughter's son; in his absence, it goes to the father; in his absence, it goes to the mother; in her absence, it goes to the brothers; in their absence, it goes to the brother's son; in his absence, it goes to the *sakulya* (distant kinsman). Kātyāyana also [says] (927):
Now, for one who has no son, a wife of noble birth or even daughters [are entitled];
in their absence, the father, mother, brother, and sons are declared [to be so].

By the word "api" (also), the son of the daughter (*dauhitr*) who is included among the category of daughters is intended. "Sons" refers to the sons of the brothers. Among brothers as well, when there is a combination of uterine and non-uterine brothers, the uterine ones alone are the heirs to the wealth; in their absence, the non-uterine brothers. For this very reason, Manu (9.187) states:
"The property of each shall belong to his nearest *sapiṇḍa*. Bṛhaspati also says:
Where there are many kinsmen, lineal descendants, and relatives,
he who is the nearest among them shall take the wealth of one who leaves no offspring.

Relatives (*jñātayaḥ*) are those who share the same *piṇḍa* (*sapiṇḍāḥ*), those of the same lineage (*sakulyāḥ*), those related through water-offerings (*samānodakāḥ*), and kinsmen (*bāndhavāḥ*) such as the daughter of one’s father’s sister (*pitr̥ṣvastrīyā*) and others. [365] In the absence of brothers, the sons of the brothers (*bhrātuḥ putrāḥ*) are the heirs to the wealth. Among them, the sons of a uterine brother (*sodarabhrātuḥ*) are the first to receive the wealth; in their absence, the sons of a half-brother (*bhinnodarabhrātuḥ*) are the heirs. When there is a coexistence of both brothers and nephews, the nephews have no right to take the inheritance. However, when a certain brother dies without a son while other brothers remain, and they are about to divide and take that wealth, if another brother should die meanwhile, his son acquires a right to take his paternal uncle’s wealth by way of his own father.

However, according to the legal principle that "for those whose father has died, the allotment of shares is according to the father" (YDh. 2.120), that wealth should be divided and taken by other paternal uncles together. In the absence of even the brother's sons, the grandmother is the heir to the wealth;
and when the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth.

Because of this statement by Manu (9.217). Although in this sentence it appears that the paternal grandmother (*pitāmahī*) follows immediately after the mother, nevertheless, since she cannot be inserted among those whose order is fixed—beginning with the brother and ending with the brother’s son—as prescribed in Yājñavalkya’s verse which is intent upon establishing sequence, one must understand from Manu’s own words that the paternal grandmother, being included within the category of *sagotra* relatives, inherits the property immediately after the sons of the brother. Nor does this contradict Manu’s statement; for that [statement] is concerned merely with the attainment of the paternal grandmother’s right to inherit, and is not intended to establish a specific sequence. In the absence of the paternal grandmother, the *sapiṇḍas* who are closest among the *sagotras*—namely the paternal grandfather and others—should take the inheritance. Among them, too, the sequence is as follows: first the paternal grandfather takes the wealth; in his absence, the paternal uncle; in his absence, his sons and so forth. In the absence of the paternal grandfather’s lineage, the great-grandfather, his sons, and so on, take the wealth according to this same sequence. In their absence as well, among the *sapiṇḍas*, whoever is closest according to this very sequence of proximity shall take it. In the absence of *sapiṇḍas*, the *samānodakas* take the wealth according to this same sequence determined by proximity. These *samānodakas* are the seven generations beyond the *sapiṇḍas*, or more, provided there is no knowledge of the births of the preceding ancestors. Thus says Vriddha-Manu: [The text continues with the citation of Vriddha-Manu.]
The sapinda relationship, however, ceases with the seventh person;
the status of being a samānodaka (a kinsman by water) ceases with the fourteenth.

"According to some, the lineage (*gotra*) is said to be that which follows from the recollection of birth and name. [366] In the absence of those related by the *udaka* rite, the kinsmen (*bandhu*) are the heirs to the property. They are of three kinds: paternal kinsmen, maternal kinsmen, and kin by marriage. Thus it is stated in another *Smṛti*:
"The sons of one's father’s sisters and the sons of one's mother’s sisters..."
One's own maternal uncles' sons should also be known as one's own kinsmen.
The sons of one's father's paternal aunt, the sons of one's father's maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's father's maternal uncle are to be known as paternal kinsmen (pitṛbandhu).
The sons of one's mother’s paternal aunt, the sons of one's mother’s maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's mother’s maternal uncle are to be known as the mother’s kinsmen (mātṛbāndhava).
Among these as well, first the paternal kinsmen (pitr-bandhu) are the sharers of the wealth; in their absence, the maternal kinsmen (mātṛ-bandhu) are the sharers of the wealth.
Where there are many cognates (jñāti), such as those belonging to the same lineage (sakulya) or other relatives, he who is the nearest among them shall take the wealth of one who has no offspring.
Because of this statement.

In the absence of relatives, the teacher (*ācārya*) is the one who takes the property. Although in Yājñavalkya’s statement—which is primarily concerned with the sequence of inheritance—the teacher is not mentioned separately from the pupil, nevertheless, by the mention of the "pupil," it is already indicated that the teacher, being even more preeminent than him, is the first to receive a share of the wealth; thus, there is no contradiction. For this very reason, Āpastamba (2.6.14.2–3) states: "In the absence of sons, a near *sapiṇḍa*; in his absence, the teacher; in the absence of the teacher, the resident pupil (*antevāsī*). In the absence of the teacher, the pupil inherits the wealth; in his absence, a fellow student, according to the previously cited statement of Yājñavalkya. In the absence even of fellow students (*sabrahmacārin*), a learned *śrotriya* shall take the property of a Brāhmaṇa. However, the property of a Kṣatriya or others, the king shall take. Thus says Gautama (28.39): "Learned *śrotriyas* shall divide the estate of a childless Brāhmaṇa. Viṣṇu also (17.12–13) says: "In his absence, it goes to a fellow student; in his absence, excluding the property of a Brāhmaṇa, it goes to the king. Manu also (9.188–89):
But in the absence of all these, Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the three Vedas, pure, and self-controlled shall be the heirs; thus the Dharma is not violated.
The property of a Brāhmaṇa is always inviolable by the king; such is the established rule. However, in the absence of all [other heirs], the king may take the property of the other castes.
Devala also says:
"The king shall take property that has no heir everywhere, with the exception of the property of a Brahmin;
however, he should cause the property of a Brahmin that has no heir to be given to those learned in the Vedas."
Bṛhaspati also says:
"Those Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are childless and deprived of wives and brothers—
the king shall be the taker of their wealth, for he is the sovereign lord of all."

Viṣṇu (15.40) states that the inheritor of the estate must necessarily perform the ancestral rites for the deceased, such as the *śrāddha*: “He who takes the wealth is declared to be the giver of the *piṇḍa*. Whoever takes someone’s property must offer the *śrāddha* for them and present the *piṇḍa* for three generations. Here, by the word *śrāddha*, the *preta-śrāddha* is intended. The wealth of forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), ascetics (*yati*), perpetual celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*), and others shall not be taken by sons, wives, or similar relatives; rather, others shall take it. Thus, Yājñavalkya (2.137), as an exception to the rule concerning sons, wives, and so forth, indicates those who inherit their property:
The heirs of forest-dwellers, renunciants, and lifelong students,
in their respective order, are the teacher, the virtuous pupil, the spiritual brother, and the fellow student of the same hermitage.

By the term *brahmacārī* here, the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) is intended, due to his association with the ascetic (*yati*). Therefore, in the absence of a son, daughter, or daughter’s son, the father and other relatives shall take the property of a temporary student (*upakurvāṇaka*) according to the previously stated order. The teacher takes the property of the lifelong student; the teacher’s property is taken by a good disciple (*sacchiṣya*). By the word "good" (*sat*), what is intended here is the state of having studied the spiritual scriptures (*adhyātmaśāstra*) and being capable of practicing their meaning—not merely good conduct—since it is established by other authorities that even a teacher of bad character is unworthy of a share. The property of a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) is obtained by a "dharma-brother who shares the same sacred site" (*dharmabhrātrekatīrthī*). A "dharma-brother" is one who has entered the same order, a brother, or one who has the same teacher. An "ekatīrthī" is one belonging to the same stage of life (*āśrama*). Thus, a "dharma-brother and an ekatīrthī" is a "dharma-brother who shares the same sacred site. In this way, the venerable Vijñāneśvara has stated that, relying on the word "order" as referring to a reverse order, the teacher and others take the property of the lifelong student and the rest. However, to us, because of the observation of Viṣṇu’s statement (17.15–16), "The teacher or the disciple shall take the property of the forest-dweller," it appears that the word "order" refers to a direct (natural) order. The fact that the disciple is declared by Viṣṇu to be the taker of the forest-dweller’s property should be understood to apply when the teacher is absent. As for Vasiṣṭha’s statement (17.52), "Those who have entered other stages of life are not entitled to shares," that is intended to mean that the property of those in other stages of life must not be taken by ascetics and the like; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with this very statement. As for Gautama’s declaration (3.10), "A mendicant (*bhikṣu*) possesses no accumulation," which implies that ascetics and the like have no connection with wealth, how can it be said that disciples and others are entitled to their property? To this we reply: [The remainder of the text follows.]
A renunciant (yati) should wear even a garment for the purpose of covering his private parts;
likewise, he may take up sandals and various requisites for yoga practice.

From this statement, it follows that even for an ascetic (yati), a connection with material objects such as clothing and books certainly exists. "Alas! One may accumulate wealth for a month, or for six months, or likewise for a year; but once it is acquired, one should abandon it in the month of Āśvayuja."

According to this statement (YDh. 3.47), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) indeed possesses a connection with wealth. Even for the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*), there is certainly a connection with goods such as clothing for the sake of maintaining the body. Therefore, the statement that disciples and others are entitled to share in that property is not contradictory.
Manu (9.210) states that among those who have reunited after partition, there is no inequality in shares caused by seniority or other such factors when they divide again:
"If those who were divided live together and should divide once more..."
In that case, the division shall be equal; there, seniority does not exist.

In this context, since the exclusion of unequal division is already established by the very rule of equal partition, the further statement that "seniority does not exist there" is intended to indicate that an unequal division based on seniority and the like does not occur; however, when there is a combination of much or little wealth, an inequality of shares arises according to the combined property. Some, however, say that at the time of combination, whatever was combined by each person, an inequality should be calculated in the division of the accumulated increase of the combined substance according to that proportion; they argue that, based on this indicative text, the combined substance itself must be divided equally because it is ordained as such. That is incorrect, because no decisive reason (*vinigamaka*) is seen for the position that the portion of the increase of the combined substance is to be divided unequally while the combined substance itself is to be divided equally, even though it is so ordained. Bṛhaspati states: "Among those who have combined their property, he who acquires more through learning, valor, or other means shall receive two shares of that substance, while the others shall receive equal shares."
But among those who have combined their efforts, whoever acquires more by means of learning, valor, or other such qualities, two shares shall be given to him; the remainder shall share equally.

And this [rule]—established by the force of the statements of Vasiṣṭha and others which prescribe the meaning "two shares for the *arjaka* (the one who acquired property)" (17.51)—is intended to make known that while what is acquired without detriment to the paternal estate is not subject to partition, this is not so; rather, even that which is acquired without detriment to the joint estate (*saṃsṛṣṭadravya*) is to be divided in this manner. The word *saṃsṛṣṭin* is derived from the sense that "those who have joint property" belong to this category. Furthermore, Bṛhaspati states that the pooling of wealth (*dhanasaṃsarga*) must be performed only with [paternal] ancestors and the like, and not with others.
"Furthermore, one who, though divided by his father or brother, resides together with him—or with his paternal uncle—out of affection, is called *saṃsṛṣṭa* (reunited). Thus [it is said].

In cases of mutual co-residence (*saṃsṛṣṭi*), because of the division of property among those who have died before the one who was reunited—provided that the sons and grandsons of the deceased exist—the rule applies: “For those whose father has died, the allotment of shares is according to the father” (YDh. 2.120). Accordingly, they should receive their paternal share after dividing it from the co-residents. However, in the case of a deceased co-resident who has no sons or grandsons, when the wife, daughters, and others would otherwise be entitled to inherit his estate according to the previously mentioned order, Yājñavalkya (2.138) provides an exception by showing that the co-resident himself shall take that inheritance, starting with the statement: “For one who has gone to heaven without a son... (2.138).
But the reunited coparcener shall inherit from the reunited coparcener, and a uterine brother from a uterine brother.

The word *tu* here is intended to indicate an exception to the rule concerning wives, daughters, and others. The meaning of the first quarter-verse is that when a *saṃsṛṣṭin* (one reunited with a kinsman) dies without a son, his property is taken by that very *saṃsṛṣṭin*, and not by his wife or other heirs. An exception to this is stated: "But for a uterine brother, a uterine brother. Here, the two terms *saṃsṛṣṭinaḥ* and *saṃsṛṣṭī* are to be supplied. Thus, the meaning is as follows: where both a uterine brother and a half-brother are *saṃsṛṣṭins*, the inheritance belongs only to the uterine *saṃsṛṣṭin*, and not to the half-brother *saṃsṛṣṭin*. Regarding the time of partitioning the reunited property, if the wife of a deceased *saṃsṛṣṭin* is pregnant but the pregnancy was unknown, a son born subsequently is indeed entitled to a share of his own father's portion. Therefore, whether he be a uterine or a half-brother, the *saṃsṛṣṭin* shall give a share of the deceased *saṃsṛṣṭin*'s portion to him; in the absence of such a son, he himself shall take it. Thus says the same author (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.138).
One should give a share and take away a share for one who is born and for one who has died.

The meaning is that when a son is born, his father shall give him his share; but when he dies, the *saṃsṛṣṭin* (one who has reunited) shall take it, provided he is devoid of sons and grandsons. Where there are *saṃsṛṣṭins* born of different wombs while the uterine brothers are not *saṃsṛṣṭins*, the distribution of the wealth occurs by dividing it, because the cause for one case—uterine brotherhood—is present in one place, while in the other case, the cause—being a *saṃsṛṣṭin*—is present elsewhere. He (Yājñavalkya himself) states that in either of these two cases, the *saṃsṛṣṭins* shall divide and take the wealth of the deceased who died without sons or grandsons (YDh. 2.139).
But a son born of the same womb is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* (one who shares in the estate); one not born of the same womb shall not take the wealth.
Even if he is not a *saṃsṛṣṭin*, he may take it; but one born of a different mother, even if a *saṃsṛṣṭin*, shall not take it.

The term *asaṃsṛṣṭī* is connected to both [parts of the sentence] like the eye of a crow (*kākākṣivat*). The word *saṃsṛṣṭa* is also connected to both. For the word *saṃsṛṣṭa* connected with the former [part], the meaning is "one born from the same womb" (*ekodarasamsṛṣṭa*), i.e., a uterine brother (*sodara*); and in that case, the masculine gender is not intended to be significant. For the latter [part], the meaning is "one who is associated" (*saṃsṛṣṭī*). The particle *eva* ("only") is to be supplied [after *anyamātr̥ja*]: "only one born of another mother. Thus, the meaning of this [verse] is as follows: "But a uterine brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* shall take the wealth; however, a non-uterine brother who is not a *saṃsṛṣṭin* shall not take the wealth. A uterine brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* shall also take the wealth; but even a *saṃsṛṣṭin* who is born of another mother shall not take the wealth. By this, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), it is stated that uterine brothers who are not *saṃsṛṣṭins*, and sisters who are *saṃsṛṣṭins*—even those born of different wombs—should divide and take [the estate] equally.
