Having introduced the division among *saṃsṛṣṭins*, Manu clarifies this very point (9.211–212): [Manu 9.211–212] "Among uterine brothers, some may be *saṃsṛṣṭins* and others not; the wealth of the deceased goes to the *saṃsṛṣṭin*, and the rest shall divide [it] equally. After the father's death, if brothers have divided the estate and live together again, they shall divide it once more according to the law in the same manner as before. In this way, Manu clearly demonstrates this very meaning by beginning with the division of *saṃsṛṣṭins*.
If the eldest or the youngest [son] is deprived of his share at the time of distribution,
or if either of them dies, his share is not lost.
The uterine brothers, having assembled together in harmony, shall divide it equally;
as shall the brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters.

[371] The meaning is that [the share] would be diminished either by the adoption of another stage of life (*āśrama*) or by such faults as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), such that one would no longer be entitled to receive one's own portion. "It is not lost" means that it is not to be taken only by those who have reunited (*saṃsṛṣṭin*); rather, it must be extracted separately. Once that portion has been extracted, even uterine brothers who have not reunited, even if residing in different regions, having come together from there—united and assembled—and even half-brothers who have reunited, as well as uterine sisters, shall divide and take it equally, without any inequality of more or less. In this regard, when both kinds of property—immovable and movable—exist, the rule is as follows: the uterine brothers and sisters who have not reunited shall divide and take the immovable property; whereas the half-brothers who have reunited shall divide and take the movable property, including hidden wealth and manifest property in the form of bipeds, quadrupeds, and so forth. Thus says Prajāpati:
Any property that has been lost shall belong to those who were joint owners;
however, land and houses shall be taken by those who were not joint owners, each according to their respective share.

By the term "property" (*dravya*), following the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*), there is the inclusion of movable property consisting of manifest bipeds, quadrupeds, and so forth. The phrase "of those who are *saṃsṛṣṭa*" implies "those born of different wombs. The phrase "those who are not *saṃsṛṣṭa*" implies "uterine brothers and others. The author of the *Smṛticandrikā*, however, cites the verse of Yājñavalkya: "A *saṃsṛṣṭin* born of a different womb shall not take the wealth from one born of a different womb; even if not *saṃsṛṣṭa*, a uterine brother shall take it, and not one born of another mother. Having read this statement of Yājñavalkya, he asserts that when there exists only immovable property or only movable property, based on this Yājñavalkya text, only the uterine brother—even if not *saṃsṛṣṭa*—takes it; but when a non-*saṃsṛṣṭa* uterine brother exists, a *saṃsṛṣṭa* brother born of a different womb shall not take it. He further states that when both types of property, immovable and movable, exist, then according to the rule of Prajāpati as stated by Manu, the non-*saṃsṛṣṭa* uterine brothers and the *saṃsṛṣṭa* brothers born of different wombs shall divide and take the inheritance. In this regard, in the opinion of the *Smṛticandrikā* author, the redundancy in Yājñavalkya’s verse would be difficult to avoid, because what was already stated by the words "a *saṃsṛṣṭin* born of a different womb shall not [take] from one born of a different womb" is repeated by the words "nor one born of another mother. Furthermore, since the intended meaning is already obtained through agreement with the text of Manu, to assume a different meaning would result in the fault of "excessive conceptualization" (*kalpanāgaurava*), as it would necessitate the assumption of a separate underlying Vedic text (*śruti*). However, where among the uterine brothers some are *saṃsṛṣṭa* and some are not, since both causes for taking the wealth—uterine status and *saṃsṛṣṭa* status—are present, the *saṃsṛṣṭa* uterine brothers shall take it, and not the non-*saṃsṛṣṭa* uterine brothers. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says: [372] (The verse of Bṛhaspati follows.)
"Furthermore, those two who are united through affection share in each other's [property]. Thus it is said.

Gautama also states: "When a *saṃsṛṣṭin* (one reunited after partition) dies, the *saṃsṛṣṭin* is the heir to the property. The phrase "when a *saṃsṛṣṭin* dies" is to be understood as "when he dies without a son. By this, the following meaning is established: when the deceased *saṃsṛṣṭin* is devoid of sons and grandsons, even though there exist closer relatives such as the wife and others, by the force of this specific text, the father who was his *saṃsṛṣṭin* takes that wealth. The same applies to the paternal uncle and the brother's son. Likewise, in the absence of sons and grandsons, *saṃsṛṣṭin* brothers inherit from one another. Similarly, among *saṃsṛṣṭin* brothers, in the absence of sons and grandsons, they inherit from each other. It should not be argued that even if there is a son who is not a *saṃsṛṣṭin*, the son who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* alone takes the father’s wealth because of his status as a *saṃsṛṣṭin*; for the cause for taking the wealth is the death of a *saṃsṛṣṭin* who is childless, and since that father has sons, that condition is absent. Nor should it be argued that in Yājñavalkya’s statement, "But the *saṃsṛṣṭin* [inherits] from the *saṃsṛṣṭin*," the word "childless" (*aputrasya*) is not heard, and therefore the mere death of a *saṃsṛṣṭin* is the cause; for the word "childless" (*aputrasya*), which is included in the phrase "of him who has gone to heaven childless" (*svaryātasya hy aputrasya*), is to be supplied (*anuṣaṅga*) to the rule concerning *saṃsṛṣṭins* just as it is to the word "gone to heaven. Nor should it be said that its supply is not desired here; for if it were not, it would follow that the wealth of a father who has sons—such as a paternal uncle—would also be taken by the *saṃsṛṣṭin* brothers and their sons. Furthermore, since the right of the wife and others pertains to the case of a childless person, while the right of the *saṃsṛṣṭin* pertains to the case of one with sons, these two would have different scopes and thus could not stand in the relationship of general rule (*utsarga*) and exception (*apavāda*). Consequently, the use of the particle *tu* ("but") in the phrase "But the *saṃsṛṣṭin*" (*saṃsṛṣṭinas tu*) to indicate its status as an exception would be inconsistent. Therefore, the qualification "childless" (*aputrasya*) must necessarily be applied there. Nor can it be argued that the qualification "childless" is applied to *saṃsṛṣṭin* paternal uncles and others because of the maxim that "a qualification is meaningful only where there is a possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and where, in the absence of deviation, it might otherwise apply"; for that qualification does not apply to a father who has a *saṃsṛṣṭin* son, because of the impossibility of deviation. Thus, it must be said that the death of the *saṃsṛṣṭin* father is indeed the cause for the son of the *saṃsṛṣṭin* to take the wealth, and therefore that wealth should be taken by the *saṃsṛṣṭin* son alone, not by a non-*saṃsṛṣṭin* son. However, this cannot be maintained, because it results in a discrepancy in the injunction (*vidhi-vaiṣamya*) that introduces a split in the text contrary to the principles of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā Śāstra: the injunction would operate with the inclusion of the qualification in the case of *saṃsṛṣṭin* paternal uncles and others, but not in the case of the *saṃsṛṣṭin* father. Furthermore, in the matter of being entitled to the paternal and ancestral property, the fact of being a son or grandson is the determining factor, and that is common to all. Thus, shares of the *saṃsṛṣṭin* father should be divided and taken by all of them. It should not be argued that the entitlement to the father’s property ceases after partition; for Hārīta’s text shows that even after partition, the sons' entitlement to the father’s property does not cease: "Or, having divided while still living, he may retire to the forest or enter the stage of a recluse; or, having divided with a small portion, he may live taking the greater share; if he should later become impoverished, he may take from them again, and he should divide those portions that have been exhausted. This demonstrates that even after partition, the sons' entitlement to the father’s property does not disappear. Nor should it be suspected that, in the case of a son born after partition (*vibhaktaja*), there will be an entitlement to the father’s property simply because he is a son; [this is not so, as the specific conditions regarding *saṃsṛṣṭin* status apply].

Those born before the partition have no authority over their father’s estate; one born after the partition has no authority over his brother’s share; and that which was acquired by the father himself with his own effort cannot be claimed by the sons who have already divided.
All that belongs to one born after partition, his elder brothers are declared to have no authority over.
Just as with wealth, so it is with debt, and in matters of giving, pledging, and buying; they have no mutual authority over one another, except regarding impurity and the water-libation rites.

By this statement of Bṛhaspati, it is established that after a division made during the father’s lifetime, only he who is born subsequently while remaining in the womb has the right to take the entire paternal estate, and not those who were already divided. Nor should it be argued that, just as when there is a reunited uterine brother, non-reunited uterine brothers are ineligible for the property of the reunited one, so too when there is a reunited son, other sons have no share in that wealth. For in that case, mere uterine brotherhood is not the determining factor for inheriting the property of a non-reunited person; rather, by the force of the text—"A reunited kinsman inherits from a reunited kinsman, and a uterine brother from a uterine brother"—it is determined that uterine brotherhood conjoined with the status of being reunited is the determining factor. However, regarding sons, mere sonship alone is the determining factor, and since that is common to all, the same does not apply here. Furthermore, because the rule concerning reunited kinsmen would otherwise result in a contradiction with the previously mentioned injunctions, it does not apply to the case of sons; thus, the status of being a son conjoined with the status of being reunited cannot be the determining factor for inheriting the property of a reunited kinsman. Therefore, it is settled that the wealth of a deceased reunited father must be taken by his sons, both those who were reunited and those who were not. The one who takes the property of the reunited kinsman must maintain the wife of the reunited kinsman and must maintain and perform the marriage rites for the daughter until her marriage. Accordingly, Śaṅkha and Nārada, referring to the property of a reunited kinsman, state: (Nārada, Dāyabhāga 25–27).
If among brothers one should die childless or renounce the world,
the remaining brothers shall divide his wealth, excluding the woman’s property.
They should provide for her maintenance until the end of her life, provided she remains faithful to her husband's bed; otherwise, they may withhold it from the other wives.
"Whatever daughter he may have, her paternal share is considered for her maintenance: until her marriage she shall take her portion; thereafter, her husband shall maintain her. Thus it is said.

"In others" means among those unchaste women who do not guard the bed. Regarding the phrase "until the sacraments" (*ā saṃskārāt*), the prefix *ā* is used in the sense of inclusion; thus, the meaning is "including marriage. In the absence of a reunited coparcener (*saṃsṛṣṭin*), a brother who was not reunited shall take the reunited property; in his absence, the mother; in her absence, the father; and in his absence, the wife shall take it. Thus says Śaṅkha: "The wealth of one who has gone to heaven without a son goes to his brothers; in their absence, the parents shall take it; in their absence, the eldest wife. Although no specific order is perceived in the word "parents" (*pitarau*) due to the formation by *ekaśeṣa*, nevertheless, since the word for mother (*mātṛ*) is seen to be placed first in the compound "mother and father" (*mātāpitarau*) which has the same meaning, such an order of recitation certainly exists here. "Eldest" refers to one endowed with qualities such as self-restraint, and not merely the first-married wife; therefore, this does not exclude the middle or other wives. In the absence of a wife, the sister shall take that wealth.
Bṛhaspati says:
"She who is his sister is entitled to receive a share from him;
this is the law for one who dies childless and without a wife or father."

The word *ca* here serves to include both the brother and the sister. Some, however, reading the text as *yā tasya duhitā* ("his daughter"), say that the daughter is intended. In the absence of a daughter and a sister, the text states: "In the absence of these, the nearest *sapiṇḍa* or others shall take the wealth" (*Manu* 9.187). Accordingly, following the previously mentioned order, they should take the property of one who was reunited (*saṃsṛṣṭin*), since no specific rule to the contrary is heard. [375] Manu describes the various types of women's property (*strīdhana*) in verse 9.194:
That which is given before the sacred fire, that which is received at the bridal procession, and that which is given as a token of affection;
that which is obtained from a brother, a mother, or a father—these are declared to be the six kinds of a woman’s property.
The mention of "sixfold" is for the purpose of excluding a smaller number, but not for the purpose of excluding a larger number. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya (2.143) states:
"That which is given by the father, mother, husband, or brother; that which is received before the fire; and that which is obtained upon supersession—this is declared to be the woman's property."

Thus, the initial phrase has been employed. Viṣṇu also states that there is more than six types of woman’s property (*strīdhana*): “That given by the father, mother, son, or brother; that received near the fire (*adhyagni*); that given upon taking a second wife (*ādhivedanika*); that given by relatives (*bandhu*); the bride-price (*śulka*); and the subsequent gift (*anvādheya*)” (ViDh 17.18). The nature of the woman’s property beginning with *adhyagni* is explained by Kātyāyana (895–899): “That which is indeed given to women at the time of marriage in the presence of the fire is proclaimed by the virtuous as *adhyagni*-woman’s property.”
Furthermore, whatever a woman receives when being led away from her father’s house is declared to be the woman’s property known as *adhyāvāhanika*.
Whatever is given out of affection by a mother-in-law or a father-in-law,
as well as that which is given upon the salutation of their feet, is called "affectionately given" (prītidatta).
That which is obtained by a woman from her husband’s family after marriage is called *anvādheya*;
likewise, that which is obtained from her own family is also so designated.
Whatever price is obtained for household utensils, vehicles, milch animals, ornaments, or articles of labor— that is declared to be the *śulka* (toll).

*Śulka* is the price of household utensils and other such items which is received from the groom and others as a condition for giving away the maiden, appearing in the form of an ornament for the bride. *Ādhivedanika* is that which is given to a previously married wife at the time of marrying another wife. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya (2.148) states: "One should give an equal amount as *ādhivedanika* to a superseded wife.
To those whose woman's property (*strīdhana*) has not been given, it is ordained that half [of the amount] be given."

[376] Regarding the specific rules for the giving of wealth to women by their father and others for the sake of her maintenance, Kātyāyana states: (902) "The father, mother, husband, brother, or kinsmen shall give property to a woman according to their ability, up to two thousand [paṇas], with the exception of immovable property."
The meaning is that immovable property and other wealth should be given according to one's capacity, up to a maximum of two thousand *kārṣāpaṇas*. Vyāsa also says:
"A gift of wealth up to two thousand [coins] should be given to a woman."

By the phrase "the gift is for another," it is shown that even from what is abundant, one should not give more than this. For this very reason, it is understood that this rule applies when [the property] is handed over repeatedly every year. Consequently, even if it exceeds this amount, that which is given for the sake of livelihood over many years—even if it be immovable property—must be given provided there is the capacity to do so. However, regarding that which is given under a condition such as "this ornament and so forth must be worn only during festivals," and that which is given to prevent deception by an heir, Kātyāyana states that these also do not constitute *strīdhana* (woman's property). (903)

In this regard, that which is given with a condition (*sopādhi*), or that which is obtained through the power of yoga (*yoga*), or that which is given by a father, brother, or husband, is not called "woman's property" (*strīdhana*).

He (Kātyāyana) states that even those two types—what is acquired by women through crafts (*śilpa*) and what is acquired out of affection from friends and others, excluding paternal kinsmen and so forth—do not possess the status of woman's property (Kāt. 904).

Whatever has been obtained through crafts, or whatever else has been received out of affection from the husband, the husband's ownership extends over that; the remainder, however, is declared to be the woman’s property.
By this [rule],
a wife, a son, and a slave are all entirely without property;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong.

This statement (*Manu* 8.416) should also be understood as referring specifically to wealth acquired through crafts and the like. Manu (9.199) states that women have no independence regarding the expenditure of their *strīdhana* (women’s property) and so forth without the consent of their husbands:
"Women should not make a withdrawal from the family property held in common by many."
And even from one's own wealth, one must not act without the permission of one's husband.

Regarding the fact that in some cases there is independence over a woman's property, Kātyāyana says (901): "That which is obtained by a married woman or a maiden, together with her husband, from the father's house, or from a brother, or from her parents, is declared to be *saudāyika* (gift of affection)."

The grammatical connection is: "by the married daughter, in the house of her husband. It is held that women attain independence upon receiving dowry property (*saudāyika*), because that was given by them [the relatives] for the sake of compassion as a means of livelihood.

"Women's independence regarding their *saudāyika* property is always proclaimed; they have full authority over its sale or gift, even in the case of immovable property. (Kāt. 905–906) The phrase "from the brother, from the parents, or [others]" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for [the husband], the paternal kinsmen, and the maternal kinsmen. Nārada states that a woman has independence over property given by her husband, with the exception of immovable property.
Whatever has been given to a woman by her husband who was pleased with her,
she may enjoy or give away at her will even after he has died, except for immovable property.

The meaning is that women whose husbands have died without partition may only enjoy the immovable property given by their husbands; they must not perform acts such as giving it away. Kātyāyana also says (921):
"A sonless widow, preserving her husband’s bed and remaining under the authority of her elders, may live there peacefully until death; after [her passing], the heirs shall take possession."

Men have no independence regarding any of a woman’s property because they lack ownership over it; thus, the same author (Kātyāyana, 911–913) states: "Neither the husband, nor the son, nor the father, nor the brothers have authority over her property, whether in its acquisition or its disposal."
If, however, any one among them should forcibly consume the woman's property,
he shall be made to pay it back with interest and shall also incur a fine.
If he should eat that very thing after having obtained permission and with a sense of pleasure,
he should be made to pay the full amount as a fine when he possesses wealth.
Devala also states that a husband lacks the fitness to enjoy his wife’s property:
"Livelihood, ornaments, the bride-price, and acquisitions shall constitute the woman’s property;
her husband has no right to this himself except in times of distress."

She may spend the woman's property at her pleasure on food, clothing, and ornaments; she may also give it with interest for the sake of liberation or enjoyment, or even when removing distress for her sons, as she is entitled to enjoy the woman's property.

*Vṛtti* is wealth given by the father or others for the purpose of livelihood. *Lābha* is that which is obtained from somewhere for the sake of affection, such as a cow or similar property. *Vṛthā* means without cause or distress. *Mokṣa* signifies relinquishment or giving away. The mention of "son" (*putra*) is intended to indicate the family (*kuṭumba*) in general. *Ārti* means suffering or affliction. Here, because it is stated that "the husband does not deserve [it] except in times of distress," it is indicated that only the husband is entitled to enjoy the wife's property in times of distress, and no one else. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya (2.147) states that in times of famine and so forth, the wife's property taken by the husband need not be returned if he lacks the capacity [to provide].
In times of famine, for religious purposes, during illness, or when there is imprisonment,
a husband is not required to give to his wife the property she acquired as a woman's separate estate.
The phrase "in matters of religious duty" implies "when they are obligatory. Regarding "obstructive acts," this refers to such things as the seizing of prisoners.
Kātyāyana states that when wealth has been seized by a husband during a time of distress, it should be returned at his own will if he possesses the means (914):
"To one who is diseased, or beset by calamity, or oppressed by creditors..."
Having ascertained that it has been granted, he should give it with affection, even by his own will.

"Granted" means consented to by the woman—this is the remainder [of the sense]. He himself (Kāt. 908–909) states that in certain cases, when a woman is obstructed by illness or other causes, whatever she has affectionately authorized must necessarily be made to be given by the man:
"Now, if he should have two wives and does not visit her again..."
Moreover, even if it was given out of affection, the husband may compel her to return it by force.
"Wherever a woman's food, clothing, and shelter are withheld, there she may take for herself her own property, as well as her share of the inheritance.

This is to be understood as applying when the woman is free from fault. He himself (Kātyāyana, 928–929) states that a woman who is at fault does not deserve any of the woman's property: "A woman who is wicked, or who has run away, or who is addicted to drinking liquor, shall lose her right to maintenance; she is not entitled to any of the woman's property."
A woman who is intent on doing harm, who is lawless, who destroys wealth, and who is addicted to adultery does not deserve to inherit her husband's property.

"Always engaged in harmful acts and intent on behaving contrary to her husband's will"— it is he [Manu] himself who states the reason why a wicked woman is unworthy of women’s property and lacks the right to participate in sacrifices and other rites: "Therefore, one should employ the wealth produced for the sake of sacrifice in places consistent with dharma, not among women, fools, or those who act against dharma."
Whatever woman's property (*strīdhana*) was taken on the promise, "I shall restore it to you," that must be given back to them by the sons as if it were a debt. And so says the same author (Kāt.
916): "Woman's property promised by the husband must be given; it is like a debt to the sons.
Regarding the seizure of woman's property by sons and others, Manu states their liability to punishment and their connection with guilt (8.29, 9.200).
If their own kinsmen should seize the property of those women while they are still alive,
a righteous lord of the earth should punish them with the penalty prescribed for thieves.
"Whatever ornament may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide that; those who do divide it fall.

The meaning is: "worn" refers to having been worn on occasions such as festivals, and "worn" [in this context] means worn without such pretext and without the motive of deceiving the heirs and so forth.

The property of a deceased woman is to be taken by her sons and daughters after dividing it equally. Thus says Manu (9.192): "But when the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the maternal inheritance equally."

[380] And this refers to property given as a subsequent gift (*anvādheya*) or wealth bestowed out of affection by the husband. For this very reason, it has been stated by that same author (Manu 9.195):
"And that which is given as a subsequent gift, and that which is given by the husband out of affection..."
That wealth shall belong to the offspring of a woman who has passed away while her husband is still living.

"Of the progeny" means of the lineage consisting of females and males. Regarding this matter of various kinds of property, Bṛhaspati states the specific rule for a situation where there is a gathering of both married and unmarried daughters:
"The woman's property shall belong to the offspring, and the daughter is entitled to a share thereof; provided she is unmarried. But if she is already married, she receives only honor."

"Of the offspring" means of the sons. "A sharer thereof" means a sharer of an equal portion with the sons. Regarding the phrase "but the married," etc., the meaning is that the married woman receives something according to her status, but not an equal share with the sons. Kātyāyana states (917): "In the absence of unmarried [sisters], the property should be divided and taken together with the married sisters who are not widows, along with the brothers.
Sisters who have husbands should divide [the property] together with their kinsmen.
At the time of this division of wealth, something should be set aside and given to the daughters of the daughter (dauhitris). And so Manu says (9.193):
"But for those who may be their daughters, something should be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth according to their merit and with affection.

Thus, the property of the mother known as *yautaka* is to be taken by the unmarried daughters alone; it is not to be taken by the sons, nor by the married daughters. And so says that same author (Manu 9.131):
But whatever may be the mother's separate property (yautaka), that indeed is the share of the unmarried daughter.

*Yautaka* is that which was obtained by two people sitting together on a single seat at the time of marriage and other such occasions; for this very reason, the authors of the *Nighaṇṭu* have stated: "The property of a couple is *yautaka*."

Daughters alone shall take the woman’s property other than that which was given as an after-gift (*anvādheya*) or by the husband out of affection, such as the *adhyagni* and other forms of female property. Among them, when there is a combination of those who are married and those who are unmarried, only the unmarried daughters shall take it. In their absence, among those who are married, only those who are childless, penniless, and unsettled shall take it. For this very reason, Gautama (28.22) states: “The woman’s property belongs to the daughters who are unmarried and unsettled. In the absence of daughters, the granddaughters (*dauhitryaḥ*) shall take it, because they possess a greater share of the female constituent. In their absence, the grandsons (*dauhitrāḥ*) shall take it. Thus say Nārada, Kātyāyana, and Yājñavalkya (YDh. 2.117; Nārada, Dāya. 2).
The daughters [inherit] the remainder of the mother's debt; in their absence, the lineage [inherits].

*Anvaya* means lineage (*santati*). And that [lineage] is understood from proximity to refer to the daughter. Because of the expression "the remainder after the debt" (*ṛṇāc cheṣam*), it is understood—based on the statement of Yājñavalkya (2.50), "When there is a debt of the mother, the debt less than the debt or equal to the debt must be paid by sons and grandsons"—that the sons and grandsons who are entitled to discharge the debt incurred by the mother must take [the property]. If there is more than the debt, then what remains after the payment of the debt is to be taken by the daughter and the others. However, in the absence of debt, it is understood that everything is to be taken. Nārada also [says this] (Dāya. 2).

In the absence of the mother, her daughters; in their absence, those belonging to her lineage; and among those of different mothers, the daughters’ daughters and the daughters’ sons shall have their shares calculated according to their respective mothers, because Gautama has stated: "Or rather, each [child] shall take [the share] of his own mother's group" (GDh 28.15). In the absence of the daughters, the daughters’ daughters, and the daughters’ sons, the sons shall take [the inheritance]; for it is said: "After the parents have passed away, the sons shall divide the estate and the debt equally."
According to the statement of Yājñavalkya (2.117):

"In the absence of daughters, however, that inheritance [goes] to the sons," and according to the statement of Kātyāyana: "In the absence of sons, the debt must be paid by the sons and grandsons," the grandsons are the ones entitled to discharge the grandfather's debt and are the heirs to that wealth. As for the wealth of a childless woman, her wife or daughter of equal or higher caste shall take it; in their absence, her offspring shall take it. And so says Manu (9.198):
Whatever property may belong to a woman, however given by her father, that a Brāhmaṇī wife shall take; or it shall belong to her daughter, or to her offspring.

The mention of the *brāhmaṇī* is an elliptical designation for a maiden born of a caste other than the lowest. Manu (9.196) states that the husband shall take the property of a woman who has been consecrated by the *brāhma*, *daiva*, *ārṣa*, *gāndharva*, or *prājāpatya* forms of marriage, provided she dies childless or leaves behind no offspring: "In the *brāhma*, *daiva*, *ārṣa*, *gāndharva*, and *prājāpatya* marriages, when she passes away without progeny, that wealth is declared to belong to the husband alone."
But the wealth of a woman who has entered into one of the *āsurā* and other such marriages belongs to her mother and father. And thus says that same [author, Manu 9.197]:
"Whatever wealth may have been given to her in the *āsurā* and other marriages, it is ordained that upon her death without offspring, it shall belong to her mother and father."
Bṛhaspati states that the property of a childless maternal aunt and others should be taken by nephews and other relatives who are equal to sons:
"A maternal aunt, the wife of a maternal uncle, the wife of a paternal uncle,
a paternal aunt, a mother-in-law, and the wife of an elder brother are proclaimed to be equal to a mother."
If these women have neither a biological son nor a daughter's son,
nor the son of such a daughter, then their wealth shall be inherited by their sister's sons and the others.

The phrase "the wealth that was given" refers to the property obtained at the time of marriage; it is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other forms of women’s property, such as that received upon taking a second wife (*ādhivedanika*). For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says (2.143):
"And that which is designated as women’s property, beginning with what is received upon taking a second wife (*ādhivedanika*), if she dies childless, her kinsmen shall obtain it. (YDh 2.144)
Having thus stated the general rule, he declares the specific determination:
"The wealth of a woman who dies childless belongs to her husband in all four [forms of marriage] beginning with the Brāhma;
however, if she has borne children, it goes to her daughters; and in the remaining [forms], it reverts to the father. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.145)

The mention of "four" is illustrative; for even in the *gāndharva* form of marriage, Manu (9.196) states that the husband is the recipient of the woman's property. Regarding the *āsura* and other forms of marriage, Kātyāyana (918) says that what was given by paternal relatives (*bandhu*) and others shall be taken by them alone, and in their absence, by the husband: "But what is given by relatives goes to the relatives; in their absence, it goes to the son [or the husband]."

The *strīdhana* known as *śulka* (bride-price) shall be taken by the uterine brothers alone; in their absence, the mother takes it—so says Gautama (28.23): “The *śulka* of a sister belongs to the uterine brothers, after the death of the mother. As for the statement of Śaṅkha, “And the husband [takes] his own *śulka*,” that should be understood to apply when she dies before the marriage. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya (2.146) states: “If she has died, one should take what was given, having cleared out the expenses of both sides.”
Regarding that which was given to the maiden by her maternal grandfather and others, such as bracelets and the like, Baudhāyana states that her uterine brothers shall take it:
"The uterine brothers shall divide equally the inheritance of a deceased maiden;
in their absence, it shall belong to the mother; in her absence, it shall belong to the father."

Paiṭhīnasi states that the wealth of a daughter who has no offspring should be taken by her uterine brother and not by her husband: “When the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) has died, the husband does not deserve the property; in the case of one who is childless, as well as in the case of an unmarried girl (*kumārī*), it should be taken by the brother. However, regarding the verse: “But when an appointed daughter who is childless has somehow died, the husband of that appointed daughter shall take that wealth without hesitation,” [this refers to a different interpretation].
Thus is the statement of Manu (Manu 9.135); it is to be understood as applying when there is no uterine brother born later [than the deceased].
Thus ends the determination of the title of law regarding inheritance in the *Vyavahāravivekoddyota* by Śrī Kodaṇḍaparaśurāma. 34.

**Possible reading of the defective text:** In the *Madanaratnapradīpa*, composed by the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīmadanasiṃhadeva— the son of the Mahārājādhirāja Śrīśaktisiṃha, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles beginning with “Śrīkodaṇḍaparaśurāma”— this is the thirty-fourth section: the determination of the legal title of inheritance (*dāyabhāga*) within the illumination of the discernment of legal procedure (*vyavahāravivekoddyota*).
Now follows the determination of the legal title known as gambling and betting.
Regarding that, Nārada defines its nature (Dyūta 1):
"Gambling with dice, sticks, stalks, and so forth, which is conducted through deceitful means..."
Playing with dice, sporting with birds, gambling, and betting on animal fights.

Dice are the stakes. A *vadhra* is a leather strap. *Śalākās* are long, square-shaped gaming pieces made of ivory or other materials; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), cowrie shells and the like are included. With these, gambling conducted through fraudulent means for a wager is called *samāhvaya*; the meaning is that it is a game played with birds such as cocks and other fowl for a stake. The mention of "birds" (*vayas*) is an illustration for living beings in general. Bṛhaspati says: "Birds, rams, bulls, and the like, when mutually seized [for combat]..."
Those who strike while having made a wager call that a *samāhvaya*.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), wrestlers and others are included. Manu also says (9.223):
"In this world, that which is performed with non-living things is called gambling (*dyūta*);
but that which is performed with living beings is to be known as betting (*samāhvaya*)."
That same author (Manu 9.221, 222, 227–228) states that gambling and betting must be prohibited by the king:
"The king shall prohibit both gambling and betting within his realm."
These two vices are the destroyers of the kingdoms of rulers.
Gambling and betting are open forms of theft;
therefore, the king should always exert effort to suppress them.
In ancient times, this gambling was seen to cause great enmity;
therefore, a wise person should not indulge in gambling, even for the sake of amusement.
Whatever man should practice that [prohibited act], whether in secret or openly,
there shall be a variety of punishments for him, as the king desires.

The classification of punishments and the determination of penalties. The word *iṣṭam* means "desire"; here the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). Yājñavalkya (2.203) states that for the purpose of identifying thieves, the king should cause gambling and betting matches to be conducted before his own men:
"Gambling should be conducted with a single stake for the sake of identifying thieves;
this same rule is to be understood as applying to betting on living creatures."

If, for some reason, a game of dice must be conducted for the purpose of identifying a thief, then it should be held in a place provided with signs such as archways and the like; so says Kātyāyana (933–935):
"One should never indulge in gambling, which increases anger and greed, produces wicked people, is cruel, and destroys the wealth of men."
Since strife inevitably arises from gambling, just as venom from the mouth of a snake,
therefore a king should desist from it, for it is indeed a vice regarding his domain.
If it should be bright, one should have an archway situated at the entrance constructed;
for the sake of preventing confusion among the noble ones, that [archway] should be made to bestow [the gift of] the hand.
